- “The education community has pointed out numerous challenges and opportunities that text-based generative AI presents to education (Cooper, 2023;Dwivedi et al., 2023;Kasneci et al., 2023). Its effect on writing assessment is especially concerning, since textbased generative AI tools can generate original content with minimal instructions from students, who could have little to no knowledge of the subject (Kohnke et al., 2023). This leads to attempts to ban these tools (Tlili et al., 2023), or to return to traditional, in-person examination (Stahl & Eke, 2024). However, a more sustainable response may be to embrace these tools by adapting them to existing pedagogies or designing new pedagogies to incorporate them into school curricula (Milano et al., 2023).   - “Research has been conducted to explore the role of a machine-in-the-loop in enhancing EFL writing… Song and Song (2023) assessed the influence of ChatGPT on the IELTS writing skills of Chinese EFL students. In a similar vein, Tsai et al. (2024) found that EFL college English majors achieved significantly higher scores on essays revised with ChatGPT's assistance.   - “For instance, Woo et al. (2024b) examined how EFL secondary school students used AI-generated text and human-generated words in narrative compositions, revealing that the number of human words and AI-generated words significantly contributed to human-rated scores of the compositions.” [37]

## Executive Summary

The direct evidence that generative AI improves K–12 reading and literacy outcomes is promising in a few narrow use cases but not yet strong enough to support a broad claim of effectiveness across literacy domains. The clearest K–12 evidence is concentrated in secondary writing-feedback and vocabulary settings, most often in EFL/ESL contexts rather than mainstream English/language arts classrooms. Across those studies, generative AI is usually implemented as a chatbot or feedback assistant that provides immediate corrective feedback, vocabulary practice, or homework support, and it is typically compared with business-as-usual instruction, paper-based practice, or teacher feedback rather than with strong non-AI digital writing tools or peer review systems. By contrast, direct K–12 evidence on reading comprehension, summarization, argumentation from sources, disciplinary literacy, and broader literacy achievement is sparse, and evidence on foundational reading skills is effectively absent. Broader reviews confirm that the school-based generative-AI evidence base is expanding rapidly but remains methodologically immature and unevenly distributed across grades, subjects, and populations [34] [8] [44] [6].

The strongest experimental K–12 finding in the pool is an RCT of GPT-4 as an English homework tutor in secondary school. In that study, GPT-4-supported homework tutoring for high-school English learning produced an overall learning gain of d=0.251 on an externally measured 24-item pre/post test, with heterogeneity by year level: d=0.603 in 3rd-year classes and d=-0.004 in 5th-year classes (RCT, n=75) [4]. The same study found higher homework interestingness (d=0.593), perceived resource availability (d=0.586), usefulness (d=0.356), and comprehensiveness (d=0.281) for the GPT-4 condition [4]. The broadest synthesis directly on ChatGPT across education reports positive average effects on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking, but it is not specific to K–12 literacy and therefore only partially answers the focal brief (meta-analysis) [6]. Likewise, broader systematic reviews indicate that generative AI and AI tutoring systems can support personalization, feedback, and engagement, but they do not isolate K–12 reading/literacy effects [15] [34] [7].

The strongest direct K–12 quasi-experimental evidence also clusters around writing and vocabulary. A high-school EFL quasi-experiment found that ChatGPT-based mobile feedback reduced ESL writing errors more than traditional teacher feedback, with a reported partial eta squared of .860 for the main effect of error category, though no direct standardized between-group effect size was reported (QED, n=132) [33]. Another high-school quasi-experiment reported that a ChatGPT-based vocabulary application outperformed a traditional paper-based condition on a 54-item vocabulary post-test among Saudi secondary students, though the exact standardized effect was not reported (QED, n=57) [47]. A newer secondary study on AI-assisted writing feedback versus traditional teacher feedback is highly relevant but under-extracted in the source pool, so it cannot bear strong quantitative weight here [27]. These positive findings are tempered by adjacent causal evidence showing that generative AI can improve revision performance while also encouraging heavier reliance on the tool and fewer metacognitive processes in postsecondary writing tasks (RCT, n=117) [24], and by pilot evidence that AI reliance can reduce reading comprehension accuracy when participants outsource processing to the model (RCT, n=32) [21].

Across the tiered research questions, Tier 1 is only partially answered: the intervention is definable as student- or teacher-facing large-language-model tools used for text generation, tutoring, feedback, revision, vocabulary support, or reading-response assistance, but the literature often blurs generative AI with broader AI, tutoring systems, and automated feedback [34] [44] [7]. Tier 2 is partially answered: the most common counterfactuals are business-as-usual literacy instruction, teacher feedback, paper-based vocabulary study, and conventional homework rather than strong head-to-head comparisons with peer review, automated writing evaluation, or human tutoring [4] [33] [47] [8]. Tier 3 is partially answered: implementation appears to matter substantially, with effects varying by degree of teacher structuring, prompt design, autonomy, and learner prior attainment, but literacy-specific classroom-process evidence is still thin [4] [14] [28] [36]. Tier 4 is only partially answered: there is some evidence of positive effects on narrow literacy outcomes, especially feedback-supported writing and vocabulary, but too little rigorous K–12 evidence on reading comprehension, broader writing quality, transfer, or subgroup differences to conclude that generative AI broadly improves K–12 literacy achievement.

Overall confidence is moderate for the narrow claim that generative AI can improve some secondary literacy-related outcomes, especially vocabulary learning, writing error reduction, and structured homework support, and low for the broader claim that it improves K–12 reading and literacy achievement in general. The single most important caveat is that the direct K–12 evidence base is small, heavily concentrated in secondary EFL/ESL contexts, and dominated by short-term studies with proximal outcomes rather than independent, durable, classroom-representative literacy measures [6] [34] [44].

## Research Report

### Research Questions Investigated

| Tier | Sub-question |
|------|-------------|
| Tier 1 | How is “generative AI” defined in K-12 literacy research, and which tool categories are studied in relation to reading and writing outcomes? |
| Tier 1 | Which literacy outcomes are most commonly examined, and how are they operationalized? |
| Tier 1 | For which K-12 populations and contexts is the literature concentrated? |
| Tier 2 | How are similar literacy outcomes developed without generative AI, and what comparison conditions are used? |
| Tier 2 | What non-generative or pre-generative technologies provide meaningful counterfactuals for evaluating generative AI? |
| Tier 2 | What are the most appropriate counterfactuals for evaluating generative AI in K-12 literacy instruction? |
| Tier 3 | How are generative AI tools implemented in K-12 literacy instruction in practice? |

## Defining the intervention and the current scope of the field

In this literature, “generative AI” most often refers to large-language-model systems that generate or transform text in response to prompts, including chatbots such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, writing-feedback assistants, question-answering tutors, vocabulary-practice tools, and systems that generate explanations or model responses [34] [20] [44]. Reviews also note that the boundary between generative AI and broader AI-in-education remains unstable, with many papers blending LLMs with older categories such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive systems, automated feedback, and conversational agents [7] [34] [8]. For this brief, the most relevant interventions are student- or teacher-facing text-generating tools used to support literacy tasks such as writing feedback, revision, vocabulary practice, summarization, reading-response activities, and homework tutoring [4] [33] [47].

The school-based literature is concentrated in secondary grades, especially high school, and in language-learning settings rather than general education ELA. The available direct K–12 studies in the source pool focus mainly on high-school English learning, EFL/ESL writing, and vocabulary [4] [33] [47] [27]. Reviews of generative AI in education similarly report strong concentration in higher education and comparatively sparse K–12 evidence, especially for younger students [34] [44] [7] [37]. Elementary and middle-school evidence exists more often in adjacent AI-literacy, writing-support, or mixed-method studies than in rigorous literacy-outcome trials [28] [36] [35].

The most frequently studied outcomes are not broad literacy achievement measures but narrower, proximal outcomes. In K–12 studies these include multiple-choice English-learning test scores, vocabulary post-tests, error reduction in second-language writing, and self-reported engagement or attitudes [4] [33] [47]. Across the wider educational literature, common outcomes also include writing quality, revision behavior, learning perception, and higher-order thinking, but these are often measured in postsecondary contexts and cannot be assumed to generalize directly to K–12 classrooms [6] [24] [9]. Foundational reading outcomes such as decoding, phonics, oral reading fluency, and early reading comprehension are largely missing from the direct generative-AI evidence in this pool. That absence is especially notable because strong non-AI literacy interventions in elementary grades often target exactly those outcomes or integrate reading-to-write in structured ways [1].

## What studies use as the counterfactual

The counterfactuals in the direct K–12 generative-AI literacy studies are usually weak-to-moderate comparators rather than the strongest plausible alternatives. In the high-school GPT-4 homework-tutor RCT, the comparison was ordinary homework without the GPT-4 tutor, not teacher conferencing, human tutoring, or a non-generative tutoring system [4]. In the high-school ChatGPT mobile-feedback quasi-experiment, the comparator was traditional teacher feedback on ESL writing [33]. In the Saudi vocabulary study, the comparator was a traditional paper-based learning condition [47]. These are relevant baselines, but they do not answer whether generative AI outperforms strong peer review, automated writing evaluation, rule-based grammar tools, or intensive human tutoring.

This comparator weakness matters because K–12 literacy outcomes are commonly developed through established non-AI pedagogies such as writing workshop, explicit strategy instruction, teacher-led feedback, peer discussion, and genre-based writing instruction. For example, a non-AI QED on college-admission essay instruction for underserved high-school students found that explicit genre-based instruction improved essay performance relative to business-as-usual, with R²=0.46 for essay outcomes and R²=0.42 for writing self-efficacy [18]. In elementary grades, a non-AI RCT of SRSD Plus for grades 1–2 found very large gains in writing quality (g=1.02), planning (g=1.40), structural elements (g=0.29), use of source text (g=0.48), number of words (g=0.82 to 1.39), and transition words (g=1.33 to 2.46) relative to business-as-usual writers workshop (RCT, n=93 randomized; posttest n=90) [1]. These studies are not generative AI studies, but they provide an important benchmark: existing human-led literacy instruction can produce large effects on writing-related outcomes, so GenAI should be judged against more than low-intensity business-as-usual conditions.

Broader reviews of AI for teachers and tutoring systems reinforce the need for careful comparator choice. Teacher-focused AI reviews indicate that many studies prioritize efficiency and automation but under-specify pedagogical comparison conditions [8]. Reviews of tutoring systems describe long-standing human-versus-machine and adaptive-versus-static comparison problems, including the fact that many AI systems appear beneficial mainly when compared to limited support rather than to well-implemented instruction [15] [16]. This is directly relevant to generative AI for literacy: a chatbot that beats paper worksheets does not necessarily beat expert teacher conferencing or structured peer response.

## Direct experimental and quasi-experimental evidence in K–12 literacy

### High-school English-learning homework tutoring

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). The study “GPT-4 as a Homework Tutor can Improve Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes” tested GPT-4 as an interactive tutor for high-school English homework in a real school setting (n=75 total; control n=39, treatment n=36) [4]. The intervention used normal homework materials seeded into GPT-4 so students could receive individualized support during homework rather than only static assignments [4]. The primary outcome was an externally measured 24-item multiple-choice pre/post test of English homework content, focused especially on grammar-syntax material [4]. The reported result was an overall effect of d=0.251, with strong heterogeneity by class level: d=0.603 in 3rd-year classes and d=-0.004 in 5th-year classes [4]. On engagement-related measures, the GPT-4 group rated the homework as more interesting (d=0.593), better resourced (d=0.586), more useful (d=0.356), and more comprehensive (d=0.281) [4]. This is the strongest direct causal K–12 evidence in the pool, but it is a homework-tutoring study in English learning rather than a classroom trial of broad reading or writing instruction.

### High-school ESL writing feedback on mobile

Design: Quasi-Experimental Design (QED). “The Impact of ChatGPT on English Language Learners’ Writing Skills: An Assessment of AI Feedback on Mobile” compared ChatGPT mobile feedback with traditional teacher feedback in an Indian senior secondary public school (n=132; ChatGPT group n=66) [33]. The intervention centered on AI-generated feedback for correcting common ESL writing errors, delivered through mobile access [33]. The reported finding is that students receiving ChatGPT feedback showed significantly greater reduction in writing errors than those receiving traditional teacher feedback, with partial eta squared=.860 reported for the main effect of error category, although no direct between-group standardized effect size was reported [33]. The study also reported positive student attitudes toward using the tool for English grammar learning [33]. This supports a narrow claim that generative AI can assist surface-level writing correction in secondary EFL/ESL contexts, but it does not establish broader improvements in writing quality, argumentation, or independent transfer.

### High-school EFL vocabulary learning

Design: Quasi-Experimental Design (QED). “The Impact of Using a ChatGPT-based Application to Enhance Saudi Students’ EFL Vocabulary Learning” compared a ChatGPT-based vocabulary application with a traditional paper-based condition among Saudi high-school students (n=57) [47]. The intervention targeted vocabulary acquisition through a chatbot-like application, and the outcome was a 54-item vocabulary multiple-choice post-test [47]. The study found that the ChatGPT-based app outperformed the traditional paper-based condition, but the exact effect size was not reported in the source pool [47]. Students in the intervention group also reported positive attitudes toward the app [47]. This is useful evidence that GenAI may support vocabulary learning in secondary EFL contexts, but the lack of an extractable effect size and the paper-based comparator limit precision.

### Secondary AI-assisted writing feedback versus teacher feedback

Design: Quasi-Experimental Design (QED). “The role of AI assisted writing feedback in developing secondary students writing skills” is directly relevant because it compares AI-assisted writing feedback with traditional teacher feedback among secondary EFL students [27]. However, the source pool does not provide extractable sample details, outcome statistics, or exact effect sizes. It can therefore only be used as evidence that this line of comparative research exists, not as firm quantitative support for effectiveness claims [27].

## What is missing in direct K–12 literacy evidence

The strongest gap is reading. No study in the available pool provides rigorous K–12 causal evidence that generative AI improves reading comprehension in ordinary classroom ELA instruction relative to business-as-usual, peer discussion, teacher-led comprehension instruction, or established digital reading supports. The existing K–12 generative-AI studies instead focus on English-learning homework, vocabulary, and writing correction [4] [33] [47]. Reviews of the broader GenAI-in-education landscape acknowledge rapid growth but do not identify a mature K–12 reading-comprehension evidence base [34] [6] [44].

There is also little direct evidence on broader writing quality as distinct from grammar correction. The mobile ChatGPT study emphasizes error reduction [33], and the Saudi study targets vocabulary [47]. The under-extracted 2025 secondary writing-feedback study may address broader writing skill, but the available summary is insufficient for exact reporting [27]. This matters because high-quality literacy instruction aims not just at correctness but also idea development, organization, evidence use, genre control, and revision depth. Non-AI writing studies show that such outcomes can be improved substantially through explicit instruction and self-regulated strategy development [1] [18].

Foundational reading skills are effectively absent. None of the direct generative-AI K–12 studies in the pool tests effects on phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, or oral reading fluency. That is a critical limitation for any claim about K–12 literacy overall, because early literacy is foundational and developmentally distinct from secondary writing support. The absence of such evidence is even more conspicuous when contrasted with the strong tradition of early-literacy RCTs in non-AI instruction [1].

## Mechanisms and implementation: how generative AI is being used

The dominant implementation models in the K–12 studies are student-facing support during a specific task rather than full curricular replacement. GPT-4 was used as an interactive homework tutor built from standard homework materials, reducing teacher setup after initial configuration [4]. ChatGPT mobile feedback was used as a corrective-feedback engine for ESL writing [33]. The Saudi vocabulary tool was used as a targeted practice application for word learning [47]. These are relatively bounded use cases: feedback, tutoring, and vocabulary support.

Across broader reviews, the main hypothesized mechanisms are increased feedback frequency, personalization, on-demand explanation, motivational support, and reduced delay between student effort and instructional response [34] [9] [15]. Teacher-oriented reviews also suggest that AI’s perceived promise lies in scalability and time-saving, especially where teacher capacity is limited [8]. In the homework-tutor RCT, the teacher reportedly benefited from reduced preparation burden after setup, illustrating a possible operational advantage [4]. But these same mechanisms can shift from scaffolding to substitution if students simply offload the work of reading, generating, or revising text to the system.

Implementation details outside literacy reinforce that effects depend on how support is structured. In two high-school RCTs on AI feedback in physics, effects differed by whether AI hints were compulsory or autonomously requested and by student prior achievement: low-achievers benefited in the compulsory AI-hint condition (d=0.673), while high-achievers benefited in the autonomous AI-help condition (d=0.378) [14]. In a QED with grades 8–9 students, a brief AI-literacy workshop improved students’ regulation of LLM interaction in school science tasks and was associated with higher task performance (r=0.19) [28]. In another high-school QED, an AI chatbot improved situational interest and self-efficacy relative to a static textbook scaffold (d=0.44) [12]. These are not literacy studies, but they support a mechanism claim highly relevant to literacy instruction: effects likely depend on structured use, student self-regulation, and the match between task complexity and AI support.

Mixed-method K–12 studies of LLM classroom use also suggest that classroom orchestration is fragile. A real-time middle-school EFL study reports that classroom constraints such as limited time, mixed proficiency, and teacher orchestration can make LLM writing support break down in practice [36]. A mixed-method paper on “grade-specific teachers” argues that default LLM outputs often fail to match student developmental level, which is especially important for younger learners and equity-sensitive implementation [35]. These studies cannot support effectiveness claims, but they add practical evidence that open-ended student-directed use may be less reliable than tightly bounded, teacher-mediated use.

## Variation by population, subgroup, and setting

The population coverage is narrow. Direct K–12 evidence is mostly secondary and EFL/ESL-oriented [4] [33] [47]. This means the literature speaks more clearly to multilingual or second-language contexts than to mainstream English-medium ELA classrooms. Reviews of EFL/ESL instruction also show strong interest in digital supports and gamified tools, indicating a broader ecosystem in which GenAI is being adopted, but these syntheses are not specific to generative AI nor to literacy outcomes in general education [5].

There is little direct evidence for students with disabilities, struggling readers, or younger children. The K–12 AI-literacy review highlights uneven inclusion and definitional ambiguity across sectors [44]. Teacher-facing AI reviews similarly note that ethical, accessibility, and equity concerns are often discussed more than empirically tested [8]. The absence of direct subgroup trials means the brief’s priority populations remain largely unresolved. Even where heterogeneity is studied, it is usually by prior attainment rather than by disability or language-support designation. The GPT-4 homework-tutor RCT found stronger gains in one year level than another [4], and the high-school physics RCTs found different optimal AI-help structures for lower- versus higher-achieving students [14]. These findings imply that subgroup variation is likely real, but direct literacy evidence is thin.

There is also limited evidence comparing teacher-mediated versus student-directed use. The GPT-4 homework tutor was partly teacher-mediated at the design stage because the teacher seeded the homework materials, but students then interacted with the tutor independently [4]. The mobile-feedback and vocabulary-app studies also appear primarily student-facing within a teacher-organized instructional setting [33] [47]. No direct K–12 literacy study in the pool cleanly randomizes teacher-mediated versus open student-directed GenAI use. That question remains open, though adjacent evidence suggests structured mediation matters [28] [14] [36].

## Adjacent evidence that informs, but does not answer, the K–12 literacy question

Because direct K–12 evidence is thin, adjacent evidence can help identify plausible benefits and risks, but it must be handled cautiously. The most relevant adjacent evidence comes from postsecondary writing and learning experiments involving generative AI feedback, revision, and tutoring.

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). “Beware of Metacognitive Laziness” tested ChatGPT, human-expert support, a checklist tool, and no support in a university essay-revision task (n=117) [24]. The ChatGPT group showed greater essay score improvement after revision, with omnibus eta²=0.108, and pairwise 95% CIs indicated advantages over checklist, control, and human-expert conditions [24]. However, process analyses showed heavier reliance on AI and relatively fewer metacognitive processes during revision [24]. For K–12 literacy, this suggests a plausible tradeoff: better immediate revision products may coexist with weaker independent regulation.

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). “Experimenting with Generative AI: Does ChatGPT Really Increase Everyone’s Productivity?” studied Thai writing analysis tasks among university students (n=121) [10]. ChatGPT increased average writing-analysis scores by 0.43 points out of 10 and reduced completion time by 1.73 minutes, but stronger econometrics students performed worse on writing tasks with ChatGPT, indicating heterogeneous effects by prior competence [10]. This aligns with the K–12 pattern that benefits may depend on learner profile rather than being uniform.

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). “Experimental Evidence on Negative Impact of Generative AI on Scientific Learning Outcomes” found lower comprehension accuracy after reading complex passages when adults used generative AI, with a 25.1% reduction under full AI reliance and a 12% reduction under partial AI reliance relative to manual work (n=32; p=0.002459 and p=0.005081, respectively) [21]. Although not a K–12 study, it directly raises concern for reading-comprehension tasks: if AI use substitutes for active processing, apparent efficiency gains may mask weaker understanding [21].

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). “The Effects of Generative AI Agents and Scaffolding on Enhancing Students’ Comprehension of Visual Learning Analytics” found that proactive GenAI agents improved comprehension relative to passive GenAI agents and non-AI storytelling supports in higher education (n=117), showing that fixed support is not equivalent to more interactive scaffolding [3]. This is relevant because literacy interventions may likewise depend on the form of AI support, not just its presence.

Design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). “Directive, Metacognitive or a Blend of Both?” tested different AI feedback types in higher education (n=329) and found effects on revision behavior but not final resource quality; directive feedback increased revision odds relative to metacognitive feedback (OR=2.93, 95% CI [1.25, 6.88]) and hybrid feedback had still higher odds (approximately OR=4.3, 95% CI [1.82, 10.0]) [31]. This suggests feedback design may shape literacy-process behaviors even when final-quality outcomes do not change.

These adjacent studies do not establish K–12 literacy effects, but taken together they imply a coherent mechanism pattern: generative AI may increase feedback volume, speed, and willingness to revise, while also raising risks of cognitive offloading, dependence, and uneven benefits by prior skill [24] [10] [21] [31].

## What broader syntheses say about likely benefits and limits

The most directly relevant broad synthesis is the 2025 meta-analysis on ChatGPT and student outcomes, which concludes that ChatGPT has positive effects on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking across education, but the source pool does not provide the specific pooled estimates or K–12-literacy moderator results needed for precise reporting here [6]. Because the meta-analysis includes elementary through undergraduate populations, it is highly relevant for general direction but only partially useful for this specific K–12 literacy brief [6].

Other reviews are broader still. A systematic review and bibliometric analysis of generative AI in education finds that the field is expanding rapidly but is still dominated by exploratory work, conceptual debate, and higher-education applications [34]. Reviews of AI in higher education report similar patterns: promise for feedback, personalization, and efficiency, but limited rigorous causal evidence and substantial concerns about ethics, assessment validity, and over-reliance [7] [20] [19] [37]. A systematic review of generative AI for automated feedback finds strong interest in scalable feedback generation, but again mainly in postsecondary settings [9]. Reviews of tutoring systems and AI-enabled personalized learning also indicate that AI can improve learning under some conditions, but they aggregate across subjects and tool types rather than isolating K–12 literacy uses of generative AI [15] [2].

Reviews focused on teachers and AI literacy add a different implication. Teacher-oriented syntheses stress that adoption decisions involve workload, ethics, oversight, and the need for pedagogical framing, not merely outcome gains [8]. AI-literacy reviews argue that students need explicit preparation to question, monitor, and regulate AI outputs, which bears directly on literacy tasks involving source evaluation, summarization, and writing from evidence [44]. Ethics-focused reviews also foreground privacy, digital divide, and sustainability issues, though they do not contribute direct learning-outcome evidence [26]. Together, these reviews support a cautious implementation stance: any literacy benefit likely depends on strong pedagogical orchestration and critical-use norms rather than unrestricted access to text generation.

## Tradeoffs relative to teacher feedback, human support, and non-AI tools

The direct K–12 evidence suggests that generative AI can sometimes match or outperform ordinary comparison conditions on narrow outcomes, but it does not yet show superiority to the strongest human supports. The mobile-feedback QED suggests better writing-error reduction than teacher feedback [33], but the reported statistic does not establish whether gains extended beyond surface correctness. The GPT-4 homework-tutor RCT shows benefits over ordinary homework [4], but it does not compare GPT-4 with human tutoring or teacher conferencing. The vocabulary study compares ChatGPT with paper practice, not with established adaptive vocabulary software or high-quality teacher-led vocabulary instruction [47]. Consequently, the evidence does not justify a broad substitution claim.

The best non-AI comparators in the pool show that strong instruction can yield large literacy effects. SRSD Plus produced large gains in early elementary writing-related outcomes [1], and genre-based essay instruction improved writing and self-efficacy for underserved high-school students [18]. These are important because they establish that pedagogically rich human-led instruction remains a high bar. Reviews of differentiated instruction and other non-AI pedagogies likewise indicate that variation in instructional quality matters greatly for outcomes [11].

There are also construct-validity and authorship tradeoffs. A large observational comparison of human-written and ChatGPT-generated high-school argumentative essays demonstrates that GenAI can produce essay-quality outputs relevant to high-school tasks, which creates challenges for interpreting writing products as evidence of student competence [29]. Assessment-focused reviews similarly note that generative AI complicates the validity of writing assessment, because a better product may reflect external support rather than internalized skill [19]. This tradeoff is central to literacy: improved draft quality under AI support is not the same as improved independent reading or writing ability.

Dependency and over-reliance are another concern. In the postsecondary revision RCT, better revised essays coexisted with fewer metacognitive processes [24]. In a high-school RCT on AI literacy, students still adopted incorrect ChatGPT recommendations 52.1% of the time overall despite an intervention, and the brief intervention did not reduce over-reliance (final n=36; d=-0.25 for over-reliance) [46]. Although that study is in mathematical numeracy rather than literacy, the mechanism generalizes directly to reading and writing tasks where students must evaluate generated explanations, summaries, or wording. The likely literacy tradeoff is therefore scale and immediacy versus independence and source judgment.

## Strength of evidence by outcome family

For writing feedback and error correction, the evidence is the strongest, though still limited. The direct K–12 QED on ChatGPT mobile feedback supports better error reduction than teacher feedback [33], and the under-extracted 2025 secondary writing-feedback study points in the same topical direction [27]. Adjacent postsecondary RCTs on revision also support the plausibility of improved revision products under GenAI-supported feedback [24] [31].

For vocabulary, there is one relevant K–12 QED showing a positive result for a ChatGPT-based app versus paper-based learning [47]. That is encouraging but too thin for a strong general conclusion.

For broader writing quality, argumentation, disciplinary literacy, and source-based writing, the evidence is weak. The available K–12 generative-AI studies do not provide strong experimental evidence on these outcomes, even though non-AI writing interventions demonstrate that they are measurable and improvable [1] [18].

For reading comprehension, the evidence is very weak. No direct K–12 RCT or QED in the pool convincingly tests a generative-AI reading intervention against a strong literacy comparator. The only related causal warning signal comes from adjacent adult evidence showing comprehension losses under AI reliance [21].

For engagement and perceptions, the evidence is more positive but should not be conflated with literacy achievement. The GPT-4 homework-tutor RCT showed better engagement-related ratings [4]. The vocabulary and mobile-feedback studies also reported positive student attitudes [47] [33]. Broader reviews often report enthusiasm and perceived usefulness around chatbots and AI feedback [34] [20]. But perceptions are indirect evidence only.

### Synthesis and Implications

The best-supported conclusion is narrow: generative AI can improve some secondary literacy-related outcomes, especially in structured uses such as English-learning homework support, vocabulary practice, and AI-generated corrective feedback, and these benefits are most visible in EFL/ESL contexts [4] [33] [47]. The evidence does not yet show that generative AI broadly improves K–12 reading comprehension, foundational reading, disciplinary literacy, or overall literacy achievement. It also does not show that GenAI reliably outperforms strong human supports such as expert conferencing, structured peer response, or well-designed strategy instruction [1] [18].

For schools and practitioners, the practical implication is to treat generative AI as a bounded support tool rather than a general literacy solution. The strongest current use cases are feedback acceleration, vocabulary practice, and guided homework tutoring [4] [33] [47]. These uses are most defensible when teachers define the task, constrain the tool’s role, and require students to remain cognitively engaged in revision or explanation. Adjacent evidence suggests that outcomes depend on scaffolding structure, student regulation, and prior knowledge, so implementation should emphasize prompt routines, verification, and reflection rather than open-ended text outsourcing [14] [28] [24].

A second implication is that evaluators should distinguish immediate product improvement from durable literacy learning. Better corrected drafts, more complete homework, or higher engagement do not necessarily mean stronger independent reading or writing skill [19] [24] [29]. Schools considering adoption should therefore prioritize outcome measures that include independent posttests, transfer tasks, and assessments completed without AI assistance.

A third implication is that comparator choice matters for policy. Evidence that GenAI beats paper worksheets or low-feedback conditions is not enough to justify large-scale replacement of teacher-mediated literacy instruction. Given the strong non-AI evidence for explicit writing instruction and strategy-based support, the most appropriate near-term role for generative AI is supplementation where human feedback is scarce, not substitution where high-quality instruction is already present [1] [18] [8].

### Limitations and Research Gaps

The evidence base has five major weaknesses. First, there are too few direct K–12 RCTs on literacy outcomes. Only one strong direct K–12 RCT in the pool targets an English-learning homework context, not broad classroom literacy instruction [4]. Second, the available K–12 studies are concentrated in secondary EFL/ESL settings, limiting generalizability to mainstream English-medium classrooms [33] [47]. Third, outcomes are often proximal and narrow—error counts, vocabulary scores, short-term homework tests, and attitudes—rather than independent standardized literacy measures or follow-up outcomes [4] [33]. Fourth, comparator conditions are often weak; there are few direct comparisons with peer review, automated writing evaluation, strong teacher conferencing, or human tutoring [8] [15]. Fifth, equity-relevant populations are largely missing: students with disabilities, struggling readers, early elementary learners, and varied socioeconomic access groups are underrepresented [44] [26].

There are also notable reporting limitations in the current pool. Several highly relevant studies are under-extracted, with sample sizes, dosage, effect sizes, or outcome details not reported in the provided summaries [27]. Some of the newest studies are preprints, which increases uncertainty about stability and peer-review status [4] [14] [28]. Publication-quality syntheses exist, but most are broad and not specific to K–12 literacy [6] [34] [37].

The highest-priority research gaps are direct K–12 trials on reading comprehension, summarization, argumentation, source-based writing, and disciplinary literacy; elementary-grade studies including foundational reading outcomes; head-to-head comparisons with teacher conferencing, peer review, and non-AI writing tools; subgroup analyses for multilingual learners in mainstream settings, students with disabilities, and struggling readers; and longer-term studies measuring independent performance after AI support is removed [44] [34] [19].

## Body of Evidence Maturity: EMERGING
Justification: The evidence base includes a small number of directly relevant K–12 studies with some positive quasi-experimental and one notable randomized finding, but coverage is narrow, heavily secondary/EFL-focused, and thin for reading comprehension, foundational literacy, and equity-priority populations. Methodological rigor and comparator strength are inconsistent, and much of the surrounding literature is broader, adjacent, or postsecondary rather than directly responsive to the K–12 literacy question.

paper_profiles.title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for quantitative evidence on the effectiveness of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in K-12 schools. Prior reviews had largely been qualitative or focused on narrower technologies, leaving unclear the overall impact of AI-supported personalized learning and the conditions under which it works best. The study therefore asks how effective AI-enabled personalized STEM education is in schools and which moderator variables explain differences in outcomes.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis following PRISMA procedures, synthesizing 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trial studies published between 2012 and 2024. The review focused on AI-enabled personalized learning interventions in school STEM subjects and coded moderators including school level, AI application type, personalized learning model, outcome type, subject area, and whether generative AI was used. The included AI applications spanned intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, AR/VR, and other AI-supported tools.

The population was K-12 students across multiple school levels, including kindergarten, elementary, junior high, and senior high school, in school-based STEM learning contexts worldwide. Because this is a meta-analysis, the paper aggregates evidence across many settings rather than reporting a single intervention site or country. The focus is explicitly on student learning outcomes in school STEM education.

The main conclusion is that AI-enabled personalized STEM education produces a statistically significant small-to-medium positive effect overall compared with non-AI approaches (reported overall g = 0.455). The strongest effects were found for junior and senior high school students, AR/VR-based tools, and more learner-centered models that combine AI with classroom or collaborative pedagogies. Effects also varied by subject, with comprehensive courses showing the largest gains. By contrast, observed outcome type and generative-AI versus non-generative-AI status did not significantly moderate effects. The authors argue for evidence-based, pedagogically aligned integration of AI in K-12 STEM education.

paper_profiles.title: The role of AI assisted writing feedback in developing secondary students writing skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves the writing performance of secondary-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students more than traditional teacher feedback alone. The authors focus on a common instructional problem in EFL writing classrooms: teachers often have limited time to provide detailed, individualized feedback, while students need frequent revision opportunities to improve grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and overall writing quality. The study also examines students’ perceptions of using an AI writing assistant as a feedback tool.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions over an 8-week period. The experimental group used Grammarly to receive immediate AI-generated feedback on drafts, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, style, sentence clarity, and coherence; after revision, the teacher also provided brief higher-order feedback. The control group followed a traditional process in which the teacher provided delayed written feedback on drafts. Both groups completed pre-test and post-test timed persuasive essays and followed the same writing curriculum with the same instructor. Writing was scored analytically across content, organization, language use, and mechanics by two independent EFL raters, and the experimental group also completed a post-study perception questionnaire.

Participants were 60 Turkish public high school students aged 15–17 enrolled in an EFL program, divided into an experimental group and a control group of 30 each. The study took place in a secondary school setting in Türkiye during regular class time, with use of the school computer lab for the AI tool. Students had little prior experience with AI-based writing tools, and parental consent was obtained because participants were minors.

The main conclusion is that AI-assisted feedback significantly improved students’ writing more than teacher-only feedback. The experimental group showed larger gains in total writing scores, especially in language use and organization, while both groups improved over time. Students also reported positive perceptions of the AI tool, including improved confidence and satisfaction with the feedback. The authors conclude that AI writing tools can effectively supplement secondary EFL writing instruction, particularly when combined with teacher guidance rather than used as a replacement for human feedback.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback system can improve lesson planning in vocational teacher education. The authors focus on a practical problem in higher education: detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is valuable for student teachers but difficult for university instructors to provide consistently and at scale. The study asks whether AI-based feedback can support or outperform human feedback on key didactic planning dimensions, and whether using such a system also influences students’ motivation, AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competence, and technology self-efficacy.

The intervention centers on EDDA, an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and teaching materials using a BERT-based model trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks. EDDA does not generate open-ended responses like a large language model; instead, it classifies lesson plans into predefined didactic categories and returns expert-level text and visual feedback tied to established criteria. In the study, the experimental group used EDDA throughout a semester and could also consult the university instructor to discuss the AI feedback, while the control group received human feedback only. Both groups completed the same lesson-planning tasks and theoretical coursework.

The population consisted of 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups to design 90-minute vocational lessons. The intervention spanned a semester, with students iteratively incorporating six focal dimensions or principles into the same lesson plan: sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization. Outcomes included coded analyses of lesson plans as well as repeated self-report surveys on AI literacy and related meta-dimensions.

The main conclusion is that analytical AI feedback can effectively supplement traditional instructor feedback and, on some lesson-planning dimensions, match or exceed human-only feedback. The experimental group showed advantages on selected planning aspects, including some sustainability-related dimensions, social competences for sustainable development, reflexivity, and several planning features highlighted in the abstract such as action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, or motivation. The authors therefore argue that analytical AI tools are promising for feedback in teacher education, but should be embedded in a broader, human-centered instructional framework rather than treated as a standalone solution.

paper_profiles.title: Current practices and future direction of artificial intelligence in mathematics education: A systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a practical and up-to-date synthesis of how artificial intelligence is being used in mathematics education. The authors argue that prior reviews often focused on broad AI categories or research-stage systems, but gave less attention to specific, market-ready tools that educators could actually implement. The review therefore asks four main questions: how AI in mathematics education studies are distributed across educational levels, what AI tools are used and how they can be categorized, which commercialized tools are available online and what they do, and what emerging trends and future directions appear in the literature.

The study uses a systematic literature review approach. The authors searched Web of Science and Scopus for English-language journal articles published between 2019 and 2024, focused on AI in mathematics education. After screening and deduplication, 32 studies were included. The review categorizes AI tools into adaptive learning systems/intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, augmented reality, virtual reality, learning analytics, serious games, and AI mathematics problem solvers. It also identifies named tools such as Khan Academy, Squirrel AI, ChatGPT, Bard, GeoGebra, GeoGebra AR, Photomath, Vuforia, and NeoTrieVR, and distinguishes between generative AI tools and pedagogical AI tools.

The population represented across the reviewed studies spans primary/elementary, middle/high school, university, and adult learners, with the largest share of studies at the middle/high school level, followed by university/adult and then primary levels. Because this is a review, the context is not one single intervention site but a synthesis of studies conducted across multiple countries, with especially strong representation from China, the United States, and Spain. The paper is situated in mathematics education broadly and examines both classroom-oriented and digital learning applications of AI.

The main conclusions are that AI in mathematics education is expanding rapidly and serves multiple instructional purposes, especially personalization, adaptive feedback, interactive visualization, and problem support. Chatbots were the most common category in recent studies, while AR/VR showed strong promise for engagement and conceptual understanding, especially for geometry and spatial learning. The authors conclude that commercialized pedagogical AI tools currently dominate the field, but generative AI tools are increasingly important. They also emphasize the need for more longitudinal research, stronger understanding of long-term effects and equity implications, and more work on how AI can complement rather than replace teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive learning systems and intelligent tutoring systems are among the AI approaches associated with enhanced mathematics learning and achievement in the literature reviewed. The paper references their personalized learning and adaptive feedback functions but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: mathematics achievement/learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The authors ask three main questions: which technological breakthroughs enabled personalized tutoring, how current systems use real-time adaptation to improve engagement and academic performance, and what ethical challenges have emerged alongside these technologies. The review is motivated by persistent global learning gaps and interest in AI-based tools that can personalize instruction at scale.

The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The authors analyze tutoring systems through a four-part framework covering artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. They also conduct a latent class analysis that groups systems into three categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal tutoring systems that combine verbal, visual, and physical interaction. Across the reviewed studies, key AI techniques include Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, natural language processing, and large language models.

The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The included literature spans multiple learner groups, with examples and discussion prominently involving younger learners, middle school mathematics students, secondary physics learners, and some higher-education contexts. The review focuses primarily on students as end users of tutoring systems in educational environments, rather than on teachers or administrators as the main participants.

The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. Computer-based ITS are more scalable and cognitively adaptive, while robot-based systems are stronger for social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems integrating both approaches may offer the greatest educational benefit. They also conclude that important challenges remain, especially around scalability, data privacy, bias, transparency, and the still-limited cognitive adaptability of robotic systems.

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence-supported programming education: Effects on learning performance, self-efficacy and processes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, improves programming education outcomes and how it shapes students’ learning processes. The authors focus on four questions: whether GenAI improves programming output quality and knowledge transfer, whether it affects programming self-efficacy, how it changes students’ programming behaviours, and how different behaviour patterns under GenAI relate to academic performance. The study responds to mixed prior findings suggesting that GenAI may improve immediate task performance but may not always support deeper learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experiment in which one group of students used a ChatGPT-based platform (ChatGPT-Next-Web using GPT-3.5-turbo) for self-directed programming learning, while a control group used other Internet resources instead of GenAI. Both groups completed the same Turtle-library programming learning tasks in a standardized computer lab setting. Measures included ratings of programming products across multiple dimensions, pre/post programming self-efficacy surveys, and fine-grained behavioural trace data captured through scripts and analysed with frequency analysis, process mining, and clustering.

Participants were 55 undergraduate Physics Education students at a public university in China. All had prior foundational Python experience but were new to the Python Turtle library. The experimental activity itself lasted 120 minutes, followed by a 40-minute post-test task completed without external resources. The study took place in university computer labs with uniform hardware, and the authors also provided the experimental group with a GenAI user guide to support interaction with the tool.

The main conclusions are that GenAI support improved short-term programming performance and increased self-efficacy, especially in self-regulation and complex programming tasks, but did not improve longer-term knowledge transfer when students later had to work without external resources. Behavioural analyses showed that GenAI-supported learners relied more on information retrieval and copying, whereas control students engaged more in independent coding and code revision. Within the GenAI group, higher-performing students used the tool more critically and interactively, showing greater epistemic agency, while lower-performing students were more likely to copy outputs directly. The authors argue that GenAI can be beneficial for programming education, but only when instructional design discourages over-reliance and supports active cognitive engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing Generative AI (GenAI) for Automated Feedback in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging use of generative AI for automated feedback in higher education. The authors note that higher education instructors face growing pressure to provide timely, personalized, and scalable feedback, especially in online and large-enrollment courses. Prior reviews had examined automated feedback or generative AI separately, but had not focused specifically on GenAI-based feedback in higher education or on how these systems are implemented in authentic instructional settings. The review therefore asks three questions: what contexts GenAI feedback systems are used in, what their main characteristics are, and what possibilities they create for higher education.

The authors conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-style procedures and Arksey and O'Malley's framework. They searched peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published from 2019 to 2023 in Academic Search Premier and Education Source, screened 1,976 non-duplicate records, and ultimately included 10 empirical studies from Q1 or Q2 journals. The reviewed studies examined GenAI-based feedback tools such as ChatGPT, chatbots, digital tutors, and specialized writing/assessment systems. These tools were used for automated feedback in contexts including language learning, academic writing, creative thinking, and STEM courses. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI systems served purposes such as personalized learning, collaborative problem-solving, self-regulated learning, and motivation/engagement.

The population and context are higher education settings, including undergraduate and some graduate-level contexts, with both students and educators implicated in implementation. The review synthesizes studies conducted in varied instructional environments, with frequent relevance to online learning and large-scale courses. It also emphasizes instructor roles in implementation, including guiding students' use of GenAI, providing higher-level or final feedback, engineering prompts, and facilitating deeper learning beyond what automated systems can provide.

The main conclusions are that GenAI automated feedback systems show strong promise for improving educational efficiency and support in higher education. The reviewed evidence suggests these systems can reduce instructor workload, provide timely and personalized feedback, improve communication, support cognitive and emotional needs, and expand access to feedback in lower-pressure environments. At the same time, the review highlights unresolved issues such as ethical concerns, accuracy, overreliance, and the need to better define instructors' roles in AI-supported feedback ecosystems. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated in ways that augment rather than replace human instruction, and they call for more research as the field develops.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of AI-Blended Learning and AI-Personalized Learning on Undergraduate Biology Students' Attitude and Performance in Climate Change Education
paper_profiles.venue: Anchor University Journal of Science and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-enhanced instructional approaches improve undergraduate biology students’ attitudes toward climate change and their academic performance in climate change education better than traditional classroom teaching. The study is motivated by the concern that conventional instruction may not sufficiently engage students or address diverse learning needs when teaching complex environmental topics.

The intervention compared three instructional conditions: AI-Blended Learning, AI-Personalized Learning, and Traditional Classroom Instruction. In the AI-Blended Learning condition, students used ChatGPT-3.5 alongside face-to-face teaching. In the AI-Personalized Learning condition, students relied on ChatGPT-3.5 as the primary instructional support in a fully AI-driven personalized environment. The comparison group received conventional face-to-face instruction without the AI intervention. Outcomes were measured using a Climate Change Attitude Assessment (CCAA) and a Climate Change Achievement Test (CCAT), with pretest and posttest scores analyzed using ANCOVA.

The study involved 70 300-level undergraduate biology students at Federal University Gusau in Nigeria. Students were drawn from existing classes and assigned into three groups: AI-Blended Learning (20), AI-Personalized Learning (20), and Traditional Classroom Instruction (30). The intervention lasted four weeks and covered climate change topics such as causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and policy actions.

The main finding is that AI-Blended Learning produced substantially stronger gains in both attitude and performance than either AI-Personalized Learning or Traditional Classroom Instruction. Post hoc analyses showed that the blended approach significantly outperformed both alternatives, while AI-Personalized Learning did not significantly differ from traditional instruction on the reported comparisons. The paper concludes that integrating ChatGPT-3.5 with teacher-led classroom instruction is more effective than relying on AI alone, and recommends that higher education lecturers adopt AI-blended approaches to improve engagement and learning outcomes in environmental education.

paper_profiles.title: Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI code generators such as OpenAI Codex help or hinder novice learners who are first learning introductory text-based programming. The authors focus on a key educational concern: although AI-generated code may improve immediate task performance, it could also create over-reliance and weaken learners’ ability to understand, modify, or retain programming knowledge. The study addresses whether novices can effectively use AI code generation, how it changes task performance, and whether prior access to such tools affects later independent coding and retention.

To study this, the researchers built a web-based Python learning environment called Coding Steps. Learners completed a three-week, 10-session remote program consisting of a Scratch-based introduction and pre-test, seven Python training sessions, and two evaluation sessions (an immediate post-test and a one-week retention test). During training, one group had access to an AI code generator powered by OpenAI Codex, while a comparison group did not. Participants worked through 45 code-authoring tasks, each followed by a code-modification task, plus multiple-choice questions on core introductory Python topics such as variables, conditionals, loops, and arrays. The system logged code edits, documentation use, errors, submissions, and AI prompt/code-generation behavior.

The population consisted of 69 novice learners aged 10-17 recruited through coding camps in two major North American cities. All reported no prior text-based programming experience, though many had experience with block-based programming environments such as Scratch. Participants were assigned to conditions using a matched-groups design based on Scratch pre-test scores to balance prior programming knowledge. The study was conducted remotely via Google Meet, with instructors available to provide support and personalized feedback during training.

The main findings were that access to Codex substantially improved performance on training-phase code-authoring tasks: learners completed more tasks, achieved higher correctness, made fewer errors, and finished faster. Importantly, prior use of the AI tool did not reduce performance on subsequent manual code-modification tasks, and learners in the Codex group performed similarly to the baseline group on the immediate post-test without access to the tool. On the one-week retention test, the Codex group showed slightly better performance, though differences were not statistically significant overall. The authors conclude that AI code generators can support novice programming learning without clear evidence of harming short-term retention, and that learners with stronger prior programming competency may benefit the most.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated feedback on student writing can be used effectively in higher education language learning, and whether students prefer it to feedback from human tutors. The authors focus on the emerging use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) learners. The study addresses two core questions: whether AI feedback produces stronger writing gains than human feedback, and whether students prefer AI-generated or tutor-generated feedback.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks. In Study 1, the intervention compared GPT-4-generated writing feedback with feedback from human tutors in a repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. ENL students completed weekly 300-word academic writing tasks, received either AI or human feedback, revised their work, and were assessed through pre- and post-writing tests scored with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI-generated and human tutor feedback on weekly assignments, then completed weekly surveys with Likert-scale and open-ended items about satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference.

The population consisted of 91 ENL university students enrolled in an academic reading and writing course at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. Study 1 included 48 students, and Study 2 included 43 different students. Human tutors were trained English language tutors from the university’s ENL Tutor Program, while GPT-4 feedback was generated using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators. The intervention occurred in the context of regular course writing assignments during a shortened Spring 2023 semester.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback. Students in both conditions improved similarly over the six-week period. Preference data showed an almost even split between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human tutors valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask immediate follow-up questions, while those preferring AI valued clarity, specificity, consistency, and detailed academic language suggestions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing instruction without harming learning outcomes, and they recommend a blended approach that combines the efficiency and specificity of AI with the interpersonal benefits of human tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Faculty and Student Perceptions of Generative AI in University Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and faculty perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to perceived ease of use, ethical concerns, intentions to use, and views about impacts on learning. The study addresses a gap in empirical evidence about how attitudes toward generative AI differ across university roles and across student subgroups defined by gender and STEM versus non-STEM disciplines.

The study used an anonymous online survey grounded in a modified UTAUT framework and supplemented with items about perceived effects on learning competencies and ethics. The survey measured constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, habit, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention, along with views about academic integrity, policy needs, and the frequency of generative AI use. The approach was descriptive and comparative rather than experimental.

Participants were 982 students and 76 faculty members at a single large land-grant public university in the southeastern United States during the Fall 2023 semester. The student sample included both undergraduate and other university students, and analyses compared students with faculty as well as four student subgroups: STEM male, STEM female, non-STEM male, and non-STEM female. Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 through voluntary online survey distribution.

The authors conclude that students and faculty were broadly similar in their attitudes toward generative AI, though students reported higher ease of use, hedonic motivation, and personal innovativeness, while faculty reported more habitual use. Both groups used generative AI at similarly low rates overall and shared concerns about negative effects on learning competencies and academic dishonesty, while also supporting the development of institutional policies. Within the student sample, male STEM students tended to express the most positive attitudes and non-STEM female students the least positive, suggesting that gender and disciplinary context shape how generative AI is received in higher education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Students’ Multimodal Representations of Ideas About Epistemic Reading of Scientific Texts in Generative AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students represent their ideas about reading scientific texts generated by generative AI tools, a process the authors call GenAI-science epistemic reading. The problem addressed is that students need to draw on both their understanding of science and their understanding of GenAI in order to critically interpret AI-generated scientific information, yet existing measures in this area are often limited to Likert-scale surveys. The study asks what students’ multimodal representations of these ideas look like in terms of presentational, organisational, and orientational meanings.

The study uses a qualitative collective case study approach and develops a multimodal instrument in which students draw and write short explanations about (1) how ChatGPT/Poe generates scientific texts and (2) how they themselves read scientific texts in these tools. The authors analyze 44 students’ drawings and written responses using Lemke’s framework of presentational, organisational, and orientational meaning, and from these data they construct an analytical framework with categories such as epistemic trust, epistemic knowledge, organisational form, and representations of the nature of science and GenAI. Although the responses were collected before an explicit-reflective instructional activity that was part of a larger project, this paper focuses on the pre-instruction representations rather than testing intervention effects.

Participants were 44 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students in Hong Kong participating in extracurricular lessons. The instructional context involved a bilingual teacher who had prior online training workshops on implementing the teaching approach. Students completed the multimodal task in two classrooms before instruction, and the broader project centered on improving students’ understanding of epistemic reading of scientific texts from sources including GenAI and online media.

The main conclusion is that a multimodal approach is useful for characterising students’ ideas about GenAI-science epistemic reading in ways that standard survey instruments may miss. Students expressed a range of epistemic trust positions, including trust, critical thinking, confusion, and non-evaluation, and used different semiotic modes to express these ideas. The paper’s core contribution is an analytical framework teachers and researchers can use to diagnose and discuss students’ epistemic understanding of AI-generated scientific texts. The authors argue that such multimodal representations can serve as a richer diagnostic and instructional tool for future intervention studies on GenAI in science education.

paper_profiles.title: AI Responses to Challenging Problems and Educator Responses to AI Availability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI tools, specifically ChatGPT and Gemini, respond to cognitively demanding secondary mathematics tasks and what educators should do in response to increasing AI availability. The authors are concerned not only with whether GenAI can produce mathematical answers, but also with the pedagogical implications of tools that can engage in open-ended reasoning, generate explanations, and revise responses after prompting. The article situates this issue within secondary mathematics education and argues that educators should move beyond a ban-oriented stance toward instructional uses that preserve student thinking and reasoning.

The approach is a conceptual and illustrative analysis rather than an empirical intervention study. The authors posed three mathematics tasks spanning middle and high school content areas—rates and proportional reasoning, geometric proof, and quadratic interpretation—to ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, and Gemini 1.0 during March–April 2024. They then analyzed the quality, strengths, and errors in the AI responses and derived two instructional strategies for educators: having students interact with GenAI to explore, clarify, and extend mathematical ideas, and having students critique AI-generated solutions and arguments. The paper includes concrete examples of prompts teachers could use to support these strategies.

The population and context are secondary mathematics education in the United States, with examples drawn from US middle school and high school mathematics curricula. However, no human participants were recruited and no classroom implementation data were collected. Instead, the article focuses on hypothetical and proposed uses of GenAI by students and educators in classroom mathematics settings.

The main conclusions are that current GenAI systems can engage with cognitively demanding mathematics tasks in ways that exceed traditional calculators or step-solving apps, but they also make substantial mathematical and logical errors. The authors therefore recommend that teachers use GenAI as a conversational and critical-thinking tool rather than as an answer engine. They argue that student learning can be supported when students are asked to interrogate, extend, and evaluate AI responses, especially in ways that preserve mathematical communication, reasoning, and proof-oriented thinking.

paper_profiles.title: Suitability of Chinese GenAI platforms for early childhood education: A multifaceted evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether currently available Chinese generative AI platforms are suitable for use in early childhood education (ECE), a context in which young children’s developmental needs, age-appropriate content, and ethical protections are especially important. The authors argue that existing AI evaluation frameworks do not adequately capture ECE-specific requirements, so they develop and apply a Chinese evaluation framework organized around three dimensions: technical performance, pedagogical adaptability, and ethical and safety considerations.

The study evaluates 10 freely accessible Chinese GenAI platforms using a mixed-methods design that combines quantitative scoring with qualitative content analysis. Platforms were assessed on multimodal support, response speed, lesson-plan generation, activity organization, personalization for different age groups, ethical compliance, content appropriateness, and algorithmic fairness. Testing was conducted under standardized hardware, network, and prompt conditions over a two-week period in February 2025, and scoring was completed through expert review and consensus. Rather than testing learning outcomes in classrooms, the study evaluates the capabilities and risks of AI tools that might be used by early childhood educators.

The context is Chinese early childhood education, especially preschool-aged children and the educators selecting tools for them. The platforms were not necessarily designed specifically for ECE, but were chosen because they are prominent, open-access Chinese GenAI systems with potential relevance to education. The paper also discusses implications for other stakeholders, including parents, developers, and policymakers concerned with AI use in early learning environments.

The main conclusions are that the proposed framework can differentiate among Chinese GenAI platforms and identify meaningful strengths and weaknesses. Doubao and iFlytek Spark showed particularly strong overall performance, with Doubao excelling broadly and Spark performing especially well in pedagogical adaptability; DeepSeek stood out for pedagogical adaptability but performed poorly technically. Across platforms, the authors conclude that improvements are still needed in multimodal support, transparency of privacy and recommendation policies, ECE-specific datasets, personalization, and ethical safeguards before GenAI can be considered fully suitable for early childhood education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can support teachers—not students—by improving lesson planning before instruction takes place. The authors focus on a common challenge in teaching preparation: novice teachers often struggle to anticipate students’ misconceptions, learning difficulties, and the kinds of classroom interactions that reveal whether a lesson plan is effective. The study asks whether an LLM can improve teaching plans by simulating teacher–student interactions, generating teaching reflections, and then revising the original plan accordingly.

The intervention is a prompt-based workflow using GPT-4 (and, in one comparison condition, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to enhance high school mathematics teaching plans. Starting from existing lesson plans, the model first simulates classroom dialogue involving students with varying ability levels and typical errors, then produces teaching reflections based on those simulated interactions, and finally refines the lesson plan using those reflections. The authors evaluate eight datasets of lesson plans, including LLM-generated plans, human expert-written plans, and plans written by pre-service teachers, with improvements produced through one or two rounds of LLM-based refinement. Human raters scored plans on a detailed framework covering problem chains, teaching activities, knowledge content, teaching methods, evaluation, interdisciplinarity, practical value, scope, and overall quality.

The context is high school mathematics in China. The evaluation corpus included 480 teaching plans drawn from 60 lessons across four knowledge modules: Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics.
