Human evaluation was carried out by mathematics teachers with teaching experience, and the paper compares baseline lesson plans against LLM-enhanced versions rather than measuring direct student learning outcomes. The workflow was implemented through web-based LLM interfaces rather than custom-coded systems, with the aim of keeping the approach accessible to ordinary teachers.

The main conclusion is that LLM-based simulation and reflection substantially improved the quality of teaching plans. In many dimensions, the refined plans matched or exceeded the quality of high-quality human-written plans, and plans originally written by pre-service teachers also improved notably after LLM enhancement. Performance varied by content area, with the strongest results in statistics and weaker performance in geometry, where visual reasoning is harder to support through text alone. Overall, the paper argues that LLMs can serve as useful pre-class rehearsal and lesson refinement tools for teachers, especially for instructional preparation, though further work is needed on challenging question design, disciplinary depth, and broader validation in authentic teaching settings.

paper_profiles.title: Reinforcing L2 reading comprehension through artificial intelligence intervention: refining engagement to foster self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an artificial-intelligence-supported reading environment can improve second-language (L2) reading comprehension, learner engagement, and self-regulated learning. The study addresses a gap in the literature on AI for reading instruction, especially for language learners, by asking whether AI-enhanced classrooms can outperform conventional instruction and how learners perceive such an environment.

The intervention centered on the ReadToMe (RTM) platform, an AI-based, multi-sensory reading system that converts curricular text into text-to-speech, synchronized highlighting, pronunciation support, concept images, dictionary support, and knowledge-graph-based scaffolds. In the experimental condition, students used RTM for homework and reading practice, while the control group received conventional reading instruction and feedback from the teacher or peers. The study used a mixed-methods design with pre/post quantitative measures and follow-up semi-structured interviews.

Participants were 60 Iranian female EFL students from two intact classes at a language institute, with 30 students in the experimental group and 30 in the control group. They were upper-intermediate/C1 learners with a mean age of 21, attending in-person classes twice weekly for about 12 weeks. Both groups used the same reading textbook, and the same instructor taught both groups to reduce teacher effects. Outcomes included an objective reading comprehension test plus self-report scales for engagement and self-regulation.

The main findings indicate that the AI-supported group significantly outperformed the control group on reading comprehension, self-regulation, and engagement. Qualitative data also suggested that most students viewed the AI platform as motivating, engaging, and helpful for personalized feedback and comprehension support, though some reported usability problems such as slow loading and navigation issues. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-enhanced reading instruction can be an effective approach for improving L2 reading outcomes and supporting learner engagement and self-regulated learning, while also noting the importance of addressing technical usability barriers.

paper_profiles.title: How do generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools and large language models (LLMs) influence language learners’ critical thinking in EFL education? A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a timely question in education: whether generative AI tools and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT support or undermine critical thinking in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. The authors note that prior work has focused mainly on technical benefits like grammar correction, vocabulary development, and writing support, while giving less attention to higher-order thinking. To address this gap, they conduct a systematic review focused specifically on critical thinking in EFL contexts.

Using the PRISMA framework, the authors searched Web of Science, Scopus, ProQuest, ERIC, and Google Scholar for studies published from 2022 to February 2025. After screening 3,243 records plus 4 additional sources, they included 15 studies. The review synthesizes evidence on the dual nature of generative AI and LLMs, the research methods used, the main thematic focuses, the theories and models applied, and the limitations and future directions in this research area. The reviewed studies concern EFL learners and teachers, with contexts including classroom teaching and language learning activities such as writing, speaking, argumentation, and literature learning.

The main conclusion is that generative AI and LLMs have both promise and risk for critical thinking in EFL education. Ten of the 15 studies (66.67%) reported positive effects, including improved argumentative writing and speaking, stronger analytical reasoning, better evaluation and problem-solving, increased engagement and confidence, and support for self-directed learning. At the same time, five studies (33.33%) warned that overreliance on AI could reduce analytical depth, creativity, autonomy, and independent reasoning. The authors conclude that AI can nurture critical thinking when used with guidance, critical evaluation, and pedagogical structure, but may hinder it when learners passively accept AI-generated content.

paper_profiles.title: Reading differently with ChatGPT: EFL learners’ use of Question-Answer Relationship strategy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners developed reading comprehension when using ChatGPT together with the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy. The core research question was how learners’ reading comprehension changed through this integration, especially across different QAR levels: locating explicit information, synthesizing across text segments, and making inferences about tone and author intent. The study addresses a practical problem in EFL reading instruction: students often need individualized support with vocabulary, sentence structure, and higher-order comprehension, but traditional instruction may not provide timely, adaptive scaffolding.

The intervention combined structured reading strategy instruction through QAR with guided use of ChatGPT. Students completed five weekly guided reading sessions in which they read texts, answered TOEFL-style comprehension questions, generated their own QAR questions and answers, asked ChatGPT to generate questions, and then compared, revised, and discussed responses through free-form interaction. The study used three rounds of semi-structured interviews across five weeks and analyzed 105 interviews thematically using the QAR framework categories (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You) alongside inductive coding.

Participants were 35 first-year undergraduate students in an academic English program at a university in northern China. They were enrolled in two EFL classes per week and also completed one guided ChatGPT-supported reading practice session per week. Most participants self-identified as low-intermediate in TOEFL-related reading proficiency and had limited prior experience with generative AI. Interviews were conducted in Chinese, transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo.

The main conclusion is that learners described a developmental progression in comprehension: ChatGPT first helped them identify explicit information and understand vocabulary and sentence structure, then supported summarizing and synthesizing across paragraphs, and finally helped them engage in inferential and interpretive reading about tone, stance, and author intention. Students did not simply accept ChatGPT outputs passively; many used it dialogically to compare reasoning and refine their own understanding. At the same time, participants identified limitations in ChatGPT, including weak handling of polysemous vocabulary, unclear parsing of long sentences, overlong summaries, and sometimes inaccurate inferential explanations. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a useful reading partner when paired with structured strategy instruction, but its value depends on critical, strategic use and AI literacy.

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Tutors Beyond K-12: An Observational Study of Adult Learner Engagement and Academic Impact
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether intelligent tutoring systems, which have mostly been studied in K-12 settings, can also benefit adult learners in postsecondary education when use is voluntary rather than required. The authors focus on two questions: how optional tutor use relates to adult learners’ academic outcomes, and what demographic or behavioral characteristics distinguish adults who choose to use intelligent tutors.

The intervention studied is the Apprentice Tutors platform, a set of adaptive College Algebra tutors integrated into Blackboard and Canvas via LTI at a state technical college. The tutors provided real-time correctness feedback, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-based adaptive problem selection, multi-layered hints, progress tracking, tutorial videos, links to textbook and YouTube resources, and a bug/Q&A feature. The study analyzed two years of platform deployment data, combining tutor interaction logs with institutional grades and demographic records. Analyses included descriptive statistics, usage analyses, learning-curve modeling, and regression analysis.

The population was adult learners enrolled in College Algebra at a 2-year state technical college in the United States, many of whom balanced work with night, hybrid, in-person, or online study. The dataset included 3,510 students overall, with 520 students using the tutors at least once and 214 using them in Unit 1, which had the greatest tutor coverage. Tutor users were more likely to be female and slightly older than non-users, and usage was concentrated in evenings, late nights, and on Thursdays, suggesting that flexibility mattered for this learner population.

The main conclusion is that voluntary use of intelligent tutors appears promising for adult postsecondary learners. Students showed reduced error rates with more practice inside the tutors, and tutor use was positively associated with higher Unit 1 assessment scores outside the tutor. However, because the study was observational and lacked random assignment, the authors emphasize that these findings are preliminary and do not establish causality. They argue that intelligent tutors are a viable supplementary resource for adult learners and recommend future randomized studies and broader tutor coverage to test long-term and more generalizable effects.

paper_profiles.title: Lecturers’ perceptions of the influence of AI on a blended learning approach in a South African higher education institution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how lecturers perceive the influence of artificial intelligence on blended learning in a South African higher education institution. The central problem is the limited understanding of lecturers’ views on how AI can enhance blended teaching and learning, what challenges arise during implementation, and what kinds of support are needed for successful integration. The study is framed by the SAMR model (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) to interpret different levels of AI integration in teaching practice.

The researchers conducted a qualitative single-case study using semi-structured focus group interviews and document analysis. The approach focused on how lecturers were already using AI within blended learning rather than testing a controlled intervention. Reported uses of AI included answering student queries, generating customized learning materials and assessments, enabling translation across languages, providing real-time feedback, supporting interactive activities, and automating some administrative tasks. The document analysis was used to corroborate lecturers’ descriptions with examples from module sites, such as adaptive quizzes, AI-generated case studies, automated feedback, and translation tools.

The study involved 15 lecturers from the College of Education at one South African higher education institution. Although the direct participants were lecturers, the educational context included their students in blended courses, and the paper discusses perceived effects on student engagement, communication, personalization, and learning support. The setting was a blended higher education environment combining face-to-face and online instruction.

The main conclusions are that lecturers generally viewed AI as beneficial for blended learning, especially for personalization, communication, quick feedback, adaptive assessment, and broader access to learning materials. At the same time, they identified substantial barriers, including resistance to change, time constraints, uneven student access to technology, ethical and privacy concerns, limited infrastructure, and the need to balance AI with traditional pedagogy. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled blended learning requires strong institutional support, professional development, management backing, reliable internet and technological infrastructure, technical support, and dedicated time for lecturers to learn and implement AI effectively.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what its capabilities, limitations, and implications may be for higher education, especially for learning, teaching, and assessment. A central concern is whether generative AI threatens traditional written assessments by enabling students to produce plausible essays and other academic responses rapidly, while also creating new opportunities for educational innovation. The authors position the debate within the longer history of educational technology hype and within the field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

The paper uses a desktop analysis approach built around an extensive literature review and the authors’ own exploratory testing of ChatGPT through a series of prompts. Rather than conducting a controlled empirical study with enrolled learners, the article reviews early academic and preprint literature on ChatGPT and related GPT systems, describes OpenAI and the development of GPT-3/ChatGPT, and demonstrates the tool’s functions through examples such as conceptual explanations, statistical problem solving, essay generation, and Chinese writing. It also situates ChatGPT alongside existing student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AIEd applications, including intelligent tutoring systems, automated essay scoring, automated writing evaluation, and tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune.

The context is higher education broadly, with discussion focused on students, teachers, and institutions rather than a defined participant sample. The article addresses implications for assessment integrity, writing instruction, feedback, and educational policy. Although the broader retrieval topic concerns K-12 literacy, this specific paper does not study school-age learners and instead concentrates on postsecondary settings, including examples and cited literature from university and professional education.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT is impressive but limited: it can generate fluent prose, support brainstorming, and offer conceptual explanations, yet it can also produce shallow analysis, errors, fabricated references, and misleadingly confident outputs. The authors argue that higher education should neither ban nor uncritically embrace the technology. Instead, institutions and educators should adapt assessment practices, strengthen feedback-rich and in-class learning designs, and treat ChatGPT as part of the evolving AIEd ecosystem rather than as a complete replacement for human teaching or judgment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed desktop analysis/literature review with illustrative experiments using ChatGPT, but it does not present a controlled empirical design, causal identification, or systematic outcome evaluation. It offers useful synthesis but only limited direct evidence under the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially substantial implications for assessment and writing support, but impact is unclear because no effect sizes or direct learner outcome estimates are reported. Overall impact remains speculative and mixed rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual and literature-review discussion of ChatGPT as a generative conversational AI for higher education learning, teaching, and assessment, including ad hoc prompting demonstrations.
Discusses AI writing assistants such as Grammarly and Wordtune, automated writing evaluation, essay scoring, and corrective feedback tools as adjacent comparator technologies for writing support.
Reviews automated essay scoring, automated written corrective feedback, and assessment-support systems that provide feedback on student writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT has major implications for higher education assessment, academic integrity, and institutional policy, presenting both threats (e.g., undermining traditional essay assessment, plagiarism-detection challenges) and opportunities (e.g., redesigning assessment and pedagogy). These conclusions are based on literature review and illustrative use experiments rather than a controlled empirical outcome study; no causal effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of implications for assessment, academic integrity, teaching, and institutional response

finding.finding_summary: Through demonstrations, the authors report that ChatGPT can generate explanations, examples, and draft prose within roughly 60-120 seconds, suggesting potential efficiency gains for producing instructional or writing-support content. However, they also note network errors, truncation, factual unreliability, and fabricated references, so the efficiency benefit is descriptive and qualified rather than experimentally validated.
finding.measure: Speed and apparent usefulness of AI-generated responses for explanation, drafting, and support tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses ChatGPT and adjacent AI writing tools as potentially useful for writing support, revision, grammar correction, and idea generation, while also emphasizing that ChatGPT-generated essays can be shallow, generic, or inaccurate and may invent references. Evidence cited for tools like Grammarly and Wordtune is adjacent and not K-12-specific; no direct literacy learning effect for ChatGPT is estimated in this paper.
finding.measure: Writing quality support, grammar correction, revision assistance, and generated essay quality

finding.finding_summary: The authors speculate that ChatGPT may create opportunities to support creativity, critical thinking, experimentation, and collaborative problem solving if used with appropriate pedagogy, but also warn that overreliance could weaken authentic demonstration of student thinking. These claims are forward-looking and not supported by direct empirical tests in the paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving opportunities discussed conceptually

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students perceive generative AI technologies such as ChatGPT in higher education. The study asks three main questions: how familiar students are with generative AI, what benefits and challenges they perceive in using it for teaching and learning, and how these tools might be effectively integrated into higher education. The paper is motivated by the rapid emergence of generative AI and the need to understand user acceptance, perceived risks, and possible educational uses from the student perspective.

The authors used an online survey with both closed-ended Likert-scale items and open-ended questions, making the study mixed-methods. The survey explored students’ knowledge of generative AI, willingness to use it, concerns about it, and perceived effects on teaching and learning. Qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses identified perceived benefits such as personalized and immediate learning support, writing and brainstorming assistance, research and analysis support, multimedia support, and administrative efficiency. Reported concerns included accuracy and transparency, privacy and ethical issues, overreliance and effects on holistic competencies, career implications, human values, and lack of institutional policies.

The population consisted of 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six universities in Hong Kong, across a range of disciplines including STEM and non-STEM fields. Data were collected through convenience sampling via an online questionnaire. The context was higher education rather than K-12 schooling, and the study focused on student perceptions rather than measuring learning outcomes or testing an instructional intervention.

The main conclusion is that students were generally positive about generative AI and saw it as useful for learning, writing, research, and future careers, while also expressing substantial concerns about reliability, ethics, privacy, and possible negative effects on skill development and employment. The authors argue that effective integration of generative AI in higher education requires improved AI literacy, attention to ethical and policy issues, and instructional designs that use AI to complement rather than replace human teaching and higher-order skill development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with descriptive statistics, correlations, and thematic analysis, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental design and does not estimate causal effects on learning outcomes. It meets limited credibility criteria appropriate to correlational/perception research.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceptions and perceived usefulness, but impacts on actual educational outcomes are unclear because no causal learning effects or standardized effect sizes were measured. Therefore impact is best classified as unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of university students' perceptions of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for learning support, brainstorming, writing assistance, research help, and student support services in higher education.
Students specifically discussed using generative AI to improve writing through grammar help, paraphrasing, polishing text, brainstorming, and feedback on written work.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive perceptions of generative AI for literacy-related tasks such as brainstorming, grammar support, paraphrasing, article polishing, and feedback on writing, especially for non-native English-speaking students. However, these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured literacy gains, and the paper also documents concerns that overreliance could undermine authentic writing development and academic integrity. Study size was n=399; no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Survey Likert items and open-ended responses about perceived writing/brainstorming support

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed generally positive attitudes toward GenAI in teaching and learning, including willingness to integrate it into learning practices (Mean=3.85, SD=1.02) and valuing 24/7 availability (Mean=4.12, SD=0.83) and anonymous support (Mean=3.77, SD=0.99). Willingness to use GenAI was positively correlated with knowledge of GenAI (r=0.189, p<0.001) and frequency of use (r=0.326, p<0.001), suggesting more familiarity is associated with greater acceptance and engagement. Sample size was n=399.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, willingness to use, perceived usefulness, and correlations with knowledge/frequency of use from survey items

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as potentially helpful for improving depth of thinking, self-directed learning, and idea generation, but many also worried it could hinder critical thinking, creativity, and other transferable skills through overreliance. Concern items about hindering development of generic or transferable skills had a mean of 3.10 (SD=1.23), indicating moderate concern rather than a clear positive or negative causal impact. Sample size was n=399; no causal effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Survey concern items and open-ended responses about critical thinking, creativity, and transferable skills
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.23 for transferable skills concern item

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as improving efficiency by saving time (Mean=4.20, SD=0.82), supporting immediate feedback, assisting with literature search and summarization, and handling repetitive administrative tasks. These findings indicate perceived productivity benefits rather than directly measured performance or time-on-task reductions. Sample size was n=399; no experimental efficiency effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Survey items and open-ended responses about time saving, immediate feedback, research support, and administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial student concern about institutional and governance issues surrounding GenAI, including academic integrity, privacy, fairness, uncertain policies, and the perceived value of university education. Students simultaneously supported future integration and called for formal institutional guidelines; concern that GenAI use undermines the value of university education had Mean=3.15 (SD=1.17). Sample size was n=399, with no effect sizes for institutional outcomes reported.
finding.measure: Survey concern items and thematic analysis of open-ended responses about policy, ethics, privacy, and institutional guidance

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/theoretical article that addresses a central question in contemporary education: whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) necessarily undermines academic integrity, or whether it can be integrated in ways that support ethical learning. The authors frame the problem around widespread concern that GAI enables plagiarism, cheating, and misuse in assessment, while also noting its growing adoption in education. They argue that these concerns should not lead to wholesale rejection of GAI, but instead to a rethinking of pedagogy, assessment, and ethical guidance.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper advances a conceptual argument grounded in ethical theory and educational theory. It draws on deontological ethics, consequentialism, constructivist learning theory, and self-determination theory to argue that GAI can be used responsibly to enhance personalized learning, formative feedback, digital literacy, motivation, and authentic assessment. The article discusses examples such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, AI-supported writing feedback, virtual lab assistants, and collaborative project tools, presenting these as ways AI might support autonomy, competence, relatedness, and active knowledge construction.

The paper does not study a defined participant sample, but discusses educational use broadly across classroom contexts, with illustrative examples from high school history, language arts, science, and business classes, alongside references to higher education and professional fields. It is therefore best understood as a broad position paper for educators, administrators, and policymakers considering AI integration in educational settings rather than as K-12 outcome research focused on a specific population.

The main conclusion is that GAI does not inherently erode academic integrity; instead, its effects depend on how it is implemented. The authors conclude that responsible use of AI, combined with ethical instruction, transparent policies, authentic assessment design, and professional development for educators, can make GAI a catalyst for better learning rather than a shortcut for misconduct. They emphasize that institutions should invest in teacher training, iterative evaluation, and explicit ethical guidance so that AI use aligns with educational goals and fairness principles.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This article is explicitly labeled as an opinion piece and provides no original empirical methodology, sample, or causal design. Although peer-reviewed, under the provided framework it fits red because it is purely conceptual/non-empirical.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper claims potentially positive but also conditional effects of generative AI on literacy, motivation, and integrity, yet provides no direct effect estimates. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated, which best fits yellow.

interventions.use_case: Opinion paper discussing responsible educational use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for classroom learning, assessment support, feedback, and interactive exploration across subjects, including language arts writing support.
Cites intelligent tutoring systems as examples of AI tools that can personalize instruction and support knowledge construction.
References adaptive learning platforms as AI-enabled systems that tailor content and pacing to student needs.
Describes AI-driven tools that provide personalized formative feedback on student drafts and skills during learning and assessment.
Discusses generative AI writing assistants that give real-time feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and creative writing development in language arts.
Mentions AI-generated interactive simulations and timelines used to support exploratory, constructivist learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This is a non-empirical opinion paper arguing that generative AI can both threaten and strengthen academic integrity depending on governance, assessment redesign, and ethical implementation. No original sample, outcome data, effect sizes, or comparative estimates are reported; claims are supported through conceptual argument and citation to prior literature rather than direct measurement.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that generative AI writing tools can enhance literacy-related outcomes by providing real-time feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and revision processes in language arts. However, the article reports no original K-12 literacy data, no sample size, and no effect size; the claim is theoretical and illustrated with examples rather than tested empirically.
finding.measure: writing quality feedback processes in language arts (conceptual, not directly measured)

finding.finding_summary: Drawing on self-determination theory, the paper contends that generative AI may improve intrinsic motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness through personalized feedback and self-directed learning. These claims are not based on original outcome measurement in this paper; no sample, validated motivation measures, or effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: intrinsic motivation, engagement, and relatedness (theoretical discussion, not directly measured)

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that responsible use of generative AI can support durable skills such as critical thinking, reflection, collaboration, and digital literacy by shifting instruction toward authentic tasks and ethical engagement with AI outputs. The article provides no original empirical evidence, effect sizes, or participant data, so the claimed benefits remain theoretical.
finding.measure: critical thinking, collaboration, metacognition, and digital literacy (conceptual, not directly measured)

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid emergence of generative AI in classrooms, especially the challenges created by tools such as ChatGPT. The author argues that educational institutions need to move beyond simple prohibition or unrestricted acceptance of AI and instead develop a more deliberate approach centered on three core capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is motivated by concerns that students and teachers may not understand AI’s limitations, may rely on it uncritically, and may lack guidance for responsible educational use.

The paper uses a conceptual discussion grounded in a case study at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, together with a narrative literature review. The institutional case focuses on the university’s response to student and staff use of generative AI, including the development of internal AI guidelines for written assignments. These guidelines allowed AI use under conditions of transparency, documentation, and critical evaluation, while prohibiting direct copy-pasting of AI-generated text. The paper also reviews practical classroom uses of AI, such as experimentation with chatbots, AI-supported case study construction, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies, and it provides an extended overview of AI literacy components and prompt engineering methods.

The population and context are primarily higher education, specifically students, lecturers, supervisors, and university leadership at a single Swiss university of applied sciences. Although the author occasionally suggests that some ideas may also be useful for children, the actual case and evidence discussed are centered on adult learners in a university setting rather than K-12 literacy contexts. The setting is a classroom and institutional environment in which AI policies, workshops, and curricular integration are being considered rather than formally tested in an intervention study.

The main conclusions are that institutions should neither ban nor fully deregulate AI use, but instead cultivate a broader “AI culture” through explicit guidelines, training, workshops, curricular integration, and attention to ethics. The author concludes that responsible AI integration in education depends on systematically teaching AI literacy, helping learners understand prompting strategies, and strengthening critical evaluation of AI outputs. The paper is primarily a practical and conceptual contribution for higher education, offering recommendations rather than causal evidence about learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a conceptual/theoretical discussion with a narrative literature review and informal case-study reflections rather than an empirical evaluation. It does not provide a rigorous causal design, clearly defined sample, validated outcome measures, or quantitative analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially beneficial but also cautionary implications for AI literacy, critical thinking, and institutional practice, yet impact remains unclear because no empirical effect estimates are reported. As a result, the practical impact is speculative rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of classroom integration of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude, emphasizing AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of chatbot outputs in educational settings.
Describes AI-driven games and immersive/virtual reality as example classroom uses to create interactive and playful learning experiences, but does not empirically evaluate them.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, based on a narrative literature review and an informal Swiss university case study, that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are important skills for education in the AI era. However, it does not report direct causal estimates, validated pre/post measures, effect sizes, or sample sizes for changes in students' critical thinking or related durable skills.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion informed by informal discussions, case-study observations, and narrative literature review; no standardized durable-skill outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The article describes an institutional response at a Swiss university that adopted AI-use guidelines rather than outright banning or fully unrestricted use, presenting this as a pragmatic middle-ground governance approach. It also reports implementation challenges such as weak compliance monitoring, lack of staff training, and absence of dedicated AI-support structures, but provides no quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline development, governance practices, and implementation challenges described qualitatively

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI tools may improve efficiency in tasks such as curriculum design, brainstorming, and case-study generation, while also noting time costs, training burdens, and resource constraints for staff. These are illustrative practice observations rather than tested productivity outcomes, and no quantitative workload or time-savings data are reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative descriptions of teacher productivity, curriculum creation support, and workflow burden

paper_profiles.title: An overview of clinical decision support systems: benefits, risks, and strategies for success
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a state-of-the-art review and conceptual overview of computerized clinical decision support systems (CDSS) in medicine. It addresses what CDSS are, how they have evolved, what kinds of functions they serve in healthcare, what benefits they can provide, and what risks or implementation challenges accompany their use. The paper is not about K-12 education or literacy; instead, it focuses on healthcare technology and clinical workflows.

The authors describe multiple forms of CDSS, including knowledge-based systems that use explicit rules and non-knowledge-based systems that use artificial intelligence, machine learning, or statistical pattern recognition. They review major use cases such as medication safety, guideline adherence, diagnostics, imaging, laboratory support, administrative documentation, and patient-facing decision support through personal health records. The paper synthesizes examples from prior literature rather than reporting a new experiment, and it concludes with practical recommendations for safer design, implementation, evaluation, and maintenance of CDSS.

No school-age student population, educator population, or education setting is studied. The context is healthcare delivery, especially hospitals, clinics, and electronic health record environments. Although examples are drawn from several countries and healthcare systems, the paper itself is a general review rather than a study of a defined participant sample.

The main conclusion is that CDSS can improve clinical decision-making, patient safety, workflow, and some aspects of cost containment, but they also introduce substantial risks such as alert fatigue, workflow disruption, overreliance, poor interoperability, maintenance burdens, and data-quality problems. The authors argue that successful CDSS require careful human-centered design, strong integration with existing systems, ongoing evaluation, user training, and active maintenance of both technical infrastructure and clinical knowledge bases.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review article about clinical decision support systems in healthcare, not an empirical K-12 education study. It does not evaluate an education intervention, lacks a school-age literacy sample, and provides no study-specific education research design that fits the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct K-12 literacy outcomes and no evaluable effect of any educational intervention. Any relevance to literacy comparators is only highly indirect and adjacent, so impact for the target education use case cannot be established.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Parental Involvement, Parental Support and Family Education on Pupil Achievements and Adjustment: A Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a literature review commissioned by the UK Department for Education and Skills to examine how parental involvement, parental support, and family education relate to pupil achievement and adjustment in school. The review addresses both naturally occurring parental involvement and interventions intended to increase it, with particular attention to educational attainment, engagement, and broader adjustment outcomes. It also considers how these relationships vary by social class, ethnicity, age, and school-home interactions.

The paper synthesizes English-language research rather than evaluating a single intervention. It distinguishes between spontaneous parental involvement—especially "at-home" parenting practices such as intellectual stimulation, parent-child discussion, high expectations, and support for learning—and formal intervention efforts such as parent training, home-school link initiatives, family learning, and community education programs. The review repeatedly contrasts stronger evidence from observational and longitudinal studies with much weaker evidence from intervention evaluations.

The populations covered span school-age pupils across primary and secondary education, along with parents and, in some intervention literature, adult learners and community education participants. Much of the cited evidence comes from the UK and the United States, with discussion of related work from other international contexts. The review emphasizes that parental involvement declines as children age, but that supportive home environments and parental aspirations remain important across developmental stages.

The main conclusion is that parental involvement—especially in the form of good parenting and learning support at home—has a substantial positive association with pupil achievement and adjustment, even after accounting for background factors such as social class. In primary years, this effect may exceed variation associated with school quality. However, the evidence base for interventions designed to increase parental involvement is judged to be technically weak, making it impossible to estimate their impact on achievement with confidence. The authors conclude that the field understands reasonably well how spontaneous parental involvement supports achievement, but lacks strong causal evidence on how best to improve it through policy or programs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a literature review drawing heavily on correlational and longitudinal observational studies rather than a meta-analysis or randomized evaluation. It demonstrates methodological awareness and cites large datasets, but the paper itself is not an experimental causal study and much of the intervention evidence it reviews is described as technically weak.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive associations between parental involvement and student achievement/adjustment, but it does not provide a pooled causal effect size and explicitly states that intervention impacts cannot be quantified reliably from the available evidence. Therefore overall impact is positive but unclear in magnitude under the framework.

finding.finding_summary: This literature review synthesizes evidence showing that spontaneous parental involvement, especially 'at-home good parenting,' home discussion, and support for learning, is consistently and positively associated with pupils' educational achievement after accounting for social class and related background factors. The report cites large longitudinal datasets such as the National Child Development Study (approximately n=17,400 in the original cohort) and the US NELS sample (approximately n=24,600), but does not provide a single pooled effect size for overall achievement outcomes in the review text excerpt.
finding.measure: General educational achievement and adjustment, including standardized reading and mathematics tests, public examination performance, and school-related adjustment measures
finding.study_size: n≈17,400 cohort in NCDS; n≈24,600 in NELS; overall review sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that parental involvement positively affects pupil adjustment and related learner dispositions, often indirectly through shaping self-concept as a learner and raising aspirations. In EPPE-related evidence, a stronger home learning environment was associated with greater cooperation, conformity, peer sociability, and confidence, and with lower anti-social and worried/upset behaviour, though no single pooled effect size is reported in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Psychological adjustment, learner self-concept, aspirations, cooperation, conformity, sociability, confidence, and behaviour ratings

finding.finding_summary: The review finds strong evidence about the importance of naturally occurring parental involvement for pupil outcomes, but concludes that intervention programmes designed to enhance parental involvement have been evaluated too weakly to estimate their impact on achievement. As a result, the paper supports policy attention to parental involvement while simultaneously concluding that the intervention evidence base is insufficient for firm institutional recommendations about programme effectiveness across stages or contexts.
finding.measure: Quality and policy relevance of intervention evaluations; institutional efforts to enhance parental involvement

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid growth of artificial intelligence in education research within higher education and asks what kinds of evidence syntheses have been conducted, what topics they cover, how methodologically rigorous they are, and what major findings, benefits, challenges, and research gaps they report. The authors argue that, given the public attention surrounding AI and the emergence of generative AI, it is important to map the existing review literature and assess the field’s conceptual and methodological foundations.

The study uses a tertiary review approach—a review of reviews—to synthesise 66 evidence syntheses published between 2018 and July 2023 that focused solely on AI in formal higher or continuing education. Searches were conducted across multiple major databases and supplementary sources, and the included reviews were coded for publication characteristics, authorship, topical focus, methodological quality, and reported findings. The authors classify the literature using a prior AIEd typology covering profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems and personalisation.

The population and context are not primary-study participants in a single intervention, but rather the higher education literature itself. Across the included reviews, the dominant user groups were students, with some focus on educators and administrators in higher education and continuing education settings. The paper reports that most reviews addressed general AIEd or profiling and prediction, but key findings across reviews most often concerned adaptive systems and personalisation, including chatbots, personalised content, recommender systems, and facial recognition or emotion-detection applications.

The main conclusions are that AI in higher education review research is expanding quickly but remains uneven in quality and scope. The field is dominated by systematic reviews, often produced by domestic research teams, with substantial attention to adaptive systems and predictive analytics. However, the authors identify recurring weaknesses, including insufficient quality appraisal, limited reporting of inter-rater reliability and coding schemes, and inadequate attention to ethics, context, and interdisciplinarity. They call for future AI in higher education research to be more rigorous, collaborative, and ethically grounded.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-systematic review of 66 reviews with explicit search, screening, and quality-appraisal procedures, which is stronger than a single correlational study. However, it is not a direct K-12 effectiveness meta-analysis or RCT, and its focus is higher education field mapping rather than causal impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper maps the field and identifies promising applications and major gaps, but it does not report pooled learning effect sizes or direct impacts on school-age literacy outcomes. Its practical impact for K-12 literacy is therefore indirect and unclear rather than demonstrably positive.

interventions.use_case: Meta-systematic review of higher education AI literature identifying adaptive systems and personalization platforms that tailor content, sequencing, and learning pathways to individual learners.
Review of higher education evidence syntheses on profiling and prediction applications such as dropout/retention prediction, student modeling, and data-driven academic support.
Review discusses AI for assessment and evaluation, including automated grading, feedback, and evaluation of student understanding and engagement.
Review situates the field historically through intelligent tutoring systems that diagnose learner strengths and weaknesses and provide personalized instructional support.
Paper references emerging generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Bard as a new wave of educational AI, but explicitly excludes GenAI review studies from the analyzed corpus.

finding.finding_summary: Across 66 higher-education evidence syntheses, the review found rapid growth in AI in education reviews but identified substantial methodological and ethical gaps. Research was concentrated on academic support services (64 of 66 reviews) rather than institutional/administrative uses (26 of 66), and average review quality was 6.57/10, prompting a call for more rigorous, ethical, and interdisciplinary research. No pooled intervention effect size was reported because this was a review of reviews rather than an effectiveness meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Distribution of review topics, methodological quality scores, publication/authorship patterns, and reported research gaps in AI higher education evidence syntheses

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI applications in higher education are used for functions such as admissions, course scheduling, retention support, automated assessment, and institutional quality assurance, suggesting potential efficiency gains. However, evidence was uneven, administrative applications were less represented than teaching/learning uses, and the authors highlighted insufficient rigor and transparency in the review base. No quantitative pooled effect on efficiency outcomes was reported.
finding.measure: Reported AI uses for administrative support, assessment automation, scheduling, retention, and quality assurance across included reviews

finding.finding_summary: Some included higher-education reviews summarized AI applications associated with critical thinking, communication, and related higher-order skills, especially in chatbot and simulation contexts. The umbrella review notes these outcomes as present but not consistently or rigorously assessed across the literature, with stronger emphasis on mapping the field than estimating impacts. No pooled effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Reported outcomes such as critical thinking, communication skills, and related higher-order competencies in included secondary reviews

finding.finding_summary: The review notes AI applications, especially chatbots and adaptive systems, were studied for outcomes such as satisfaction, anxiety reduction, engagement, motivation, and affect detection. At the same time, the authors emphasize that affective and social aspects remain under-evaluated and require more research attention and better study designs. No aggregate effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Engagement, satisfaction, anxiety, motivation, and affective indicators reported in included reviews

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in the artificial-intelligence-in-education literature by examining AI from the perspective of teachers rather than focusing primarily on student-facing systems. The authors ask how research on teachers’ use of AI has developed over time, what kinds of teacher data have been used in AI studies, what roles teachers play in AI development and implementation, what benefits AI offers teachers, what challenges teachers face, and which AI methods are most commonly used. The goal is to clarify how AI supports planning, instruction, and assessment in teaching practice and to identify what is still missing for effective school adoption.

The study uses a systematic review approach. The authors searched the Web of Science for English-language empirical studies published over roughly the prior 20 years through 14 September 2020 and selected 44 articles that focused on AI in pre-service or in-service teacher education, teachers’ use of AI applications, or AI analysis of teacher data. The reviewed studies covered applications such as intelligent tutoring, automated grading and essay scoring, feedback systems, monitoring tools, and machine-learning models predicting teacher-related variables. The analysis examined publication trends, data types, teacher roles, AI benefits and challenges, and the AI methods used.

The population and context are not a single sample but a body of prior empirical studies involving mainly K-12 teachers, with some attention to students and very limited inclusion of pre-service teachers. The review emphasizes school-based educational contexts, especially K-12 settings, while excluding higher education studies. Across the reviewed literature, teachers appeared in multiple roles: as models for training AI systems, as sources of data about teaching or professional development, as graders validating automated scoring, and as pedagogical guides for selecting materials or criteria.

The main conclusions are that AI can support teachers in lesson planning, instructional implementation, and assessment by helping identify student needs, monitor learning, provide immediate feedback, reduce workload, and automate some evaluation tasks such as essay scoring. At the same time, the literature shows important constraints: limited reliability and technical capacity of AI systems, weak portability across contexts, insufficient school infrastructure, and limited teacher technological knowledge for AI integration. The authors also conclude that teachers are not yet sufficiently involved in AI design and that more research is needed on pre-service teacher use, multimodal data, and pedagogically robust AI systems for diverse educational settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not estimate pooled causal effects. The synthesis is largely descriptive/qualitative across heterogeneous studies, so it fits yellow rather than green or blue under the provided framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally promising but mixed and non-quantified impacts, especially around teacher efficiency and literacy assessment support, with important implementation limitations. Because no pooled effect sizes or clear magnitude estimates are provided, impact is best classified as unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of K-12 teacher-facing AI applications and machine-learning methods used for planning, implementation, and assessment, including automated essay scoring, monitoring dashboards, predictive models, and adaptive support tools.
Teacher-facing AI systems that provide immediate feedback, automated scoring, and assessment support, especially automated essay scoring and online writing evaluation.
Machine-learning analysis of teacher and student data to predict engagement, performance, risks, and critical moments requiring intervention.
AI-supported platforms that adapt learning content, text complexity, or exercises to student needs and help teachers select appropriate materials or activities.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 44 studies in the systematic review, AI was commonly reported to reduce teacher workload by supporting timely monitoring, immediate feedback, and automated scoring. The review synthesizes qualitative and descriptive evidence rather than pooled causal estimates, so no meta-analytic effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, efficiency of monitoring/feedback/assessment, automation of scoring and planning support

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies literacy-relevant AI uses such as automated essay scoring, online writing evaluation, and text readability classification, suggesting potential benefits for assessment and instructional planning. However, it also notes limitations in validity and technical capacity, including concerns that AI may improperly evaluate text structure, logic, coherence, or multimodal texts; no pooled literacy achievement effect was reported.
finding.measure: Essay scoring, writing evaluation, text readability/complexity classification, ICT literacy support

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that research on teachers' AI use has increased sharply since 2017 and that AI offers meaningful promise for school adoption, but implementation remains constrained by limited infrastructure, teacher AI knowledge, reliability, and context transferability. These findings indicate institutional potential alongside substantial barriers, without quantitative institutional impact estimates.
finding.measure: Research trend, implementation barriers, teacher participation in AI development, school infrastructure and adoption conditions

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective/theoretical article that examines the emerging role of ChatGPT in higher education. Framed by constructivist learning theory, it asks two main questions: what key benefits ChatGPT may offer for the future of higher education, and what major challenges its adoption may create. Rather than reporting an empirical evaluation, the paper synthesizes prior literature and develops propositions for how institutions, educators, and researchers should think about generative AI in tertiary education.

The approach studied is the potential integration of ChatGPT and other large language models into higher education teaching, learning, assessment, research support, and administrative support. The authors organize the discussion into five proposed benefits—adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research/writing/data-analytics support, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment design—and five challenges—ethical and equity concerns, academic integrity risks, bias and falsified information, inability to assess graduate skills well, and difficulties in assessing student learning outcomes. The paper repeatedly argues that ChatGPT may support personalized and scaffolded learning, but only when used carefully and in conjunction with human educators and sound institutional policy.

The context is higher education rather than K-12, with discussion applying broadly to tertiary institutions. The paper refers to students, academics/educators, and administrative staff as relevant user groups, but it does not describe a recruited sample or a specific implementation site. It also does not report any intervention duration, training protocol, or measured outcomes, because its primary contribution is conceptual: a constructivist interpretation of ChatGPT's affordances and risks, along with 19 propositions for practice and future research.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT has meaningful potential to enhance higher education through personalization, feedback, and support for teaching and administration, but it also introduces serious risks related to academic integrity, misinformation, inequity, and superficial learning. The authors conclude that higher education institutions should educate users about responsible AI use, redesign assessments to emphasize authentic learning processes, address bias and access issues, and build AI literacy into graduate preparation. Overall, the paper argues for cautious, ethical, and complementary use of ChatGPT rather than uncritical adoption or outright prohibition.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed perspective/theoretical paper, but it does not report an empirical study, sample, comparison group, or measurable outcomes. Under the K-12 evidence framework, it lacks clear empirical methodology and therefore falls in the lowest evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits and risks, but provides no causal estimates or direct outcome data. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Perspective paper discussing ChatGPT as a conversational generative AI tool in higher education for adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research/writing support, administrative support, and assessment design.
ChatGPT is described as automating or augmenting formative feedback and grading-related feedback processes for student work.
ChatGPT is discussed as a writing and language support tool for drafting, summarizing, translating, and assisting with academic writing tasks.
The paper proposes integrating ChatGPT APIs into learning management systems to support personalized and adaptive learning pathways.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration when used for scaffolded, authentic, and collaborative learning tasks, but may also undermine these same skills if used for shortcutting or superficial learning. No original empirical data, sample sizes, or effect sizes are reported; the claims are conceptual and based on prior literature and propositions for future research.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and graduate skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that ChatGPT could improve efficiency by automating elements of feedback, grading support, research assistance, and administrative communication, potentially reducing staff time and costs. However, these are perspective-based claims rather than findings from a reported empirical study, and no sample size or effect estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of workload reduction, efficiency, cost savings, and administrative productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies institution-level opportunities and risks of ChatGPT, including potential improvements to pedagogy and support services alongside concerns about academic integrity, equity, bias, copyright, and assessment redesign. The evidence presented is not based on original institutional outcome data; instead, it synthesizes concerns and recommendations from a theoretical perspective.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, assessment design, academic integrity, equity, and AI literacy considerations

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the evidence base for within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education. The authors note that differentiated instruction is widely promoted as a way to address student heterogeneity, but that its empirical support in secondary schools is unclear. The review asks what kinds of differentiated instruction have been studied in secondary education, how those approaches are operationalized, what effects they have on student academic achievement, and which contextual or personal factors appear to support or hinder effectiveness.

The paper uses a systematic review with a best-evidence synthesis approach covering literature from 2006 to 2016. The authors define differentiated instruction as planned adaptations to content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time based on assessed student needs. Included studies had to involve mainstream secondary education, use quantitative outcome measures of academic achievement, and compare differentiated instruction to business-as-usual or another condition. Fourteen papers representing 12 unique empirical studies met inclusion criteria. The reviewed interventions varied substantially, including generic teacher training in adaptive teaching, ability grouping and tiering, individualized instruction, mastery learning, heterogeneous grouping, and remediation in flipped classroom settings.

The population and context were mainstream secondary school students and teachers, with studies conducted across multiple regions including the United States, several European countries, Taiwan, and African countries. Subjects included mathematics, science, reading, and other academic domains. The review also considers school- and teacher-level conditions such as teacher knowledge, preparation time, collaboration, class size, and leadership support as possible moderators of implementation and outcomes.

The main conclusion is that differentiated instruction in secondary education shows small to moderate positive effects on student academic achievement overall, with summarized effect sizes ranging from d = +0.741 to +0.509 when omitting an outlier. However, the literature base is small, heterogeneous, and methodologically uneven, and differentiated instruction is operationalized in many different ways across studies. The authors therefore conclude that differentiated instruction appears promising, but stronger and more consistent research is still needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about which forms are most effective in secondary school settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using explicit inclusion criteria and quantitative effect-size synthesis, but it is not a clean meta-analysis of a single intervention and includes heterogeneous quasi-experimental and survey evidence with notable limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports mostly small to moderate positive effects on academic achievement, with synthesized effects generally above 0.20, indicating meaningful average impact for differentiated instruction overall.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 12 unique empirical studies (reported in 14 papers) on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education, not AI tools. Across studies, the majority of findings were small to moderate positive effects on academic achievement, with summarized effect sizes reported as ranging roughly from d = +0.741 to +0.509 after omitting an outlier. Outcomes spanned multiple non-literacy academic domains including mathematics, science, and other school subjects, typically compared against business-as-usual or standard instruction.
finding.measure: Academic achievement tests across subject areas (e.g., mathematics, science, reading, other curriculum-aligned achievement measures)
finding.effect_size: range reported approximately d=+0.741 to +0.509 (with outlier omitted)

paper_profiles.title: Business (Teaching) as Usual amid the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Case Study of Online Teaching Practice in Hong Kong
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators in Hong Kong maintained teaching and learning during the early COVID-19 school closures, with a focus on the strategies used for rapid online transition and the challenges perceived by educators and other stakeholders. The study is motivated by the abrupt suspension of face-to-face schooling and the need to understand how schools and universities could continue instruction under emergency conditions.

The authors use a qualitative multiple-case study with naturalistic inquiry, drawing on school visits, personal communication, unstructured interviews, and descriptive documents. Three cases are analyzed: a primary school, a secondary school, and a university. Across the cases, educators initially relied on asynchronous instruction such as prerecorded videos, LMS-based worksheets, and online exercises, and then moved toward blended online approaches combining asynchronous materials with synchronous tools such as Zoom webinars, discussion functions, breakout rooms, and messaging. The paper also describes support strategies including parental involvement, IT-team technical assistance, device lending, alumni tutoring, and use of social and gamified platforms.

The population and context span Hong Kong elementary, secondary, and undergraduate settings during class suspension from approximately February to April 2020. Participants include teachers, students, parents, and institutional staff in government-funded mainstream schools and a university. The study emphasizes differences by educational level: younger students required greater teacher presence and parental support, secondary students could handle more diverse digital activities, and university students preferred greater autonomy and asynchronous learning.

The main conclusions are that effective emergency online teaching depended on a blended model combining synchronous and asynchronous methods, with teachers playing a central organizing role in sustaining social and cognitive engagement. The study identifies three major non-teaching challenges in the rapid transition: digital divide, data privacy, and professional leadership/technical support. The authors conclude that online learning can function as a practical continuity strategy during crisis, but its success depends heavily on infrastructure, teacher support, student self-regulation, and family capacity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative multiple-case study using naturalistic inquiry and interviews, which provides useful descriptive evidence but no experimental or quasi-experimental causal design. It meets limited credibility criteria and does not report standardized outcome estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially beneficial but mixed and context-dependent impacts for online/blended instruction, especially for continuity and social interaction, yet impact magnitude is unclear because no effect sizes or controlled comparisons are reported.

interventions.use_case: Online school instruction delivered through learning management systems, prerecorded lessons, discussion tools, webinars, and web conferencing during COVID-19 school closures across primary and secondary settings.
Use of game-based digital learning tools such as Code.org, Codecombat, and a gamified e-quiz reading platform to support engagement and subject learning in remote instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across three qualitative cases in Hong Kong (primary, secondary, tertiary), educators reported that a blended mix of asynchronous and synchronous online teaching was workable for maintaining 'teaching as usual,' but implementation was constrained by digital divide, data privacy, and leadership/capacity issues. Findings are based on case observations, interviews, and stakeholder perceptions rather than causal estimates; no effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Educator and stakeholder perceptions of online teaching implementation, institutional challenges, continuity of instruction
finding.study_size: n=3 educator cases; stakeholder feedback sample not systematically reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that asynchronous materials, LMS workflows, and parent checking of assignments sometimes reduced teacher marking burden and enabled continuity of instruction, but teachers also experienced increased workload during the abrupt transition online. Evidence comes from qualitative case descriptions and interview testimony; no standardized productivity metrics or effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload, assignment handling, continuity of teaching operations

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students described synchronous sessions and blended approaches as helping social interaction and reducing isolation, while motivation and attention were uneven, especially among younger students learning from home. The evidence is perception-based, with no controlled comparison or quantitative engagement effect sizes reported.
finding.measure: Perceived motivation, attention, social interaction, isolation
finding.study_size: n=3 educator cases; student/parent comments reported but not systematically sampled

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that online learning demanded and sometimes supported autonomy, self-direction, time management, and collaboration, particularly for older students, but younger learners often struggled with self-regulation and organization. These findings are descriptive and qualitative, without validated durable-skills scales or effect-size estimates.
finding.measure: Perceived self-directed learning, time management, organization, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Yes, they can: Developing transcription skills and oral language in tandem with SRSD instruction on close reading of science text to write informative essays at grades 1 and 2
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a longstanding debate in early literacy instruction: whether students in the primary grades should first master foundational transcription and oral language skills before being taught higher-level composing processes, or whether these can be developed simultaneously. The study also examines whether first- and second-grade students can learn to do close reading of informational science texts and then use those texts to plan and write informative essays—an area the authors note is rarely emphasized in early elementary classrooms despite standards expectations.

The intervention studied was “SRSD Plus,” a multicomponent instructional approach that combines Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) for close reading, planning, and informative writing with explicit instruction in transcription and oral language. The “Plus” elements included handwriting fluency, spelling, vocabulary, and sentence proficiency; the SRSD component emphasized strategy instruction, self-regulation, discussion, modeling, planning, and genre knowledge for writing informative essays from source texts. Students in the treatment condition received teacher-led instruction in small groups for 45 minutes, three times per week, over 10 weeks, while comparison students received business-as-usual writing instruction described by teachers as writers workshop. Teachers delivering SRSD Plus received practice-based professional development and ongoing implementation support.

The study was conducted in one high-poverty elementary school in the southeastern United States with 93 first- and second-grade students, who were randomly assigned within class to SRSD Plus or business-as-usual. Outcomes included writing quality, planning, structural elements of informative essays, use of source text, transition words, number of words written, spelling, handwriting fluency, vocabulary, sentence proficiency, and discourse knowledge. Assessments were administered before and immediately after the intervention, and treatment fidelity was monitored through structured observations.

The main conclusion is that young students can successfully develop transcription skills, oral language, and composing abilities at the same time. Compared with business-as-usual writers workshop, SRSD Plus produced moderate to large positive effects on writing outcomes, oral language skills, spelling, and discourse knowledge, with especially strong gains in writing quality and planning. The findings support integrated, explicit, evidence-based literacy instruction in the early grades rather than delaying composition instruction until foundational skills are fully developed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial with student-level random assignment, blinded assessors, fidelity data, and a clearly defined business-as-usual comparison in a relevant K-2 literacy context. Although some comparator implementation details were missing, the design meets the standard for a strong RCT with high relevance to K-12 literacy instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced medium-to-large effects on multiple literacy outcomes, including writing quality (g=1.02), planning (g=1.40), and other writing measures, in a high-poverty early elementary population. These effect sizes indicate substantial educational impact relative to business-as-usual writers workshop.

finding.finding_summary: This randomized controlled trial compared teacher-led SRSD Plus with business-as-usual writers workshop for Grade 1-2 students (n=93; posttest n=90) in a high-poverty school. SRSD Plus produced statistically significant improvements across writing-related literacy outcomes, including writing quality (effect size g=1.02), planning (g=1.40), structural elements in informative essays (g=0.29), use of source text (g=0.48), number of words written (g=0.82 in Grade 1; g=1.39 in Grade 2), and transition words (g=1.33 in Grade 1; g=2.46 in Grade 2). The intervention also improved spelling and discourse knowledge, supporting stronger early literacy composition performance than business-as-usual writing workshop.
