finding.measure: Timed source-based informative essay writing tasks; writing quality rubric; planning rubric; structural elements rubric; number of words written; transition words; use of source text; spelling dictation; discourse knowledge interview
finding.effect_size: g=1.02 (writing quality); g=1.40 (planning); g=0.29 (structural elements); g=0.48 (use of source text); g=0.82 to 1.39 (number of words); g=1.33 to 2.46 (transition words)
finding.std_deviation: Sample mean age SD=0.48; outcome SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: SRSD Plus improved oral-language-related outcomes relative to business-as-usual writers workshop in this Grade 1-2 RCT (n=93). The abstract and methods/results summary report moderate to large positive effects for vocabulary and sentence proficiency, indicating that integrating oral language instruction with writing strategy instruction benefited early language development alongside writing.
finding.measure: Researcher-developed proximal vocabulary task and sentence proficiency task
finding.effect_size: moderate to large effect sizes reported, exact values not_reported in provided text
finding.std_deviation: Sample mean age SD=0.48; outcome SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The intervention embedded close reading of science texts aligned to NGSS and asked students to write informative essays from science-related source texts, so science-content learning was part of the instructional context. However, the study did not report a standalone science reasoning or science achievement outcome; instead, science text comprehension was inferred through planning and use of source text, making evidence for scientific reasoning indirect rather than definitive.
finding.measure: Indirect indicators through comprehension/use of science informational source texts in planning and writing

finding.finding_summary: The study's theoretical framing emphasized self-regulation, motivation, persistence, and self-efficacy as targets of SRSD instruction, and fidelity observations suggested strong student responsiveness and engagement during implementation. However, no direct student-reported or validated social-emotional outcome measure was reported in the provided text, so the evidence is supportive but indirect.
finding.measure: Instructional fidelity ratings of student responsiveness/engagement; self-regulation emphasized in intervention design

paper_profiles.title: Making a case for college: A genre-based college admission essay intervention for underserved high school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether explicit genre-based instruction can improve underserved high school seniors’ college admission essay writing and their self-efficacy for writing in that genre. The authors frame college admission essays as a high-stakes, gate-keeping form of writing that many low-income and ethnically diverse students are expected to produce for college access, yet often do not receive direct instruction on in regular secondary English classes. The study asks whether teaching the specific features of college admission essays helps students write better essays and feel more confident writing them.

The intervention was a six-week features-based writing workshop built around explicit teaching of genre elements in college admission essays. Students in the treatment condition received 10 instructional sessions including skill lessons, models/examples, practice, sharing, peer or instructor feedback, and revision. The curriculum taught features such as selecting a strong topic, audience awareness, introductions, dialogue, description, explaining significance (the “so what?”), connecting to outside texts or events, and writing conclusions. The comparison group completed the same pre/post essay and self-efficacy measures but otherwise received business-as-usual English instruction from their regular teacher, described as mostly literary analysis and not college admission essay instruction.

Participants were 41 12th-grade students at one urban public high school in the southwestern United States, primarily low-income and multi-ethnic, with many first-generation college-bound students and many previously classified as English Language Learners. Two intact classrooms were assigned by coin toss to treatment or comparison conditions. The intervention was delivered by a doctoral student in English Education, with assistance from the regular classroom teacher. Outcomes included rubric-scored pre/post college admission essays and a self-efficacy survey specific to college admission essay writing.

The study found that students who received the genre-based intervention scored significantly higher on posttest essay quality than the comparison group after controlling for pretest scores, and they also showed significantly greater gains in writing self-efficacy. The authors conclude that explicit, features-based instruction in authentic high-stakes writing genres may be a promising way to support underserved high school students’ writing development and college access. They also argue that college admission essay instruction should be incorporated into secondary writing curricula, especially in schools serving low-income and ethnically diverse students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental group comparison study in K-12 with pre/post measures, a comparison condition, and reported statistical tests, but it is not a randomized controlled trial at the student level and has notable limitations including small sample size, convenience sampling, and some analytic assumption violations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are substantial, with between-group variance explained of R²=0.46 for essay quality and R²=0.42 for self-efficacy, indicating a medium-to-large impact in a priority population of low-income, multi-ethnic high school students.

finding.finding_summary: This quasi-experimental study examined a non-technology, features-based genre-writing intervention for 12th-grade college admission essays. Students in the treatment group outperformed the comparison group receiving business-as-usual English instruction on posttest essay quality after controlling for pretest, F(1,38)=29.74, p<0.05, with R²=0.46; adjusted posttest means were 4.91 (SD=0.71, n=17) for treatment versus 3.68 (SD=0.78, n=22) for comparison on a 6-point holistic rubric.
finding.measure: Holistic rubric-based quality of college admission essays (6-point writing rubric assessing ideas/content, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, conventions)
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; analytic table reports treatment n=17 and comparison n=22 for essay outcome
finding.std_deviation: Treatment posttest SD=0.71; comparison posttest SD=0.78; treatment pretest SD=0.60; comparison pretest SD=0.90

finding.finding_summary: The genre-based writing intervention also increased students’ writing self-efficacy relative to business-as-usual instruction. On self-efficacy difference scores, treatment and comparison groups differed significantly, F(1,36)=48.50, p<0.01, with R²=0.42; mean self-efficacy rose from 5.91 to 8.06 in the treatment group and declined slightly from 5.85 to 5.69 in the comparison group.
finding.measure: Self-reported college-admission-essay writing self-efficacy using a 15-item Likert-type confidence scale
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; analytic table reports treatment n=16 and comparison n=21 for self-efficacy outcome
finding.std_deviation: Treatment posttest SD=1.05; comparison posttest SD=1.71; treatment pretest SD=1.88; comparison pretest SD=1.79

paper_profiles.title: Assessing the Writing of Struggling Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article addresses how teachers can more effectively assess the writing of struggling learners, especially students with disabilities and other students who experience persistent writing difficulties across K-12 schooling. The paper argues that writing is a complex, multi-level process involving handwriting, spelling, vocabulary, sentence construction, paragraphing, text organization, and elements of the writing process such as planning, revising, and editing. Because struggling writers show diverse profiles of strengths and weaknesses, the authors emphasize that writing assessment should be purpose-driven rather than based on a single test or generic measure.

The paper does not evaluate an intervention experimentally; instead, it provides a practitioner-oriented framework for assessment. The authors describe major purposes of writing assessment—screening, instructional planning and modification, summative assessment, progress monitoring, and eligibility determination for special education—and then review practical methods teachers can use to assess writing at multiple levels of language. These include holistic, analytic, and primary-trait rubrics for text quality; teacher-developed paragraph checklists; informal sentence-level analyses; spelling inventories and error analysis procedures; vocabulary profiling; handwriting legibility and fluency measures; portfolios; norm-referenced tests; and curriculum-based measurement. The emphasis is on aligning assessment tools to instructional goals and using multiple data sources.

The population and context are K-12 school settings, with particular attention to struggling writers and students with learning disabilities in typical educational and special education contexts. The article draws on research and examples spanning elementary through secondary grades, and it is written primarily for teachers and school personnel who assess and support student writing. It also references parents and specialists as potential sources of contextual information during assessment.

The main conclusion is that no single writing assessment is sufficient for understanding struggling learners. Effective assessment should be ongoing, use multiple tools, and target specific writing components so that teachers can design better, more individualized instruction. The authors also conclude that more comprehensive and systematic assessment practices are especially important for students with writing difficulties, because broad quality scores alone often fail to reveal the specific instructional supports those students need.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/practice article on writing assessment, not an empirical study evaluating a technology or instructional intervention. It does not present original methods, sample, causal design, or quantitative results for the focal topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper is potentially useful conceptually for identifying business-as-usual literacy assessment and feedback practices, but it provides no direct causal evidence of impact on student outcomes. Any practical impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a practitioner-oriented review of K-12 writing assessment for struggling learners rather than an intervention evaluation. It synthesizes prior literacy research to argue that writing outcomes should be assessed across letter/word, sentence, paragraph, and text levels, and notes adjacent evidence such as poorer keyboarded than handwritten composition through grade 6 in some cited studies and the limited sensitivity of some rubrics for progress monitoring; however, it does not report a new sample, effect size, or original outcome analysis.
finding.measure: Writing assessment approaches and literacy-related indicators including handwriting fluency/legibility, spelling, vocabulary, sentence quality, paragraph/text quality, and progress-monitoring measures

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses the practical utility of different writing assessment tools for screening, instructional planning, progress monitoring, and eligibility decisions. It suggests some methods are more efficient but less instructionally useful (e.g., holistic rubrics are quicker and economical), whereas richer approaches such as analytic rubrics, portfolios, and detailed error analyses provide better instructional guidance but require more teacher time; no original empirical comparison or quantitative efficiency estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Assessment usability and efficiency considerations such as ease/speed of administration, scoring time, and instructional usefulness

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing EFL/ESL instruction through gamification: a comprehensive review of empirical evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how gamification has been used in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and English as a Second Language (ESL) instruction, what factors shape its relationship to language-learning outcomes, and which gamification elements are most commonly employed. The authors note growing interest in digital and game-based supports for English learning, alongside mixed findings in prior research and practical barriers such as limited teacher time, technological constraints, and uncertainty about which game elements are most effective.

The study uses a rapid evidence assessment with PRISMA procedures to systematically review 30 empirical studies published between 2010 and 2022 and indexed in Web of Science. The review focuses specifically on gamification rather than full educational games or serious games. Across the included studies, the reviewed interventions involved platforms and tools such as Kahoot, Edmodo, ClassDojo, Moodle, Raz-Kids, Padlet, mobile apps, augmented reality tools, and self-designed gamified systems. Common gamification features included points, badges, leaderboards, quizzes, progress bars, feedback, rewards, challenges, avatars, collaboration, and competition.

The populations covered in the reviewed literature span primary, secondary, and higher education, though the review reports that most studies were conducted in higher education, with fewer in secondary and primary settings. The studies came from multiple countries including China, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, Korea, the Netherlands, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Spain, Turkey, and Ecuador. Language outcomes examined included vocabulary, grammar, speaking, writing, listening, reading, morphological awareness, literature, and business English, with a strong emphasis on English language learning in technology-supported instructional settings.

The main conclusions are that gamification generally shows positive effects on English proficiency, motivation, engagement, attitudes, anxiety reduction, learner autonomy, and classroom dynamics, although results are not uniformly positive across all contexts. The review also highlights that outcomes depend on implementation context, learner characteristics, and the specific gamification elements used. The authors conclude that gamification is a promising but context-sensitive pedagogical strategy for EFL/ESL instruction and that more research is needed to identify optimal designs and extend evidence across educational settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using PRISMA-style procedures over 30 empirical studies, which strengthens credibility. However, it is not a formal meta-analysis, does not provide pooled quantitative effects, and includes heterogeneous study designs and populations, so it falls below blue-tier evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broadly positive but variably measured impacts, especially for motivation and EFL/ESL outcomes, yet the magnitude of effects remains unclear because no pooled effect sizes are reported. The evidence indicates promising but not precisely quantified impact.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of gamification platforms and game-like digital learning environments used in EFL/ESL instruction (e.g., Kahoot, Edmodo, ClassDojo, TipOn, self-designed games) to support English learning outcomes such as vocabulary, writing, speaking, listening, grammar, and reading.

Reviews ICT-supported English instruction delivered through digital classroom tools and online platforms that provide quizzes, feedback, and structured practice but are not necessarily adaptive or AI-based.
Includes mobile and app-based English learning tools such as handheld language learning systems and vocabulary apps used for EFL/ESL practice and reinforcement.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 30 reviewed empirical studies, the review reports generally positive effects of gamification on literacy-related EFL/ESL outcomes including writing, reading, vocabulary learning, and broader English proficiency. However, results are narrative rather than meta-analytic, and some cited studies suggest stronger engagement than achievement gains, with no pooled effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations reported.
finding.measure: Writing performance, reading motivation/performance, vocabulary acquisition and retention, English proficiency measures
finding.study_size: n=30 studies (aggregate review sample size not_reported)

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that gamification generally improves EFL/ESL language fluency outcomes such as speaking, listening, grammar, and overall English proficiency. It highlights examples such as Hwang et al. (2017), where 77 ninth-grade students in a quasi-experiment showed improved English listening motivation and achievement in a game-based condition relative to traditional instruction, but no standardized pooled effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Listening comprehension, speaking performance, grammar learning, oral scores, overall English proficiency
finding.study_size: n=30 studies; specific example n=77 for Hwang et al. (2017)

finding.finding_summary: The strongest and most consistent finding in the review is that gamification improves motivation, engagement, attitudes, and reduces anxiety in EFL/ESL learning contexts. The review synthesizes 30 empirical studies and cites repeated positive perceptions toward tools like Kahoot and other gamified platforms, though it also notes mixed evidence in the broader literature and no pooled effect estimates.
finding.measure: Motivation surveys, engagement measures, attitude questionnaires, anxiety scales, classroom participation/behavior
finding.study_size: n=30 studies (aggregate review sample size not_reported)

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that gamification may support learner autonomy, collaboration, focused attention, and self-directed learning habits in EFL/ESL settings. These findings are based on narrative synthesis across multiple studies rather than pooled estimates, and the evidence appears less consistent and less central than for motivation or language outcomes.
finding.measure: Learner autonomy, collaboration, focused attention, self-directed learning, communication ability
finding.study_size: n=30 studies (aggregate review sample size not_reported)

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses implementation-level issues such as teacher attitudes, institutional constraints, curriculum rigidity, access to technology, and tensions with exam-oriented schooling. While some studies suggest gamification can enhance teacher professional competency, others report teacher resistance and concern about alignment with high-stakes assessment, yielding a mixed institutional picture.
finding.measure: Teacher attitudes, implementation barriers, professional competency perceptions, curriculum/institutional constraints
finding.study_size: n=30 studies (aggregate review sample size not_reported)

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can successfully complete national high school English reading comprehension exams, and what that implies for educational assessment. The author positions the study as a benchmark evaluation of large language models’ capabilities on a realistic, high-stakes school task, with particular concern about whether such systems can undermine the validity of computer-based or minimally proctored exams.

The study applied ChatGPT GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to three 2022 Dutch VWO national exams in English reading comprehension. The exams included multiple-choice items, short open-response items, and multi-part questions based on reading passages. GPT-3.5 was initially tested through the ChatGPT web interface with occasional re-prompting when the model failed to give a valid answer; GPT-4 was tested via the OpenAI API using an automated script and no re-prompting. The author also ran a bootstrapped self-consistency analysis with GPT-4, repeating each exam 50 times at a higher temperature setting to examine whether output variability could help identify uncertain or potentially incorrect answers.

The population and context are Dutch high school students in the VWO track, the most academically rigorous secondary education pathway in the Netherlands, although no human participants were directly recruited for the experiment. Instead, ChatGPT’s performance was compared against official scoring rubrics and, for one exam, publicly available student score distributions. The setting was effectively an online/API-based test-taking environment using official national exam materials from 2022, selected partly to avoid contamination from the model’s training data because ChatGPT’s knowledge cutoff predated the exams.

The main findings were that GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without it, while GPT-4 achieved 8.3 and 8.1 across two model versions, outperforming the average Dutch student score available for one exam. The author concludes that large language models are already capable of performing at or above average human levels on some high school reading comprehension assessments, which raises serious concerns for assessment integrity. At the same time, the paper notes possible educational opportunities for using such systems to support writing, summarization, explanation, and personalized feedback, though these applications were discussed rather than empirically tested in this study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmark study with clear methods, but it is not an intervention study with K-12 learners and does not use randomized or quasi-experimental designs. Evidence is based on AI performance on exam materials rather than student learning outcomes in classroom implementation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial capability of an LLM on a K-12 literacy-related assessment, but the impact is indirect for the retrieval topic because no student literacy intervention was implemented and no learner effect size was estimated. Institutional implications are important but still exploratory and unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) on Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exams to evaluate its ability to answer literacy assessment items and implications for assessment integrity, with some analyses of re-prompting and self-consistency.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed strongly on Dutch high-school English reading-comprehension exams, a literacy outcome domain. GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 across three 2022 VWO English exams (or 6.5 without re-prompting), compared with the national student mean of 6.99 on Exam 1; GPT-4 scored 8.3 (March 2023) and 8.1 (June 2023) without re-prompting. For Exam 1 specifically, GPT-4 scored 44/49 versus the student mean of 35.88/49 (SD=6.48; n=35,698), indicating above-average performance on reading-comprehension assessment items.
finding.measure: Scores/grades on Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exams (multiple-choice and open-response items)
finding.study_size: 124 exam questions across 3 exams; student comparison for Exam 1 n=35,698
finding.std_deviation: Student Exam 1 SD=6.48 points; item-level student SDs for subsets reported as 10.5%-13.2%

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence that LLMs can compromise the integrity of computer-based or minimally proctored literacy assessments because ChatGPT generated valid answers at or above average student performance within minutes. At the same time, the paper identifies institutional opportunities, such as using self-consistency/bootstrapping to flag uncertain AI responses and potentially inform exam design and difficulty calibration, though these applications were exploratory rather than validated interventions.
finding.measure: Assessment-performance comparisons, self-consistency/bootstrapping behavior across repeated exam attempts, and implications for exam security and design
finding.study_size: 124 exam questions across 3 exams; 50 GPT-4 repetitions per exam in bootstrapping analysis

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of using large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and related transformer-based systems, in education. The central question is how these models might support learning and teaching across educational levels while also introducing new pedagogical, ethical, and governance challenges. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the paper synthesizes existing examples and proposes a forward-looking agenda for responsible educational integration.

The paper outlines a broad set of possible educational applications. For students, it describes potential uses such as reading and writing support, summaries and explanations of complex texts, question and quiz generation, personalized practice, collaborative writing support, remote tutoring, and accessibility supports for learners with disabilities. For teachers, it highlights lesson planning, differentiated content creation, feedback on student writing, assessment support, plagiarism checking, and professional development. The paper also reviews selected recent studies involving LLMs and NLP systems in educational contexts, but its main contribution is conceptual: it proposes that effective use of LLMs requires explicit pedagogical strategies, human oversight, fact-checking, and critical thinking instruction.

The population and context discussed are broad rather than tied to one sample. The authors explicitly refer to elementary, middle, high school, university, professional training, remote learning, and inclusive learning scenarios. The institutional affiliations are in Germany, but the paper does not report a single participant location because it is not an empirical intervention study. The discussion is therefore cross-contextual and intended for educational stakeholders considering adoption of LLMs.

The main conclusions are that LLMs have substantial promise for personalization, feedback, engagement, and content generation, but they also pose serious risks related to bias, overreliance, privacy, plagiarism, inequitable access, and misinformation. The authors argue that LLMs should be used as supplements rather than replacements for teachers or authoritative sources. They recommend teacher and student training, curriculum designs emphasizing critical evaluation, human monitoring, transparency, and institutional policies for ethical, secure, and equitable implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, challenges, and selected prior studies rather than reporting an original empirical design, sample, or causal evaluation. It therefore does not meet criteria for empirical evidence quality in the K-12 framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes potentially meaningful impacts on literacy, feedback, personalization, and teacher efficiency, but does not provide original effect estimates or direct outcome evidence. As a result, practical impact is plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on uses of large language models such as ChatGPT in education, including question answering, summaries, explanations, personalized guidance, remote tutoring, discussion support, and conversational assistance for learners across grade levels.

Describes LLM use for literacy-related assistance such as grammatical and syntactic correction, writing-style improvement, summaries, translations, vocabulary/grammar explanation, and support for reading and writing tasks.
Discusses LLM/NLP-based use for semi-automated grading, highlighting strengths and weaknesses in student writing, adaptive feedback on student responses, and reducing teacher grading burden.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to generate up-to-date, engaging, and personalized English reading comprehension exercises for Chinese middle school learners, given teachers’ reports that existing materials are often reused year after year and are difficult to customize. The authors position large language models, especially ChatGPT, as a potential solution for producing both reading passages and multiple-choice comprehension questions that fit student level, topic interests, and instructional needs. The study also asks whether such generated materials are of sufficient quality for real educational use.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system built around ChatGPT, with a graphical user interface for non-technical users such as teachers and students. Using manually designed prompts, the system generates reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, with controls for topic, length, genre, difficulty level, and referenced passage. It also generates multiple-choice questions, answer options, and explanations, and includes a toxicity check before content is released. For comparison, the paper also develops a baseline using fine-tuned GPT-2 plus PPLM for controlled passage generation.

The population and context center on middle school English education in China, especially Grades 7-9 in Beijing, with the system intended for middle school teachers and students. Evaluation involved several groups: Chinese college students with prior experience completing middle school English exercises, native English speakers recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system for one week and were interviewed. The paper also draws on reading materials collected through collaboration with the Municipal Education Commission and eight local middle schools in Beijing.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were judged highly coherent, readable, engaging, and topic-aligned, and in several human evaluations were rated as equal to or better than existing human-written textbook passages. Generated questions were relevant to passages but weaker than human-written questions, especially because distractor options were often repetitive or low quality. Teachers nevertheless viewed the system very positively, describing it as useful for reducing preparation time and expanding access to diverse, personalized reading materials. The authors conclude that LLM-based systems show strong promise for practical educational use, while noting that question generation and larger-scale deployment still need improvement and further study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation study with multiple human-rating experiments and teacher interviews in a relevant K-12 context, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes. Evidence is mainly based on passage-quality judgments, comparative ratings, and small-sample qualitative feedback rather than causal classroom impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but still unclear impact: strong positive evidence on quality and teacher efficiency, but no direct effect sizes on student reading comprehension or broader literacy achievement are reported. The paper demonstrates feasibility and perceived value for a priority K-12 literacy population rather than established learning gains.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized middle-school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions, with teacher-specified prompts for topic, genre, length, difficulty, and optional reference texts.
A graphical reading-exercise generation system used by teachers to create, edit, and assign AI-generated reading materials and comprehension questions.

finding.finding_summary: For middle school English reading materials, ChatGPT-generated passages were rated higher than human-written textbook passages by Chinese student evaluators on readability (4.61 vs 4.52), correctness (4.60 vs 4.32), coherence (4.65 vs 4.39), engagement (4.37 vs 4.07), and overall quality (4.46 vs 4.18). In pairwise comparisons on 10 topic-matched passage sets, evaluators preferred ChatGPT zero-shot passages over human-written passages (0.87 vs 0.13) and judged them highly topic-coherent (0.97) and suitable for Chinese middle school learners (0.77 vs 0.40 for human-written in that comparison setup); however, generated multiple-choice questions were somewhat weaker than human-written ones on usefulness (3.25 vs 3.93) and suitability (3.48 vs 3.92).
finding.measure: Human ratings of generated reading passage quality (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality), pairwise passage preference, topic coherence, suitability for middle school learners, and exercise-question quality ratings
finding.study_size: 30 human-written + 30 ChatGPT + 30 GPT-2 passages in Example Set 1; 10 human-written passages + 30 generated passages in Example Set 2; 10 question sets; 9 Chinese college students, 36 native English speakers, and 3 experienced teachers

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated passages received higher engagement ratings than both human-written passages and GPT-2 passages in the Chinese student evaluation (4.37 for ChatGPT vs 4.07 human-written and 2.78 GPT-2). The paper also reports teacher beliefs that more diverse and personalized reading materials could increase student enthusiasm for learning, though no direct student motivation or engagement outcome was experimentally tested in classrooms.
finding.measure: Human evaluator engagement ratings of reading passages; teacher feedback about expected learner enthusiasm
finding.study_size: 90 passages in multi-dimension evaluation; 9 Chinese college student raters; 3 experienced teachers for system feedback

finding.finding_summary: Experienced middle school teachers reported that the system substantially reduced the cost and time required to produce diverse, personalized English reading exercises and described it as a valuable personalized resource library. After using the system for one week, teachers gave strongly positive qualitative feedback and one reported an overall system rating of 80/100, though no quantitative workload time savings were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews and qualitative feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and time/cost reduction

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what its capabilities, limitations, and implications might be for higher education, especially for learning, teaching, and assessment. The authors position the tool within broader debates about educational technology and artificial intelligence in education (AIEd), with particular concern about whether generative AI undermines traditional written assessments and how institutions should respond. The article also briefly recounts OpenAI’s development and business model shift, and reviews early academic and preprint literature on ChatGPT and related large language models.

The paper uses a desktop analysis approach rather than a primary intervention study. Its approach consists of an extensive literature review plus informal experimentation with ChatGPT using varied prompts, such as conceptual explanations, mathematical examples, essay writing, and Chinese composition. The authors use these demonstrations to illustrate strengths such as rapid text generation, conceptual explanation, and potential support for brainstorming and writing assistance, alongside weaknesses such as factual inaccuracy, fabricated references, shallow analysis, language limitations, and network or length constraints.

The context is higher education rather than K-12. The discussion concerns students, teachers, and higher education institutions, and frames ChatGPT within student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AIEd applications. Much of the paper focuses on possible educational uses already familiar from AI writing tools, including automated feedback, essay scoring, grammar support, revision assistance, and adaptive or personalised learning, and then considers how ChatGPT extends these possibilities while also intensifying risks around cheating, assessment validity, and overreliance on machine-generated text.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is disruptive but should not be understood in purely alarmist or utopian terms. The authors argue that higher education should adapt by rethinking assessment, strengthening instructional design, and using AI tools pragmatically rather than banning them outright. They suggest that ChatGPT may support innovation through feedback, experimentation, collaboration, and more student-centred pedagogies, but they also stress the need for caution because the system can generate inaccurate, biased, or superficial content and may challenge existing plagiarism detection and conventional essay-based assessment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed article, but it is primarily a narrative review/opinion piece with desktop analysis and informal experimentation rather than a systematic empirical study. It provides no controlled design, sample-based outcome analysis, or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful but highly uncertain effects on writing support, efficiency, and institutional assessment practices. Because no direct empirical effect sizes or outcome estimates are reported, impact remains unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion and informal experimentation with ChatGPT as a general-purpose conversational AI for higher education tasks such as answering questions, generating essays, brainstorming, and supporting learning/assessment activities.
Reviews AI writing assistants such as Grammarly and Wordtune as adjacent examples of AI-supported writing, revision, grammar correction, and feedback in education.

Discusses automated essay scoring, automated writing evaluation, and automated written corrective feedback systems as teacher-facing AI applications for assessing and providing feedback on student writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports anecdotal experimentation showing ChatGPT can generate coherent prose, explain concepts, and draft essays quickly, suggesting potential usefulness for writing support. However, the authors also found the generated essay output generic, shallow, and sometimes fabricated references, and they provide no controlled literacy outcome data, effect sizes, or learner performance measures.
finding.measure: Author-conducted demonstrations of generated writing quality, conceptual explanations, and multilingual text generation; narrative literature review of AI writing tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT and related AI tools can increase efficiency by producing responses, explanations, and draft text within seconds to minutes, and by potentially reducing teacher workload through automated support and feedback. This is based on descriptive examples and literature discussion rather than empirical comparison, so no quantitative productivity gains are reported.
finding.measure: Task completion speed and perceived workload/productivity benefits described in author trials and literature review

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that ChatGPT poses substantial institutional challenges for traditional higher education assessment, academic integrity policies, and future governance of teaching and learning. The paper also frames this as an opportunity for assessment redesign and institutional innovation, but presents no direct institutional outcome data or causal estimates.
finding.measure: Narrative analysis of implications for assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and institutional practice

finding.finding_summary: In its literature review of Grammarly and similar tools, the paper cites prior studies suggesting automated writing support may improve engagement, motivation, self-efficacy, and writing autonomy. These are secondary findings drawn from other studies rather than outcomes directly measured in this paper, and no pooled quantitative estimates are provided here.
finding.measure: Engagement, grit, self-efficacy, academic emotions, and writing autonomy measures as described in cited prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes prior literature indicating that AI writing tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune can support revision, grammar correction, idea formulation, and English writing quality, especially for EFL learners. These are review-based claims rather than new empirical results from the present article, and no effect sizes or sample sizes are synthesized.
finding.measure: Writing quality, error correction, revision support, and idea formulation in prior studies of AI writing tools

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits: A Pilot Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI literacy intervention using ChatGPT can help adolescents better understand the capabilities and limitations of large language models while reducing fear and negative attitudes toward AI. The authors argue that public excitement about generative AI is often accompanied by misconceptions, including overconfidence in the technology’s abilities and limited awareness of problems such as hallucinations, weak reasoning, and difficulty following complex instructions. The study is framed as an early exploration of how prompting instruction and hands-on use of ChatGPT might support more critical, realistic understanding of AI in school settings.

The intervention was a two-hour workshop conducted in a high school. It included an introductory presentation on intelligence, AI, large language models, and differences between human and artificial intelligence, followed by two practical ChatGPT activities. In both activities, students were asked to prompt ChatGPT to act as a personal teacher explaining democracy in an interactive, natural, non-boring way while meeting specified instructional goals. The first activity allowed students to freely explore ChatGPT’s strengths and limitations. After this, the instructor explicitly discussed ChatGPT’s limitations and introduced prompting strategies; students then repeated the task using improved prompting techniques. Data came from pre/post questionnaires, post-activity user-experience measures, and open-ended responses.

The population consisted of 21 students aged 16 to 18 in a formal school setting in Palermo, Sicily, Italy. The study therefore concerns secondary education rather than literacy instruction specifically, but it is relevant as adjacent evidence on teacher-guided prompting, classroom AI literacy, and student interaction with generative AI. The instructional model was teacher-led and workshop-based: students received direct instruction, then guided practice with ChatGPT, and reflected on the system’s limitations. Some students also worked in pairs due to technical issues.

The authors report encouraging preliminary findings. Students showed reduced perceived realistic and identity threats from AI after the workshop, reported mostly positive emotions, and viewed the experience as enjoyable and manageable. They perceived ChatGPT as useful and capable, but also unnatural, repetitive, and limited in conversational quality. Students judged the second interaction, after prompting instruction, as clearer and better than the first, suggesting that explicit prompting guidance improved interaction quality. The paper concludes that classroom workshops combining explanation of AI concepts with hands-on prompting practice may help students develop more realistic expectations of generative AI and better understand its limits, though the findings are preliminary and require larger, more controlled studies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot pre/post classroom study with n=21, no control group, limited uploaded interaction logs, and mostly self-report plus qualitative measures. It is peer-reviewed and has a clear method, but causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: statistically significant reductions in AI threat perceptions and perceived improvements in interaction quality were reported, but no standardized effect sizes or direct literacy achievement outcomes were provided. The study is also outside literacy instruction per se, so practical impact for K-12 literacy remains indirect.

interventions.use_case: High school AI-literacy workshop using ChatGPT as a conversational 'personal teacher' on democracy, with students first interacting freely and then applying prompting strategies to improve response quality and understand LLM limitations such as hallucinations, weak instruction-following, and limited conversational flexibility.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot workshop with high school students, the intervention improved students' perceived understanding of LLM limitations and prompting as a strategy for interacting more effectively with ChatGPT. After the prompting lesson, students rated the second interaction as better (mean=2.45, SD=1.19 on the reported comparison scale), clearer (mean=5.25, SD=1.11), and slightly more natural (mean=4.55, SD=1.61), and qualitative responses indicated greater awareness of unreliability, repetition, and difficulty following complex instructions. No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Pre/post surveys on perceived AI limitations and interaction improvement; qualitative open-ended reflections about prompting and ChatGPT limitations
finding.std_deviation: reported for selected survey items: SD=1.19, 1.11, 1.61

finding.finding_summary: The workshop reduced negative attitudes and threat perceptions toward AI among participating adolescents. Realistic threat decreased from mean=4.17 (SD=1.39) pre to 3.73 (SD=1.42) post for n=20, and identity threat decreased from mean=4.08 (SD=1.39) to 3.57 (SD=1.54), both reported as statistically significant (p<0.05); students also reported higher positive than negative emotions after interacting with ChatGPT (positive mean=3.48, SD=1.79 vs negative mean=1.35, SD=0.91, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Pre/post perceived realistic threat and identity threat scales; post-interaction self-reported emotions questionnaire
finding.study_size: n=20 for threat measures; n=21 for emotions
finding.std_deviation: Realistic threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.42; identity threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.54; positive emotions SD=1.79; negative emotions SD=0.91

finding.finding_summary: The ChatGPT activity was embedded in instruction about democracy, and students perceived the chatbot as responsive, useful, and capable of providing explanations and summaries on request. However, the study did not directly assess learning gains in democracy knowledge with a content test, and students also reported repetitive, overly encyclopedic, and sometimes unsatisfactory responses, so evidence for domain learning outcomes is inconclusive. Sample size was 21 students.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of instructional usefulness and response quality during a democracy-focused teaching task; no direct academic achievement test reported

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate high-quality, personalized reading comprehension exercises for English learners in Chinese middle schools. The authors motivate the work by noting a practical problem in schools: teachers often reuse outdated reading materials, while creating new, level-appropriate passages and multiple-choice questions is time-consuming. The study asks whether a ChatGPT-based system can generate reading passages and accompanying questions that are suitable for real classroom use and how those outputs compare with both a GPT-2-based baseline and existing human-written textbook materials.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. Users can specify features such as topic, length, genre, difficulty level, and, in a one-shot mode, provide a reference passage to guide generation. The system also generates multiple-choice comprehension questions and includes a toxicity check before outputs are shown to users. For comparison, the authors also built a baseline using fine-tuned GPT-2 with PPLM control. Evaluation combined automatic text metrics, structured human ratings of generated passages and questions, pairwise comparisons against human-written materials, and interviews with practicing teachers who used the system.

The study context is middle school English education in China, with datasets drawn from grades 7-9 reading materials provided through collaboration with Beijing schools and the Municipal Education Commission. Human evaluators included Chinese college students with prior experience completing middle school English exercises, native English speakers recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system for one week. The intended end users of the system were middle school teachers and students.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were judged to be high quality, often outperforming both the GPT-2 baseline and, in some evaluations, existing human-written textbook passages on readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. Teachers also viewed the system as useful for reducing preparation time and producing more diverse, personalized reading materials. However, question generation was weaker than passage generation: while generated questions generally matched passage content, distractor options were often low quality, repetitive, or too easy. The authors present the system as an early real-world educational application of ChatGPT with promise for practical use, while acknowledging that broader deployment and further refinement are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical evaluation study with substantial human assessment and authentic teacher feedback, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes. Evidence is based mainly on comparative content evaluation and small-scale qualitative implementation feedback rather than causal impact on K-12 learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests promising but still unclear educational impact: generated reading passages were rated very highly and teachers saw practical value, yet no direct student achievement effect sizes or classroom outcome gains were reported. Impact on literacy learning remains inferred from content quality and usability rather than demonstrated through intervention trials.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized middle school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercise questions, with teacher-editable outputs for classroom use.
Fine-tuned GPT-2 plus PPLM baseline for controlled generation of English reading passages used as a comparison model against ChatGPT and human-written materials.

finding.finding_summary: For middle school English reading materials, ChatGPT-generated passages were rated higher than human-written and GPT-2 baseline passages on overall quality by Chinese student evaluators (4.46 vs. 4.18 human-written vs. 2.84 GPT-2) and by native English speakers (4.06 vs. 3.89 vs. 3.75). In pairwise comparisons on 10 topic-matched sets, ChatGPT passages beat human-written passages on relative quality in zero-shot generation (0.87 vs. 0.13) and one-shot generation (0.80 vs. 0.20), and were judged highly topic-coherent (0.97), suggesting strong promise for producing suitable reading-comprehension texts, though question generation remained weaker than human-written items.
finding.measure: Human ratings of reading-passage quality (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality), pairwise relative quality, topic coherence, suitability for middle school English reading exercises, and question quality ratings
finding.study_size: n=30 passages in Example Set 1; n=10 topic-matched passage sets in pairwise comparison; n=10 exercise sets for question evaluation; 9 Chinese college student evaluators, 36 native English speakers, and 3 middle school teachers for system feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teacher interview feedback after one week of system use indicated that the ChatGPT-based system could substantially reduce the cost and time required to create diverse, personalized reading exercises for middle school English classes. Three experienced teachers described the tool as a 'personalized resource library' that could ease resource preparation and improve access to tailored reading materials, although these gains were based on qualitative feedback rather than quantified time-savings.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative feedback on usefulness, time/cost reduction, and ease of use after first-hand system use

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers believed more up-to-date, engaging, and personalized reading materials could stimulate student enthusiasm for English learning, and ChatGPT-generated passages received higher engagement ratings than human-written passages in student evaluations (4.37 vs. 4.07) and native-speaker evaluations (3.93 vs. 3.77). However, these results reflect perceived engagement of materials rather than direct measurement of student motivation or behavior in classroom learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Human ratings of passage engagement/interestingness
finding.study_size: 9 Chinese college student evaluators and 36 native English speakers evaluating passage sets

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support second/foreign language writing development, specifically by serving as a feedback tool to improve vocabulary and grammar for socially vulnerable learners with refugee/migrant backgrounds. The authors position the study in the context of growing interest in generative AI for language learning and the additional instructional challenges faced by multilingual students who must overcome language barriers in school.

The intervention was a short classroom-based pilot conducted within the regular German-as-a-foreign-language syllabus. Students first wrote a personal email in German about their favourite sport. Researchers then used ChatGPT to revise each text for vocabulary and grammar, and students received these improved versions to study and discuss. In a final stage, students wrote a new personal email on a similar topic related to sports and healthy life, with the intention that they would apply the language improvements modeled by ChatGPT. Outcomes were assessed by comparing pre- and post-intervention writing characteristics such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence.

The study took place in a junior high school in Patras, Greece, with eight 15-year-old students of refugee/migrant background enrolled in German language classes. Although the paper refers to the school as junior high, the participants were in the third grade of Gymnasium and aged 15, which corresponds most closely to secondary/high-school-age learners for this extraction scheme. The instructional context was a multilingual, multicultural classroom in a single urban school.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT showed promise as a language-learning and writing-support tool. Students' later writing samples were longer, used more unique words, and generally contained longer sentences, which the authors interpret as improvements in L2 writing performance. At the same time, they emphasize that this was a pilot study and caution that findings are limited by the very small sample, short duration, and lack of generalizability. They also note broader concerns around misuse, accuracy, and the need for human teacher supervision when using ChatGPT in educational settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot pre-post classroom study with 8 students and no control group, randomization, or robust statistical testing. It provides some direct K-12 evidence in an authentic school setting but has major credibility limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported descriptive gains on writing output measures are promising and occur in a priority population (migrant/refugee-background adolescents), but impact magnitude is uncertain because no standardized effect sizes or comparison group were provided.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as an AI writing support and feedback tool to revise junior high school students’ German L2 email writing, specifically improving grammar and vocabulary after an initial draft, with students then studying the revised version before producing a new similar text.

ChatGPT functioned as a generative conversational AI that produced revised versions of student texts in response to teacher/researcher prompts, serving as a guided classroom support tool rather than an autonomous tutor.

finding.finding_summary: In this pilot classroom study of 8 migrant/refugee-background junior high school students (n=8), use of ChatGPT-mediated feedback was associated with improved German L2 writing indicators on a follow-up writing task. Reported gains included a mean 38% increase in total words, an average increase of 19.1 unique words per student, and an approximately 42% increase in average words per sentence; however, no standardized writing assessment, inferential statistics, or formal effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Writing-product metrics: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and descriptive word-frequency comparisons in German foreign-language email writing

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits: A Pilot Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI literacy intervention can help adolescents better understand the capabilities and limitations of large language models such as ChatGPT, while also reducing fear and negative attitudes toward AI. The authors argue that public excitement about LLMs often coexists with misleading assumptions that these systems can reliably solve problems across domains, despite known weaknesses such as hallucinations, limited reasoning, and imperfect instruction-following. The study therefore asks whether a classroom-based prompting workshop can improve students’ interactions with ChatGPT and foster a more realistic understanding of AI.

The intervention was a two-hour school workshop combining instruction and hands-on practice. Students first received a presentation on intelligence, AI, and LLMs, then completed an activity using ChatGPT to act as a personal teacher explaining the concept of democracy in an engaging way. This initial activity was designed to expose limitations in ChatGPT’s ability to follow complex instructions. The instructor then explicitly discussed ChatGPT’s limits and introduced prompting strategies, after which students completed a second, similar prompting activity. Data collection included pre/post questionnaires on perceived AI threat, post-workshop self-reported emotions, user-experience ratings, perceptions of ChatGPT functionality, and open-ended responses about the interaction.

The study involved 21 high school students aged 16 to 18 in a formal school setting in Palermo, Sicily, Italy. The context was a single high school workshop rather than a full curricular implementation. The activity was teacher- or instructor-led, with guided practice using ChatGPT during class time. Although the paper is relevant to K-12 AI literacy and classroom uses of generative AI, it is not primarily a literacy-instruction study; instead, it focuses on prompting, AI understanding, and student attitudes.

The main conclusions are that the workshop was well received and associated with reduced perceived realistic and identity threat from AI, more positive than negative emotions after interaction, and student-reported improvement in the quality and clarity of ChatGPT interactions after learning prompting strategies. Students appreciated ChatGPT’s responsiveness and usefulness but also noticed important limitations, especially repetitiveness, lack of natural conversational quality, and difficulty following requests precisely. The authors conclude that hands-on AI literacy workshops can help students develop more critical and realistic views of LLMs, but they emphasize that the pilot nature of the study, technical issues, and limited sample require larger and more controlled future research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot pre/post field study in one high school classroom (n=21) without a control group, randomization, or direct validated academic learning outcomes. It provides empirical evidence with clear methods, but credibility is limited to a single-group exploratory design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: there were statistically significant improvements in AI attitudes and perceived interaction quality, but no reported effect sizes and no direct K-12 literacy achievement outcomes. Overall impact is positive but modest/uncertain for the target literacy-use agenda.

interventions.use_case: High school AI literacy workshop using ChatGPT as a conversational 'personal teacher' on democracy content, with explicit instruction in prompting strategies so students can experience both improved prompting and the limitations of LLM outputs.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT to learn and discuss concepts of democracy in a classroom task, and after prompting instruction they perceived the second interaction as better, clearer (mean=5.25, SD=1.11), and slightly more natural (mean=4.55, SD=1.61). However, the study did not report direct pre/post learning gains on democracy knowledge or standardized academic assessments, so evidence for academic improvement in this subject-area outcome remains indirect and perception-based.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of interaction quality during a democracy learning task; no direct content-learning assessment reported
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.11 to 1.61 for selected comparative perception items

finding.finding_summary: The two-hour workshop was associated with reduced negative attitudes and threat perceptions toward AI. Realistic threat decreased from pre to post (mPre=4.17, SD=1.39; mPost=3.73, SD=1.42; n=20; p<0.05), and identity threat also decreased (mPre=4.08, SD=1.39; mPost=3.57, SD=1.54; n=20; p<0.05); after interaction, students reported higher positive than negative emotions (mPositive=3.48, SD=1.79 vs. mNegative=1.35, SD=0.91; n=21; p<0.05).
finding.measure: Pre/post threat perception scales about AI; post-interaction self-reported emotions
finding.std_deviation: Realistic threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.42; identity threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.54; positive emotions SD=1.79; negative emotions SD=0.91

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students' perceived ability to interact productively and critically with an LLM by teaching prompting strategies and highlighting AI limitations such as unreliability and constrained understanding. Students rated the second interaction as better (mean=2.45, SD=1.19 on the comparison item as reported by authors), clearer (mean=5.25, SD=1.11), and somewhat more natural (mean=4.55, SD=1.61), and qualitative evidence suggested a better grasp of limitations and more structured prompts over time, although no direct performance rubric for prompting skill was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interaction improvement, perceived understanding of ChatGPT capabilities/limits, qualitative analysis of student reflections
finding.study_size: n=21; uploaded chat logs for 9 students
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.19 to 1.61 for selected prompting-related comparison items

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines the opportunities, risks, and implementation considerations associated with large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT, in education. The core question is how LLMs might support learning and teaching across educational levels while also introducing new challenges related to bias, overreliance, privacy, academic integrity, access, and pedagogical fit. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes existing examples and proposes a conceptual agenda for responsible educational use.

The paper discusses a wide range of potential educational uses for LLMs. For learners, these include support for reading and writing, summaries and explanations of complex texts, question and quiz generation, conversational practice, curiosity prompting, remote tutoring, adaptive support, and inclusive applications for learners with disabilities. For teachers, the paper highlights lesson planning, personalized materials, feedback on student work, assessment support, content generation, and professional development. It also reviews selected prior studies on quiz generation, feedback, conversational AI, automatic assessment, and pedagogical dialogue, while emphasizing that this research base is still emerging.

The context is broad and cross-sector rather than tied to a single implementation site. The authors explicitly discuss educational applications spanning elementary school, middle and high school, university, professional training, remote learning, and inclusive education. From a K-12 literacy perspective, the paper is relevant because it identifies practical uses such as grammatical and syntactic correction, summaries and explanations for reading comprehension, prompts and questions to stimulate critical reading and writing, vocabulary and grammar support, and personalized feedback on student writing. However, these uses are presented as opportunities and examples rather than as tested classroom interventions.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial potential to enhance personalization, feedback, content creation, engagement, and access in education, but only if they are integrated with strong pedagogical approaches and sustained human oversight. The authors argue that teachers and students need new competencies to understand model limitations, verify outputs, and use LLMs critically rather than passively. They recommend curriculum design that emphasizes fact-checking, critical thinking, ethical awareness, and hybrid human-AI instructional models, and they call for further research on effective integration, safeguards, and equitable access.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and selected prior studies rather than reporting an original empirical design, sample, or causal analysis. It does not provide a clear study methodology or direct evaluative evidence for a specific intervention implementation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful educational benefits, but it does not present original effect estimates or direct impact data. As a result, practical impact remains unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on educational uses of large language models such as ChatGPT for student support, conversational assistance, content generation, question answering, summarization, personalized guidance, and remote tutoring across K-12 and higher education contexts.
Discusses LLM/NLP use for semi-automated assessment, adaptive feedback, scoring of student answers, and support for revision of written or domain-specific responses.
Describes LLMs as writing and language supports for grammar correction, style improvement, summarization, translation, vocabulary support, reading comprehension support, and writing assistance.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can be integrated into K-12 learning in ways that support both disciplinary learning and AI literacy. The authors argue that although there is growing interest in AI literacy and in using AI for learning, there is little empirical research on the actual processes by which students use GenAI in classroom learning. The study therefore asks two questions: how high school students incorporated ChatGPT into knowledge-building work, and how their AI literacy developed through that process.

The intervention was a teacher-designed integration of ChatGPT into a high school World Religions course structured around Knowledge Building pedagogy. Across roughly two phases of classroom activity, students used ChatGPT first to explore the problem space by critiquing AI-generated essays and generating inquiry questions, and later to deepen inquiry through guided conversations with ChatGPT, fact-checking, peer discussion, and collaborative posting in Knowledge Forum. The teacher explicitly scaffolded use through class discussions, prompts, a steering prompt for ChatGPT interaction, expectations for fact-checking, and requirements to document and cite AI use. The instructional model was teacher-led and classroom-based, with collaborative small-group work and individual use of ChatGPT embedded in ongoing inquiry and writing.

The study took place with 10 consented high school students and one teacher in a K-12 setting in a major South American city. Students came from three different schools and were enrolled in an elective course conducted in English. Data consisted primarily of end-of-semester semi-structured student interviews, supplemented by classroom artifacts from Miro and Knowledge Forum and teacher planning/reflection documents. The analysis used qualitative coding focused on students' uses of ChatGPT and dimensions of AI literacy.

The main conclusions are that students used ChatGPT in multiple ways: for information search, brainstorming, generating questions, supporting writing, summarizing, and keeping up with discussion. Students also developed emerging AI literacy, including awareness of strengths, weaknesses, risks, and some mechanisms of ChatGPT, though their understanding was often partial and sometimes inaccurate. The paper concludes that GenAI can productively support collaborative knowledge building when educators provide structured pedagogical guidance, opportunities for critique and reflection, and explicit scaffolds for mindful, ethical human-AI partnership rather than simple answer-getting.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample qualitative classroom study using interviews, artifacts, and teacher notes in a real K-12 setting, but it lacks a comparison group, standardized outcome measures, and causal identification. It provides useful implementation and mechanism evidence, meeting only limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impacts: students perceived gains in efficiency, idea generation, and critical AI use, but outcomes were not quantified and academic gains were not directly measured. As a result, overall impact remains modest or uncertain.

interventions.use_case: High school students used ChatGPT as a conversational learning partner within a teacher-designed knowledge building pedagogy to generate inquiry questions, obtain brief explanatory answers with multiple perspectives, receive follow-up questions, support research and discussion, and assist with essay planning and writing in a World Religions course.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative study of 10 high school students in a World Religions course, interviews and classroom artifacts suggested ChatGPT supported domain learning by helping students search for information efficiently, surface diverse perspectives, and keep up with discussions. However, students also reported misinformation, dated content, and difficulty fact-checking convincing outputs, so evidence for improvement in subject-matter learning was process-based rather than tied to measured achievement gains. No standardized achievement outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student interview reports and classroom artifacts about learning support in a World Religions course; no direct achievement test reported

finding.finding_summary: Students described using ChatGPT to support literacy-related tasks including generating essay outlines, revising drafts, summarizing texts, gathering arguments, and correcting minor writing mistakes. Some students viewed it as a useful support for starting and improving writing, whereas others warned that overreliance, copying outputs, and inaccurate content could undermine authentic writing quality and learning; no direct reading or writing performance measures were collected. The paper therefore provides implementation evidence rather than causal evidence on literacy gains.
finding.measure: Student self-reports and artifacts on essay writing, revision, summarization, and writing support; no standardized literacy assessment reported

finding.finding_summary: The study found qualitative evidence that structured ChatGPT use, combined with teacher scaffolds, supported durable skills such as critical evaluation, prompt engineering, fact-checking, metacognitive reflection, collaboration, and configuring an appropriate human-AI partnership. Students described learning to refine prompts, compare outputs against external sources, discuss AI-generated ideas with peers, and set boundaries on use, though these outcomes were not quantified with validated scales. Evidence comes from interviews, Knowledge Forum posts, and teacher scaffolds with n=10 students.
finding.measure: Interview evidence and classroom artifacts concerning critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, prompt engineering, and fact-checking practices

finding.finding_summary: About 70% of interviewed students reported that ChatGPT increased efficiency in information search by allowing natural-language queries, maintaining conversational context, and providing concise answers more quickly than search engines. Students also used it to reduce workload in routine tasks such as outlining essays, summarizing text, and getting quick help during class, although no time-on-task or productivity metrics were formally collected.
finding.measure: Student self-reported efficiency in information search and task completion

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT could increase engagement by making interactions feel personal, helping them participate in class discussions, and sparking interest through idea generation. At the same time, some students voiced concern about dependence, reduced attention span, and passive shortcut use, indicating potential downsides for self-regulation and healthy engagement. These findings are qualitative and based on interviews rather than validated motivation or self-regulation instruments.
finding.measure: Student interview reports about engagement, personal connection, dependence, and self-regulation concerns

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether using ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool improves academic writing skills among ESL undergraduate students. The author positions the study as an early empirical test of generative AI for writing instruction, addressing the lack of intervention-based evidence on ChatGPT’s effects on writing quality. The research asks whether, when instructional time and tasks are held constant, ChatGPT-supported feedback leads to significantly better writing outcomes than comparison instruction, and how students perceive its impact.

The study used a mixed-methods intervention design with quantitative and qualitative components. Two sections of first-year science and engineering students at a private university in India served as the experimental and comparison groups. The experimental group received a short training session on using ChatGPT for self-assessment and peer-assessment, then used ChatGPT during six hours of instruction on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph writing. ChatGPT was used to support brainstorming, idea development, checking genre features, and feedback on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary. The comparison group received instruction without this ChatGPT-supported feedback process. Writing performance was measured with pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test tasks scored using validated rubrics; focus group discussions captured student perceptions.

The final analytic sample included 35 students in the experimental group and 37 in the comparison group, all aged 18–19 and studying in English-medium higher education. The setting was a university classroom in India, not a K-12 context. Quantitative results showed statistically significant gains for the experimental group across time and significantly higher post-test and delayed post-test scores than the comparison group. Qualitative findings indicated that students viewed ChatGPT positively for helping with idea generation, staying on topic, organization, grammar explanations, and faster writing, although some also worried about dependence on the tool and reduced creativity.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can function effectively as a formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes when students are trained to use it.
