The author argues that its dialogic, immediate, and customizable feedback can support improvements in content, organization, and grammatical accuracy, with benefits sustained at delayed post-test. However, the study also notes constraints on generalizability because it was conducted at a single elite university, focused on only three writing genres, and involved a short intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with a comparison group, pre/post/delayed post testing, reported statistical assumptions, and sizable effects, but it is not a randomized K-12 trial and uses an intact higher-education sample with attrition from initial consent to analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported literacy effects are large, with very large within-group effect sizes and substantial post-test and delayed post-test differences favoring the ChatGPT condition. However, relevance to the target K-12 evidence question is indirect because the sample is undergraduate ESL students rather than school-age learners.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a formative feedback tool for self- and peer-assessment in an undergraduate ESL academic writing course, providing feedback on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary during paragraph writing tasks.

Conversational use of ChatGPT to give dialogic, on-demand explanations and guidance during writing, including brainstorming, checking topic sentences, supporting details, conclusions, grammar, and vocabulary choices.

finding.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental mixed-methods intervention, the ChatGPT group outperformed the comparison group on academic writing assessments after a 6-hour intervention and again at delayed post-test. Experimental-group scores increased from pre-test M=12.581 (SD=0.833, n=37) to post-test M=19.216 (SD=2.485) and delayed post-test M=20.419 (SD=2.575), with within-group RM ANOVA F(2,72)=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902; Bonferroni comparisons showed very large gains from pre to post (d=3.300) and pre to delayed post (d=3.898), and a smaller continued gain from post to delayed post (d=0.598). Between groups, the experimental group exceeded the comparison group at post-test, t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e-7, and delayed post-test, t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e-14.
finding.measure: Rubric-scored academic writing tests on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph writing; rubric dimensions included content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
finding.study_size: n=72 analyzed total; experimental group n=37, comparison group n=35
finding.std_deviation: EG pre SD=0.833; EG post SD=2.485; EG delayed post SD=2.575; CG delayed post SD=1.897; CG post SD=1.695

finding.finding_summary: Focus group data indicated overwhelmingly positive student perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact, including increased motivation, reduced anxiety about asking for feedback, and greater confidence in obtaining immediate writing support. However, a minority of students reported concerns about reduced motivation to think independently and increased machine dependence, so the evidence is perception-based and somewhat mixed in nuance despite the overall positive direction.
finding.measure: Student focus group discussions on perceived motivation, anxiety reduction, and attitudes toward ChatGPT-supported feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT-supported self- and peer-assessment promoted learner autonomy, collaboration, and explicit reflection on writing decisions, especially around idea generation, organization, and grammar explanations. These findings come from qualitative coding rather than causal quantitative estimates, and some students also expressed concern that overreliance on the tool could dampen independent thinking and creativity.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes related to learner autonomy, collaboration, self-monitoring, and metalinguistic reflection

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative evidence suggests ChatGPT made brainstorming and feedback cycles faster, helped students complete writing tasks more efficiently, and was framed by the author as potentially useful in large classes where individualized feedback is difficult. These outcomes were not quantified experimentally, so the finding is based on user reports and author interpretation rather than measured time-on-task or workload reductions.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of faster writing, reduced brainstorming time, and perceived efficiency of feedback processes

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool in higher education language learning, focusing on two questions: whether AI-generated writing feedback improves student writing more than human tutor feedback, and whether students prefer AI or human feedback. The study is positioned in response to growing interest in ethical and practical uses of generative AI for writing instruction, especially in English as a new language (ENL) contexts.

The authors report two longitudinal studies using GPT-4 to generate feedback on student writing. In Study 1, a six-week quasi-experimental repeated-measures design compared ENL students who received weekly feedback from GPT-4 with students who received feedback from human tutors. Students completed pre- and post-writing assessments scored by human raters using an analytic rubric covering content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence. In Study 2, a separate group of ENL students received both human and AI feedback each week and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

Participants were 91 undergraduate ENL students at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region, all with at least B1 English proficiency. Study 1 included 48 students aged 20 to 30; Study 2 included 43 students aged 19 to 36. The intervention involved weekly 300-word academic writing tasks. Human-feedback students met with trained tutors in 30-minute one-on-one sessions, while AI-feedback students received individualized GPT-4 feedback by email generated from a structured prompt designed by experienced language educators.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce superior writing gains relative to human tutor feedback: both groups improved similarly, with no significant between-group difference. Student preferences were nearly evenly split between AI and human feedback. Students valuing human feedback emphasized face-to-face interaction, engagement, and opportunities for follow-up questions, while those favoring AI emphasized clarity, specificity, consistency, and convenient access. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing instruction without harming learning outcomes, and they recommend a blended approach that combines AI’s detailed written feedback with human tutoring interaction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed longitudinal quasi-experimental study with a comparison group and repeated measures, but it is nonrandomized, small-sample, and conducted in higher education rather than K-12. It provides some causal leverage but has relevance limitations for the requested K-12 literacy evidence base.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main causal literacy finding shows no significant advantage of generative AI feedback over human tutor feedback, with very small or null between-group differences. Preference outcomes were mixed and do not demonstrate clear positive impact on literacy achievement.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated automated feedback on university ENL students' academic paragraph writing, covering topic sentence, idea development, academic language, transitions, sources/evidence, and grammar error explanations.
Use of ChatGPT/GPT-4 as an automated writing evaluation and language-feedback tool for ENL essay revision in an academic writing course.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, a 6-week quasi-experimental repeated-measures comparison found no significant difference in writing improvement between students receiving GPT-4 feedback and those receiving human tutor feedback. Writing scores increased in both groups (EG: 27.522 to 33.370; CG: 26.820 to 33.680), but the group-by-time interaction was not significant, F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063; posttest group difference was also nonsignificant, t(46)=-0.539, p=0.591, d=-0.156.
finding.measure: Analytic writing rubric scores on pre/post academic writing assessments evaluating content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence (maximum score 40).
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063; posttest Cohen's d=-0.156
finding.std_deviation: Pretest SDs: EG=1.301, CG=1.391; Posttest SDs: EG=1.908, CG=2.066

finding.finding_summary: The same study also supports a no-difference conclusion when GPT-4 is framed specifically as an AI writing/language tool: students receiving AI feedback did not outperform peers receiving tutor feedback on posttest writing quality after 6 weeks. Both groups improved substantially over time, but there was no significant between-group effect, F=0.241, p=0.626, and no significant pretest or posttest mean differences.
finding.measure: Pre/post scored academic writing performance using a 4-domain analytic rubric.
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.005 for between-subject group effect; pretest Cohen's d=0.520; posttest Cohen's d=-0.156
finding.std_deviation: Pretest SDs: EG=1.301, CG=1.391; Posttest SDs: EG=1.908, CG=2.066

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2, ENL students' preferences for AI-generated versus human tutor feedback were nearly evenly split across six weeks, indicating broadly comparable acceptance of both forms of feedback. Grand means were very similar on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference items (e.g., satisfaction: human 4.28 vs AI 4.26; preference item: human 4.20 vs AI 4.13), with item 9 averaging 1.53 on a binary preference scale where 1.5 indicates an even split.
finding.measure: Weekly learner perception survey on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and feedback preference using 5-point Likert items plus forced-choice preference item and open-ended responses.
finding.std_deviation: Grand mean SDs ranged approximately 1.10-1.14 across survey items; Q9 SD=0.50

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can successfully complete Dutch national high school exams in English reading comprehension, and what that implies for educational assessment. The central question is not whether students learn more with AI, but whether generative AI systems can perform at or above the level of human secondary students on a high-stakes literacy-related assessment. The study also compares performance across GPT-3.5 and two versions of GPT-4 and explores whether repeated sampling with stochastic settings can reveal when the model is uncertain or likely to be wrong.

The approach involved administering three 2022 Dutch VWO national English reading comprehension exams to ChatGPT. GPT-3.5 was tested through the web interface in December 2022, sometimes with re-prompting when the model failed to give a valid answer. GPT-4 was later tested through the API in March 2023 and again with the June 2023 update using a fully automated prompting procedure and no re-prompting. The exams included multiple-choice and open-response comprehension items based on texts, with scores converted to official Dutch grades. The paper also used a bootstrapping/self-consistency method by repeating GPT-4 responses 50 times at a nonzero temperature to see whether inconsistent answers signaled likely errors.

The population and context are Dutch upper-secondary students in the VWO track, the most academically rigorous high school pathway in the Netherlands, although the direct test taker in the experiment was the AI model rather than human participants receiving an intervention. Human student score distributions were used as a benchmark for one exam, where public exam data were available. The literacy domain studied is English reading comprehension, including identifying main ideas, making inferences, and interpreting vocabulary in context.

The main conclusion is that GPT-3.5 performed roughly at the level of the average Dutch student on these exams, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student and achieved high passing grades without re-prompting. The author argues that these results raise concerns about the security and validity of computer-based assessments, while also suggesting potential educational uses of large language models. However, the study does not provide causal evidence about student literacy improvement from generative AI, and its findings are limited to AI exam performance in one national exam context rather than impacts on K-12 learners’ literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with clear methods and objective scoring, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental study of student outcomes and includes no intervention assigned to K-12 learners. It provides descriptive comparative evidence about model performance on exams, not educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially important but indirect implications for literacy assessment and educational systems, yet it does not estimate student learning gains or report effect sizes on K-12 outcomes. Impact on actual student literacy is therefore unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) was used as a conversational large language model to answer Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exam questions, benchmarking model performance against student exam norms and comparing prompting conditions and model versions.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test whether K-12 students improved their literacy through using generative AI; instead, it benchmarked ChatGPT on high-school English reading-comprehension exams. GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 across three Dutch VWO English exams (6.5 without re-prompting), compared with the national student mean of 6.99 on one exam, while GPT-4 scored 8.3 (March version) and 8.1 (June version), indicating strong model performance on literacy assessment tasks rather than causal effects on student literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Scores/grades on Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exams; item-level correctness on multiple-choice and open-response reading questions
finding.study_size: 3 exams, 124 total questions; student comparison available for Exam 1 only (n=35,698)

finding.finding_summary: The findings suggest substantial institutional implications for assessment integrity: ChatGPT could pass or outperform average student performance on high-stakes English reading-comprehension exams, implying potential risks for unsupervised or computer-based assessment. GPT-4 scored 8.3/8.1 on the Dutch 1-10 grading scale without re-prompting, and the author argues this raises concerns about exam security and the need to redesign assessment practices.
finding.measure: LLM exam performance relative to official passing thresholds and student norm distributions; implications for assessment security
finding.study_size: 3 exams, 124 total questions; student comparison for Exam 1 (n=35,698)

paper_profiles.title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and teachers perceive the acceptable use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process, with a focus on ChatGPT. The core problem is not whether GenAI improves writing outcomes, but rather what different educational stakeholders consider appropriate or inappropriate use across tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, giving feedback, and evaluating writing. The authors position the study in response to growing concerns about academic integrity, plagiarism, and the lack of clear institutional guidance for AI use in education.

The study used a cross-sectional questionnaire survey. Participants were shown example prompts and outputs from ChatGPT for six writing-related tasks, then asked to rate the appropriateness of four kinds of use: offloading a task the person already knows how to do, using AI output as a model for ideas, submitting AI-generated output with disclosure, and submitting AI-generated output without disclosure. The survey also included items about beliefs regarding AI utility, concerns about AI in education, openness to new technology, and familiarity with AI.

The sample included 226 participants: 158 students, mostly undergraduate students from a public research university in the United States, and 68 teachers recruited from multiple institutions worldwide, primarily adult/university-level language teachers. Most teachers were teaching in the United States or China, though some were in other countries; only a very small number taught in K-12 settings. The study context was educational writing, but overwhelmingly in higher education rather than school-age settings.

The main conclusion is that students and teachers broadly agree that GenAI is more acceptable when used to support early or assistive stages of writing, such as brainstorming, outlining, or generating models, and less acceptable when used to complete assignments for submission, especially without disclosure. Both groups also reported that institutions and classrooms were largely unprepared for GenAI, with very limited AI-related policy, training, or student instruction. The authors argue for explicit institutional guidelines and teacher professional development on ethical and transparent AI use in writing education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey study with clear methods and sample reporting, but it is nonexperimental and does not provide causal or quasi-experimental evidence on learning outcomes. It offers descriptive/comparative perception data rather than impact estimates on K-12 literacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows unclear practical impact because it does not estimate effects of generative AI on literacy or other student outcomes. Its main contribution is documenting stakeholder perceptions and institutional readiness, with no direct outcome effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based evaluation of perceptions of ChatGPT/genAI use across stages of the writing process, including brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, teacher feedback, and evaluation of student writing.
ChatGPT is presented as a conversational generative AI chatbot producing writing-related outputs in response to prompts, though the paper studies perceptions rather than tutoring effects.

finding.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 226 participants (158 students, 68 teachers), both groups reported broadly similar views that genAI use is more acceptable for idea generation/modeling than for undisclosed submission of AI-produced work, while also indicating substantial institutional unpreparedness. Only 5.9% of teachers reported their institution had an AI policy, 4.4% reported receiving AI training, and 10.3% reported educating students about appropriate AI use; no causal effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Perception survey on acceptable genAI use in writing tasks; yes/no items on institutional AI policy, training, and teacher instruction about AI

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students generally saw genAI as more acceptable for supportive or efficiency-oriented uses—such as brainstorming, outlining, and using AI-generated feedback/evaluation as a model—than for replacing core authorship. Teachers were significantly more favorable than students toward teacher-side efficiency uses such as modeling feedback and evaluation, but the study measured perceptions only and did not report actual workload reduction or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Likert ratings of appropriateness of genAI for feedback and evaluation tasks; perceived utility of AI for teachers and students
finding.std_deviation: Reported for item/task means in paper, but not outcome-specific

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about perceptions of using generative AI in the writing process rather than testing whether genAI improves writing quality, revision quality, or literacy achievement. Although writing-related tasks were central to the survey, no student literacy performance outcomes, experimental contrasts, or effect sizes on writing/reading measures were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived appropriateness of genAI use for brainstorming, outlining, writing, and revising
finding.std_deviation: Reported for survey task means only

paper_profiles.title: Challenges for higher education in the era of widespread access to Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how widespread access to generative AI systems, especially tools such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, is challenging traditional higher education. The authors aim to discuss both the opportunities and risks of generative AI in university teaching and learning, including its usefulness for information acquisition, writing, problem solving, and programming, as well as concerns about hallucinations, misinformation, academic dishonesty, and erosion of critical thinking. The paper also considers broader implications for curriculum redesign, digital literacy, and the future role of universities and educators.

The empirical component is a survey of 143 university students drawn from multiple universities and disciplines. The survey asks about students’ prior use of AI tools, purposes for using ChatGPT and other systems, trust in AI-generated content, willingness to interact with chatbots, opinions about AI in education, and attitudes toward AI partially replacing teachers or grading exams. The paper also includes a conceptual discussion of generative AI capabilities across text, image, and sound generation, and uses an example of an AI-generated factual error to illustrate the problem of hallucinations.

The population studied consists of higher education students, including both bachelor’s and master’s students, in fields such as computer science, management, administration, and related areas. The context is higher education rather than K-12, and the study is framed around university transformation in response to pervasive generative AI. The participant pool appears to be based in Poland, given the institutional affiliations and publication context, though the survey is described as including students from diverse universities.

The main conclusions are that students are already using generative AI extensively, generally support allowing and teaching AI use in universities, but often overestimate their ability to detect AI errors. The authors argue that universities should not simply prohibit AI, but should adapt by strengthening factual knowledge, critical thinking, digital literacy, and responsible AI use. They emphasize that examinations should verify students’ own knowledge without AI assistance, and that higher education must prepare students to work with AI while avoiding overreliance on statistically generated outputs that may contain convincing falsehoods.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed survey study with descriptive analysis, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental evaluation and provides no controlled comparison of learning outcomes. It offers some empirical evidence but only one of the three main credibility criteria for strong causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear practical impact: students perceive benefits and institutional relevance, but the evidence is descriptive and mixed, with no reported effect sizes or demonstrated improvements in academic outcomes. It is therefore best classified as unclear impact rather than proven positive or negative impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based examination of university students' use and perceptions of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT/GPT-4 for educational tasks including information search, problem solving, essay generation, summarization, translation, and class preparation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports survey results from 143 university students on perceptions of generative AI in higher education. A majority supported allowing and teaching AI use in universities (55%), and 76% believed AI systems would be useful in education in the future, but students were divided on whether AI tools might replace teachers and 51% opposed AI grading of exams. No causal estimates or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student survey responses on perceptions of AI integration, teacher replacement, and AI grading in higher education

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using ChatGPT for efficiency-oriented academic tasks such as finding solutions to problems (63%), information search (62%), programming (52%), and preparing for classes, homework, projects, and exams. These findings indicate perceived productivity benefits, but the study did not experimentally compare performance or time savings against a non-AI condition and reported no effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-reported uses of ChatGPT for academic task completion and preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents indirect evidence suggesting risks to critical thinking and verification skills: although 50% of students said they verify dubious AI-generated content and 24% said they always scrutinize it, only 21% detected a major factual error in a GPT-generated biography, while 50.7% failed to identify it. Among students claiming alertness or consistent verification, nearly half still missed the error (47.8% and 45.7%, respectively), suggesting overconfidence and weak real-world evaluation of AI outputs. No causal identification or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy in detecting factual hallucination in AI-generated text; self-reported trust and verification behavior

paper_profiles.title: Complementary Advantages of ChatGPTs and Human Readers in Reasoning: Evidence from English Text Reading Comprehension
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how two versions of ChatGPT (ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 and ChatGPT Plus/GPT-4) compare with human readers in text-based reasoning during English reading comprehension. The authors focus on three kinds of inference central to comprehension of narrative texts: commonsense inference, emotional inference, and causal inference. Rather than testing whether AI improves student learning, the study asks whether AI systems and Chinese high school ESL learners show different strengths and weaknesses when answering reading-based reasoning tasks.

The approach was a direct comparative performance study. The researchers administered three offline reading tests to 114 senior secondary students in China and also prompted ChatGPT and ChatGPT Plus to generate comparable sets of responses. Test 1 assessed commonsense inference using items about local Chinese culture and everyday life; Test 2 assessed emotional inference using adapted narrative stories requiring identification of characters' emotions; Test 3 assessed causal inference using a suspense story with questions about causes and consequences. The authors also explored whether more elaborate prompting improved the chatbots' causal reasoning, especially for ChatGPT Plus.

The population consisted of grade-11 Chinese students (about age 17) in a single mid-level high school, described as English-as-a-second-language learners preparing for the national college entrance examination. Students had studied English for at least six years and had prior classroom experience with reading comprehension strategies. The study took place in a school setting during flexible class time and involved objective task performance rather than self-report.

The main conclusions are that human readers and ChatGPT systems showed complementary strengths rather than one uniformly outperforming the other. Students performed best on local-culture commonsense items and on causal reasoning, suggesting advantages in culturally grounded knowledge and logical narrative analysis. ChatGPT Plus performed strongest on daily-life commonsense items and emotional inference overall, outperforming students on many positive-emotion tasks, while students were relatively better on negative emotions. ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) generally performed worst of the three. When prompts were elaborated, ChatGPT Plus improved substantially on causal inference, while ChatGPT showed little change. Overall, the paper argues that human readers and generative AI have different but potentially complementary reasoning advantages in English reading comprehension.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative performance study, not a causal or quasi-experimental evaluation of a K-12 instructional intervention on student outcomes. It includes a defined sample and measures, but lacks randomization, a business-as-usual or non-AI instructional comparator, and does not estimate treatment effects on learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mixed comparative performance of ChatGPT/ChatGPT Plus versus students on literacy-related reasoning tasks, but the practical impact on K-12 literacy achievement is unclear because no instructional implementation or effect size on student learning was reported.

interventions.use_case: Direct comparison of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4) against Chinese senior high school ESL students on English narrative-text reading comprehension inference tasks (commonsense, emotional, and causal reasoning), including prompt-updated causal reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: This comparative study assessed English reading-comprehension inference performance rather than an instructional treatment effect. Among 114 Chinese senior-2 ESL students and repeated chatbot runs (87 valid runs for commonsense; 82 for emotional and causal tests), students outperformed both ChatGPT versions on local-culture commonsense inference (86.83% vs. 61.98% ChatGPT vs. 66.58% ChatGPT Plus) and on several causal-inference items, while ChatGPT Plus outperformed students on daily-life commonsense inference (93.33% vs. 67.66%) and showed stronger emotional-inference accuracy overall. No causal effect on students' literacy outcomes versus business-as-usual instruction was estimated, and no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on researcher-developed English reading comprehension inference tasks: commonsense inference (local culture, daily life), emotional inference from narrative stories, and causal inference from a suspense text
finding.study_size: n=114 students; chatbot outputs: n=87 valid runs for commonsense, n=82 valid runs for emotional and causal tasks

finding.finding_summary: For text-based reasoning, findings were mixed across inference types. Students showed stronger logical analysis on causal-inference items and better performance on locally grounded knowledge, whereas ChatGPT Plus performed better on some deductive and emotional-inference tasks and improved after more elaborate prompting; ChatGPT remained largely unchanged under prompt updating. These results suggest complementary rather than uniformly superior reasoning performance by the LLMs.
finding.measure: Reasoning/inference accuracy on commonsense, emotional, and causal inference tasks derived from narrative reading
finding.study_size: n=114 students; chatbot outputs: n=82-87 repeated valid runs depending on task

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that "AI literacy" has become a prominent but inconsistently defined concept in education, especially after the rise of generative AI. The authors ask how researchers conceptualize and approach AI literacy in K-12 and higher education, and what new trends have emerged since generative AI became widely available. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes the literature to clarify what counts as AI literacy and how different studies define its goals.

The authors conduct an integrative review of 124 studies published between 2020 and July 2024. They systematically searched ERIC and Scopus, supplemented by purposive citation tracing, and included both empirical and theoretical studies in K-12 and undergraduate contexts. From these studies, they derive a conceptual framework with three perspectives on AI—technical details, tool use, and sociocultural impact—and three perspectives on literacy—functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial. They then use this framework to organize patterns in the literature, including machine-learning-focused K-12 curricula, AI ethics instruction, comprehensive K-12 AI curricula, postsecondary AI literacy without generative AI, and newer studies focused on generative AI tool use and prompt engineering.

The review covers students in K-12 and undergraduate education internationally, though it excludes graduate, professional, and teacher-focused AI literacy studies. It is not a causal study of literacy outcomes; instead, it maps how AI literacy interventions and frameworks are being designed across educational levels. The paper repeatedly distinguishes learning about AI from learning with AI, and excludes studies that only use AI as an instructional tool rather than teach AI literacy itself.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy is best understood as an umbrella term encompassing substantially different educational aims and practices. Since the advent of generative AI, research has shifted strongly toward viewing AI as a tool—especially in higher education—while earlier work more often emphasized technical understanding and sociocultural critique in K-12 settings. The authors conclude that the field needs more precise terminology than the generic label "AI literacy," and they highlight gaps such as limited work on critical literacy for AI tools and comparatively less postsecondary research beyond generative-AI tool use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed integrative review synthesizing 124 studies, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental evaluation of a specific K-12 literacy intervention and does not provide a formal meta-analysis of literacy outcomes. Its methods are transparent for literature identification and thematic synthesis, yet it does not meet higher-tier causal evidence standards for the user’s target question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate the effect of generative AI on K-12 literacy outcomes and reports no pooled effect sizes or direct comparative impacts on reading or writing achievement. Its contribution is primarily conceptual and field-mapping, so practical impact on the target literacy outcome domain is indirect and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: One-Topic-Doesn’t-Fit-All: Transcreating Reading Comprehension Test for Personalized Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large-language-model-generated personalized reading comprehension materials can improve English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning outcomes by aligning reading passages with students’ interests. The authors argue that EFL reading materials are often culturally or topically mismatched to learners, which may reduce engagement and comprehension. They focus on reading comprehension and motivation, asking whether interest-aligned transcreated texts can support better performance and sustain motivation when students later encounter less interesting materials.

The intervention is a structured "personalized transcreation" pipeline built with OpenAI’s gpt-4o. Starting from passages and multiple-choice questions in the RACE-C dataset, the system extracts passage topics, classifies question types using Bloom’s taxonomy, identifies linguistic features, and then rewrites passages and questions so they are semantically aligned with each learner’s interests while preserving linguistic difficulty and cognitive demand. An English expert validated the generated materials and corrected the small number of unanswerable items. In the experiment, one group received transcreated passages matched to their interests, while a comparison group received transcreated passages on randomly assigned topics.

The study was conducted with 20 Korean college EFL learners at a college in South Korea. Students were divided into two groups of 10 with similar TOEFL profiles. Both groups first completed a transcreated test and then an original test with less-preferred topics. Quantitative outcomes included comprehension test scores, turnaround time, and the Instructional Materials Motivation Survey (IMMS); qualitative data came from open-ended written reflections analyzed thematically.

The main conclusion is that personalized, interest-aligned reading materials were associated with better comprehension gains, stronger performance on higher-order analytical questions, faster completion times on the later test, and better retention of motivation than non-personalized materials. However, the evidence comes from a very small, single-site higher-education sample and captures only short-term effects. The paper supports the promise of generative AI for personalized literacy-related instruction, but it does not provide K-12 evidence and does not test long-term learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small controlled experiment with n=20 and a non-K-12 college EFL sample, using group comparison but without a clearly randomized K-12 causal design, reported effect sizes, or strong external validity for the target population. It provides suggestive causal evidence with substantial limitations, so it does not meet green-tier rigor for the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings are directionally positive for reading comprehension, motivation retention, and efficiency, but effect sizes are not reported and the sample is very small and not K-12. The magnitude therefore remains unclear for the target school-age literacy population.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated personalization of EFL reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions so that passages are transcreated to match each learner’s stated topic interests while preserving linguistic features and question structure.
GPT-4o is used behind the scenes to generate and transcreate reading passages and questions for personalized assessment/instruction, though students do not interact dialogically with the model.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled comparison with Korean EFL college learners, the group receiving interest-aligned personalized reading materials improved from 73.33±15.12 to 86.67±8.28 on reading comprehension tests, while the group receiving randomly assigned transcreated materials showed a smaller, non-significant change from 76.50±11.11 to 83.00±9.39. The personalized group also showed larger gains on higher-order Analyze questions (+1.33±0.71 out of 5) than the non-personalized group (+0.00±0.45), suggesting better performance on analytical reading comprehension items.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension test scores on two 20-item EFL reading assessments derived from RACE-C, including performance on Analyze-level multiple-choice questions
finding.std_deviation: Test 1 personalized group 15.12; Test 2 personalized group 8.28; Test 1 comparison group 11.11; Test 2 comparison group 9.39; Analyze gain SDs 0.71 and 0.45

finding.finding_summary: Students exposed first to personalized reading materials retained motivation better across the shift to less engaging texts, with IMMS scores changing only from 4.68±0.66 to 4.61±1.04, compared with a larger decline in the non-personalized group from 4.82±0.38 to 4.44±0.85. Confidence increased in the personalized group (4.30±0.66 to 4.57±1.19) but decreased in the comparison group (5.01±0.82 to 4.30±0.66), and qualitative reflections described higher engagement and sustained interest among personalized-condition participants.
finding.measure: Instructional Materials Motivation Survey (IMMS) on a 7-point Likert scale, confidence subscale/item, and qualitative written reflections on engagement and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The personalized group completed the follow-up test faster after receiving interest-aligned reading materials, reducing turnaround time from 30.78±7.60 to 27.78±5.30 minutes, whereas the non-personalized group’s time increased from 24.50±11.04 to 32.00±17.77 minutes. This suggests personalized content may improve task efficiency during reading comprehension work.
finding.measure: Test turnaround/completion time in minutes

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Inference Making Questions for Reading Comprehension Assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model can automatically generate reading-comprehension assessment questions that target specific kinds of inference making, an important component of literacy assessment. The authors focus on bridging inference questions because these are central to reading comprehension and can help educators diagnose students’ comprehension difficulties more precisely. The study is motivated by the need for scalable, high-quality reading-comprehension items for school-age learners, especially in grade 3-12 contexts.

The authors first develop a taxonomy of inference-question types for reading comprehension assessments, including pronominal bridging, text-connecting, and gap-filling inferences, and validate it by annotating an existing operational item bank. They then use GPT-4o with few-shot prompting to generate multiple-choice reading-comprehension questions for expository passages, comparing prompting conditions with and without chain-of-thought rationales and with different numbers of examples. Three expert raters evaluated the generated questions on overall item quality, whether each item matched the requested inference type, and whether the model’s reasoning was adequate.

The work is situated in K-12 assessment rather than classroom instruction. The target context is diagnostic reading-comprehension assessment for students in grades 3 through 12, using expository passages similar to those in an ETS-developed assessment. However, the empirical evaluation is based on generated items and expert judgments, not on student learning outcomes or classroom use. The paper discusses implications for educators because better diagnostic items could support more targeted literacy instruction and intervention.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4o can generate many reading-comprehension questions of sufficiently high general quality for potential operational use, but it is much less reliable at generating items that truly match a requested inference type. Across 357 generated questions, 93.8% were judged acceptable in general quality, but only 42.6% matched the intended inference type, and reasoning quality was also limited. The authors conclude that automatic generation combined with human expert review is promising for scalable diagnostic literacy assessment, but current generative AI is not yet reliable enough to replace expert judgment for inference-specific item development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation with a clear methodology and structured human-rating procedure, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental study of K-12 learners and reports no student outcome effects. As an arXiv preprint focused on item-generation performance rather than educational impact, it fits yellow rather than green/blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mixed practical impact: strong gains in assessment-item production efficiency and item quality, but unclear educational impact on students and weak precision in generating the intended inference type. Because no student learning effects are measured, impact remains unclear overall.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automatic generation of multiple-choice reading comprehension assessment items targeting specific inference types (pronominal bridging, text-connecting, gap-filling) for grades 3-12 diagnostic reading assessments using GPT-4o.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated whether GPT-4o could generate reading-comprehension assessment items suitable for grade 3-12 use, rather than whether students' literacy improved. Across 357 generated items, 93.8% were judged by expert raters to be good-quality questions for operational use, but only 42.6% accurately matched the requested inference type, indicating strong item-writing quality but limited construct precision. No student literacy outcome data, effect sizes, or causal estimates on reading achievement were reported.
finding.measure: Expert human ratings of generated reading-comprehension item quality and inference-type accuracy for diagnostic literacy assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that GPT-4o can substantially support scalable assessment development by producing high volumes of acceptable reading-comprehension items: 93.8% of 357 generated items were rated as good quality, with the best condition reaching 96.7% (87/90 items). Authors conclude that automatic generation combined with human review is more scalable than fully manual authoring, though construct-targeting remains imperfect because only 42.6% of items matched the requested inference type.
finding.measure: Expert-rated acceptability of generated assessment items; suitability for operational use; scalability of item generation workflow

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle school students can effectively regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT for science learning. The authors focus on three core question-asking behaviors that are important for meaningful learning with generative AI: recognizing effective versus ineffective prompts, evaluating the quality of AI-generated answers, and deciding whether to continue asking follow-up questions or stop. The study is motivated by concern that generative AI may create an illusion of understanding, encouraging over-reliance and weak metacognitive regulation rather than deeper learning.

The study used six science investigation tasks in which students interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 during a one-hour school session. For each task, students were shown either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, judged whether it was a good question, interacted freely with ChatGPT, rated each AI response for usefulness, and then wrote a short answer in their own words. The researchers also collected questionnaire data on metacognition and attitudes toward AI, and they coded the quality of prompts, AI responses, and final task answers. The design did not compare ChatGPT against business-as-usual instruction or a non-AI alternative; instead, it analyzed variation in students' interaction quality and its association with outcomes.

Participants were 63 French students aged 14-15 recruited from four middle-school institutions in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. The setting was school-based during normal class hours, with students working individually on laptops while task materials were also provided on paper. The subject area was science inquiry rather than literacy. Researchers monitored use in real time for safety, but there was no teacher-led instructional intervention or formal teacher training component.

The main conclusion is that students showed weak metacognitive regulation when using ChatGPT. On average, they performed near chance in distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts and in evaluating high-quality versus low-quality AI answers. They rarely asked follow-up questions, often stopped inquiry prematurely, and achieved only moderate task success despite unrestricted AI access. More positive attitudes toward AI were associated with poorer prompt and answer discrimination, while stronger metacognitive regulation predicted better sensitivity to prompt quality. The authors argue that effective AI literacy education should emphasize metacognitive regulation and epistemic vigilance, not just technical familiarity with AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear measures and analyses, but it is a single-group observational/correlational design without a causal comparator, random assignment, or quasi-experimental counterfactual. It therefore provides useful descriptive evidence about how students use ChatGPT, but limited causal evidence on impact versus business-as-usual or non-AI alternatives.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Observed outcomes under ChatGPT-supported inquiry were generally weak or negative: students performed at chance on key regulation measures and achieved only moderate science-task success despite unrestricted AI access. Because no positive causal effect is demonstrated and the central findings emphasize over-reliance and poor inquiry regulation, the practical impact is best classified as negative/no demonstrated benefit.

interventions.use_case: Middle school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as an unrestricted conversational inquiry tool during science investigation tasks; the study examined students’ prompt quality judgments, evaluation of AI answers, follow-up questioning, and resulting conceptual understanding.

finding.finding_summary: In a single-group study of French middle school students (N=63, ages 14–15), science task performance with unrestricted ChatGPT access was only moderate: the mean success rate across six investigation problems was 0.51 (SD=0.25), despite tasks being solvable with effective prompting. Success was higher when students obtained more expert-rated high-level AI answers (β=0.52, p<0.001), better discriminated answer quality (β=0.10, p<0.001), and asked follow-up questions after low-level answers (β=0.40, p=0.004), indicating that weak regulation of AI-supported inquiry constrained science understanding.
finding.measure: Binary-coded success on six science investigation tasks; final written explanations judged for depth, clarity, accuracy, and alignment to the problem

finding.finding_summary: Students showed near-chance ability to regulate inquiry with ChatGPT. Prompt-quality discrimination was low (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.80; one-sample t=1.77, p=0.08), answer-quality discrimination was also at chance (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.20; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions (22 total follow-ups across 6 tasks). Higher metacognitive regulation was associated with better prompt sensitivity (r=0.30, p=0.022), whereas more positive AI attitudes predicted worse prompt discrimination (β=-0.39, p=0.015) and worse answer evaluation (β=-0.30, p=0.018).
finding.measure: Signal-detection sensitivity (d′) for prompt and answer discrimination, counts of follow-up questions, metacognition questionnaire (Jr. MAI), AI attitude scales, path/correlation analyses

finding.finding_summary: Behavioral persistence and self-regulatory engagement during AI-mediated inquiry were weak. Even when students identified an answer as unsatisfactory, they asked follow-up questions only 31.8% of the time, and students who saw AI as more useful and effortless were less likely to regulate inquiry deeply, while more critical perceptions of AI fairness/usefulness and higher perceived effort predicted more follow-up behavior (β values approximately -0.33, -0.26, and 0.30, respectively).
finding.measure: Follow-up questioning/persistence during QA cycles; AI perception subscales related to fairness, usefulness, and effort

paper_profiles.title: Automated Scoring for Reading Comprehension via In-context BERT Tuning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses automated scoring of open-ended reading comprehension responses, focusing on whether a single language-model-based scorer can accurately score student answers across multiple reading comprehension items rather than training a separate model for each item. The authors argue that standard automated scoring approaches are inefficient for reading comprehension because multiple items may share the same passage, and item-specific models fail to exploit this linkage. The work was developed as the authors’ solution to the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) automated scoring challenge.

The intervention studied is a technical scoring approach called meta-trained BERT with in-context tuning. The model uses a shared BERT-based architecture that takes as input the student response, question text, passage-related information, and in-context examples consisting of prior student responses paired with scores. The authors compare this approach against several baselines, including feature-engineering models, LSTM models, item-specific BERT models, a multi-task BERT model, and variants with and without passage/question/context inputs. Performance is evaluated using five-fold cross-validation on the challenge training data and quadratic weighted kappa as the main outcome metric.

The population consists of grade 4 and grade 8 students whose human-scored reading comprehension responses appear in the NAEP challenge dataset. The dataset includes 20 reading comprehension items, with over 18,000 responses per item on average, drawn from U.S. NAEP assessment data. The context is large-scale educational assessment rather than classroom instruction, and the task is scoring students’ literacy-related constructed responses rather than improving literacy outcomes directly.

The main conclusion is that the shared in-context BERT model outperforms non-language-model baselines and modestly improves over item-specific and other BERT-based alternatives, achieving average QWK of 0.841. The gains are strongest for items shared across grades, suggesting that leveraging linkage across related items is beneficial. At the same time, the authors note important limitations: the best-performing model does not truly perform reading comprehension because it effectively relies on the response, question, and in-context examples more than the full passage; it may struggle to generalize to unseen items; it remains somewhat biased across demographic groups; and it offers limited interpretability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical machine-learning evaluation with cross-validation on an assessment dataset, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental study of student learning and lacks a business-as-usual or non-AI instructional comparator. It provides technical performance evidence for automated scoring, with some subgroup bias analysis, but not strong educational effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest, clear gains in operational scoring performance relative to other automated scoring models, but impact is limited to assessment efficiency rather than demonstrated literacy improvement for students. For the user’s literacy-effect question, educational impact remains unclear because no student achievement effects are estimated.

interventions.use_case: Automated scoring of K-12 open-ended reading comprehension responses on NAEP grade 4 and grade 8 items using a shared in-context BERT model to approximate human scoring and reduce grading effort.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a shared in-context BERT automated scoring model improves scoring accuracy over alternative automated scoring baselines while potentially reducing model storage and human grading effort. On the NAEP training data across 20 items, meta-trained BERT with in-context tuning achieved average QWK=0.841 versus 0.828 for item-specific BERT(response), 0.833 for BERT in-context, and 0.833 for BERT multi-task; human inter-rater agreement was 0.878. The model is presented as replacing 20 separate item-specific models with one shared model, reducing storage requirements by about 20x.
finding.measure: Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) agreement with human scores; model storage scalability; implied grading-efficiency gains
finding.study_size: ~20 items; average >18,000 human-scored responses per item
finding.effect_size: QWK improvement of +0.013 over BERT(response) and +0.008 over BERT in-context/multi-task

finding.finding_summary: Although the task domain is reading comprehension, the paper does not test whether the system improves students' literacy learning. Instead, it evaluates automated scoring accuracy on reading-comprehension responses, and the authors explicitly note that the best-performing model does not actually master reading comprehension or improve student outcomes. No causal or quasi-experimental evidence on reading comprehension, writing quality, revision, or literacy achievement is provided.
finding.measure: Automated scoring agreement on reading-comprehension constructed responses, not student learning outcomes
finding.study_size: ~20 items; average >18,000 human-scored responses per item

paper_profiles.title: Can LLMs Grade Short-Answer Reading Comprehension Questions? An Empirical Study with a Novel Dataset
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative large language models can accurately grade short-answer reading comprehension responses, addressing a practical problem in formative literacy assessment: open-ended questions are informative but burdensome for teachers to score consistently and quickly. The study also introduces a new short-answer reading comprehension dataset from Ghana, motivated by the lack of publicly available datasets from low- and middle-income countries and the need to test AI systems beyond the high-income contexts on which they are often developed and benchmarked.

The approach was an empirical evaluation of several prompting configurations of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 for automated short-answer grading. Models were given a passage, a reading comprehension question, and a student answer, then asked to classify the answer as correct/incorrect or incorrect/partially correct/correct. The authors compared zero-shot and few-shot prompting and assessed agreement with expert human ratings using F1 and weighted kappa metrics. The work did not test effects on student literacy learning; instead, it tested the grading performance, reliability, and possible demographic bias of the models.

The population consisted of 162 students in Ghana ages 9 to 18, with 130 students completing written reading comprehension assessments and 48 providing spoken responses. Students completed reading tasks based on released 2016 PrePIRLS items, including a 400-word fictional story followed by short-answer comprehension questions. Responses were transcribed and scored by human raters to create ground-truth labels. The context is literacy assessment in an LMIC setting, with particular relevance to formative reading comprehension assessment.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4, especially with few-shot prompting, achieved very strong agreement with human raters and near-parity with expert grading, including QWK of 0.92 on the 3-class task and LWK of 0.89 on the 2-class task. GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5, and few-shot prompting modestly improved performance. The authors found weaker performance on partially correct answers and observed very high but not perfect repeatability across reruns. They did not detect statistically significant differences in misclassification by gender or English-at-home status, though they caution that the sample was limited. Overall, the paper concludes that generative LLMs show strong promise for grading short-answer formative literacy assessments, especially in low-stakes settings, but generalizability and practical deployment constraints remain important concerns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmarking study with a clear methodology and real student data, but it is not a causal or quasi-experimental evaluation of student learning outcomes versus a comparator condition. It supports validity and feasibility of an AI assessment tool rather than causal impact on K-12 literacy achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong operational promise and scoring accuracy, but it does not estimate effects on students' literacy outcomes, engagement, or achievement relative to business-as-usual or non-AI alternatives. As a result, educational impact is promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Generative LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) automatically grade K-12 students' short-answer reading comprehension responses for formative literacy assessment, compared against expert human raters.

finding.finding_summary: On a novel Ghanaian dataset of short-answer reading comprehension responses from secondary-age students, GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved near-human scoring performance for literacy assessment: QWK=0.92 on the 3-class rubric and LWK=0.89 on the 2-class rubric, with average F1=0.88-0.95 depending on task. The study size was 1,068 student responses from 162 students (130 completing the written assessment), and the model matched or slightly exceeded expert-human agreement on the 3-class task (human QWK=0.91), suggesting strong validity for automated scoring of reading-comprehension items rather than direct gains in student literacy.
finding.measure: Agreement and classification accuracy of LLM grading on short-answer reading comprehension items versus expert human ratings (QWK, LWK, precision, recall, F1)

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that GPT-4 can automate grading of open-ended formative reading-comprehension responses with near-expert accuracy using minimal prompt engineering, implying reduced teacher marking burden and greater feasibility of using short-answer formative assessment at scale. This efficiency finding is indirect but empirically grounded in high agreement with human raters across 1,068 responses, with GPT-4 few-shot reaching QWK=0.92 and LWK=0.89.
finding.measure: Automated grading performance as a proxy for feasibility and teacher workload reduction in formative assessment

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing across subject areas. The central question is the extent to which the tool can help students improve writing through formative feedback aligned to teacher expectations. The study is motivated by concerns about declining writing performance and by the limited evidence on how generative AI feedback tools function in secondary school settings.

CyberScholar is a rubric-aligned AI assistant designed to provide formative feedback on student writing. Unlike generic AI tools, it was configured using teachers’ instructional materials, prompts, and rubrics through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering so that feedback reflected classroom content and evaluation criteria. The study used an exploratory multiple-case qualitative design with observations, surveys, and interviews, alongside iterative development during pilot implementation.

The pilot involved 121 students and 4 teachers in four U.S. public schools: one middle school and three high schools. The participating classes included English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History in Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11. Schools represented varied socioeconomic contexts in the Midwest and Northwest United States. Although all 121 students used the tool and revised writing with AI feedback, post-survey data came from 54 students and 3 teachers, and interviews were completed with 8 students and 1 teacher.

The main conclusion is that students and teachers perceived CyberScholar as a useful support for writing, especially because it delivered detailed, specific feedback, enabled interactive follow-up questions, and made rubric criteria more visible during revision. Students reported perceived improvements in grammar, transitions, argument clarity, conclusions, and overall writing quality. At the same time, the paper notes limitations including exploratory scope, convenience sampling, small numbers of schools and classrooms, inconsistent AI ratings in some cases, and the absence of causal comparison or long-term outcome evidence. The authors emphasize that the tool is intended to complement, not replace, teacher feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative multiple-case pilot with convenience sampling, no control/comparison group, low post-survey completion relative to participants, and no standardized pre/post causal outcome analysis. It provides useful implementation evidence but does not meet causal or quasi-experimental standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact on student writing and engagement based mainly on perceptions and illustrative cases, with no reported effect sizes or rigorous comparative estimates. The direction is generally positive, but the magnitude of impact is not established.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI writing feedback tool (CyberScholar) providing rubric-aligned formative feedback on student drafts across ELA, social studies, and history assignments in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11.
CyberScholar allowed some students to ask follow-up questions and engage in dialogic clarification about revision suggestions during writing improvement.
GenAI writing assistant used to help students revise grammar, transitions, sentence structure, clarity, conclusions, and argument presentation in school writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In this exploratory pilot, students generally perceived CyberScholar as helpful for improving writing quality, especially through detailed, rubric-aligned feedback on grammar, transitions, conclusions, clarity, and argumentation. Evidence is based on qualitative themes, selected student examples, and post-survey responses rather than standardized writing assessments; 23 students explicitly reported perceived writing improvement, 19 praised detailed feedback, and one illustrative case showed rubric score improvement after revision, but no causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Post-survey responses, interviews, classroom observations, qualitative coding of student perceptions of writing improvement, and illustrative rubric score changes on revised drafts
finding.study_size: n=121 participants in implementation; post-survey n=54 students; interviews n=8 students and n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable engagement with the tool, particularly valuing its interactivity and willingness to use it again. Of post-survey respondents, 36 students said they would like to use CyberScholar again, while 11 were hesitant; qualitative comments suggested the conversational feedback process made revision more engaging, though no validated engagement scale or causal comparison was used.
finding.measure: Post-survey willingness to reuse the tool, interview comments about engagement and interactivity, classroom observations
finding.study_size: post-survey n=54 students; full implementation n=121

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that CyberScholar may support self-regulation, metacognition, and revision-oriented reflection by making feedback dialogic and tied to rubric criteria. This conclusion is inferred from qualitative themes and participant comments about using feedback iteratively, asking clarifying questions, and identifying where to focus revisions, but no direct validated measure of metacognition or critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview and survey data on revision practices, follow-up questioning, self-directed learning, and perceived understanding of rubric criteria
finding.study_size: n=121 implementation participants; analyzable post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students and n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: Participants described the tool as providing quick feedback and potentially saving time relative to peer review or self-analysis, and the authors suggest it may help support teacher workload by delivering timely formative comments. However, this was not directly tested with time-on-task or workload metrics, so evidence for efficiency gains remains perception-based and preliminary.
finding.measure: Qualitative comments about speed, convenience, and perceived time savings; teacher and student post-surveys/interviews

paper_profiles.title: Experimenting with Generative AI: Does ChatGPT Really Increase Everyone’s Productivity?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, improves user productivity across tasks that are outside the model’s strongest commonly studied domains. Rather than focusing on English writing or Python/SQL coding, the authors examine performance on Thai-language writing analysis tasks and math/data analysis tasks using Stata, asking whether ChatGPT improves task quality and speed for all users or whether benefits vary by student characteristics.

The intervention was access to ChatGPT during task completion, compared directly against completing equivalent tasks without ChatGPT. The study used an experimental within-subject design with counterbalancing: 121 economics undergraduates completed writing analysis and math/data analysis task sets both with and without ChatGPT, and task order and set order were randomized across four groups to reduce order effects and task-set bias. Outcomes were objective task scores out of 10, averaged across three expert raters, and time to completion under a 20-minute session cap. Participants also completed a background questionnaire including grades and self-rated skills.

The study was conducted with economics students from Chulalongkorn University and Thammasat University in Thailand. The writing tasks included brainstorming, reading and giving feedback on texts, composing tweets, and summarizing documents in Thai. The math/data tasks included Stata coding for visualization, variable generation, regression, hypothesis testing, and equation derivation. Although the broader research topic here concerns K-12 literacy, this paper does not study school-age populations; it studies university students in a higher education context.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT improved average performance and reduced completion time overall, but benefits were unevenly distributed. Average writing scores increased by 0.43 points and math/data scores by 1.65 points, while completion times decreased in both domains. However, 34% of students did not improve on writing tasks and 42% did not improve on math/data tasks. Higher-ability students, proxied by econometrics grades, tended to perform worse with ChatGPT on writing analysis tasks, while students with stronger digital skills tended to benefit more, especially in math/data analysis. The authors argue that generative AI can raise productivity on average, but its value depends on task domain and user characteristics, underscoring the continuing importance of human skill and digital competence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a causal experiment with randomized order/task-set assignment and within-subject comparison of ChatGPT versus no-ChatGPT conditions, which strengthens internal validity. However, it is not K-12, uses a small university sample from two Thai institutions, and reports limited design details typical of a strong peer-reviewed RCT for education evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Average impacts are positive but heterogeneous and reported mostly as raw score/time differences rather than standardized effect sizes; literacy gains appear modest and a substantial minority did not benefit or did worse. Relevance to the K-12 literacy question is also limited because the sample is higher education, not school-age students.

interventions.use_case: Students used ChatGPT as a generative writing assistant for Thai-language writing analysis tasks, including brainstorming, reading and giving feedback on texts, composing tweets, and summarizing documents.
Students interacted directly with ChatGPT as a general-purpose conversational generative AI to support task completion across writing analysis and quantitative/data-analysis tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized within-subject experiment with 121 university economics students, ChatGPT use increased average scores on Thai writing analysis tasks by 0.43 points out of 10 and reduced completion time by 1.73 minutes (from 19.19 to 17.46 minutes). However, 41 of 121 students (34%) did not improve, and higher-ability students, proxied by econometrics grades, showed significantly smaller gains or worse performance when using ChatGPT (OLS coefficient about -0.54 to -0.57 on score difference; p<0.10; LPM and logistic models also significant).
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing analysis score (0-10 average of 3 raters) and task completion time for Thai-language tasks including brainstorming, feedback, tweet composition, and summarization
finding.std_deviation: Score Diff SD=1.98; Time Diff SD=3.43

finding.finding_summary: Across tasks, ChatGPT improved efficiency by reducing time to completion while also raising average performance. For writing analysis, mean completion time fell by 1.73 minutes (19.19 without ChatGPT vs. 17.46 with ChatGPT), and for math/data analysis, time fell by 0.99 minutes (18.26 vs. 17.27), indicating productivity gains under a 20-minute task limit.
finding.measure: Task completion time in minutes under timed experimental conditions; paired with task scores
finding.std_deviation: Writing Time Diff SD=3.43; Math/Data Time Diff SD=2.90

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests heterogeneous effects on higher-order performance: students with stronger econometrics achievement performed worse on writing tasks with ChatGPT, whereas students with stronger digital skills performed better with ChatGPT, especially in math/data tasks. Because the study operationalizes these as moderators rather than direct outcome measures of critical thinking or metacognition, evidence for durable skills effects is indirect and mixed.
finding.measure: Indirect proxies via heterogeneous treatment effects by econometrics grade and self-rated digital skills, not direct durable-skills assessments
finding.effect_size: Writing: econometrics coefficient about -0.54 to -0.57 on score difference; Math/Data: digital skills coefficient about +0.70 to +0.73 on score difference

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models, especially GPT-4, can accurately grade K-12 students’ short open-ended responses to formative assessment questions. The central problem is that open-response questions can be educationally valuable but are expensive and time-consuming for teachers to score at scale. The study asks whether LLMs can perform this grading task at a level close to expert human raters across different school stages, subjects, and question difficulties.

The researchers built a novel dataset from Carousel, a UK-based online quizzing platform, containing 1,710 student responses to 12 short-answer questions in Science and History. The questions spanned Key Stage 2, Key Stage 3, and Key Stage 4, corresponding roughly to elementary, middle, and high school ages. Student answers were marked by qualified teachers, with disagreements resolved by a third rater to create a ground-truth label of correct versus incorrect. The authors then compared several LLM configurations—GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, each in zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions—on the same binary grading task.

The main finding is that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved Cohen’s kappa of 0.70, close to human interrater agreement of 0.75. GPT-4 substantially outperformed GPT-3.5, largely because it had much higher recall while maintaining strong precision. The paper reports only small differences in model performance by subject, key stage, and question difficulty, suggesting relatively stable performance across the sampled K-12 contexts.

The authors conclude that GPT-4 shows promise as a tool for low-stakes formative assessment in K-12 education, particularly because it can approximate expert teacher scoring much faster than manual grading. However, the study does not test impacts on student literacy or learning outcomes directly; instead, it provides evidence about AI-supported assessment accuracy and efficiency using real student work in a UK online assessment context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmarking study using real K-12 student responses and expert human comparison, but it does not estimate causal effects on student literacy or learning outcomes and lacks a treatment-control or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful performance evidence for automated scoring, not intervention effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful operational benefits and near-human grading accuracy, but impact on student learning is indirect and unclear. No causal effect sizes on literacy achievement, writing quality, or reading outcomes are reported.

interventions.use_case: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 used to automatically score/mark K-12 students' short-answer open-text formative assessment responses in science and history, compared against expert teacher ratings.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved near-human scoring performance while substantially reducing marking time for low-stakes formative assessment. On a dataset of 1,710 student responses, GPT-4 few-shot reached Cohen's kappa=0.70 versus human interrater kappa=0.75; the authors estimate teachers would need at least 11 hours to mark the dataset manually versus about 2 hours using GPT-4 after script setup.
finding.measure: Agreement with expert ground-truth ratings (Cohen's kappa, percent agreement, precision, recall, F1) and estimated teacher time savings for marking
finding.effect_size: kappa=0.70 for GPT-4 few-shot vs human kappa=0.75; percent agreement=0.85

finding.finding_summary: For science short-answer items, the paper reports that model grading performance remained strong and showed only small variation by subject area.
