finding.effect_size: rs=-0.41 for over-reliance vs incorrect-task decision time; rs=0.35 for under-reliance vs correct-task decision time; d=0.78 for increased under-reliance
finding.std_deviation: Decision confidence SD=0.46 intervention vs 0.76 control; total decision time SD=0.77 intervention vs 1.12 control

paper_profiles.title: A Human-Centered Approach to Ethical AI Education in Underresourced Secondary Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how AI education can be designed ethically and equitably for students in under-resourced secondary schools. The authors argue that simple access to AI tools or exposure to AI concepts is insufficient, especially in Title I and Title I-eligible contexts, because such approaches may reproduce inequities and fail to develop students’ ability to reason about fairness, privacy, accountability, and other social consequences of AI. The study asks whether a human-centered course model can support ethical judgment, academic agency, and college-oriented confidence in these settings.

The intervention studied was a college credit-bearing course, Responsible & Ethical AI, offered through a partnership between the University of Notre Dame and the National Education Opportunity Network (NEON). The course used a bichronous model with asynchronous prerecorded instructional content and synchronous discussion-based learning. It emphasized ethical judgment rather than technical mastery, using case analyses, debates, role-plays, reflective writing, and applications of ethical frameworks to real-world AI issues such as bias, privacy, surveillance, automation, and generative AI. Instruction was supported by school-based co-teachers and undergraduate near-peer teaching fellows, with teaching fellows also grading work under faculty supervision.

The population included nearly 180 high school students from 12 Title I and Title I-eligible U.S. high schools, along with 8 co-teachers and 12 teaching fellows. The schools served largely low-income and historically marginalized student populations across multiple states. The paper reports end-of-course survey data from students, co-teachers, and teaching fellows, combining Likert-scale responses and open-ended reflections. Because teaching fellows were undergraduate students serving instructional roles, they are also part of the studied population.

The main conclusions are that students reported strong academic agency, high support and comfort in the learning environment, and especially strong engagement with ethical reasoning about AI tradeoffs. Co-teachers and teaching fellows also described the course as rigorous, meaningful, and supported by the relational structure of mentorship and dialogue. The authors conclude that ethical judgment can be intentionally taught as a core outcome of AI education and that human-centered supports such as mentorship, synchronous discussion, and local classroom facilitation are important equity mechanisms in under-resourced schools. However, the evidence is descriptive rather than causal because it relies on self-reported end-of-course survey data without a control group or pre/post comparison.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods program evaluation using end-of-course self-report surveys and qualitative reflections, with descriptive statistics and triangulation across stakeholder groups. It lacks a control group, pre-post baseline, direct learning measures, and causal identification, so it fits correlational/qualitative evidence rather than rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings are directionally positive and especially relevant for a priority population—students in Title I and Title I-eligible schools—but impact magnitude is unclear because no causal effect sizes or validated pre-post gains are reported. The evidence suggests promising but not well-quantified impact.

interventions.use_case: Bichronous AI literacy and ethics course delivered through Canvas with prerecorded instructional content, structured assignments, and synchronous discussion sessions for secondary students in Title I and Title I-eligible schools.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the Responsible & Ethical AI course reported strong perceived preparedness for college-level academic work and engagement with course content in AI ethics/civics-type subject matter. Student survey composites showed high academic agency (mean=4.37, SD=0.74) and high judgment-oriented AI engagement (mean=4.65, SD=0.60) on 5-point scales, based on 122 student responses; however, these are self-reported descriptive outcomes without pre-post comparison or causal estimates.
finding.measure: End-of-course student Likert survey composites on academic agency and AI judgment-oriented engagement in a college-credit AI ethics course

finding.finding_summary: The course was associated with positive self-reported durable skill development, especially ethical reasoning, applying learning to new cases, weighing multiple viewpoints, planning, help-seeking, and time management. Students rated AI judgment-oriented engagement highly (mean=4.65, SD=0.60) and academic agency highly (mean=4.37, SD=0.74) on 5-point scales; qualitative responses and educator reports converged that students engaged in sophisticated reasoning about fairness, privacy, accountability, and tradeoffs, though no direct performance-based assessment or causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student end-of-course Likert composites and open-ended reflections; educator perceptions of rigor, discussion, and ethical reasoning
finding.study_size: n=122 students; n=8 co-teachers; n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.60 (AI judgment-oriented engagement); SD=0.74 (academic agency); SD=1.12 (postsecondary trajectory expansion)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported a highly supportive and comfortable learning environment and educators perceived strong engagement and meaningfulness. Student ratings were high for learning support (mean=4.59, SD=0.68) and comfortable learning environment (mean=4.79, SD=0.50), while co-teachers rated perceived student engagement at mean=4.25 and course meaningfulness at mean=4.88; these findings suggest positive effects on engagement, confidence, and belonging, but are based on post-course perceptions only.
finding.measure: End-of-course surveys on learning support, comfort, engagement, and perceived meaningfulness
finding.study_size: n=122 students; n=8 co-teachers; n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.68 (learning support); SD=0.50 (comfortable environment); teacher/fellow SDs reported for some items but not all focal student outcomes

finding.finding_summary: At the implementation level, the course achieved very high completion and was successfully delivered across 12 underresourced U.S. secondary schools through a university-nonprofit partnership model. Nearly 180 students completed the course with a 97.8% completion rate, suggesting feasibility and institutional viability of this human-centered AI education model in Title I and Title I-eligible contexts, though no comparison benchmark was provided.
finding.measure: Program completion rate and stakeholder perceptions of college preparation and postsecondary trajectory expansion
finding.study_size: nearly n=180 course completers; survey subsamples n=122 students, n=8 co-teachers, n=12 teaching fellows
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.12 for student postsecondary trajectory expansion; other implementation metrics not reported with SD

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Program Alongside AI: Critical Thinking, AI Ethics, and Gendered Patterns of German Secondary School Students
paper_profiles.venue: 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE-SEET ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary school students critically engage with generative AI tools in programming and how they perceive ethical responsibility when using those tools. The authors argue that most prior work has focused on university students, leaving a gap in understanding how younger learners—who are encountering programming alongside GenAI early in their development—approach issues such as trust, responsibility, privacy, and code comprehension. The study also examines whether these patterns differ by gender in the German context, where AI use is shaped by strong data protection and regulatory discourse.

The study uses a survey-based mixed-methods design combining Likert-scale items with open-ended questions. Survey items measured programming and AI tool usage, critical thinking practices in AI-assisted programming, and ethical learning related to AI. Quantitative analyses described response distributions and tested gender differences with chi-square tests, while qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. The paper does not test an instructional intervention; rather, it examines students’ existing practices and perceptions while attending extracurricular software development workshops.

Participants were 84 German secondary school students aged 16–19 attending one-day and five-day extracurricular software development workshops. All reported using GenAI tools for programming, primarily ChatGPT, for tasks such as code generation and debugging. The context was informal rather than regular school instruction, with students working collaboratively on small software projects in Germany. The sample was composed of students already interested in computer science and likely more motivated and tech-engaged than the broader student population.

The main conclusion is that students show an “AI paradox”: they express strong ethical awareness about transparency, accountability, legal standards, privacy, and testing, yet many also report practices that may undermine learning, such as integrating AI-generated code they do not fully understand. Boys were more likely to use AI frequently and to consult AI before teammates, while girls were more skeptical of AI outputs and more likely to emphasize peer collaboration and accountability. The authors conclude that software engineering education should strengthen critical AI literacy by connecting ethical principles to concrete programming practice, including code explanation, privacy-conscious workflows, and collaborative review.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-method study based primarily on self-reported survey data with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and thematic analysis, not a causal design. It provides useful direct K-12 evidence but meets only limited credibility criteria because there is no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison and no objective learning outcome measure.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful but mixed associations, especially around durable skills and ethical awareness, with medium gender-effect sizes on selected attitudes/behaviors but no direct achievement effect estimates. Overall impact is unclear because outcomes are perceptual and behavioral rather than demonstrated learning gains.

interventions.use_case: Secondary school students use general-purpose generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and similar tools for AI-assisted programming tasks including code generation, debugging, explanation, and problem-solving support during software development workshops.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory mixed-method survey of German secondary school students (n=84, ages 16-19), students reported strong endorsement of some critical-thinking-aligned programming practices such as testing code even if others already tested it (88% agree/strongly agree), checking code for defects (86%), and considering alternative solutions (61%). At the same time, a substantial minority reported risky dependence on AI outputs: 21% agreed they use code they do not fully understand and 32% were neutral, and boys were significantly more likely than girls to ask GenAI before a teammate (chi-square(4)=10.45, p=.034, Cramer's V=0.42, medium effect), suggesting an 'AI paradox' of ethical/critical awareness coexisting with shallow code integration.
finding.measure: Self-report Likert survey on critical thinking practices in AI-assisted programming; open-ended thematic responses about privacy and AI use
finding.effect_size: Cramer's V=0.42 for gender difference on AI-first help-seeking; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Students showed strong support for institutional and governance-oriented AI ethics principles in programming contexts: 95% agreed GenAI systems should be rigorously tested, 90% agreed users should be informed about purpose/how the system works/limitations, and 88% agreed systems should meet ethical and legal standards. Qualitative responses emphasized shared responsibility across politics, companies, developers, and users, with girls placing somewhat stronger emphasis on accountability; a gender difference was reported for accountability perceptions (chi-square(4)=9.68, p=.046, Cramer's V=0.41, medium effect).
finding.measure: Self-report Likert survey on AI ethics/accountability plus qualitative thematic analysis of responsibility attribution
finding.effect_size: Cramer's V=0.41 for gender difference on accountability item; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In the vocational/computer-science domain of programming education, students reported that GenAI tools are widely used for code creation (78%) and debugging (62%), but the study did not directly measure learning gains, programming performance, or achievement outcomes. Findings instead suggest potential tradeoffs for programming learning, with self-reported quality-assurance behaviors coexisting alongside willingness by some students to integrate incomprehensible AI-generated code.
finding.measure: Programming-related self-reported use patterns and attitudes; no direct academic achievement measure

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary-school English as a foreign language (EFL) students use generative AI text when composing writing, and whether particular patterns of human-AI text integration are associated with better writing quality. The authors frame the study around concerns that AI may both support writing and distort students’ demonstrated proficiency, especially when students rely heavily on AI-generated text. The research questions focus on the linguistic features of AI-generated text embedded in student compositions, the interaction patterns students use with AI-generated text, and whether these patterns benefit different types of learners differently.

The study analyzed 59 compositions written by Hong Kong secondary school students from seven schools with different academic achievement profiles. Students attended a two-hour workshop on attempting a writing task with ChatGPT support, learned either a genre-based or process-based writing approach plus prompt engineering, and then completed a feature article task within two weeks. Students were required to include both their own words and AI-generated text, and to self-highlight which portions came from chatbots. The researchers then conducted content analysis of the compositions, multiple linear regression examining associations between text features and scores, and cluster analysis to identify learner profiles and interaction patterns.

Across the sample, compositions relied heavily on AI text: on average, 63.39% of words were AI-generated, and many compositions contained 70% or more AI-generated text. The main quantitative finding was that total word count—whether AI-generated or human-written—was the strongest predictor of writing scores, whereas the particular chunking pattern of AI text was generally less predictive. However, this relationship differed by academic profile. Students from higher-banding schools appeared better able to benefit from either AI-generated or human-authored words and were more capable of writing independently. In contrast, students from lower-banding schools often relied more heavily on AI-generated text, and revising AI output with their own words was sometimes associated with lower scores.

The authors conclude that generative AI can enhance EFL writing, but benefits are uneven and depend on students’ preexisting writing competence and AI literacy. Higher-achieving students seem better positioned to use AI strategically to support writing, while lower-achieving students may become more dependent on AI without gaining comparable improvement in writing quality. The paper argues that educators should emphasize independent writing ability, process-writing skills, and effective prompting so that AI enhances rather than replaces student writing effort.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear methods, human-rated outcomes, and statistical analyses, but it is observational/correlational without a control group or causal identification strategy. It provides direct secondary-school evidence but only meets limited causal credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially beneficial but heterogeneous associations between generative AI-supported writing and literacy outcomes, with clear tradeoffs by student achievement level and no standardized causal effect size. Overall impact is promising but unclear and uneven, especially for lower-achieving students.

interventions.use_case: Secondary school EFL students used ChatGPT and other generative AI chatbots to co-compose a feature article by integrating AI-generated text with their own writing, including drafting and revision in a machine-in-the-loop writing process.
Students interacted with conversational generative AI chatbots through prompt engineering to generate writing content and support idea development and revision during article composition.

finding.finding_summary: In 59 Hong Kong secondary EFL students composing feature articles with AI support, overall writing quality was mainly predicted by total number of words, whether AI- or human-generated; partial correlations between total score and AI words (0.417, p<0.01) and human words (0.424, p<0.01) were positive. However, benefits differed by learner profile: for students from high-banding schools, scores were more strongly associated with both AI and human word counts (e.g., total score partial correlations 0.578 and 0.544, both p<0.01), whereas for low-banding schools AI word count was not significantly associated with higher scores and human revision of AI text was associated with lower content/organization performance.
finding.measure: Human-rated HKDSE feature article writing scores: content, language, organization, and total score; composition structure including AI-generated vs human-written words and chunks
finding.effect_size: partial correlations reported (e.g., total score with AI words r=0.417; with human words r=0.424; high-band subgroup total score with AI words r=0.578; with human words r=0.544)
finding.std_deviation: Total score SD=3.28; Content SD=1.27; Language SD=1.02; Organization SD=1.10

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests students differed in their ability to independently draft, revise, and strategically integrate AI-generated text, indicating variation in process-writing and AI-literacy-related skills. Cluster analyses identified profiles with high scores under either high or low AI use, but low-achieving students appeared less proficient at revising AI output and more dependent on verbatim AI text, implying uneven development of self-regulated writing and evaluative judgment; no standardized durable-skills effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed interaction patterns with AI-generated text, prompt use, chunk integration, and inferred drafting/revision strategy quality from regression and cluster analysis

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how free generative AI tools such as ChatGPT may affect the development of writing competence and personal writing voice in secondary education. The authors focus on a central tension: AI may support students during writing, but it may also encourage dependency, plagiarism, and reduced engagement in the cognitive work needed to develop authentic literacy skills. The paper asks both how AI can function as a partner in writing development and how schools can prevent uses of AI that undermine learning.

Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention study, the paper presents a conceptual and practice-oriented discussion of how AI might be integrated across phases of the writing process: pre-writing, drafting, revision, feedback, self-assessment, and peer assessment. The authors suggest that AI may be useful for brainstorming, generating counterarguments, clarifying vocabulary, and providing rapid formative feedback on drafts. At the same time, they argue that the core drafting phase should remain centered on students producing text in their own words, and they emphasize process-based assessment, clear task criteria, authentic writing prompts, and controlled testing conditions as ways to preserve learning and authorship.

The population of interest is students in secondary education, especially those in study-preparatory programs, along with teachers responsible for writing instruction. The discussion is grounded largely in the Norwegian and broader Nordic school context, including references to Norwegian secondary students, language arts teaching, and school assessment practices. The paper also draws adjacent evidence from higher education, language learning, and human-AI writing support studies to inform implications for school-age literacy instruction.

The main conclusion is that AI should be treated as a supplementary educational tool rather than a replacement for teacher guidance or student thinking. The authors argue that AI may offer practical benefits such as immediate feedback, support for revision, and reduced teacher workload, but current evidence is insufficient to show that it reliably improves writing competence. They stress significant tradeoffs, including hallucinated information, plagiarism risk, loss of student ownership, weak detection of AI-generated text, and the possibility that overuse could diminish motivation or the development of writing voice. Overall, the paper recommends a balanced approach combining technological controls, thoughtful assignment design, teacher oversight, and an emphasis on critical thinking and authentic expression.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/conceptual paper that synthesizes literature and practical implications but does not present a clear original empirical methodology, sample, or causal design. Although it cites peer-reviewed studies, the paper itself is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful but currently unclear effects of generative AI on writing, feedback, and school assessment, with substantial tradeoffs and no reported effect sizes. Overall impact is uncertain rather than clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT-like generative AI as a conversational writing partner in secondary education for brainstorming, generating counterarguments, giving revision feedback, and supporting self-/peer-assessment during the writing process.
Use of generative AI and adjacent tools such as Grammarly-like writing assistants for editing, grammar/language support, and improving content structure in student writing.
AI-generated formative feedback on student drafts, including paragraphing, topic sentences, tone, and revision suggestions intended to supplement teacher feedback and reduce feedback delays.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a narrative/theoretical discussion rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not report original effect sizes or tested impacts on secondary students' writing outcomes. It synthesizes adjacent evidence suggesting possible literacy benefits from AI for idea generation, revision, structure, and feedback, while also emphasizing risks to authentic authorship, writing voice, plagiarism, shallow engagement, and overreliance. The paper explicitly states that there are not yet solid studies clarifying whether AI effectively improves writing competence in secondary education.
finding.measure: not_reported; discussion centers on writing competence, writing voice, revision quality, and feedback processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that generative AI may support critical thinking when used to generate counterarguments, act as a devil's advocate, and support reflective revision, but may also undermine independent thinking if students outsource idea generation or drafting. No original empirical estimates are provided, and the authors frame this as a balance between augmentation and dependency rather than a demonstrated causal effect.
finding.measure: not_reported; discussion centers on critical thinking, self-assessment, reflective revision, and ownership of ideas

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior literature and practical examples suggesting AI can improve feedback speed and potentially reduce teacher workload by providing immediate formative feedback on drafts and handling routine support tasks. However, it also notes that human educators provide better-quality feedback than generative AI in adjacent research, so efficiency gains may come with quality tradeoffs and require close teacher oversight.
finding.measure: not_reported; discussion centers on immediacy of feedback, teacher workload, and handling of routine instructional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights institutional implications of generative AI for assessment, cheating detection, task design, and exam security in secondary schools. It argues that schools may need process-based assessment, authentic task redesign, and technological controls because AI-generated text is difficult to detect and can outperform real students in some adjacent higher-education assessment contexts, but it provides no original K-12 causal evidence.
finding.measure: not_reported; discussion centers on exam integrity, plagiarism detection, assessment design, and school policy responses

paper_profiles.title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.venue: 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on CI for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning and addresses how to introduce computational intelligence concepts to younger learners, especially high-school students, through a co-learning framework that combines human learning with AI and robotics. The authors position the work as part of outreach and education in computational intelligence, with a focus on helping pre-university students understand foundational concepts such as fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation.

The intervention combined lectures and hands-on AIoT workshops built around AI-Fuzzy Markup Language (AI-FML), the IEEE 1855 standard, and co-learning with devices such as the Kebbi Air robot, AIoT-FML-LT, and MoonCar. The paper also presents a machine-human co-learning model and a learning framework for workshops in which students used AI-FML learning tools, built or trained fuzzy-system knowledge and rule bases, interacted with robots, and explored real-world applications such as intelligent air conditioning, speaking English, and brain-computer interface applications.

The participant pool was broad rather than limited strictly to high-school students. Of 214 registrants, the sample included elementary, junior high, senior high, university, and graduate students, as well as teachers, parents, and other attendees from Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and a small number from other countries. The event was conducted physically in Taiwan and virtually through Zoom, making the setting blended. Outcomes reported included attendance, certificate completion, submitted reports, and participant feedback.

The main conclusion is that the summer school and AIoT workshops were successful in engaging participants and helping them understand core computational intelligence concepts. Based on short reports and feedback surveys, the authors conclude that participants gained understanding of computational intelligence, fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation, and that the workshop provided useful experience applying AI-FML tools to real-world problems. However, the evidence is primarily descriptive and based on reports and feedback rather than rigorous learning assessments or controlled comparisons.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a descriptive report of a summer school and workshop with informal feedback, attendance counts, and anecdotal comments. It lacks a clear empirical study design, validated outcome measures, comparison group, or statistical analysis, so it does not meet credibility criteria for stronger evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests positive but unclear impact on participants' understanding and motivation, with no reported effect sizes or rigorous causal evidence. Reported benefits are promising but too weakly measured to justify green or blue impact tiers.

interventions.use_case: High-school and younger students interacted with the AI-FML robot Kebbi Air during an AIoT workshop to explore fuzzy-system outputs, robot expressions, and human-robot co-learning activities.

Students used the AI-FML learning platform, AI-FML Lab, and Blockly-based tools to learn computational intelligence concepts and experiment with AIoT applications such as intelligent air conditioning, speaking English, and BCI demonstrations.
The workshop asked students to simulate robot perception/cognition and vary fuzzy-system and PSO parameters to observe effects on learning performance and system behavior in applied AIoT scenarios.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants' short reports and feedback surveys indicated they understood principles of computational intelligence, neural networks, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary computation to a higher degree than in previous summer schools. However, no validated pre/post assessment, statistical test, or effect size is reported, so the evidence is descriptive rather than causal. The total number attending at least two-thirds of lectures/workshops was 78, with 80 short reports and 77 feedback surveys submitted.
finding.measure: Participant short reports, feedback surveys, attendance/certificate completion, and informal judgments of understanding of computational intelligence concepts
finding.study_size: n=78 attendees completing at least two-thirds; n=80 reports; n=77 surveys

finding.finding_summary: Teacher and organizer feedback suggests the summer school and AIoT workshop increased student motivation and interest in computational intelligence, with comments describing the event as stimulating involvement in rapidly evolving fields and fostering future research interest. These findings are based on anecdotal feedback rather than standardized motivation measures, and no comparative statistics are provided.
finding.measure: Anecdotal teacher comments and participant feedback about motivation, engagement, and interest
finding.study_size: n=77 feedback surveys; qualitative remarks from teachers/participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents the summer school as a successful outreach model that expanded computational intelligence exposure to high-school and even elementary students across Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and other countries. Institutional reach is evidenced by 214 registrants and international participation, but the paper does not provide formal evaluation of policy change, sustained adoption, or downstream institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Registration counts, cross-country participation, certificate completion, and narrative claims about outreach and alignment with STEM/education policy goals

paper_profiles.title: Exploring AI-Generated Text in Student Writing: How Does AI Help?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI-generated text contributes to secondary school English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students’ story writing. The core question is not whether AI can write for students, but how students actually use AI-generated text inside their own compositions and whether different patterns of use are associated with better human-rated writing quality. The authors frame the work as human-AI collaborative writing, or “machine-in-the-loop,” where students retain full agency and may choose whether and how to incorporate AI outputs.

The intervention involved two workshops in which students from two Hong Kong secondary schools first learned to build simple AI natural language generation tools using Python, Gradio, Hugging Face, and open-source language models, and then used those tools to write short stories. Students had 45 minutes in the second workshop to write with AI support, using prompting and editing strategies, and later could complete stories for submission to a contest. The analyzed dataset consisted of 23 stories under 500 words, with students marking which text was their own and which was AI-generated. Researchers then analyzed counts and types of AI-generated text, and experts scored each story on content, language, and organization.

The population was 23 Hong Kong secondary school students from two schools serving students with different prior academic achievement levels. The context was EFL creative writing in school workshops rather than a controlled experiment. Quantitative analyses included descriptive statistics, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to identify learner profiles based on writing quality and AI usage patterns.

The main conclusion is that both human-written word count and AI-generated word count were significantly associated with higher writing scores, but benefits depended strongly on student competence and strategy. More proficient writers generally relied less on AI yet used it more effectively through editing and selective integration. Some lower-performing students appeared to benefit somewhat, especially in language quality, but heavy AI use did not guarantee strong writing and did not erase underlying differences in writing ability. The authors argue for differentiated pedagogy: stronger writers may benefit from fine-grained instruction in prompting and revision, while weaker writers need more foundational writing support alongside guidance in using AI text strategically.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, single-group correlational study of secondary students with expert scoring and regression/cluster analyses, but no control group, randomization, or causal identification. It provides direct K-12 evidence, yet credibility is limited by the very small sample and observational design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially beneficial but inconsistent effects of AI-generated text on writing quality, with no standardized effect size and substantial heterogeneity across students. Impact is therefore unclear rather than convincingly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used self-built AI natural language generation writing tools to generate editable story text and integrate AI-produced passages into short-story compositions during a machine-in-the-loop writing task.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 23 Hong Kong secondary school students, both the number of human-written words and AI-generated words were significantly positively associated with expert-rated writing quality in stories written with AI support. Multiple linear regression showed strong partial correlations between human words and writing scores (Content r_partial=0.937, Language=0.914, Organization=0.943, CLO total=0.951) and moderate positive partial correlations for AI words (Content=0.49, Language=0.537, Organization=0.532, CLO total=0.586), but cluster analyses showed that high AI use did not reliably produce strong writing; some heavy AI users scored highly while others produced short, incomplete, low-scoring stories.
finding.measure: Expert-rated EFL story-writing quality using rubric scores for content, language, organization, CLO total, plus counts of AI-generated words/chunks and total story length
finding.std_deviation: Grand total SD=5.94; CLO SD=4.74; AI words SD=90.56; human words SD=164.69

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an AI-based writing feedback tool, CGScholar AI Helper, can support high school students’ writing development in English Language Arts. The study addresses a gap the authors identify in K-12 research on AI-supported writing, arguing that while AI writing tools are increasingly common, there is limited empirical evidence on their effects for school-age students. The authors are also interested in the design question of how generative AI can be recalibrated for education rather than used as unrestricted "AI in the wild." 

The intervention was a pilot implementation of CGScholar AI Helper, a web-based tool that gives AI-generated feedback on student writing using retrieval-augmented generation and teacher customization. The system was loaded with the teacher’s prompt, rubric, and source readings so that feedback would align with classroom expectations. Students submitted an initial draft of a 200-word comparative paragraph, received AI feedback tied to six rubric criteria, revised, received a second round of AI feedback, and then submitted a final version to the teacher. Data came from students’ initial and revised writing, a student focus group, a teacher post-survey, and researcher observations, analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.

The study took place in one public high school in the Midwest United States in an 11th-grade ELA class serving a socioeconomically underserved community. Six students who consented from a class of twenty-three participated, along with one female ELA teacher. The implementation was embedded in normal classroom instruction around two assigned readings on Indigenous values and culture. The research team interviewed and trained the teacher and students on using the platform, and researchers were present during implementation to provide technical support and observe use.

The authors conclude that CGScholar AI Helper showed promise as a mediated AI writing support tool. Five of the six students improved on at least one rubric criterion after AI feedback, with gains especially in compare/contrast, composing claims, analysis, and introducing/connecting evidence. Student and teacher feedback suggested that the tool provided direct, actionable feedback and motivated revision, which the teacher described as otherwise difficult to elicit. At the same time, the paper notes that the AI feedback was sometimes too long and linguistically complex, and the authors emphasize that the tool is still under development. Overall, the study presents early, direct school-age evidence that rubric-aligned generative AI feedback may support revision and writing development in high school ELA, but only in a very small, single-site pilot without a comparison group.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative case study with one teacher and six consenting 11th-grade students, using draft comparisons, focus groups, observations, and a teacher survey but no control group, randomization, validated outcome instruments, or statistical testing. It provides direct K-12 evidence, but credibility is limited by the tiny sample and descriptive design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unclear impact: most students improved on at least one writing criterion, but gains were uneven, some criteria showed no improvement, and no effect sizes were reported. Given the very small pilot sample of struggling writers in a low-income school, the evidence suggests possible modest benefit but not a quantified or clearly generalizable impact.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-calibrated AI writing feedback for 11th-grade ELA paragraph writing, using a RAG-based system and the teacher's rubric/materials to generate iterative feedback on compare/contrast, claims, evidence, conventions, and analysis.
Generative AI writing support embedded in the CGScholar platform to help students revise drafts through rubric-aligned textual feedback and optional follow-up clarification features.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of 11th-grade ELA writing, 5 of 6 students improved on at least one rubric criterion after receiving CGScholar AI Helper feedback, and 1 student improved on three criteria. Improvements were reported in compare/contrast (3 students), composing defensible claims (2 students), analysis (2 students), and introducing/connecting evidence (1 student), while no improvements were identified for writing conventions or support of evidence; no standardized effect sizes or inferential statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-rubric-aligned AI ratings (0-4 stars) across six writing criteria, comparison of initial vs revised drafts, focus group feedback, teacher post-survey, and researcher observations

finding.finding_summary: Student focus group data and teacher post-survey suggested the tool increased motivation to revise and made revision feel more actionable. Students described the feedback as helpful, direct, and specific, and the teacher reported that the tool encouraged revision, though these findings are perception-based and derived from a very small sample without validated engagement scales.
finding.measure: Student focus group perceptions of helpfulness and revision support; teacher post-survey comments about motivation to revise

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines how different configurations of generative AI support affect students’ writing self-efficacy, with a particular focus on whether the stage of AI intervention matters more than simply whether AI is present. The paper is motivated by a tension in academic writing: generative AI may improve efficiency and confidence, but it may also reduce ownership, agency, and independent writing capacity. The authors specifically ask whether AI support for idea generation, sentence construction, both, or neither produces different self-efficacy patterns over repeated writing tasks.

The intervention was a 2 × 2 experimental design crossing AI support for idea generation and AI support for text construction, yielding four conditions: No AI, Sentence AI, Ideation AI, and Full AI. Participants used ChatGPT under tightly constrained prompts that limited responses to their assigned support type and excluded motivational or evaluative feedback. Students completed two 30-minute argumentative essays in a 100-minute online session, with writing self-efficacy measured after each task on a 0–100 scale. The study also included exploratory qualitative observations from post-task reflections and interaction logs, though these were not formally coded.

The population was 13 Korean undergraduate students, recruited by voluntary response sampling after exclusions from an initial 21 recruits. The context was higher education, not K-12: participants were sophomore- to senior-level undergraduates completing online argumentative writing tasks in Korean via Google Meet. The study was conducted in the Republic of Korea using the free web interface of ChatGPT during November and December 2025.

The main conclusion is that generative AI assistance does not uniformly improve writing self-efficacy; instead, effects depend on where AI enters the writing process. Full AI support produced the highest but largely stable self-efficacy, yet qualitative evidence suggested reduced ownership and authenticity. Ideation-level support appeared most promising, combining relatively high self-efficacy with positive change over time while preserving learners’ sense of writing in their own words. Sentence-level AI support was associated with a consistent decline in self-efficacy across all participants in that condition, suggesting that revision-focused AI may operate as a discouraging comparison standard rather than a scaffold. The authors argue that AI configuration shapes both confidence and agency and that larger, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these pilot findings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot experimental study with a between-subjects design, but only 13 analyzed participants and no statistically conclusive effects; it provides some empirical credibility but substantial precision and generalizability concerns. It is also postsecondary rather than direct K-12 evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Observed effects on writing self-efficacy were potentially large in some comparisons, but estimates were highly imprecise, confidence intervals crossed zero, and findings were mixed across AI configurations. As adjacent postsecondary evidence, it implies possible benefits and risks for literacy support but does not establish clear impact for K-12 populations.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a generative writing assistant for undergraduate argumentative writing, with experimentally varied support at ideation-only, sentence-level revision/drafting, or full-process assistance.
Conversational ChatGPT interaction used to scaffold idea generation and/or text construction through dialogue during essay writing, though not as a full tutor with pedagogical sequencing.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot experiment with 13 Korean undergraduates found that generative AI support affected writing self-efficacy differently by configuration rather than uniformly improving it. Full AI support showed the highest average self-efficacy (M=82.2, SD=6.4) versus no AI (M=61.8, SD=24.0), with a large but imprecise effect (g=1.23, 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]); ideation AI showed the strongest positive change over time (ΔM=+11.1, SD(Δ)=16.2), while sentence-level AI was the only condition with universal decline across participants (5/5 declined; ΔM=-5.7, SD(Δ)=5.6). Because all confidence intervals spanned zero and cell sizes were very small, results are exploratory.
finding.measure: Post-task writing self-efficacy on a 0-100 scale across writing ability, process management, and writing experience subscales, measured after two argumentative writing tasks
finding.effect_size: g=1.23 (Full AI vs No AI); g=0.73 (Full AI vs Sentence AI); g=0.99 (Sentence AI vs No AI); g=0.31 (Ideation AI vs Sentence AI)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for Full AI vs No AI: [-0.60, 3.07]; other pairwise CIs not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Full AI SD=6.4; Ideation AI SD=16.1; Sentence AI SD=7.2; No AI SD=24.0; Ideation AI SD(Δ)=16.2; Sentence AI SD(Δ)=5.6; No AI SD(Δ)=2.4; Full AI SD(Δ)=6.7

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies argumentative writing contexts but measures perceived writing capability rather than direct writing quality gains, so literacy effects are indirect and mixed. Qualitative observations suggested ideation AI preserved students’ use of their own language and agency, while full AI support raised concerns about reduced ownership and personal voice; no standardized writing-performance effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay writing tasks (two essays of 1,000-1,500 Korean characters) with qualitative reflections on voice, ownership, and writing process; no direct scored literacy outcome reported

finding.finding_summary: The study provides exploratory evidence of tradeoffs in learner agency and independence during AI-assisted writing. Full AI support was associated with stable high self-efficacy but qualitative signs of diminished ownership and authenticity, whereas ideation-only AI appeared to support planning while preserving responsibility for sentence construction; sentence-level AI may have undermined confidence via upward comparison to AI output.
finding.measure: Qualitative post-task reflections and ChatGPT interaction logs concerning ownership, authenticity, independent problem solving, and use of personal language during writing

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI chatbots responsibly for learning, rather than simply giving them access to such tools. The authors focus on “prompting literacy,” defined as understanding what AI can do for learning, when it is appropriate to use AI, and how to write effective prompts for different learning situations. The study is motivated by concerns about misuse of AI in schools, including cheating and poor-quality information, alongside the growing demand from educators for practical AI literacy instruction for students.

The intervention was a web-based instructional module for secondary students that used scenario-based practice with an LLM. Students worked through hypothetical learning scenarios in biology, geography, and math, wrote prompts to an AI chatbot, viewed the chatbot’s response, and then received immediate AI-generated rubric-based feedback on the quality of their prompt. The module emphasized active learning and elaborated immediate feedback. The authors conducted two iterative classroom deployments: Study 1 examined the auto-grader’s accuracy, student prompt performance, confidence changes, and learner perceptions; Study 2 revised the assessment design and evaluated whether new true/false and open-ended items better measured prompting literacy than the original multiple-choice questions.

The population consisted of secondary school students in 11 authentic classrooms in East Asia, with teachers facilitating the in-class activity. Study 1 included valid data from 111 students in 6 classrooms; students completed pre/post measures, interacted with the prompting module, and provided open-ended reflections. Teachers were part of implementation as classroom facilitators and were instructed to warn students that the auto-grader could make mistakes. The paper reports classroom-based deployment rather than a controlled comparison against another instructional method.

The main conclusions are that the AI-based auto-grader achieved generally strong grading performance, with average accuracy around 0.92, though it was weaker on some dimensions such as identifying prompt purpose and whether a student was seeking a direct answer. Students improved particularly in including background/context in prompts and reported higher confidence in using AI for learning after the activity. Qualitative findings suggested students learned basic principles of responsible AI use, appreciated the interactive design and immediate feedback, but also experienced challenges related to prompt writing, platform friction, limited scenario diversity, and typing/computer skills. The revised assessment in Study 2 showed better item difficulty and discrimination than the original multiple-choice assessment, supporting further refinement and broader future deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom deployment study with pre/post, correlational, psychometric, and qualitative analyses but no randomized comparison group. It provides direct K-12 evidence in authentic settings, yet causal inference is limited and some reporting is incomplete.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but mostly modest or unclear impacts: confidence improved and one prompting dimension improved significantly, while conceptual test scores showed no effect and effect sizes were not reported. Overall impact is positive but not quantified strongly enough for green or blue.

interventions.use_case: Web-based prompting literacy module for secondary students that lets learners interact with an AI chatbot in biology, geography, and math scenarios to practice responsible AI use for learning.
LLM-based auto-grader that evaluates student-written prompts against rubric dimensions and provides immediate elaborated feedback on prompt quality.
Structured web instructional module delivering scenario-based practice, pre/post assessment, and guided AI literacy activities in classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: The module improved students' prompting literacy performance on at least one targeted dimension: inclusion of background/context information increased significantly from the first to the third practice task (McNemar p=.039). However, no significant gains were found for relevance (p>.90), conciseness (p=.286), or purpose (p=.617), suggesting selective rather than broad-based skill improvement. Study 1 included 111 valid student participants, with 483 unique prompts analyzed for grading-related evaluation.
finding.measure: Student-written prompt quality scored on rubric dimensions (relevance, purpose, conciseness, background, elaboration, no direct answer) across three scenario-based practice tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after the activity, with average self-reported confidence rising by 10.4% and the change significant on a Wilcoxon test (p<.001). Qualitative responses also indicated strong interest in interacting with AI and appreciation for immediate feedback, though some students reported challenges such as typing burden, login issues, and slow system response. The confidence change was reported for the Study 1 classroom deployment with 111 students.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-report confidence item on knowing how to use AI to help learning; open-ended reflections on interest, benefits, and challenges

finding.finding_summary: The AI auto-grader showed satisfactory grading performance, achieving average pass/fail accuracy of 0.92 overall and explanation accuracy averaging 0.95 across rubric dimensions, supporting the feasibility of scalable immediate feedback. Accuracy varied by dimension, with strongest performance in relevance (0.98) and background (0.96) and weaker performance for purpose (0.85) and no direct answer (0.88), indicating useful but imperfect automation. These analyses were based on 483 student prompts from Study 1.
finding.measure: AI auto-grader agreement with human rubric scoring, including pass/fail classification accuracy and explanation accuracy by prompt dimension

finding.finding_summary: Prompting literacy conceptual test performance did not improve from pre- to post-test in Study 1 because of an apparent ceiling effect: both pre- and post-test means were 4.4 out of 6, with no significant difference (p=.377). The authors interpret this as students already having some conceptual understanding of prompt quality despite uneven ability to generate strong prompts. This result was based on the 98 students who completed both tests.
finding.measure: Scenario-based prompting literacy assessment scores (initial six multiple-choice items); assessment quality analyses in Study 2 including difficulty, discrimination, and Cronbach's alpha
finding.study_size: n=98 students for matched pre/post test; Study 2 sample size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students prompt ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots while completing a writing task. The authors focus on the problem that effective use of generative AI for writing requires prompt engineering, yet non-technical users often lack instruction and must learn through trial and error. The study asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge in their prompt engineering pathways during a classroom writing task.

The study uses a qualitative multiple-case design centered on students’ turn-by-turn interactions with chatbots. Four secondary school students completed the same timed blog-writing task using iPads, Google Docs, and the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. Data came primarily from screen recordings, supplemented by the students’ written products. The researchers transcribed and coded each prompt, identifying prompt types such as auto-complete prompts, natural language instructions, questions, search-engine-like prompts, greetings, and combinations of these forms. They then visualized each student’s prompt sequence to analyze patterns within and across cases.

The population consisted of four high-achieving form one students in a Hong Kong secondary school, all using state-of-the-art chatbots for the first time in writing, though they had some prior experience with other generative AI tools. The activity took place in an after-school classroom session lasting up to 45 minutes, taught by the first author. Students received no explicit instruction on chatbot capabilities or prompting before the task, allowing the study to observe natural trial-and-error behavior in a school-age literacy context.

The main conclusion is that students followed distinct prompt engineering pathways, with some pathways appearing more sophisticated than others. Students used a limited set of prompt types and often relied on iterative trial-and-error, sometimes repeating or slightly modifying prompts across different chatbots. The authors argue that these patterns show a need for explicit prompt engineering education in EFL writing classrooms so students can move beyond unsystematic experimentation and better leverage chatbot capabilities. The paper does not evaluate learning gains against a comparison condition; instead, it provides descriptive evidence about how school-age students actually use generative AI during writing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative multiple-case study with clear procedures, coding, and triangulation, but it uses a very small purposive sample (n=4) and does not estimate causal effects on learning outcomes. It provides useful direct secondary-school evidence, but only meets limited credibility criteria under the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful benefits for writing support and prompt engineering skill development, but impact on student literacy outcomes is unclear because no effect sizes, validated outcome gains, or comparison conditions are reported. The practical impact is therefore suggestive but not established.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots (via the POE app, including ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly) for the first time to complete a blog-writing task, with the study examining their prompt engineering pathways during human-AI collaborative writing.
Chatbots were used as writing support tools to generate ideas and text for an English writing assignment, functioning as AI-assisted writing companions rather than as fully instructional tutors.

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative case study found that four secondary EFL students successfully used ChatGPT and similar chatbots to complete the same blog-writing task, but their prompt engineering pathways varied substantially in sophistication, prompt types, and number of turns (36 coded turns across 4 students). The paper does not report standardized writing-quality gains, effect sizes, or comparative achievement outcomes; instead, it concludes that students relied on trial-and-error and often used limited prompting strategies, implying both affordances for writing support and limitations in unaided use.
finding.measure: Prompt content and sequence during completion of a writing task; completed blog entries collected for triangulation

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main empirical finding is that students demonstrated emergent prompt engineering behavior while using chatbots for writing, showing distinct pathways that ranged from simple autocomplete or search-like prompting to more complex prompts combining exemplars, natural-language instructions, and questions. Across 36 coded turns from 4 students, the authors identified six distinct prompt-content types and argued that some students appeared to learn more sophisticated prompting strategies through trial-and-error, supporting the need for explicit prompt engineering education.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of prompt types, sequencing, and sophistication in screen-recorded chatbot interactions

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy intervention can help adolescents use large language models more critically and effectively in schoolwork. The authors focus on a central concern in generative AI for education: students may over-trust fluent but inaccurate AI outputs, accept poor answers too quickly, and offload too much reasoning to the system. The study asks whether explicit instruction about how LLMs work, how they fail, and how to regulate interactions with them can improve students’ problem-solving behavior and performance.

The intervention was a two-hour workshop delivered under regular school conditions. It combined a conceptual component about LLM mechanisms and limitations, including hallucinations, bias, and sycophancy, with procedural guidance on prompting and evaluating responses. Students were taught transferable heuristics such as adding context and constraints, asking follow-up questions, requesting step-by-step explanations, and checking answers for plausibility and consistency. Two days later, students completed six individual science inquiry tasks with access to an LLM-based chatbot. The intervention group completed the workshop beforehand, while the control group completed the same task session without prior training.

The study took place in one French middle school during regular class hours. The final sample included 116 students in grades 8 and 9, ages 13–15. Students worked individually on computers during a 90-minute exercise session. Behavioral measures captured whether students accepted or replaced suggested prompts, whether they asked follow-up questions, and how accurately they judged the correctness of AI answers. Performance was based on the quality of students’ final written science answers.

The authors conclude that a short, scalable AI literacy workshop can modestly but reliably improve middle-school students’ regulation of LLM use and their task performance. Trained students were less likely to accept underspecified prompts, more likely to ask follow-up questions when needed, and better at judging whether AI responses were correct. Self-reported AI attitudes, knowledge, and metacognitive measures did not predict performance, suggesting that effective AI use depends more on explicit training in interaction regulation than on perceived competence. The paper provides direct school-age evidence that instruction can reduce uncritical reliance on generative AI, while also showing that overall performance remained only moderate even with AI support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled K–12 classroom intervention study with a comparison group and behavioral/performance outcomes, which is stronger than correlational work. However, it is not clearly randomized, comes from a single school, has attrition/exclusions, and is currently an arXiv preprint, so it has credible quasi-experimental evidence but some important design and generalizability concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic effect is positive but modest: science performance improved by about 1.1 points on a 20-point scale with a reported effect size of r=.19. Effects on regulation behaviors are meaningful, but overall impact appears modest rather than medium-to-large.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used a generative AI chatbot during six science inquiry/problem-solving tasks, and the study tested whether a brief AI literacy workshop improved how students regulate prompting, evaluate responses, ask follow-up questions, and produce better final answers when working with the LLM.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with grades 8–9 students, the intervention group that received a 2-hour AI literacy workshop scored higher on LLM-supported science problem solving than controls (n=76 vs. n=40). Final-answer scores on a 0–20 scale were higher for trained students (M=11.38, SD=3.87) than controls (M=10.29, SD=3.04), with Mann–Whitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19, indicating a modest positive effect on science task performance.
finding.measure: Science investigation task performance; final written answer validity scored 0–20 across six exercises

finding.finding_summary: The workshop improved students’ regulation of LLM interaction in several behavioral measures: trained students accepted fewer suggested prompts overall, were less likely than controls to accept underspecified prompts (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044), judged AI answer correctness more accurately (condition × prompt-specificity interaction p=.012), and asked more follow-up questions after accepted underspecified prompts (59.2% vs. 27.9%, p<.001). These results indicate stronger critical evaluation, metacognitive regulation, and strategic interaction with GenAI after training.
finding.measure: Behavioral indicators of interaction regulation, including prompt acceptance/rejection, follow-up questioning, and correctness judgments during LLM-supported tasks
finding.confidence_interval: For prompt discrimination predicting performance: sensitivity beta=1.76, 95% CI [1.06, 2.46]; response bias beta=1.65, 95% CI [0.25, 3.05]

finding.finding_summary: The intervention did not significantly change students’ GenAI self-report dimensions, and self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge and metacognitive awareness did not predict task performance. A repeated-measures MANOVA in the intervention group found no overall workshop effect on GenAI self-reports (Pillai’s trace=.116, F(6,62)=1.36, p=.247), with only small non-robust changes in Attitude and Fairness & ethics after FDR correction.
finding.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaire dimensions (attitude, trust, social influence, fairness/ethics, usefulness, effort/ease of use) and Jr. MAI metacognitive self-report
finding.study_size: n=112 for questionnaire analyses; n=116 for performance correlations

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) students, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback or feedback from human tutors. The broader problem motivating the study is the rapid emergence of generative AI in education and the need for evidence about how it can be incorporated ethically and effectively into writing instruction and assessment.

The authors report two longitudinal studies centered on feedback on student writing. In Study 1, a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental design compared AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback on weekly writing assignments. GPT-4 was prompted to provide structured feedback on topic sentence quality, idea development, academic language, transitions, use of sources/evidence, and grammar. The control group met weekly with trained human tutors in 30-minute one-on-one sessions, while the experimental group received individualized GPT-4 feedback by email and revised their drafts accordingly. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI and human feedback over six weeks and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

The population consisted of 91 undergraduate ENL students at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region, all enrolled in an academic reading and writing language course and assessed at CEFR B1 or above. The context was course-based academic writing instruction focused on 300-word paragraphs tied to class readings and topics. Human tutors were trained English language tutors, and AI feedback was produced using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback over the six-week period. Student preferences were nearly evenly split: some valued human tutors for interaction, engagement, and opportunities to ask follow-up questions, while others preferred AI for its clarity, specificity, consistency, and availability. The authors argue that a blended model may be most beneficial, combining the detailed and efficient feedback generation of AI with the interpersonal and dialogic strengths of human tutoring.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a comparison group, repeated measures, pre/post testing, and reported statistics, but it is not an RCT and is conducted in higher education rather than K-12. The methodology is stronger than correlational work, though external validity for the requested K-12 context is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic literacy finding shows no significant advantage of AI-generated feedback over human tutor feedback, with a negligible posttest effect size (d=-0.156). Perception findings are mixed and near evenly split, so overall impact is best characterized as no clear positive impact.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated automated feedback on university ENL students' academic paragraph writing, including comments on topic sentence, idea development, academic language, transitions, source use, and grammar error tables for revision.
Use of ChatGPT/GPT-4 as an AI writing support tool for corrective feedback and essay evaluation in second-language writing.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, a 6-week quasi-experimental repeated-measures comparison found no significant difference in writing improvement between students receiving GPT-4-generated feedback and those receiving human tutor feedback. The group-by-time interaction was not significant (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063), and posttest scores were similar between groups (EG n=23, M=33.37, SD=1.91; CG n=25, M=33.68, SD=2.07; t=-0.539, p=0.591, d=-0.156) on an analytic writing rubric assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence.
finding.measure: Pre/post academic writing test scores on analytic rubric (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence)
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 for interaction; Cohen's d=-0.156 at posttest
finding.std_deviation: EG pre SD=1.301, CG pre SD=1.391, EG post SD=1.908, CG post SD=2.066

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2, student preference between AI-generated and human feedback was nearly evenly split across 6 weeks among ENL learners receiving both forms of feedback (n=43; weekly responses ranged from 32 to 41). Mean ratings for satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference were all above 4 out of 5 for both feedback sources, with slightly higher grand means for human feedback on satisfaction (4.28 vs. 4.26), clarity (4.32 vs. 4.24), helpfulness (4.31 vs. 4.23), and preference (4.20 vs. 4.13), while the forced-choice preference item averaged 1.53 on a 1=human/2=AI scale, indicating a near-even split; qualitative responses suggested human feedback increased engagement while AI feedback was valued for clarity and specificity.
finding.measure: Weekly Likert surveys on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference; qualitative preference explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-generated writing feedback can likely be incorporated without reducing learning outcomes and may save educator time by reducing the burden of reviewing and responding to each student's writing, especially in larger classes. However, this efficiency claim was not directly tested with workload or time-use data, so the evidence is inferential rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Author-reported potential for reduced teacher time/workload; no direct workload metric collected

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating AI in foreign language education: An investigation into ChatGPT’s effect on foreign language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT affects foreign language learning experiences and how students perceive its strengths, limitations, and possible uses in language education. The authors position the study as a response to growing interest in generative AI for language learning, especially the need to understand its practical benefits and drawbacks in authentic instructional settings. The research questions focus on how ChatGPT influences students’ learning experiences and what advantages, challenges, and recommendations emerge from student perspectives.

The intervention consisted of a four-week ChatGPT-integrated foreign language program embedded in online English classes. ChatGPT was used in reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary lessons through activities such as warm-ups, pre-reading exploration, vocabulary practice, social media post creation, story generation, creative writing, grammar exercises, research proposal brainstorming, and essay feedback. The teacher initially provided prompts and later encouraged students to write their own prompts, with an emphasis on using ChatGPT responsibly and incorporating original ideas rather than simply copying outputs.

The study involved 13 preparatory-class university students at a School of Foreign Languages in a foundation university in Ankara, Turkey. The participants were 18–20 years old, came from multiple academic departments, and had English proficiency levels ranging from A2 to B2. Because of administrative concerns about ChatGPT use, the study was limited to a single classroom. The instructional setting was online due to emergency distance education after the February 2023 earthquake in Turkey. Data came from semi-structured interviews conducted after the four-week implementation and were analyzed thematically.

The main conclusions are that students generally perceived ChatGPT as beneficial for writing, grammar, and vocabulary learning, and as supportive of motivation, engagement, creativity, and quick access to information. Students valued immediate feedback, idea generation, and support for cultural and creative activities. At the same time, they reported important drawbacks, including possible over-reliance, encouragement of shortcuts, technical and access problems, limited usefulness for speaking and listening, and concerns about misuse. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can serve as a useful supplementary tool in language learning, but should be integrated carefully alongside teacher guidance and authentic communicative practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study with a clearly described methodology, four-week implementation, and intercoder agreement, but it uses a very small convenience sample (n=13) and relies on self-reported interview data without objective outcome measures or a comparison group.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests generally positive but unclear impacts, especially for writing-related literacy and motivation, alongside limitations for speaking/listening and risks of over-reliance. Because no effect sizes or validated quantitative outcomes are reported, impact remains modest/unclear rather than established.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was integrated into four weeks of online foreign-language instruction for university preparatory students to support reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary activities, including brainstorming, story generation, pre-reading exploration, research proposal drafting, vocabulary practice, grammar practice, and interactive discussion.

Students used ChatGPT specifically as a writing and language support tool for classification and cause-and-effect essays, brainstorming ideas, planning drafts, receiving written feedback, and expanding vocabulary and sentence structures in EFL learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across interviews with 13 university preparatory EFL students after a four-week ChatGPT-integrated course, participants consistently reported perceived improvements in writing, grammar, and vocabulary-related literacy tasks. The evidence is based on qualitative self-report rather than standardized literacy assessments; no effect sizes or inferential statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on writing improvement, grammar enhancement, vocabulary learning, and use of ChatGPT for essay planning/feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students reported limited impact of ChatGPT on speaking and no impact on listening, even while describing benefits for broader language learning. Specifically, speaking was noted as only weakly supported by some participants and listening showed no perceived benefit, based on qualitative interview data from 13 students over four weeks.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on speaking and listening skill development

finding.finding_summary: Most participants described ChatGPT as increasing motivation and engagement through instant feedback, accessibility, and interactive activities during online EFL lessons. However, a minority reported no increase in motivation, so the overall pattern is positive but based entirely on qualitative perceptions without validated motivation scales.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on motivation, engagement, and learning experience

finding.finding_summary: Students and authors proposed that ChatGPT may support creativity, self-regulated learning, and personalization through brainstorming, prompt writing, and guided independent use, but they also raised concerns that it encourages shortcuts, over-reliance, and possible deterioration in critical thinking and learner autonomy. These findings are speculative and perception-based rather than directly measured with durable-skill instruments.
finding.measure: Interview reports on creativity, independence, over-reliance, shortcuts, and perceived autonomy/self-regulation
