finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT made research and information access faster and more efficient, highlighting time-saving benefits in language-learning tasks. At the same time, occasional connection issues and access problems limited reliability, so the efficiency benefit is positive but qualified and based on self-report.
finding.measure: Interview reports on time-saving, faster access to information, efficiency, and technical/access issues

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and implementation considerations associated with large language models such as ChatGPT in education. The core problem it addresses is how these systems might be integrated into teaching and learning in ways that improve educational experiences while avoiding harms related to bias, over-reliance, misinformation, privacy, integrity, and inequitable access. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes emerging examples and proposes a conceptual agenda for responsible adoption.

The paper discusses a wide range of possible educational uses of large language models. For literacy-related and language-intensive tasks, it highlights support for reading and writing development through grammatical and syntactic correction, style suggestions, summaries and explanations of complex texts, question and prompt generation, vocabulary and grammar support, translations, outlines, practice quizzes, and feedback on student writing. From the teacher side, it describes potential uses for personalized learning materials, lesson planning, adaptive feedback, assessment support, semi-automated grading of essays and other written work, and generation of reading-comprehension materials. The authors also discuss remote tutoring, collaborative writing, and accessibility uses, including speech-to-text/text-to-speech combinations for learners with disabilities.

The population and context are broad rather than tied to a single implemented intervention. The paper explicitly refers to elementary, middle school, high school, university, professional training, group learning, remote tutoring, and inclusive learning contexts. It discusses both student-facing and teacher-facing applications, with many examples relevant to K-12 literacy instruction, such as summaries of difficult texts, reading-comprehension quizzes, writing improvement, feedback, and differentiated support. The paper also cites prior studies involving children, primary school students, high school students, pre-service teachers, and higher-education learners, but these are used illustratively rather than as part of a formal systematic review.

The main conclusion is that large language models have substantial promise for personalization, feedback, content generation, engagement, accessibility, and instructional support, but only if used with strong human oversight and explicit pedagogical design. The authors argue that successful implementation requires AI literacy for both teachers and learners, critical thinking and fact-checking routines, attention to bias and fairness, privacy protections, and curricular strategies that prevent over-reliance and misuse. They frame large language models as tools that should complement rather than replace teachers, and they call for further research and responsible governance before widespread educational adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, challenges, and selected prior studies rather than reporting an original empirical study with a defined sample, intervention protocol, or outcome analysis. It therefore does not meet empirical credibility criteria for causal or observational evidence in the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes potentially meaningful benefits and risks, but it does not provide original effect estimates or direct impact evidence. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive, null, or negative.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on educational uses of large language models such as ChatGPT for student support, including question answering, summaries, explanations, practice generation, conversational assistance, and personalized guidance across K-12 and higher education contexts.
Discusses LLM/NLP systems for semi-automated assessment and adaptive feedback on student writing and open-ended responses, including revision support and teacher-facing evaluation tools.

Describes LLMs as writing and language assistants for syntactic/grammatical corrections, style suggestions, summaries, translations, vocabulary and grammar explanations, and support for reading comprehension and writing tasks.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can improve second/foreign language writing, particularly for socially vulnerable learners with refugee/migrant backgrounds who may face additional language barriers. The research question focused on the extent to which ChatGPT could contribute to better L2 writing in vocabulary and grammar.

The intervention was a short classroom pilot in which students first wrote a personal email in German. Researchers then used ChatGPT to revise each text for vocabulary and grammar, and students received the improved version to study and discuss. After reviewing ChatGPT’s revisions and suggestions, students completed a second writing task on a similar topic. The analysis compared pre/post writing products using quantitative text features such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence.

The study took place in a junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 students aged 15 in a German as a foreign language class. All participants had refugee/migrant backgrounds and were learning German at approximately A2 level. The intervention lasted two weeks and was integrated into the regular syllabus in a classroom setting under educator supervision.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT showed promising potential as a feedback tool for foreign language writing. Students’ post-intervention texts generally contained more total words, more unique words, and longer sentences, suggesting improvement in vocabulary use and written expression. The paper argues that ChatGPT may support language learning and provide helpful scaffolding for multilingual classrooms, especially for refugee/migrant learners, while also emphasizing the need for teacher oversight and caution regarding inaccurate responses, cheating, and other ethical concerns. The authors stress that the findings are preliminary and that more research in diverse contexts is needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small classroom pilot/pre-post study with 8 students, no control group, no randomization, and limited statistical reporting. It provides some empirical evidence but only meets low credibility standards due to the very small sample and descriptive analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings indicate modest positive improvements in a priority population (migrant/refugee-background adolescents) on writing-related measures, but impact magnitude is uncertain because no standardized effect sizes or rigorous causal estimates are reported.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as an automated foreign-language writing improvement tool to revise junior high students' German email drafts for vocabulary and grammar, after which students studied the revised version and wrote a new similar email.

The study specifically evaluates ChatGPT as a feedback tool that generated corrected/enhanced versions of students' L2 writing, focusing on grammar and vocabulary feedback rather than open-ended tutoring dialogue.

finding.finding_summary: In this 2-week pilot with 8 migrant/refugee-background junior high students learning German, post-ChatGPT-supported writing showed increases in total words (mean +38%, ranging from +2% to +62%), unique words (mean +19.1 words per student, except one student with -1), and average words per sentence (mean about +42%, with one student decreasing). The outcome suggests improved foreign-language writing production in vocabulary richness and sentence expansion, but no standardized test, inferential statistics, or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Writing output characteristics from student email tasks: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and frequent-word analysis

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to generate high-quality, personalized English reading comprehension materials for school learners using large language models, especially in real educational contexts where teachers need fresh, level-appropriate materials. The authors focus on middle school English instruction in China, motivated by teacher reports that reading exercises are often reused year after year and that creating customized passages and questions is labor-intensive. The study asks whether a ChatGPT-based system can generate reading passages and multiple-choice comprehension questions that are suitable for classroom use and how those outputs compare with both a GPT-2 baseline and existing human-written textbook materials.

The intervention is a reading comprehension exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. Teachers or users can specify passage length, genre, CEFR difficulty level, and topic, and can either generate a passage from scratch or adapt a referenced passage in a one-shot setting. The system also generates multiple-choice questions, answers, and explanations for a given passage, includes a toxicity check, and presents outputs in an editable interface so teachers can revise the materials before use. The study evaluates the system through automatic text metrics, human ratings of generated passages and questions, pairwise comparisons against textbook materials, and interviews with experienced middle school teachers after using the system for one week.

The main educational context is Chinese middle school English learning, especially reading comprehension practice for Grades 7-9 students. Human evaluators included Chinese college students with prior experience doing middle school English exercises, native English speakers, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system directly. The system was reportedly used by middle school English teachers and designed for real school use, though the formal evaluation centered more on content quality and user feedback than on measured student learning gains.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were judged highly coherent, readable, engaging, topic-aligned, and often superior to both a fine-tuned GPT-2 baseline and the sampled human-written textbook passages. Teachers viewed the system as useful for reducing time and cost while expanding access to personalized and diverse reading materials. However, the study also finds that generated multiple-choice questions were weaker than human-written ones, especially in the quality and variety of distractor options, meaning teacher review remains necessary. Overall, the paper presents a promising early implementation report of generative AI for differentiated literacy materials in middle school English instruction, with personalization, faster material creation, and teacher customization as key proposed mechanisms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system evaluation study with multiple human evaluation components and teacher interviews, but it is not a classroom experiment measuring student learning gains with randomized or quasi-experimental comparison. The evidence is mainly evaluative/qualitative and task-performance based, so it fits yellow rather than green or blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but still unclear educational impact: generated literacy materials were rated highly and teachers perceived efficiency benefits, but no direct student achievement effect sizes or classroom learning outcomes were reported. Because impact is inferred from material quality and implementation feedback rather than demonstrated learning gains, the impact remains yellow.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized middle school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions, with teacher-set prompts for topic, length, genre, difficulty, and optional reference passage adaptation.
GUI-based classroom support system that delivers AI-generated reading passages and exercises for teacher editing and student practice in middle school English reading instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT-generated English reading passages for Chinese middle school learners were rated as higher quality than both a fine-tuned GPT-2 baseline and, in several human evaluations, even higher than human-written textbook passages. In Human Evaluation 1, Chinese student raters gave ChatGPT passages higher overall quality scores (4.46/5) than human-written passages (4.18/5), and in pairwise comparisons ChatGPT zero-shot passages were preferred over human passages 0.87 vs. 0.13; topic coherence was also very high (0.97), suggesting strong suitability for reading-comprehension material generation, though question generation quality lagged behind human-written items.
finding.measure: Human ratings of reading passage readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality; pairwise preference scores; topic coherence; suitability of passages; human ratings of generated multiple-choice question quality
finding.study_size: 30 human-written + 30 ChatGPT + 30 GPT-2 passages in Example Set 1; 10 human-written passages paired with 30 generated passages in Example Set 2; 10 reading exercises for question evaluation; 9 Chinese college students, 36 native English speakers, and 3 experienced teachers for system feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback indicated that the system could substantially reduce the time and cost of producing diverse, personalized reading materials, functioning as a 'personalized resource library' for English teachers. After one week of use, 3 experienced teachers reported the system exceeded expectations and was easy to use, although they noted that teachers still needed to review and select suitable generated questions because distractor quality and question-type variety were imperfect.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usefulness, ease of use, time/cost reduction, and quality of generated instructional materials

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and indirectly supports that personalized, up-to-date reading materials may increase learner engagement and enthusiasm, with engagement explicitly included as a human-rated quality dimension. ChatGPT-generated passages received higher engagement ratings than human-written passages among Chinese student evaluators (4.37 vs. 4.07) and native speakers (3.93 vs. 3.77), though no direct student learning or motivation outcome was measured in classrooms.
finding.measure: Human ratings of passage engagement/interest as a quality dimension
finding.study_size: 9 Chinese college students and 36 native English speakers evaluating passage sets

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Exploring Ways of Harnessing Pedagogical Practices with the Assistance of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Changes in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how generative artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT, can be harnessed to enhance pedagogical practices in higher education. Rather than examining a K-12 literacy intervention, the paper focuses on higher education broadly and aims to identify potential educational affordances of AI for teaching, learning, and research support. A secondary aim is methodological: the author explores the use of ChatGPT itself as a research assistant to help generate and organize possible pedagogical use cases.

The study uses a qualitative approach in which the author "interviewed" ChatGPT using prompts about how AI can support higher education, including how it can assist university tutors and students. The AI-generated responses were then reviewed by the author and used to derive major categories, which were subsequently explored through recent literature searches in Google Scholar. The resulting categories include personalized learning, automated assessment and feedback, virtual assistants and chatbots, content creation, resource recommendation, time management, language translation and support, research assistance, simulations and virtual labs, collaboration and communication, accessibility and inclusivity, and broader teaching and learning support.

The population and context are higher education stakeholders rather than school-age learners: university students, tutors/educators, faculty, administrators, and policy actors. The paper is not an empirical classroom pilot with student outcome measures; instead, it is a qualitative, conceptually oriented exploration grounded in AI-generated text and supporting references from recent higher education literature. The author is based in Greece, but the discussion is framed as internationally relevant and does not report a participant sample from a specific institution.

The main conclusion is that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT have substantial potential to support higher education through personalization, faster feedback, accessibility, content generation, and administrative support, but they should be used as complementary tools rather than replacements for human educators. The paper repeatedly emphasizes the need for human oversight, critical evaluation of AI outputs, training in AI literacy, and institutional guidelines to address ethical risks such as inaccuracies, bias, privacy issues, plagiarism, misuse, and overreliance. The author also notes that stronger evidence-based research is needed to test the actual effectiveness of these proposed affordances.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/conceptual review that uses ChatGPT as an interviewee/research assistant and synthesizes literature, but it does not present primary empirical evaluation, comparison groups, or quantitative outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially beneficial but largely unmeasured impacts on efficiency, policy, and skills; because no empirical effect estimates are reported, impact remains unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of ChatGPT as a conversational generative AI tool and research assistant in higher education, discussing uses such as personalized support, answering student questions, content generation, feedback, and administrative assistance.
Discusses ChatGPT and related AI tools for writing assistance, language translation, proofreading, vocabulary/grammar support, and support for academic writing and language learning tasks.
Reviews potential uses of AI for automated grading, automated assessment, and rapid feedback generation on assignments, quizzes, and tests in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can improve efficiency by saving educator time in content creation, grading, administrative support, and feedback provision. However, this is based on a qualitative, non-empirical review of ChatGPT outputs and cited literature rather than direct measurement; no sample, effect size, or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual claims about time savings, automated grading, content generation, and administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper concludes that integrating generative AI in higher education has implications for curriculum design, university policy, educator training, assessment redesign, and ethical governance. It also highlights institutional risks including privacy, bias, plagiarism, and widening the digital divide, but provides no direct institutional outcome data or causal estimates.
finding.measure: Conceptual/policy implications for curricula, governance, ethics, and institutional adoption

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that AI may support durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, time management, and self-directed learning when used with human guidance. At the same time, it warns that overreliance on AI may undermine critical thinking and that AI literacy training is necessary; these claims are not tested empirically in the study.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, time management, and AI literacy

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Voices on Generative AI: Perceptions, Benefits, and Challenges in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university students perceive generative AI technologies such as ChatGPT in higher education. The study asks three main questions: how familiar students are with generative AI, what benefits and challenges they perceive in using it for teaching and learning, and how it might be effectively integrated into higher education. The paper is framed by Biggs’ 3P model, emphasizing that students’ perceptions of learning environments and tools can influence learning approaches and outcomes.

The study used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions, making it a mixed-methods observational study. The survey covered knowledge of generative AI, willingness to use it, concerns about its use, and perceived effects on teaching and learning. Students described a range of uses for generative AI, including personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming assistance, research and analysis support, multimedia generation, and administrative help. Reported perceived benefits included immediate feedback, tailored support, efficiency, idea generation, and support for self-directed learning.

Participants were 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from multiple disciplines across post-secondary institutions in Hong Kong. The sample included students from ten faculties, with both STEM and non-STEM representation. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlations, and thematic analysis of open-ended responses. The study was conducted through an online questionnaire rather than a classroom intervention, and it focused on student perceptions rather than measured learning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that students generally held positive attitudes toward generative AI and saw strong potential for personalized support, writing help, brainstorming, and research assistance. At the same time, they expressed substantial concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking and creativity, and broader impacts on careers and human values. The authors argue that institutions should support responsible integration of generative AI through AI literacy education, clearer policies, and safeguards around ethics, privacy, and transparency.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with descriptive, correlational, and qualitative thematic analyses of student perceptions. It is empirical and peer-reviewed, but it does not estimate causal effects of GenAI on learning outcomes and relies on self-report data from a convenience sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly perceived benefits and concerns rather than measured learning impacts, and no intervention effect sizes on academic outcomes are provided. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of university students' perceptions of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for personalized learning support, brainstorming, assignment help, feedback, and research assistance.

Students describe using generative AI for writing assistance including brainstorming, grammar/paraphrasing help, polishing articles, feedback on drafts, and second-language vocabulary/text generation support.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived generative AI positively for literacy-related tasks such as brainstorming, writing improvement, grammar/paraphrasing, and feedback on drafts, based on survey responses from n=399 Hong Kong university students. However, these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured reading/writing gains, and students also expressed concerns about plagiarism, inaccurate content, and reduced independent thinking; no causal learning effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of GenAI usefulness for writing, brainstorming, and feedback via online survey and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive attitudes toward GenAI, including willingness to integrate it into learning practices (Mean=3.85, SD=1.02) and belief that it can improve motivation and support learning independently. Perceived willingness to use GenAI was positively correlated with knowledge of GenAI (r=0.189, p<0.001) and frequency of use (r=0.326, p<0.001), though this reflects attitudes and intentions rather than observed behavioral outcomes.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of willingness, attitudes, and perceived motivational/support benefits

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed concern that GenAI may undermine critical thinking, creativity, and transferable skills, with concern items showing moderate endorsement: undermines value of university education (Mean=3.15, SD=1.17), hinders development of generic/transferable skills (Mean=3.10, SD=1.23), and over-reliance concerns (Mean=2.85, SD=1.13). These findings are based on perceptions rather than direct assessments of skill decline, but the paper substantively centers these risks as a challenge of implementation.
finding.measure: Survey items and qualitative responses on critical thinking, creativity, over-reliance, and transferable skills

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as improving efficiency by saving time (Mean=4.20, SD=0.82), providing 24/7 availability (Mean=4.12, SD=0.83), and supporting faster completion of writing, research, and administrative tasks. Qualitative responses emphasized immediate answers, rapid feedback, literature summarization, and help with repetitive work, but no objective productivity or workload metrics were collected.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of time saving, availability, and efficiency benefits from survey and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The study identified substantial institutional implications around policy, ethics, privacy, academic integrity, and future curriculum design. Students were moderately concerned that GenAI use undermines the value of university education (Mean=3.15, SD=1.17), and qualitative responses highlighted plagiarism, transparency, privacy, and teacher-student relationship concerns alongside support for institutional AI literacy training and policy development.
finding.measure: Survey concern items and thematic analysis of open-ended responses about policy, ethics, privacy, and educational value

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate high-quality reading comprehension exercises for school English instruction, addressing a practical problem identified through teacher interviews in Beijing: middle school students often receive repetitive, outdated reading materials, while teachers face substantial effort in creating new, appropriately leveled passages and multiple-choice questions. The study focuses on whether a large language model can produce more diverse, personalized reading materials suitable for classroom use.

The authors built a reading exercise generation system for Chinese middle school English learners. The system uses carefully designed prompts to generate reading passages and corresponding multiple-choice questions with ChatGPT, allowing customization by topic, length, genre, difficulty level, and question type. The interface is intended for non-technical users, especially teachers, and allows educators to edit the generated content before use. The paper also compares ChatGPT outputs with a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline and with human-written textbook materials, using both automatic text metrics and multiple forms of human evaluation. An additional toxicity check is included before exercises are released.

The primary educational context is middle school English reading instruction in China, especially Grades 7-9. Human evaluators included Chinese college students with prior experience doing similar reading exercises, native English speakers, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system for one week and then participated in interviews. The paper reports that the system had already been used by middle school English teachers and was intended to support real school practice by generating personalized reading passages and exercises.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were judged to be high quality and, in many comparisons, better than both the GPT-2 baseline and existing human-written textbook passages on dimensions such as readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. Teachers reported that the system could save time and reduce the cost of creating diverse, personalized reading materials. However, the study also found weaknesses in multiple-choice question generation: question types were not rich enough, distractor options were often weak or repetitive, and teachers would still need to review and select suitable items. Overall, the paper presents an early implementation report suggesting that generative AI can support differentiated reading-passage creation and reading-response activities in middle school literacy instruction, mainly through personalization and reduced teacher workload.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system evaluation with structured human ratings and qualitative teacher feedback, but it is not a causal study of student learning outcomes in K-12 classrooms. It lacks random assignment, a quasi-experimental design on learner outcomes, and broader real-world implementation data, though methods are clearly described and peer reviewed as a conference paper.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mostly indirect impact: strong improvements in perceived quality and suitability of AI-generated literacy materials, plus positive teacher reports on efficiency. However, no student achievement effect sizes or validated classroom learning gains are reported, so educational impact remains unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized middle school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercises, with teacher-specified topic, length, genre, difficulty, and optional reference passages, plus editable outputs for classroom use.
A teacher-facing reading exercise generation system with graphical interface that delivers AI-generated reading materials and practice questions for student use in middle school English instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT-generated reading passages for middle school English learners were rated as equal to or better than human-written textbook passages on literacy-relevant quality dimensions. In Human Evaluation 1, Chinese student raters scored ChatGPT passages higher than human-written passages on readability (4.61 vs 4.52), correctness (4.60 vs 4.32), coherence (4.65 vs 4.39), engagement (4.37 vs 4.07), and overall quality (4.46 vs 4.18); native speakers also gave ChatGPT the highest overall quality score (4.06 vs 3.89 for human-written). In pairwise comparisons, ChatGPT zero-shot passages were preferred over human-written passages 0.87 to 0.13, and suitability for Chinese middle school learners was rated higher for generated than human passages (0.77 vs 0.40 in zero-shot; 0.77 vs 0.53 in one-shot), although generated multiple-choice questions were weaker than human-written questions on usefulness and suitability.
finding.measure: Human ratings of reading passage quality (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality), pairwise relative quality, topic coherence, suitability, and question quality ratings for reading comprehension exercises
finding.study_size: 30 human-written + 30 ChatGPT + 30 baseline passages in Example Set 1; 10 human-written + 30 generated passages in Example Set 2; 10 benchmark exercises for question evaluation; 9 Chinese college student raters, 36 native English speakers, plus 9 additional student raters for pairwise comparison

finding.finding_summary: Engagement was directly evaluated as one dimension of passage quality, and ChatGPT-generated passages received higher engagement ratings than human-written passages from both Chinese students (4.37 vs 4.07) and native speakers (3.93 vs 3.77). The paper also reports teacher and author interpretations that up-to-date, personalized materials may spark students’ enthusiasm, but no direct student motivation or behavior outcomes were measured in classroom use.
finding.measure: Human engagement ratings of generated reading passages
finding.study_size: Example Set 1 rated by 9 Chinese college students and 36 native English speakers

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback indicated that the system could substantially reduce the time and cost of preparing diverse reading comprehension materials while allowing teachers to edit and customize outputs. After a one-week hands-on trial, 3 experienced middle school teachers described the system as a valuable personalized resource library and reported that the quality of generated exercises exceeded expectations, though they noted shortcomings in question-option quality that still required teacher selection and oversight.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher interview feedback on usefulness, ease of use, time/cost reduction, and workload support after system use

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents this system as an early real-world school implementation of ChatGPT in middle school English education and reports that teachers viewed it as promising for broader use. However, institutional impact was inferred from educator feedback and implementation feasibility rather than measured through school-level outcomes, adoption metrics, or policy changes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback about school applicability, feasibility, and potential for wider use

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can support second/foreign language writing improvement, with particular attention to socially vulnerable learners with refugee/migrant backgrounds. The research question asks to what extent ChatGPT can improve L2 writing in vocabulary and grammar for these students, motivated by the challenge of supporting multilingual classrooms where learners have diverse language needs.

The intervention was a short classroom pilot in which students first wrote a personal email in German. Researchers then used ChatGPT to improve the students’ texts specifically for vocabulary and grammar. Students received these revised versions, studied them, and discussed the revisions and suggestions. After that, they completed a second writing task on a similar topic, allowing the researchers to compare features of the initial and subsequent writing samples.

The study took place over two weeks in a single junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 students aged 15 attending German as a foreign language. All participants had refugee/migrant backgrounds and were learning at approximately A2 level. The classroom was multilingual and multicultural, and the broader school context included substantial experience serving students from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

The main findings were positive but preliminary. After the ChatGPT-supported feedback process, students’ later writing showed increases in total words, unique words, and average words per sentence, which the authors interpret as improvement in L2 writing performance. The paper concludes that ChatGPT shows promise as a feedback and language-support tool for foreign language writing, especially for refugee/migrant learners, but also emphasizes the need for human supervision, caution about possible misuse and inaccurate outputs, and further research with larger samples and more diverse settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot classroom study with a pre/post descriptive design, no control group, no randomization, and no reported inferential statistics. It is empirical and peer-reviewed, but credibility is limited by the very small sample and short duration.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains on writing-related text measures are positive and occur in a priority population (refugee/migrant students), but the impact magnitude is unclear because no standardized effect sizes were reported and outcomes are based on descriptive text metrics rather than validated writing assessments.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a foreign-language writing support tool to improve students' German email drafts by revising vocabulary and grammar, after which students studied the revised model and wrote a new text on a similar topic.
The study specifically evaluates ChatGPT as an automated feedback mechanism that generates corrected/improved versions of students' writing for grammar and vocabulary enhancement.
A post-2022 generative AI chatbot (ChatGPT, GPT-3.5) was prompted by researchers to provide language improvements for adolescent L2 learners in a classroom writing task.

finding.finding_summary: In a 2-week pilot with 8 junior high school students (age 15) with refugee/migrant backgrounds learning German, post-ChatGPT-supported writing showed increases in several text features. Mean total words increased by 38% (range 2%-62%), unique words increased by an average of 19.1 words per student, and average words per sentence increased by about 42%, suggesting improved vocabulary richness and sentence elaboration in L2 writing; no standardized effect sizes or inferential tests were reported.
finding.measure: Text-based writing indicators: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words in pre/post writing samples

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of using large language models such as ChatGPT in education. The core problem it addresses is how these models might support teaching and learning while also creating new pedagogical, ethical, and practical challenges. Rather than reporting results from a new empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes emerging examples and proposes a conceptual framing for responsible educational use of large language models.

The paper discusses a wide range of possible educational applications. For literacy-related uses in school-age populations, it suggests that large language models could support reading and writing through grammatical and syntactic corrections, writing-style improvement, summaries and explanations of complex texts, question and prompt generation, vocabulary and grammar explanations, translations, style suggestions, and feedback on written work. It also describes teacher-facing uses such as personalized material creation, lesson planning, adaptive feedback, semi-automated assessment of essays and other writing assignments, and generation of reading-comprehension questions. The authors propose mechanisms including personalization, faster and more frequent feedback, scaffolding, explanation, accessibility support, engagement, and support for critical thinking when paired with human oversight.

The paper addresses learners and teachers across multiple educational levels, explicitly mentioning elementary, middle, high school, university, remote learning, disability support, and professional training contexts. However, it does not report a single implemented classroom study with a defined sample, duration, or setting. Instead, it draws on prior studies and examples from the broader literature to illustrate where large language models may fit into educational practice.

The main conclusion is that large language models have substantial promise for improving personalized learning, content generation, feedback, and inclusive access, but they should not be adopted uncritically. The authors emphasize major barriers and risks including bias, over-reliance, plagiarism, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work, privacy concerns, cost, limited adaptability, and the ongoing need for human oversight and fact-checking. They recommend responsible integration grounded in teacher and student AI literacy, critical thinking, verification practices, and clear pedagogical strategies rather than treating language models as replacements for teachers or authoritative knowledge sources.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and prior studies rather than reporting an original empirical design, sample, or causal evaluation. It does not provide a clear study methodology for the paper itself or direct outcome estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes potentially meaningful educational benefits and mechanisms, but does not present original effect estimates or direct evidence of impact. As a result, real-world impact is unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on educational uses of large language models such as ChatGPT for student support, including reading comprehension support, summaries/explanations of texts, question generation, personalized practice, remote tutoring, and dialogue-based assistance across K-12 and higher education.

Discusses LLM/NLP systems for semi-automated assessment and adaptive feedback on student writing and open-text responses, including rubric-like identification of strengths/weaknesses and revision support.

Describes LLMs as writing and language assistants for grammar/style correction, vocabulary and translation support, summaries, syntactic corrections, and support for reading/writing development, including accessibility-oriented text/speech support.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid emergence of generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, in teaching and learning. The author argues that educational institutions need to move beyond either banning AI or allowing unrestricted use, and instead cultivate three core capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is positioned as a conceptual discussion focused mainly on higher education, motivated by practical challenges observed after ChatGPT’s release.

The approach combines a case study of Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, with a narrative literature review. The case material comes from unstructured informal discussions with students and staff, the author’s teaching experience, and institutional experience in an AI taskforce. The paper describes the university’s response to student AI use, including internal AI guidelines requiring transparency about which models were used, how and why they were used, how outputs were critically evaluated, and where AI contributed to written work. It also discusses possible institutional supports such as workshops, regular updates, budgets, written best practices, and dedicated AI-related roles.

The context is a single Swiss higher-education institution rather than a K-12 school, although the author suggests some ideas may also be useful for children. The populations directly reflected in the case are students, teachers/lecturers, and university leadership or administrators. The paper does not report a formal sample size, intervention duration, controlled comparison, or objective student learning outcomes. Instead, it uses the institutional case to frame broader discussion of AI literacy components, practical prompting methods, and the importance of critical evaluation of AI outputs.

The main conclusions are that effective educational integration of AI requires systematic development of AI literacy, explicit teaching of prompt engineering, and strong emphasis on critical thinking and ethical use. The author recommends an institutional “AI culture” supported by workshops, curriculum integration, guidance documents, and training for both staff and students. The paper is primarily a conceptual and practice-oriented contribution rather than a direct comparative study of student literacy outcomes, and it focuses on policy and pedagogy for responsible AI adoption in higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion grounded in a narrative literature review and an informal institutional case study with unstructured discussions, not a direct empirical evaluation with clear sampling, measures, or causal design. It is peer-reviewed, but under this evidence framework it lacks the methodological features needed for yellow or above.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful practices for AI governance and classroom integration, but it provides no direct student outcome effects or quantified impacts. As a result, practical impact is plausible but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion and case-study-informed narrative review on integrating generative AI in higher-education classrooms, emphasizing AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation rather than evaluating a specific student-facing learning tool.

Discusses use of ChatGPT and similar LLM chatbots as conversational partners or 'sparring partners' for brainstorming, source discovery, and classroom experimentation, but does not empirically test them on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are important future-oriented competencies, but it does not present empirical estimates of improvement in these skills. Evidence comes from informal discussions and a narrative literature review rather than direct measurement of student skill gains.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The case study describes an institutional response at a Swiss university in the form of AI-use guidelines intended to balance prohibition and unrestricted use, with perceived benefits around transparency and critical reflection. However, the paper also reports major implementation problems such as uncertain student compliance, lack of training, and difficulty monitoring AI use, without formal institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline implementation observations and informal stakeholder discussions

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the unsettled question of whether ChatGPT meaningfully improves student outcomes in education. The authors note that prior empirical studies have reported mixed findings, with some showing gains in learning performance, perception, and higher-order thinking, while others found null or even negative effects. To provide a more robust synthesis, the study conducts a meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental research published from November 2022 through February 2025.

The approach was a PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of 51 studies, yielding 72 independent effect sizes. Included studies had to compare an experimental group using ChatGPT with a control group not using ChatGPT, and both groups had to use the same learning method. Outcomes were grouped into learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking. The authors also coded moderators including grade level, course type, learning model, duration, role played by ChatGPT, and application area.

The evidence base spans primary, secondary, and college education, though the included studies are concentrated heavily in higher education, with only a small number from K-12 and only one primary-level study for learning performance. The studies covered STEM, language/writing, and skills courses, and included a range of uses such as tutoring, assessment/feedback, and personalized recommendation. The paper itself is a review rather than a direct intervention study, so it synthesizes outcomes across multiple educational contexts rather than reporting one implementation.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT has a large positive overall effect on learning performance (g = 0.867) and moderate positive effects on learning perception (g = 0.456) and higher-order thinking (g = 0.457). Effects on learning performance were stronger in skills and competencies courses, in problem-based learning, and in interventions lasting 4–8 weeks. For learning perception, longer interventions produced stronger effects, especially those lasting more than 8 weeks. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support student learning when integrated thoughtfully, especially with scaffolds and sustained use, but they also caution that evidence for learning perception and higher-order thinking is based on fewer studies and should be expanded in future research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis synthesizing 51 experimental or quasi-experimental studies with explicit inclusion criteria, effect-size computation, heterogeneity testing, moderator analyses, and publication-bias/sensitivity checks. It meets the framework's highest tier for study design, although relevance to K-12 literacy specifically is only partial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effects reported are medium to large, including g=0.867 for learning performance and about g=0.46 for learning perception and higher-order thinking, which exceed the blue-tier threshold of 0.20. However, these impacts are broad and not specific to direct K-12 literacy populations.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT used in educational settings as a conversational learning support, including roles such as intelligent tutor, learning partner, and learning tool across tutoring, assessment/feedback, and personalized recommendation contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across 51 quasi-experimental/experimental studies published from Nov 2022 to Feb 2025, the meta-analysis found a large overall positive effect of ChatGPT on learning performance (Hedges' g = 0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052]). A subset of included studies involved language learning and academic writing, where moderator analysis showed a positive mean effect for that course type (g = 0.531), though this paper does not isolate K-12 literacy-only samples or provide a pooled CI for the literacy subgroup in the reported table.
finding.measure: Learning performance measured primarily through tests and exams; includes language learning and academic writing course outcomes within the broader meta-analysis
finding.effect_size: g=0.867 overall; g=0.531 for language learning and academic writing subgroup
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [0.683, 1.052] for overall learning performance; subgroup CI not fully reported in extracted text

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis reported a moderate positive effect of ChatGPT on learning perception (g = 0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625]) across 19 independent effects. Duration moderated this outcome, with interventions lasting more than 8 weeks showing the largest gains in learning perception (g = 1.054), suggesting stronger benefits for motivation/attitudinal outcomes with sustained use.
finding.measure: Learning perception assessed primarily through scales and questionnaires, including motivational and attitudinal dimensions
finding.effect_size: g=0.456 overall; g=1.054 for >8 week duration subgroup

finding.finding_summary: For higher-order thinking, the meta-analysis found a moderate positive overall effect of ChatGPT (g = 0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650]) based on 9 independent effects. Moderator analyses indicated stronger effects in STEM-related courses (g = 0.737) and when ChatGPT functioned as an intelligent tutor (g = 0.945), though the higher-order-thinking evidence base was smaller than for learning performance.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking measured mainly through scales and questionnaires, including constructs such as critical and creative thinking
finding.effect_size: g=0.457 overall; g=0.737 in STEM subgroup; g=0.945 when ChatGPT served as intelligent tutor

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines the promises, challenges, and research needs surrounding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning. The central question is how GenAI may transform learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment, while also creating risks related to hallucinations, ethics, privacy, equity, and the disruption of traditional educational assessment. Rather than reporting a primary intervention study, the paper synthesizes conceptual arguments and examples from prior literature to outline a human-centred agenda for learning with and about GenAI.

The paper discusses GenAI as an enabling approach across four broad educational functions: personalised learning support, generation of diverse learning resources, scalable feedback, and adaptive/authentic assessment. It draws on examples such as AI tutoring, multimodal content generation, automated feedback on writing and programming, and agent-based assessment systems. The authors frame these possibilities through learning theory, including Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, inquiry-based learning, constructivism, and feedback theory, and argue that GenAI should be designed to augment rather than replace human teaching and learning processes.

The paper is not tied to a single participant sample or empirical site. Instead, it addresses broad educational stakeholders including learners, educators, administrators, parents, policymakers, researchers, and technologists across educational contexts, with particular attention to implications for K-12 and higher education. Its discussion spans formal education generally rather than one country, setting, or implementation environment.

The main conclusion is that GenAI has substantial potential to improve personalisation, access, feedback, and assessment, but this potential is inseparable from serious risks. The authors argue that rigorous evidence, methodological standards, AI literacy, human-in-the-loop design, and ethical governance are necessary before strong claims about educational benefit can be made. They conclude that GenAI should be integrated in ways that preserve learner agency, critical thinking, creativity, and metacognitive autonomy, positioning AI as a support for human learning rather than a substitute for human intellectual work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed perspective article synthesizing promises, challenges, and research needs for generative AI in learning, but it does not report an original empirical study design, sample, comparator, intervention implementation, or direct student outcome analysis. Because it is not a direct comparative K-12 literacy impact study and provides no evaluable causal or quasi-experimental methodology, it falls in the red tier for this evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article discusses potentially positive and negative impacts of generative AI on learning and cites external studies, but it does not estimate impact from its own data or provide effect sizes. As a result, impact is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative, warranting a yellow tier.

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review of reviews that maps the scope, methods, quality, and findings of artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHEd) evidence syntheses. The authors argue that, given rapid growth in AI applications and public debate around generative AI, the field needs a stronger research foundation. Their central question is what kinds of review evidence exist in higher education AI, how rigorous that evidence is, what applications are being studied, and what benefits, challenges, and gaps are emerging.

To address this, the authors conducted a meta-systematic review of secondary research published in English from 2018 to July 2023. They searched major databases and platforms including Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, EBSCOHost, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, OpenAlex, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar. Reviews were included if they focused solely on formal higher or continuing education, addressed AI applications, and contained an explicit method section. Sixty-six publications were included, most of them systematic reviews. The paper synthesizes publication trends, review types, author geography and collaboration, review quality, and substantive AI application areas using categories such as profiling and prediction, adaptive systems and personalisation, assessment and evaluation, and intelligent tutoring systems.

The population and context are not primary-study participants in a single intervention, but bodies of prior research focused on higher education and continuing education settings. Across the included reviews, the paper identifies students as the main end users, with educators and administrators also implicated in AI applications. The review reports that adaptive systems/personalisation and profiling/prediction dominate the literature, while intelligent tutoring systems and assessment/evaluation receive less focused review attention. It also notes that most evidence syntheses are team-authored, often domestic rather than international collaborations, and that many reviews fail to report key methodological details such as inter-rater reliability, data extraction schemes, or quality appraisal.

The main conclusions are that AIHEd review research is growing quickly but remains uneven in quality and coverage. The authors call for stronger methodological rigour, more ethical and contextual consideration, greater interdisciplinary and international collaboration, and clearer reporting practices. They also argue that future research should move beyond broad overviews toward more carefully designed primary and secondary studies that better address implementation, transparency, and the real educational value of AI applications.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed tertiary review with a clear methodology, but it is not a direct K-12 comparative study and does not provide causal student-level evidence on literacy outcomes. It synthesizes secondary literature focused on higher education, so it offers only indirect evidence for the target K-12 generative AI question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate direct student literacy impacts for a K-12 intervention and reports no effect sizes tied to the target population. Its practical impact for the requested knowledge graph is therefore unclear and indirect rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a Personal Tutor for English Language Learning: A Review of Benefits and Concerns
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Changes in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging question of how generative artificial intelligence tools can function as personal tutors in English language teaching and learning, especially in English as a foreign language contexts. The authors aim to synthesize the main educational functions, benefits, concerns, and practical implications of using tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Khanmigo for personalized English learning. Rather than reporting a new intervention study, the article draws on existing literature to discuss the promise and risks of generative AI in language education.

The paper’s approach is a qualitative secondary-data review of academic articles, case studies, and reports. It organizes prior literature into several tutoring functions of generative AI, including dialogue-based tutoring, cognitive tutoring, example-based tutoring, speech-recognition tutoring, grammar and writing support, reading comprehension tutoring, vocabulary tutoring, and collaborative learning support. It also summarizes claimed benefits such as immediate feedback, personalized instruction, increased motivation, reduced anxiety, improved speaking and writing support, adaptable reading materials, and vocabulary learning in context. In addition, the paper briefly discusses three example tools—ChatGPT, Gemini, and Khanmigo—as illustrative AI personal tutors.

No direct participant sample is studied in this paper. The population and context are therefore broad and literature-based, centered on English language teaching and learning settings, particularly EFL/ELT contexts, and on the roles of students and teachers as AI users. The article does not report a bounded school, university, or country-specific empirical sample, though the authors are affiliated with institutions in the United States and Cambodia and discuss applications across varied educational settings.

The paper concludes that generative AI has substantial potential to support English language learning through personalization, feedback, engagement, and flexible practice opportunities, but that its use raises serious concerns. The main concerns identified include academic dishonesty, misinformation and hallucinations, biased assessment, weak feedback quality, accessibility inequities, psychological and social risks, cultural and identity issues, insufficient teacher and student preparedness, and overreliance on AI. The authors recommend cautious, ethical, and balanced integration of AI with human teaching, more training for teachers and students, stronger institutional policies, improved infrastructure for equitable access, and future empirical and longitudinal research on effectiveness and long-term impacts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review based on secondary sources and does not report a systematic review protocol, original data collection, comparative design, or quantitative synthesis. It is peer-reviewed, but under the provided framework it does not provide empirical causal evidence meeting blue/green/yellow standards for direct student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper makes broad claims about potential benefits and concerns of generative AI in English learning, but it does not present original effect estimates or direct comparative student outcome evidence. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Narrative review of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Khanmigo functioning as personal tutors for English language learning through conversational support, personalized practice, and feedback.

Review discusses generative AI for grammar, writing, vocabulary, pronunciation, and reading-comprehension support in English language teaching, including writing assistance and speech/language feedback functions.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging promises, risks, and future implications of ChatGPT and related generative AI technologies in education. Rather than evaluating a direct intervention or measuring student outcomes, the authors aim to provoke critical reflection on how generative AI may reshape teaching, learning, assessment, educator roles, equity, ethics, and educational systems more broadly. The central question is how education should respond to increasingly capable AI systems that can perform tasks once reserved for human educators and learners.

The paper uses a speculative methodology built around fictional storytelling and collective writing by a large, globally diverse group of education scholars. Contributors each wrote positive and negative future-oriented narratives about educational uses of conversational AI, and the authors analyzed these narratives to identify key themes. The approach is explicitly not an empirical effectiveness study; instead, it is an intellectual and future-oriented exercise intended to surface possible scenarios, tensions, and design considerations for AI in education.

No participant sample, school-based intervention, or comparative condition is reported. The context is the educational landscape in general, spanning formal and informal education and including examples from different imagined settings such as schools, universities, and online learning environments. The discussion is therefore conceptual and cross-contextual rather than tied to a specific grade band, institution, or country of implementation.

The main conclusions are that generative AI offers substantial opportunities for personalized learning, accessibility, collaboration, language support, and efficiency, but also raises serious concerns around bias, privacy, ethics, academic integrity, inequitable access, overdependence on technology, and the possible dehumanization of education. The authors argue that education needs new literacies, updated assessment strategies, and a clear reaffirmation of human agency and the central role of educators. They conclude that the key issue is not whether AI should be used in education, but how, when, by whom, and for what purposes it should be adopted responsibly.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a speculative, collective reflection using fictional narratives rather than an empirical study. It reports no direct comparative design, no K-12 sample, no intervention implementation data, and no measured student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses possible future educational implications of generative AI but provides no causal evidence of student impact. Because impact is entirely speculative and unmeasured, it is best treated as unclear rather than demonstrated positive or negative impact.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper examining the opportunities and risks of using large language models (LLMs), especially systems such as GPT-3 and ChatGPT, in education. The authors aim to synthesize emerging possibilities for both learners and teachers while also identifying major pedagogical, ethical, legal, and practical challenges. Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention, the paper argues for responsible, human-supervised integration of LLMs into educational settings.

The paper discusses a wide range of potential educational applications of LLMs. For learners, these include support for reading comprehension, writing improvement, question generation, language learning, collaborative learning, tutoring, and accessibility. For teachers, the paper highlights uses such as lesson planning, personalized material generation, feedback provision, assessment support, and professional development. It also briefly reviews selected prior studies that used language models or conversational AI in education, but these are discussed as examples from the literature rather than as original data collection in this paper.

The population and context are broad and conceptual rather than tied to a single study sample. The authors explicitly discuss educational use across elementary school, middle school, high school, university, professional training, remote learning, and support for learners with disabilities. The perspective is international in authorship, but no participant sample or implementation site is reported because this is not an empirical study.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial potential to enhance teaching and learning, but only if their use is guided by clear pedagogical goals, critical thinking, fact-checking, teacher oversight, and attention to privacy, bias, fairness, sustainability, and equitable access. The authors recommend training educators and learners in AI-related literacies, developing governance and mitigation strategies, and pursuing further research on effective and ethical classroom integration.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and prior literature rather than reporting an original empirical study with a defined sample, intervention implementation, comparator, or outcome analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate causal impacts on student outcomes. Its practical influence may be conceptual or agenda-setting, but empirical educational impact is unclear and not directly measured.

interventions.use_case: Position paper discussing prospective uses of ChatGPT and other large language models in education for student support, content generation, question answering, personalized learning, and conversational assistance across K-12 and higher education.
Discusses LLM/NLP systems for semi-automated grading, adaptive feedback, and evaluation of student answers and writing-related tasks from the teacher perspective.
Describes LLMs as writing and language support tools for grammar correction, style improvement, summaries, translations, and assistance with reading and writing development.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid emergence of generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, by emphasizing three core competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The author argues that educational institutions face a difficult balance between banning AI and allowing unrestricted use, and that neither extreme is adequate. The paper is framed as a conceptual discussion focused primarily on higher education, informed by a case study at a Swiss university of applied sciences and supplemented by a narrative literature review.

The main approach studied is the introduction and discussion of institutional AI guidance and practices at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland. The paper describes the university's internal AI guidelines for student use in written work, including requirements for transparency about which AI tools were used, how and why they were used, how outputs were critically evaluated, and where in the manuscript AI was applied. It also discusses informal, unstructured discussions with students, lecturers, and university staff about attitudes toward AI, institutional responses, and practical classroom uses such as AI experiments, case study generation, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive learning applications.

The population and context are primarily higher education students, lecturers, supervisors, and institutional leadership at a single Swiss university. Although the author occasionally suggests implications for children and schools more broadly, the empirical grounding is not in K-12 settings. The methods described are informal discussions and a locally grounded case study rather than a controlled intervention or formal comparative evaluation. No student literacy outcomes, achievement tests, or direct K-12 generative AI comparisons are reported.

The main conclusions are that institutions should not rely on simple prohibition or permissive laissez-faire policies, but should instead cultivate an 'AI culture' through training, workshops, guidelines, curriculum integration, and explicit instruction in AI literacy and prompt engineering. The author concludes that students and educators need structured support to use AI responsibly, critically evaluate outputs, and understand risks such as hallucinations and bias. The paper is therefore best understood as a practice-oriented higher education discussion and institutional case, rather than a direct student-outcome study of generative AI for literacy learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with an informal university case study, not a direct empirical evaluation of a K-12 AI intervention. It lacks a clear student outcome design, comparator, validated measures, and quantitative causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful institutional and pedagogical implications, but impact on learners is unclear because no direct student outcome evidence or effect sizes are reported. Its relevance is mainly conceptual and policy-oriented rather than demonstrably impactful.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of classroom use of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude for prompting, idea generation, classroom activities, and AI literacy development, primarily in higher education rather than a tested K-12 implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are important skills for modern education, and describes a Swiss university case in which AI guidelines were developed to encourage critical evaluation of AI outputs. However, it does not report a formal empirical study, no student-level pre/post measures, no comparison group, and no effect sizes; therefore claims about gains in critical thinking or AI literacy remain untested in this article.
finding.measure: Informal discussions, narrative literature review, and institutional case-based observations about AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The article presents an institutional response at a Swiss university, including AI-use guidelines requiring transparency about model use, purpose, critical evaluation, and manuscript locations where AI was used. The paper reports perceived relevance of these guidelines and identifies implementation challenges such as voluntary compliance, lack of training, limited monitoring, and absence of dedicated staffing, but provides no quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline development and reported implementation challenges from a university case study

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines the potential role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning. Rather than reporting a primary intervention study, it synthesizes emerging ideas and prior literature to address a central question: how GenAI may transform learning support, learning resource creation, feedback, and assessment, while also introducing substantial risks. The paper frames GenAI as both an opportunity and a challenge for education systems, especially in relation to personalization, scalability, ethics, and the changing nature of assessment.

The authors discuss GenAI as an approach that could support learners through adaptive tutoring, generate multimodal instructional resources, provide timely and personalized feedback, and enable more authentic and adaptive assessment. Across these areas, the paper draws on examples from prior studies and tools such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Khanmigo, text-to-image systems, and multi-agent AI systems. The article is conceptual and integrative: it uses learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction perspectives to propose how GenAI might function as a cognitive facilitator, content co-creator, feedback provider, and assessment agent.

The paper does not study a single participant sample or intervention context. Instead, it addresses broad educational populations and stakeholders, including learners, educators, administrators, parents, researchers, policymakers, and technologists, with explicit discussion spanning K-12 and higher education. It is therefore best understood as a high-level framework for thinking about GenAI in education rather than as direct evidence on student literacy outcomes or school-based comparative effects.

The main conclusions are that GenAI has real promise for enhancing learning through personalization, resource diversification, feedback, and assessment innovation, but that these benefits remain insufficiently validated by rigorous long-term empirical research. The authors emphasize major concerns including hallucinations, bias, privacy, inequality, opacity, overreliance, and disruption of conventional assessment. They argue that future progress depends on AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, human-centered design, stronger methodological rigor, and careful integration of GenAI to augment rather than replace human cognition and educator judgment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed perspective article, not an empirical evaluation. It does not report an original study design, sample, comparator, intervention implementation, or outcome analysis for K-12 learners.
