The population consisted of undergraduate students at a single North American research-focused institution in Canada, across an introductory computer science course, an upper-year operating systems course, and a small upper-year writing course on AI topics. Valid survey responses included 176 students in CS2, 80 in operating systems, and 7 in the writing course. Human feedback came from teaching assistants in some courses and the course instructor in the writing course.

The main conclusions are that AI-generated feedback, especially from the SLM, was often perceived as clear, structured, and actionable in large technical courses, while human feedback was preferred when assignments required personalized, context-sensitive, and nuanced guidance. In the small writing-intensive course, all respondents preferred instructor feedback. Students could often, but not always, identify whether feedback came from AI or humans. The authors argue that AI feedback is promising for scalability and efficiency, but that hybrid human-in-the-loop models are likely the most pedagogically effective approach.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative study with quantitative survey data and some statistical testing, but it is not a K-12 study, lacks random assignment, and focuses on student perceptions of feedback rather than direct learning outcomes. It appears to be an arXiv preprint/grey literature source with limited causal credibility for the requested K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but context-dependent perceived benefits of AI feedback, especially for efficiency and some feedback-quality dimensions, but impact on actual writing achievement is unclear and no standardized effect sizes are reported. Results are mixed across contexts, with human feedback preferred in the small writing-intensive course.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-based automated feedback on students’ technical writing submissions in computer science courses, comparing GPT-4 and LLaMA 3.1 8B with human TA/instructor feedback using a rubric-aligned prompt and retrieval-augmented generation.
LLM/SLM writing-feedback tool for technical documentation and report-writing, generating criterion-by-criterion comments, reasoning, and revision suggestions for student writing.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined perceived quality of feedback on student technical writing rather than objective writing achievement. In the operating systems course (n=80 valid responses), students most often preferred SLM feedback (61.25%) over LLM (15%) and human (23.75%), with statistically significant advantages for SLM on readability (p=0.005), actionability (p=0.040), and overall quality (p=0.004), while in the small writing course (n=7) all students preferred instructor feedback across all writing-feedback dimensions. In the CS2 course (n=176 valid responses), humans had the best readability mean (1.83), but SLM feedback was rated more favorably on most other feedback dimensions; no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student ratings of feedback quality for technical writing (readability, detail, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, overall quality), plus feedback preference selections

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported feedback generation substantially reduced time demands relative to human marking. For the operating systems course (143 enrolled students), humans reportedly spent about 35 hours writing feedback plus 5 hours training, whereas the SLM system generated all feedback in about 1.8 hours; for the 13-student writing course, SLM generation took about 10 minutes versus about 4.5 hours of instructor marking, and GPT-4 averaged roughly 25 seconds per response. These findings suggest strong efficiency gains, though they are descriptive and not tied to randomized productivity comparisons.
finding.measure: Time to generate feedback, estimated staffing time/cost, scalability of feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly assessed students’ ability to evaluate and discern feedback sources, which relates to judgment and critical evaluation rather than direct academic performance. Students identified feedback origin with 100% accuracy in the small writing course, 69.58% overall accuracy in operating systems, and lower accuracy in CS2 for LLM (34.66%) and SLM (52.84%) identification, suggesting variable student capacity to critically distinguish AI from human feedback depending on context. No validated durable-skills measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy in identifying whether feedback was AI- or human-generated

paper_profiles.title: Will ChatGPT get you caught? Rethinking of Plagiarism Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether essays generated by ChatGPT can be detected as plagiarized by conventional plagiarism-detection software. The core question is whether generative AI-produced academic writing would be flagged by widely used systems, and what this implies for academic integrity in education. The study is motivated by growing concern that students may use ChatGPT to generate essays and submit them as their own work.

The authors generated 50 essays by prompting ChatGPT to write approximately 500-word essays on different topics. These outputs were then checked using two plagiarism-detection tools: Turnitin for 25 essays and iThenticate for 25 essays. As an additional exploratory step, the authors also asked ChatGPT itself whether the essays had been generated by a chatbot, treating this as a kind of reverse-engineering detection approach. The analysis focused on descriptive statistics of similarity/originality scores rather than learning outcomes or writing improvement.

No human student participants were studied; instead, the unit of analysis was AI-generated text. The context is educational assessment and academic writing, but not a classroom intervention. The paper does not report a school-based implementation, grade band, or instructional setting, and it is therefore not a direct comparative K-12 writing outcomes study.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated essays often appear highly original to standard plagiarism detectors, with most essays receiving similarity scores low enough that they might not raise concern in typical academic settings. The authors argue that conventional plagiarism detection based on text similarity may be insufficient for generative AI content, and they suggest that institutions reconsider plagiarism-detection practices and policies in light of large language models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative descriptive study with a clearly described procedure and reported sample of 50 essays, but it is not a K-12 comparative intervention study and lacks a student sample, control group, validated outcome design, and inferential statistics. It provides limited empirical evidence on tool performance rather than educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests unclear but potentially meaningful institutional impact by showing that AI-generated writing may evade existing plagiarism systems, yet no student learning or writing-process effects were measured and no standardized effect sizes were reported. Impact is therefore important but empirically under-specified.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used to generate 50 short academic essays on assigned topics in order to test whether AI-generated writing could evade plagiarism-detection systems in educational settings.
Turnitin and iThenticate were used as automated plagiarism/similarity detection tools to evaluate the originality scores of ChatGPT-generated essays.
ChatGPT was additionally prompted to judge whether pasted essays were generated by a chatbot, functioning as an AI-based text-origin detector rather than as a learning support tool.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that conventional plagiarism-detection tools often rated ChatGPT-generated essays as highly original: 40 of 50 essays had similarity scores of 20% or less across Turnitin and iThenticate, suggesting these systems may fail to efficiently flag AI-generated writing. In a reverse-engineering check, ChatGPT reportedly identified 46 of 50 essays as generated by itself (>92% accuracy), outperforming the traditional similarity tools for this specific task; however, no inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or validated accuracy benchmarking were reported.
finding.measure: Plagiarism/similarity scores from Turnitin and iThenticate; count of essays identified by ChatGPT as AI-generated

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that ChatGPT can generate essays that are difficult for standard institutional plagiarism systems to detect, with 40 out of 50 essays receiving similarity scores at or below 20%. The authors interpret this as a threat to academic integrity systems and argue that institutions may need new AI-origin detection policies and revised assessment practices, but no causal institutional outcome metrics were measured.
finding.measure: Similarity/originality outcomes interpreted as implications for institutional plagiarism policy and academic integrity enforcement

paper_profiles.title: Complementary Advantages of ChatGPTs and Human Readers in Reasoning: Evidence from English Text Reading Comprehension
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how two generative AI systems, ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4), compare with human readers on reasoning during English text reading comprehension. The authors focus on three kinds of inference-making that are important for reading: commonsense inference, emotional inference, and causal inference. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the study asks whether AI and human readers show different strengths and weaknesses when interpreting English narrative texts and whether more elaborate prompting improves chatbot performance.

The approach was a direct performance comparison between human students and the two chatbot versions across three researcher-designed tests. Test 1 measured commonsense inference using local-culture and daily-life items; Test 2 measured emotional inference using adapted narrative stories requiring identification of characters' emotions; and Test 3 measured causal inference using a suspense story with questions about antecedents and likely outcomes. The authors also added an updated prompting condition for the chatbots in the causal inference task, asking them to analyze plot structure, key details, and focal characters before revising their answers.

The population was 114 second-year senior high school students in a single middle-level high school in China, around age 17, studying English as a second language. The students had studied English for at least six years and completed the assessments during school flexible class time. The chatbot outputs were generated repeatedly to create the same number of valid responses as the student datasets for comparison. The setting was essentially school-based classroom/offline testing for students, with chatbot comparison conducted separately by the researchers.

The main conclusion is that human readers and ChatGPT systems have complementary strengths rather than one clearly dominating the other. Students performed better on local-culture commonsense inference and causal reasoning requiring holistic logical analysis, while ChatGPT Plus performed best on daily-life commonsense and many emotional inference tasks, outperforming both students and ChatGPT. ChatGPT generally performed worst and was more prone to fabricated or contradictory explanations. With more elaborate prompting, ChatGPT Plus improved substantially on causal inference, whereas ChatGPT remained largely unchanged. Overall, the paper argues that AI and human readers differ in the kinds of reasoning they do well, with implications for understanding both the promise and limitations of LLM-based text reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative empirical study with a described method and sample, but it is not an intervention study in an educational setting, lacks random assignment/control of exposure, and reports mostly descriptive accuracy percentages without effect sizes or stronger causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings show mixed and context-dependent differences between students and LLMs on literacy-related reasoning tasks, with no clear educational treatment effect magnitude and no reported effect sizes, so overall impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Direct comparison of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4) against Chinese senior high school ESL students on English narrative-text reasoning tasks, including commonsense, emotional, and causal inference, with additional prompt-updating to test whether elaborated commands improve model reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The study compared 114 Chinese senior high school ESL students with ChatGPT and ChatGPT Plus on English reading-comprehension inference tasks. Students outperformed both chatbots on local-culture commonsense inference (86.83% accuracy vs. 61.98% ChatGPT and 66.58% ChatGPT Plus) and on causal inference/logical analysis in several items, while ChatGPT Plus outperformed students on daily-life commonsense inference (93.33% vs. 67.66%) and generally on emotional inference accuracy/frequency. No standardized effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on three English narrative reading inference tests: commonsense inference (local culture and daily life), emotional inference from short stories, and causal inference from a suspense story
finding.study_size: n=114 students; ChatGPT/ChatGPT Plus generated 82 valid questionnaires for emotional and causal tasks and 87 for commonsense task

finding.finding_summary: On reasoning-related outcomes embedded in reading tasks, students showed stronger logical analysis and culture-grounded inference in some contexts, especially causal antecedent reasoning and local-culture judgments, whereas ChatGPT Plus showed stronger performance on some deductive and lexical-demanding tasks and improved under more elaborate prompting. The paper argues that human readers and LLMs show complementary strengths rather than one uniformly outperforming the other. Effect sizes were not reported.
finding.measure: Reasoning/inference performance from text reading: commonsense, emotional, and causal inference accuracy; responsiveness to updated prompting in causal reasoning
finding.study_size: n=114 students; chatbot repeated-response samples of 82 or 87 depending on task

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Code Explanations Created by Students and Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can generate code explanations that are useful for students learning introductory programming, and how those explanations compare with explanations written by students. The authors focus on code comprehension and explanation as foundational programming skills, noting that producing high-quality example explanations at scale is difficult for instructors. Their research questions ask whether student- and LLM-generated explanations differ in accuracy, understandability, and length, and what characteristics students value in a good explanation.

The study used GPT-3-generated explanations and student-generated explanations for three short C functions. In a first lab activity, students wrote explanations of the functions’ intended purposes. In a second lab, two weeks later, students rated a random set of explanations drawn from a pool containing both student-written and GPT-3-written examples on ease of understanding, accuracy, and ideal length using Likert scales. The study also included an open-ended prompt asking students what makes a code explanation useful, which the authors analyzed thematically.

Participants were students in a first-year programming course at the University of Auckland, with approximately 1000 students enrolled and 954 participating in the evaluation activity. The context was an in-person lab-based introductory programming course using the C language. The quantitative component compared ratings of LLM and student explanations using Mann-Whitney U tests, while the qualitative component analyzed 100 randomly selected open-ended responses about valued explanation features.

The main conclusion is that GPT-3-generated explanations were rated significantly easier to understand and more accurate than student-generated explanations, while perceived and actual length did not differ significantly. Students tended to prefer detailed, often line-by-line explanations that clearly described inputs, outputs, and how the code works. The authors conclude that LLM-generated explanations may be useful as scalable scaffolds or examples in introductory programming education, especially for novice learners, while also noting important limits related to generalizability, the simplicity of the code tasks, and the lack of direct learning-outcome measures.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative study with quantitative analysis, but it is not K-12, not a randomized impact evaluation of learning outcomes, and mainly measures student perceptions of explanation quality rather than direct achievement gains. The design supports descriptive comparative inference but has important external-validity and causal limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper finds small positive advantages for LLM-generated explanations on perceived quality, but effect sizes are weak and the outcomes are proxy measures in higher education computing rather than direct K-12 writing or literacy impacts. Impact on the target evidence base is therefore unclear.

interventions.use_case: Large language model (GPT-3) generation of code explanations that students compare against peer-written explanations in an introductory programming course; the model is used as an on-demand generator of exemplar explanations rather than as a tutor or writing assistant.

finding.finding_summary: In a first-year university programming course, students rated GPT-3-generated code explanations as easier to understand and more accurate summaries of code than student-generated explanations. Among 954 students evaluating sampled explanations, Mann-Whitney tests showed significant advantages for LLM explanations on understandability (U=1421596.0, p=3.010×10^-31, RBC=0.206, CLES=0.397) and accuracy (U=1568575.5, p=2.866×10^-12, RBC=0.123, CLES=0.438), with no statistically significant difference in perceived ideal length after Bonferroni correction; effects were small.
finding.measure: Student ratings of code explanation understandability, accuracy, and ideal length on 5-point Likert scales in an introductory programming context

paper_profiles.title: From Model to Classroom: Evaluating Generated MCQs for Portuguese with Narrative and Difficulty Concerns
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether current generative AI models can produce usable multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for Portuguese elementary reading comprehension, especially questions targeting narrative elements and varying difficulty levels. The authors are motivated by the practical challenge of creating high-quality MCQs for classroom use and by the lack of evidence about how AI-generated questions perform in real educational settings, particularly outside English. The study asks whether generated MCQs are acceptable to experts, how their psychometric properties compare with human-authored items, and whether model-assigned difficulty aligns with expert and student performance.

The intervention is an AI-based MCQ generation pipeline applied to Portuguese narrative texts. The authors compare three generation approaches: GPT-4o in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup, Gemma-2-27B in a similar one-step setup, and a two-step method combining a fine-tuned ptt5-v2-large model for wh-question generation with Gemma-2 for answer options and difficulty annotation. Generated MCQs are evaluated against human-authored MCQs from Porto Editora materials. Evaluation includes expert review of item quality (well-formedness, narrative alignment, option clarity, answerability, plausibility, and perceived difficulty) and quantitative psychometric analysis of student responses using classical test theory metrics such as difficulty and discrimination.

The population and context are Portuguese elementary school students and education professionals. Expert review involved 18 native Portuguese-speaking participants with professional expertise in Portuguese language education, including teachers and publishing professionals. Student testing involved 284 students across 14 classes in a school group in the Valongo region of Portugal, using grade-appropriate reading materials for 2nd to 4th year elementary education. The study took place in authentic school classrooms, with paper-based administration under teacher supervision.

The main conclusion is that large language model-generated MCQs, especially from GPT-4o and Gemma-2, are broadly comparable to human-authored MCQs in overall quality, though they still exhibit issues with semantic clarity, answerability, and distractor design. Human-authored MCQs were slightly more difficult, more discriminative, and had distractors that engaged students somewhat better, but differences were generally not statistically significant. The two-step ptt5-v2+Gemma-2 method performed worse, especially on answerability and distractor reliability. Overall, the authors conclude that current LLMs can generate classroom-relevant Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs of comparable quality to human-authored items, but careful validation remains necessary before classroom deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a structured comparative empirical study with expert review and classroom psychometric validation in elementary schools, but it is not a randomized trial of student learning outcomes and is currently an arXiv preprint under review. It fits a quasi-experimental/validation evidence level with meaningful empirical methods but some credibility concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mixed evidence: generated MCQs were broadly comparable to human-authored ones, yet no clear student-learning effect sizes were reported and some quality dimensions favored human-authored items. Impact is therefore operationally promising but substantively unclear for student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI for automatic multiple-choice question generation in Portuguese reading comprehension, producing curriculum-aligned narrative-element and difficulty-controlled MCQs for elementary students and comparing them with human-authored items.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated reading-comprehension MCQ quality for elementary Portuguese language assessment rather than a learning intervention on students' writing or literacy growth. Expert review found LLM-generated MCQs broadly comparable to human-authored ones on several quality dimensions, and psychometric analysis of student responses (14 classes; 284 students, with 124 validated MCQs and about 45 responses per MCQ) showed no statistically significant differences in estimated item difficulty (Kruskal-Wallis H=1.249, p=0.741) or discrimination (reported H=0.854, p>0.05), though human-authored items were slightly more difficult and discriminative and had better distractor engagement.
finding.measure: Expert review of MCQ well-formedness, narrative alignment, option clarity, answerability, distractor plausibility, perceived difficulty; student-response psychometrics for reading-comprehension MCQs (difficulty 1-P, discrimination D, distractor usage, 3-rule option-quality test)
finding.study_size: n=284 students; 18 expert reviewers; 124 validated MCQs used in student testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions generative MCQ generation as a way to reduce the time and cost of manually authoring reading-comprehension assessments, and empirical comparison suggests current LLMs can generate items of comparable overall quality to human-authored ones after validation. However, because generated items still exhibited semantic clarity, answerability, and distractor-quality problems, the efficiency gains appear contingent on expert screening rather than fully autonomous deployment.
finding.measure: Comparative item-generation quality relative to human-authored MCQs as a proxy for feasibility of automating assessment authoring
finding.study_size: 18 expert reviewers; 180 MCQs in expert review, 124 validated MCQs in student psychometric analysis

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Small LLMs for Argument Mining in Education: Argument Component Identification, Classification, and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether small, open-source large language models can be used for educational argument mining on student essays. The core problem is how to automatically segment argumentative essays into components, classify those components by rhetorical type, and assess their quality in ways that could eventually support targeted feedback for student writing. The authors position this as an accessibility, privacy, and efficiency problem in education: high-performing models often require substantial computational resources, whereas smaller open-source models could potentially run locally on students’ computers.

The study evaluates three small LLMs—Qwen 2.5 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemma 2 9B—using two adaptation approaches: few-shot prompting and fine-tuning. These models are applied to three tasks on argumentative essays: segmentation into argument components, classification into seven Toulmin-inspired categories, and quality assessment into three levels. Performance is compared against encoder-based baselines from prior work (Longformer and BERT variants) and against GPT-4o mini as a commercial benchmark. The work is framed as an empirical model-comparison study rather than a classroom intervention trial.

The population consists of essays written by U.S. students in grades 6–12 from the Feedback Prize / PERSUADE 2.0-related dataset. The subset used includes about 6,900 essays overall, with the reported train/validation/test splits drawn from prior work. The educational context is secondary student argumentative writing in English, but the models are evaluated offline on an existing benchmark dataset rather than being deployed with teachers or students in live instruction.

The main conclusions are that small open-source LLMs outperform the reported encoder baselines for argument segmentation and argument-type classification, especially when fine-tuned. Fine-tuning was particularly helpful for segmentation and type classification, while few-shot prompting worked better than fine-tuning for quality assessment. The authors argue that these results show promise for privacy-preserving, locally run writing-support tools, but they also note important limitations: poor performance on quality assessment, inference instability in some setups, and uncertain generalizability beyond English essays from U.S. grade 6–12 students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/model-comparison study on an annotated corpus of student essays, not a K-12 intervention trial with learners receiving treatment versus comparison instruction. It has clear methods and quantitative results, but no causal design or direct student outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising task-performance gains for automated writing feedback components, but impact on actual student writing outcomes is indirect and unclear. Reported gains are model-performance improvements rather than student learning effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Small open-source LLMs and GPT-4o mini are used to automatically segment student essays into argument components, classify argument types, and assess argument quality as a pipeline for potential real-time writing feedback on argumentative essays.
LLM-based analysis of student argumentative writing to support improvement of essay structure and argumentation quality, positioned as a writing-support tool rather than a full tutor.

finding.finding_summary: On benchmark argumentative essay processing tasks using essays from grade 6–12 students, fine-tuned small LLMs outperformed encoder baselines for segmentation and argument-type classification. The best small open model (fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B) reached segmentation macro-F1=87.52, improving 18.05 points over Longformer; for type classification with inferred segmentation it achieved macro-F1=51.45, 12.27 points above the Longformer+BERT baseline. For quality assessment, results were weaker: the best small open model under inferred segmentation (Gemma 2 9B, 3-shot) was only roughly comparable to baseline, indicating gains are task-dependent.
finding.measure: Macro-averaged F1 for argument segmentation, argument type classification, and argument quality assessment on student argumentative essays
finding.study_size: test set: 419 essays, 3,711 arguments; training set: 3,353 essays, 29,440 arguments; validation set: 419 essays, 3,614 arguments
finding.effect_size: segmentation +18.05 F1 points vs baseline; type classification +12.27 F1 points vs baseline; quality assessment improvement not clearly established under inferred segmentation
finding.std_deviation: reported as error bars across 3 runs, exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that small open-source LLM pipelines can run locally and efficiently enough for educational deployment, including fine-tuning on a single A100 GPU and inference on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with 32GB RAM via Ollama. However, this is demonstrated as computational feasibility and accessibility rather than with direct classroom productivity or teacher-workload outcome data.
finding.measure: Technical feasibility/accessibility indicators such as local inference capability, model size, and computational setup

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that automated argument mining feedback could support students' argumentation and critical analysis of essays by identifying strengths and weaknesses in claims, evidence, counterclaims, and rebuttals. Empirically, the study measures model performance on argument-structure identification rather than direct student gains in critical thinking, so evidence for durable-skill improvement is indirect.
finding.measure: Automated identification/classification of argumentative components and their quality in student essays

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized grading and formative feedback for complex constructive geometry tasks in online mathematics learning. The authors focus on tasks that require students to create geometric constructions, explain reasoning, and apply concepts such as the circumcenter in inquiry-based contexts. They ask whether a large language model-based system can deliver teacher-aligned grading and useful adaptive feedback at scale, especially for open-ended explanations and multi-step geometry work.

The intervention is a personalized auto-grading and feedback system integrated into Algeomath, a Korean web-based dynamic geometry platform. The system uses rule-based grading for closed-ended and construction-based items, and GPT-4 with few-shot prompting for grading open-ended explanations. Feedback is generated from teacher-authored exemplar responses and adapts to students’ answer history and remaining attempts, with up to four attempts per item. The feedback becomes progressively more explicit across attempts, moving from hints to direct explanation.

The study was conducted with 79 middle-school students in four middle school classes in South Korea during November 2024. Students completed an 18-question sequence spanning closed-ended items, constructive geometry tasks, and open-ended explanations. The authors compared system grading to teacher judgments, analyzed attempt-by-attempt correction patterns, examined psychometric properties of items, and qualitatively reviewed cases of answer refinement and feedback quality.

The main conclusions are that the system showed strong alignment with teachers overall, especially for rule-based items and for detecting correct open-ended responses. Feedback often helped students correct errors on subsequent attempts, with about one-third of initially incorrect responses converting to correct after feedback, though gains were strongest early and longer-term transfer to later questions was unclear. The authors conclude that LLM-supported formative assessment is promising for scalable, teacher-aligned support in mathematics, but that improvements are needed in terminology precision, feedback scaffolding, and avoiding overly revealing or poorly phrased feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-group field study/pilot with teacher-agreement benchmarking and within-student attempt analyses, but no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison condition. It provides useful quantitative evidence, yet causal inference about learning impact is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising short-term improvement and operational benefits, but effect sizes are mostly not reported and longer-term transfer effects were unclear or non-significant. Overall impact appears modest or uncertain rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based auto-grading and adaptive formative feedback for middle-school constructive geometry tasks on the Algeomath platform, using GPT-4 few-shot prompts to evaluate open-ended explanations and teacher-authored exemplars to generate attempt-sensitive feedback across up to four tries.
Prompt-conditioned GPT-4 generates short, personalized, progressively scaffolded feedback messages that resemble conversational tutoring during iterative geometry problem solving.
Students solve inquiry-based constructive geometry tasks in the Algeomath web platform with interactive dynamic-geometry tools and automated response checking.

finding.finding_summary: In a November 2024 field study with 79 South Korean middle-school students, the system supported substantial within-item correction: the cumulative proportion solved rose from about 0.60 on first attempt to about 0.73 after the second, 0.78 after the third, and 0.80 by the fourth attempt. Immediate post-feedback correctness conversion across all initially incorrect attempts was 36.7% (260/708), but evidence for longer-term transfer to later geometry items was not statistically significant (e.g., Q10 p=0.547 overall correctness; Q11 p=0.643; Q18 p=0.624), so short-term gains were clearer than durable transfer.
finding.measure: Constructive geometry task correctness by attempt, cumulative success curves, post-feedback conversion rate, later-item correctness/transfer tests

finding.finding_summary: The automated grading system closely matched teacher judgments while enabling scalable real-time assessment. For open-ended explanatory questions, overall agreement with teacher scoring was 0.866 with Cohen's kappa=0.737 across 878 responses; closed-ended and constructive geometry tasks graded rule-based achieved 100% agreement with teachers.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher grading, Cohen's kappa, rule-based grading accuracy
finding.study_size: 878 open-ended responses from 79 students; 79 students overall

finding.finding_summary: Student self-assessment survey results were favorable, with average Likert ratings ranging from 4.1 to 4.5 out of 5 across items about understanding and using circumcenter concepts with the digital tool. The paper also reports that feedback was intentionally framed in encouraging language and that students broadly endorsed the activity, though no validated engagement or motivation effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student Likert self-assessment/satisfaction survey and open-ended comments

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative and attempt-level analyses suggest the system helped some students refine explanations toward greater specificity and conceptually accurate geometric reasoning within a problem, such as moving from vague statements to explicit equidistance-based justification. However, transfer of feedback-supported reasoning to subsequent more complex items was not statistically demonstrated, indicating gains in iterative reasoning but unclear durability beyond the immediate task.
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement examples, later-question transfer analyses, attempt number of first success

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive the use of generative AI to support creative mathematical writing. The central problem addressed is that while creative mathematical writing may help students express mathematical ideas imaginatively, many young learners struggle to generate and develop such stories. The authors argue that before designing effective GenAI-powered classroom tools, it is necessary to understand how students and teachers experience these tools in real instructional settings, including both perceived benefits and challenges.

The study investigated a researcher-developed GenAI-powered learning platform used within a three-step instructional routine: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed a provided math story, then visually represented mathematical ideas using a canvas tool, and finally used generative AI to draft and revise culturally relevant math stories by entering story goals, characters, settings, and events. The system leveraged OpenAI GPT-4 for story generation and DALL·E 3 for image generation, using structured prompts, active prompting, and a curated database of grade-appropriate math stories to guide output.

The participants were 79 fifth-grade students and six elementary school teachers across two U.S. schools. One school on the U.S. West Coast implemented four class sessions of 45–60 minutes focused on fraction division, and one school in the Southeast implemented eight 35-minute sessions focused on multiplication of fractions. Data came from focus group interviews with 10 students, individual interviews with all six teachers, open-ended student surveys, and classroom observation notes. The analysis used qualitative thematic analysis and produced six themes and 19 subthemes.

The authors conclude that students and teachers perceived GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing as beneficial for fostering creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and positive affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, they identified challenges including weak student critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent prompts and story ideas, insufficient pedagogical feedback from the AI system, reduced autonomy, limited social interaction, and accessibility issues. Overall, the paper presents this intervention as promising but emphasizes that educational value depends on careful instructional and interface design rather than AI generation alone.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom implementation study with thematic analysis triangulated by surveys and observations. It provides useful practice-based evidence but lacks a comparative design, validated quantitative outcome measures, and causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive but perception-based impacts without quantitative effect sizes or direct comparisons. Because impact magnitude is unclear and based on subjective reports rather than measured achievement gains, the appropriate tier is yellow.

interventions.use_case: Researcher-developed GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 powered platform supporting 5th-grade students’ creative mathematical writing through structured story generation, prompt-based co-writing, and image creation within an Ask-Represent-Transform workflow.

The classroom platform also functioned as a structured digital learning environment with question prompts, visual representation tools, and checklists guiding mathematical story writing activities beyond the generative AI component.

finding.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews, surveys, and classroom observations from 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, participants reported that GenAI-supported mathematical story writing improved problem understanding, mathematical representation, and surfacing of misconceptions. Evidence is perception-based rather than causal or test-score based; no standardized achievement effects, effect sizes, or inferential statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, representation, and misconceptions from interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI-supported activity as fostering creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, AI literacy, and critical evaluation of AI outputs, though some students also struggled to critique AI-generated content effectively. Findings were derived from thematic analysis of interviews triangulated with surveys and observations, with no quantitative effect estimates reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes on creativity, flexible thinking, AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning during GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing. At the same time, participants noted challenges related to reduced autonomy and limited social connection, so the affective picture is positive overall but not uniformly so; no scales or effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of interest, curiosity, enjoyment, ownership, autonomy, and social connection from interviews, surveys, and observations

paper_profiles.title: Which Feedback Works for Whom? Differential Effects of LLM-Generated Feedback Elements Across Learner Profiles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which design elements of large language model (LLM)-generated feedback are most effective for learners, and whether feedback preferences differ by learner personality traits. Rather than comparing AI feedback with human feedback, the study focuses on six feedback element conditions—Baseline, Keywords, Actionability, Novelty, Coverage, and Positivity—and asks which elements best support answer revision, which are most positively evaluated by students, and how those evaluations vary across Big Five personality-based learner profiles.

The intervention consisted of GPT-5-generated feedback for multiple-choice high school biology questions. Feedback was pre-generated for each answer option using prompts that systematically varied the included pedagogical element. Students answered biology questions in a web-based system, received immediate feedback tied to their selected response, rated that feedback on six subjective criteria, and, if incorrect, revised their answers iteratively until correct. Learning outcomes were assessed through first revised-attempt accuracy and an effectiveness metric based on number of attempts required to reach the correct answer; subjective evaluations covered trustworthiness, review guidance, expression quality, ease of understanding, key points clarity, and new knowledge.

Participants were 321 first-year high school students from nine basic biology classes in Japan. The activity was assigned as winter-break homework, so the context was school-related but completed through an online system outside normal class time. Students also completed a pre-questionnaire including a Japanese Big Five personality scale, allowing the authors to cluster learners into three personality profiles and analyze differences in feedback acceptance across those groups.

The study concludes that feedback elements emphasizing clear correction targets and focused guidance were most effective. Baseline feedback produced the strongest learning outcomes, with Coverage and Keywords also supporting revision, while Keywords, Baseline, and Actionability tended to receive the highest subjective ratings. Preferences differed across personality clusters: for example, some learners rated novelty more highly, whereas positivity was consistently rated relatively low. The authors argue that effective LLM-generated feedback should be designed not only around pedagogical principles but also with learner characteristics in mind, though they note important limits in generalizability due to the single-subject context, use of one LLM, and lack of broader learner measures or long-term follow-up.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with a sizable sample and structured intervention, but it does not present a clear randomized controlled or strong quasi-experimental comparison against a non-LLM condition at the student level. The paper is also an arXiv preprint, with limited causal identification and incomplete reporting of effect sizes/statistical detail for the main learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows promising but uneven effects across feedback designs, with substantial descriptive gains for some feedback variants but no reported standardized effect sizes or clean comparison to business-as-usual instruction. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear rather than firmly established.

interventions.use_case: GPT-5-generated automated feedback for high school biology multiple-choice answer revision, varying six feedback elements (Baseline, Keywords, Actionability, Novelty, Coverage, Positivity) and delivered iteratively after incorrect responses.
Use of GPT-5 as the generative engine to produce personalized-style explanatory feedback within a web-based revision workflow, though not as a full conversational tutor.

finding.finding_summary: In a learning experiment with 321 first-year high school students, LLM-generated feedback supported answer revision on basic biology multiple-choice items, but effects differed by feedback element rather than showing one overall treatment effect against a non-AI comparator. Among students who answered incorrectly initially, first-revision accuracy was 65.66% for Baseline (n=198), 53.22% for Coverage (n=171), 52.94% for Keywords (n=204), 52.11% for Novelty (n=213), 49.01% for Actionability (n=202), and 46.63% for Positivity (n=208); 95% CIs are shown graphically, but exact interval values and standardized effect sizes are not reported.
finding.measure: Biology item revision performance: first revised attempt accuracy after feedback; additional 'Effectiveness' metric based on number of attempts required to reach the correct answer

finding.finding_summary: Students' subjective acceptance of feedback varied across feedback elements and personality-based learner clusters. Keywords ranked first on four of six subjective criteria and, together with Baseline and Actionability, was generally rated more favorably, while Positivity received relatively low ratings; Kruskal-Wallis tests found significant cluster differences across all six criteria (p < .05), and Dunn post hoc tests showed differences for Trustworthiness, New Knowledge, and Expression Quality, especially involving Cluster 1.
finding.measure: Student subjective evaluations on six 3-point criteria: Trustworthiness, Review Guidance, Expression Quality, Ease of Understanding, Key Points Clarity, and New Knowledge; cluster-based differences by Big Five personality profiles

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined revision-oriented guidance and learners' ability to use feedback to move toward correct answers, suggesting some feedback formats better support review and answer revision processes than others. Baseline, Coverage, and Keywords were strongest on revision performance, while Actionability was subjectively valued, indicating a mismatch between perceived usefulness and measured revision success; however, no standardized metacognition or transfer measure was reported.
finding.measure: Revision process indicators, especially answer revision after feedback and perceived review guidance

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for students’ open-ended mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: SBERT-Canberra, a prior similarity-based automated assessment method; GOAT, a fine-tuned Mistral 7B model trained on student responses with teacher scores and feedback; and GPT-4 Turbo, used in a zero-shot configuration with a rubric-based prompt. The central questions are how these models compare in predicting teacher-assigned scores and which model produces feedback that human evaluators prefer.

The intervention is not a classroom teaching intervention but a comparative evaluation of automated feedback systems for math education. The dataset came from an online learning platform using Illustrative Mathematics-style open-ended items. The authors selected 50 open-response math problems, each with 100 student responses, teacher feedback, and teacher scores, for a total of 5,000 entries. GOAT was fine-tuned on 4,000 entries and tested on 1,000 entries. GPT-4 received a prompt including the problem, student answer, and a 0-4 scoring rubric; GOAT was fine-tuned to output teacher-like scores and feedback; SBERT-Canberra retrieved similar historical responses to infer scores and feedback. Quantitative evaluation used AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa for scoring, while qualitative feedback evaluation used two human evaluators rating 100 sampled test entries on accuracy, relevance, motivation, and model preference.

The study context is middle-school mathematics in an online learning platform, with teacher-written feedback serving as the reference standard. The paper also includes educator participants as evaluators: two raters with prior teaching experience, one with middle-school teaching experience and one with graduate-level teaching experience. The student data were drawn from classrooms of about 50 teachers who frequently used open-ended questions, but the paper does not report a direct classroom implementation with students receiving the feedback in real time.

The main conclusions are that the fine-tuned GOAT model performed best for auto-scoring, outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on AUC (0.697), RMSE (1.119), and kappa (0.422). For feedback quality, however, GPT-4 was preferred by human evaluators and achieved the highest consensus accuracy (86%) and relevance (91%), while being selected as the preferred model 77.5% of the time. The authors conclude that fine-tuned open-source LLMs show promise for score prediction, but general-purpose GPT-4 currently provides stronger feedback quality. They also emphasize that model performance is limited by the quality and consistency of teacher-provided training data.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv preprint focused on algorithm comparison using teacher-score agreement and human ratings, not a K-12 causal impact study on student outcomes. It has a clear method and quantitative evaluation, but no randomized or quasi-experimental design measuring learner effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect operational benefits for automated feedback quality and scoring accuracy, especially for GPT-4 feedback preference and GOAT scoring performance. However, it reports no student learning effect sizes or direct classroom impact, so real-world impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Automated scoring and qualitative feedback generation for students' open-ended middle-school mathematics responses using a fine-tuned Mistral-based model (GOAT), compared with SBERT-Canberra retrieval-based feedback and zero-shot GPT-4.
Use of GPT-4 Turbo in a zero-shot prompting setup to score student math open responses and generate concise rubric-aligned feedback as a generative comparator.

finding.finding_summary: On automated scoring of open-ended middle-school math responses, the fine-tuned GOAT model outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all reported scoring metrics using a 1,000-response test set drawn from 50 problems (teacher-scored dataset total 5,000 entries). GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Cohen's kappa=0.422, compared with SBERT AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, kappa=0.362 and GPT-4 AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, kappa=0.266; however, this is model-evaluation evidence rather than student learning impact evidence.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher-assigned math open-response scores using AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen's kappa
finding.study_size: n=1000 test responses; 5000 total response records from 50 problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that generative and automated feedback systems can reduce scoring/feedback burden by producing rubric-aligned scores and comments for open-ended math responses, with GPT-4 strongly preferred by human evaluators for feedback quality. In a human review of 100 sampled test responses, GPT-4 feedback was preferred 77.5% of the time on average versus 12% each for GOAT and SBERT, and achieved higher consensus accuracy (86%) and relevance (91%) than GOAT (68%, 88%) or SBERT (52%, 76%).
finding.measure: Human evaluator judgments of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, and overall preference as proxies for usefulness in teacher feedback workflow
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled responses rated by 2 evaluators

finding.finding_summary: The study assessed the motivational tone of generated feedback rather than student motivation directly. Across 100 sampled responses, consensus motivating feedback rates were similar across systems—SBERT 46%, GOAT 48%, GPT-4 52%—while demotivating feedback rates were lowest for GPT-4 (1%), followed by GOAT (5%) and SBERT (11%), suggesting generative feedback may be somewhat better on affective tone but with no direct student outcome evidence.
finding.measure: Human-coded motivational and demotivational qualities of generated feedback messages
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled responses rated by 2 evaluators

paper_profiles.title: Content vs. Form: What Drives the Writing Score Gap Across Socioeconomic Backgrounds? A Generated Panel Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why writing scores differ across socioeconomic status (SES) groups: whether score gaps mainly reflect differences in the substance of students’ ideas and argumentation (content) or differences in expression, polish, and linguistic form (style). The authors argue that writing assessments reward both what students say and how they say it, making it difficult to determine how much observed SES score gaps are attributable to underlying reasoning versus surface expression. The study focuses on decomposing a writing-score gap rather than evaluating an instructional intervention.

To address this problem, the authors introduce a "generated panel" approach using large language models. For each student essay, they generate multiple rewritten versions intended to preserve the original arguments and meaning while altering stylistic realization. They then use predictive scoring models trained on human-rated essays to estimate how much of the SES score gap is associated with content, style, and differences in scoring functions. Rewrites include SAT score-tiered stylistic rewrites and neutral rewrites generated with GPT-4o, with an additional GPT-4o verification step used to filter out rewrites judged to alter substantive content.

The study uses the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus of 25,996 argumentative essays written by U.S. students in grades 6-12, with SES-linked data available for 20,759 essays. The context is large-scale persuasive writing assessment in U.S. secondary schooling rather than a classroom intervention. Essays were originally scored by trained expert raters on a 1-6 SAT-style rubric, and the authors analyze middle- and high-school students across multiple prompts and demographic subgroups.

The main conclusion is that the SES writing-score gap is driven primarily by content differences rather than style differences. The paper reports an average SES gap of 0.67 points on a 1-6 scale, with about 69% attributed to content, 26% to style, and 5% to differences in scoring functions. The authors conclude that while stylistic polish matters, most of the disparity reflects differences in argument quality, reasoning, and evidence use. They further argue that LLM-based polishing tools alone would be unlikely to eliminate SES writing-score gaps, because improving expression without changing underlying content would leave much of the disparity intact.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational, methodological decomposition study using a large essay corpus and LLM-generated rewrites, not a direct comparative K-12 intervention evaluation. It has a clear empirical method and large sample, but no randomized or quasi-experimental causal design for student outcomes and appears to be a 2026 arXiv preprint.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial descriptive differences in writing-score components, but it does not estimate a causal educational impact of a student-facing intervention on writing outcomes. Impact is therefore important conceptually but unclear under the K-12 intervention evidence framework.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated essay rewriting and content-verification used as a research measurement instrument to create stylistic variants of student persuasive essays and decompose score gaps into content, style, and scorer-function components; not an instructional writing intervention delivered to students.

finding.finding_summary: Using 20,759 SES-linked U.S. middle- and high-school persuasive essays scored on a 1-6 rubric, the paper finds an observed SES writing-score gap of 0.67 points. A decomposition using GPT-4o rewrites attributes about 69% of the gap to content quality differences, 26% to style differences, and 5% to scorer-function differences; the study analyzes writing assessment patterns rather than intervention effects on students' writing improvement. The style share rises by grade, from about 25% in grade 6 to over 40% in grade 11.
finding.measure: Holistic persuasive essay scores on a 1-6 scale; decomposition of score gap into content, style, and scorer-function components using predicted scores from rewrite panels
finding.effect_size: Observed gap = 0.67 points on a 1-6 scale; decomposition shares: content 69%, style 26%, scoring-function 5%

finding.finding_summary: The paper's institutional/fairness finding is that score disparities in writing assessment appear to be driven primarily by underlying content differences, with a smaller but non-trivial role for stylistic conventions rewarded by scoring systems. It further argues that universal access to LLM polishing tools would likely raise predicted scores for low-SES essays but would not eliminate the gap because content dominates; no causal policy evaluation or effect size for such a policy is reported.
finding.measure: SES-group differences in assessed writing scores; decomposition into content, style, and evaluator/scoring-rule components
finding.effect_size: Observed gap = 0.67 points; 69% content, 26% style, 5% scoring-function

paper_profiles.title: The Psychosocial Impacts of Generative AI Harms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential psychosocial harms of generative language models when they produce classroom-related narratives about students. The central problem is not writing improvement or instructional effectiveness, but whether biased AI-generated text can reinforce harmful representations of learners from marginalized groups through erasure, subordination, and stereotyping. The authors argue that as generative AI tools are increasingly introduced into educational settings, there is a need to understand how their outputs may affect users' social and psychological well-being.

The study analyzes 150,000 short stories from the existing “Laissez-Faire Harms” dataset, using outputs from five major generative language models: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Claude 2.0, Llama 2, and PaLM 2. These models were prompted with 30 open-ended classroom-related prompts about students across 15 academic subjects, including both power-neutral and power-laden versions. The authors combine quantitative pattern analysis of generated names and subject associations with qualitative purposive analysis of especially egregious examples. They also classify subjects into STEM and humanities/social sciences to examine stereotype patterns more closely.

The educational context is simulated rather than based on direct interventions with human learners. The prompts concern American students in classroom scenarios, and the paper discusses implications for K-20 settings, especially students and teachers who may encounter such tools in schools. Although no human participants were recruited into an intervention, the analysis focuses on how generated depictions may affect students from historically marginalized groups, including Indigenous/Native American, Latine, and Asian/Asian American learners.

The main conclusion is that the five language models frequently generate biased educational narratives that risk psychosocial harm. The paper finds strong evidence of Indigenous erasure, Latine subordination, and stereotypes such as the “white savior” and “model minority.” The authors conclude that generative AI tools used in education may reproduce and amplify social bias, and they call for more empirical research, teacher preparation, and policy attention to mitigate these harms before broader classroom adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical computational content-analysis study with a described dataset and analytic approach, but it is not a K-12 comparative intervention study and does not estimate causal effects on student outcomes. It provides some methodological transparency but lacks experimental educational outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper documents potential harms and argues for risk mitigation; it does not show positive educational impact and its substantive finding is negative risk in generated content. No effect size on learners, teachers, or institutions is reported.

interventions.use_case: Evaluation of five generative language models (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Claude 2.0, Llama 2, PaLM 2) generating short classroom-related stories in response to open-ended prompts, to analyze representational and psychosocial harms in educationally themed text outputs rather than student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that leading generative language models can produce biased classroom narratives that risk reinforcing representational harms in educational contexts, including erasure of Indigenous/Native American learners, subordination of Latine learners, and stereotyping such as 'white savior' and 'model minority' portrayals. Evidence is based on analysis of 150,000 model-generated 100-word stories from 30 classroom-related prompts across five models; no causal effect sizes, confidence intervals, or learner outcome statistics are reported because this is not an intervention trial with students.
finding.measure: Content analysis of LM-generated classroom narratives for representational harms (erasure, subordination, stereotyping) across prompts and character depictions

paper_profiles.title: Neural Authorship Attribution: Stylometric Analysis on Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the problem of neural authorship attribution: identifying which large language model generated a given piece of text. The authors are motivated by concerns about AI-generated misinformation and argue that forensic methods are needed not only to detect machine-written text, but also to attribute it to specific source models. A central question is whether proprietary LLMs and open-source LLMs exhibit distinct writing signatures that can be measured and used for attribution.

To study this, the authors generated a corpus of 6,000 AI-written news articles using six large language models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 1, Llama 2, and GPT-NeoX. They prompted each model with 1,000 human-authored news headlines sampled from CNN and the Washington Post source data, using generation settings of top-p = 0.9 and temperature = 0.8. They extracted 60 stylometric features spanning lexical, syntactic, and structural properties of the generated texts, and compared several classification approaches, including XGBoost with bag-of-words or stylometric features, RoBERTa-based models, and a fusion model combining RoBERTa embeddings with stylometric features.

The study does not involve educational participants, schools, or writing instruction contexts; instead, it is a computational analysis of AI-generated news text. The empirical context is a machine-generated text corpus rather than a human population. Results showed clear separation between proprietary and open-source LLM outputs, especially when stylometric features were used. The best-performing fusion model achieved near-perfect initial attribution between proprietary and open-source classes, and also outperformed alternatives for within-category attribution.

The main conclusion is that stylometric analysis provides interpretable and effective signals for attributing AI-generated text to its source LLM. Lexical diversity, parts-of-speech usage, punctuation, and paragraph structure were especially informative. The authors also conclude that attribution within open-source models is harder because some models have overlapping writing styles, although Llama 2 appeared more distinct and closer in style to proprietary models. Overall, the paper contributes a forensic methodology for analyzing LLM writing signatures rather than an educational intervention or K-12 writing outcomes study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv preprint focused on neural authorship attribution and stylometric analysis of AI-generated news articles, not a K-12 education intervention study. It does not evaluate any educational use of AI, student sample, classroom implementation, or learning-related causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong technical classification performance for attributing LLM-generated text, but it does not measure educational outcomes or intervention effects in learners. Educational impact is therefore unclear and not directly assessable within the K-12 evidence framework.

paper_profiles.title: Simulation Streams: A Programming Paradigm for Controlling Large Language Models and Building Complex Systems with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to better control large language models in long-running simulations and agentic workflows. The authors argue that straightforward prompting approaches for simulation are fragile because LLMs can drift from required formats, fail to maintain state consistency, improperly include or exclude information, and violate world rules over many iterations. The paper therefore focuses on a systems and programming question: how to create a minimally interfering framework that preserves the generative capabilities of LLMs while improving consistency, modularity, and control.

The proposed approach, Simulation Streams, is a state-based programming paradigm in which variables are updated sequentially by operators. Each operator specifies a state transition formula, whether and when the LLM is invoked, what prior context is queried, and what operator runs next. The framework also uses substreams to keep prompts structured and in-distribution, and it supports an Entity-Component-System architecture to organize simulations into reusable entities and components. A custom editor and Python/Flask implementation are described to support simulation authoring, execution, and analysis.

The paper does not study a student, teacher, or school population and is not an education intervention study. Instead, it demonstrates the framework through technical examples: reinforcement-learning benchmark tasks, a three-character social simulation, and a longer-running market economy simulation. These demonstrations compare model behavior across Gemini variants and illustrate the framework's ability to maintain structured outputs and support multi-agent simulations over tens to hundreds of steps.

The main conclusion is that Simulation Streams offers a practical and flexible method for controlling LLM-driven simulations with greater consistency and rule adherence than unconstrained prompting. The authors conclude that newer Gemini models, especially Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp and its thinking version, are well suited to this framework, showing strong consistency in the social simulation and competitive performance on benchmark tasks. Overall, the paper is primarily a technical framework paper with illustrative empirical demonstrations rather than a human-subjects evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv technical paper describing an LLM simulation programming paradigm, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It lacks education-relevant comparative study design, participant/sample details for learners, and peer-reviewed causal evidence on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful system-level efficiency benefits for simulation workflows, but it provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 writing, literacy, or other learner outcomes. Educational impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: LLM-controlled simulation framework for building and benchmarking multi-agent/social, market, and reinforcement-learning-style simulated environments using structured state updates and operator-driven generation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that within the authors' simulation framework, Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp showed perfect adherence to producing one correctly formatted simulation row in the social simulation across 10 runs, which the authors argue reduced excess tokens, resampling, and overall cost/speed burdens. However, this is a systems benchmarking result rather than an educational outcome, and no standardized productivity effect size or inferential statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Simulation consistency/format adherence, need for resampling, and qualitative claims about speed/economy in LLM-driven simulation workflows
finding.study_size: 10 runs for social simulation; 10 runs of 25 steps each across 6 RL benchmark tasks
finding.std_deviation: reported graphically for some benchmark-task traces, exact values not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Analyzing ChatGPT’s Aptitude in an Introductory Computer Engineering Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT/GPT-3 can answer the range of assessments used in an introductory undergraduate computer engineering course, rather than a single exam. The authors are interested in both the opportunities and limitations of generative AI in coursework, especially for tasks that go beyond text generation and require diagrams, truth tables, circuit representations, or hands-on lab work. The study also introduces an "accuracy-per-minute" metric to compare correctness with speed of solution generation.

The approach compares three sources of answers within the course: ordinary student work completed without ChatGPT, student-submitted secondary solutions produced with ChatGPT assistance, and answers generated automatically through the OpenAI API using text-davinci-003. The evaluation covers six quizzes, three homework assignments, four laboratory projects, and planned but not yet fully analyzed exam components. Assessment was based on instructor/teaching-assistant grading of the generated work, and the paper reports average scores, completion times, and efficiency metrics.

The context is a single introductory computer engineering course (EENG 201) at Yale University in the United States, typically taken by freshmen and sophomores, with some more senior students from computer science and a small number from other fields. Students were allowed to submit ChatGPT-assisted versions of their work separately from their graded coursework under explicit rules, enabling comparison between conventional work and AI-assisted responses in an authentic class setting.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT performs relatively well on short, text-based quiz questions and can sometimes generate plausible written responses quickly, but performs poorly on homework and other tasks that depend on figures, diagrams, or physical lab activities. The authors conclude that in its current text-only form, ChatGPT could not pass the full course, though its speed makes it highly efficient on a percentage-per-minute basis. They also warn that plausible but incorrect answers could mislead students, and argue that multimodal capabilities would be necessary for much stronger performance in this domain.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical course-based evaluation with quantitative results, but it is not a K-12 comparative intervention study, lacks a clearly reported analytic design and sample size for outcome estimation, and includes substantial risk of grading and selection bias. It provides descriptive performance evidence rather than rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear educational impact overall: strong apparent efficiency gains but mixed academic performance, with good results on simple text quizzes and very poor results on more complex coursework. No standardized effect sizes or causal comparisons are reported, so impact remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Evaluates GPT-3/ChatGPT as a conversational answer generator for quizzes, homework, exams, and lab-manual questions in an introductory university computer engineering course, including student-mediated use of ChatGPT and scripted OpenAI API completions.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT/GPT-3 performed well on short text-based quiz items but poorly on more complex homework and lab tasks requiring diagrams, figures, or hands-on work. Student ChatGPT-assisted quiz scores reached 87-100% across six quizzes, but ChatGPT-assisted assignment scores were only 8-27% and lab-question scores 60-70%; OpenAI API-generated solutions showed a similar pattern with quiz scores 43-83%, assignments 8-37%, and labs 44-56%.
finding.measure: Course assessment performance on quizzes, homework assignments, and laboratory questions in introductory computer engineering

finding.finding_summary: Automated GPT-3 solution generation was dramatically faster than human completion, leading the authors to propose an 'accuracy-per-minute' metric favoring the model despite lower correctness on many tasks. API-generated solutions took about 0.2-0.5 minutes for quizzes, 1.7-3.0 minutes for assignments, and 0.3-0.5 minutes for labs, versus student completion times of 5 minutes for quizzes, 380-800 minutes for assignments, and 68-79 minutes for labs.
finding.measure: Time to generate solutions and derived accuracy-per-minute efficiency metric

paper_profiles.title: Multi-Task Instruction Tuning of LLaMA for Specific Scenarios: A Preliminary Study on Writing Assistance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether open-source large language models can be efficiently adapted for a targeted vertical application rather than broad general-purpose instruction following. The authors focus on writing assistance and ask whether instruction tuning LLaMA on scenario-specific writing data improves performance across multiple writing-related tasks. They also examine a narrower question: whether it is worthwhile to use an LLM for a single task such as grammatical error correction, given the training and deployment costs.

The intervention is multi-task instruction tuning of LLaMA using a mixture of about 52,000 generic Stanford Alpaca instruction examples and about 60,000 writing-specific examples spanning six writing tasks: grammaticality, fluency, clarity, coherence, simplification, and neutralization, while paraphrasing is treated as a hold-out task. The paper evaluates tuned models on benchmark datasets for seven writing tasks and compares them with untuned LLaMA, Alpaca-style instruction-tuned LLaMA, larger off-the-shelf LLMs such as GPT-3, InstructGPT, and ChatGPT, and task-specific smaller models for grammatical error correction. The paper also analyzes factors such as generic instruction data, model size, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and resource costs.

There is no human educational participant population in this study. The context is an AI/NLP benchmark evaluation using publicly available datasets and GPU-based model training rather than a classroom, school, or learner-facing implementation. The writing datasets include learner essays for some tasks, but these are benchmark corpora rather than recruited study participants in an education intervention.

The main conclusions are that scenario-specific instruction tuning substantially improves LLaMA’s performance on targeted writing-assistance tasks and can allow a small tuned model to outperform much larger untuned or general-purpose LLMs on many benchmarks. However, the authors conclude that using LLMs for a single focused task may not always be justified, because task-specific smaller models can remain more efficient and competitive, especially for grammatical error correction. They highlight training and inference cost, as well as hallucination risk, as important constraints when deploying LLMs for specialized writing tasks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv preliminary technical model-evaluation paper, not a K-12 empirical study. It reports benchmark experiments without learner participants, classroom implementation, or educational causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising benchmark improvements for AI-assisted writing tasks, but educational impact on learners is unclear because no K-12 outcomes or effect sizes on student writing are reported.

interventions.use_case: Instruction-tuned LLaMA used as a writing assistant for text revision and editing across seven writing tasks: grammaticality correction, fluency improvement, clarity, coherence, simplification, neutralization, and paraphrasing.
