finding.finding_summary: Across benchmark writing/editing tasks, scenario-specific instruction tuning improved LLaMA’s average score from 43.07 for Alpaca-7B to 48.65 for Writing-Alpaca-7B, and from 30.64 for base LLaMA-7B to 48.65 overall. Task-level gains included CoNLL F0.5 19.21→55.88, BEA F0.5 22.42→46.35, JFLEG GLEU 41.14→59.93, and STS paraphrasing SARI 32.34→43.30; however, results are benchmark/model-evaluation outcomes rather than K-12 learner outcomes and no inferential effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: NLP benchmark performance on writing-related text editing tasks using F0.5, GLEU, and SARI across CoNLL14, BEA19-dev, JFLEG, ITERATER subsets, TurkCorpus, ASSET, WNC, and STS

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that instruction-tuned LLaMA can outperform much larger off-the-shelf LLMs in the targeted writing-assistant scenario, suggesting efficiency gains in model size for deployment. However, task-specific LLM adaptation remained costly relative to smaller specialized models: for GEC, LLaMA-13B-GEC required 397 GPU hours and 0.7 instances/second inference versus RoBERTa-Large at 21 GPU hours and 274.7 instances/second, indicating substantial deployment and runtime disadvantages.
finding.measure: Training GPU hours, inference speed (instances/second), and comparative model-size/performance tradeoffs

paper_profiles.title: Improve Large Language Model Systems with User Logs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to improve deployed large language model systems using real-world user interaction logs rather than only static pretraining data or curated supervision. The authors argue that user logs contain valuable feedback and procedural knowledge, but they are noisy, unstructured, and difficult to learn from safely. A central concern in the paper is what they call the "Signal-or-Noise Dilemma": user feedback may represent either useful novel information or harmful noise, and language models may struggle to tell the difference.

To address this, the paper proposes UNO (User log-driveN Optimization), a framework for continual learning from user logs. UNO first filters and distills raw logs into semi-structured rule sets and preference pairs, then clusters log data using both query and rule features, and finally estimates a "cognitive gap" between the model's prior understanding and the extracted user feedback. Based on this assessment, UNO routes clusters into either a Primary Experience Module, which trains an expert LoRA adapter with preference optimization, or a Reflective Experience Module, which trains a critic LoRA to provide revision suggestions without directly updating the base model. At inference time, the system either applies the expert adapter directly or uses the critic in a refinement loop.

The empirical evaluation is conducted on MemoryBench, a benchmark for user log-driven continual learning across multiple tasks, domains, and languages. The study is not situated in a K-12 or education setting and does not report human participant demographics such as grade level or institutional role; instead, it evaluates system performance using benchmark-generated user logs and simulated interactions. Experiments compare UNO against RAG methods, memory-based baselines, and standard training approaches such as SFT and DPO.

The main conclusion is that UNO achieves state-of-the-art performance on MemoryBench and is more robust than baseline methods when learning from noisy user logs. The authors conclude that adaptive clustering, cognitive gap assessment, and the dual-path optimization strategy are important for safely leveraging user feedback. They also report that UNO supports online evolution over successive batches of user logs, suggesting potential for continual improvement of deployed LLM systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical computer science paper on improving deployed LLM systems with user logs, not an education intervention study. It does not report a K-12 sample, classroom implementation, or direct educational comparison relevant to writing instruction outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports benchmark gains for LLM system optimization, but not educational impact on learners, teachers, or institutions. For the education knowledge graph, impact is therefore unclear and not directly applicable.

paper_profiles.title: Automated Code Review Using Large Language Models at Ericsson: An Experience Report
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models (LLMs) can help automate software code review in an industrial setting, reducing the burden on experienced developers while still producing useful review comments. The authors frame code review as an important but time-consuming quality assurance activity and investigate how LLMs might generate timely, relevant, and concise feedback on code changes made in Ericsson projects.

The intervention is a lightweight automated code review pipeline that combines static program analysis with open-source LLMs such as Llama 2, Code Llama, and Mixtral. Instead of sending only changed lines to the model, the system extracts the enclosing Java method for each code diff using Tree-Sitter and includes that context in prompts designed for succinct critical review. The tool was integrated into Ericsson workflows through Gerrit, a web interface, and a VS Code plugin. The study also compared outputs from different LLM sizes and variants and gathered feedback on prompt quality and practical usability.

The population consisted of experienced Ericsson software developers, primarily senior software engineers or above with at least three years of experience, working in an industry context rather than an educational one. Evaluation included surveys in which experts reviewed LLM-generated comments on real Ericsson code snippets, pairwise comparisons of reviews from different models, and a 15-day practical use period with the tool. Quantitative counts and qualitative comments were both reported.

The main conclusions are that the approach is promising but still imperfect. Experts provided a mix of positive, neutral, and negative feedback; larger Code Llama models appeared to perform best in the reported pairwise comparisons; and some developers felt the tool saved time and improved efficiency. However, reviews were sometimes irrelevant, factually incorrect, or overly explanatory. Overall, the paper presents an early-stage industrial experience report suggesting that context-aware prompting with lightweight open-source LLMs can support automated code review, while also highlighting the need for further refinement and broader evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an industry experience report with survey-based and small-scale exploratory evaluations, but no experimental or quasi-experimental design, no validated outcome measures, and no causal identification strategy. It provides some empirical evidence, yet credibility is limited by small samples, subjective measures, and preliminary analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially useful but inconsistent benefits for efficiency and review quality, with mixed self-reports and no reported effect sizes. Impact appears promising but unclear and modest at best based on the available evidence.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted automated code review for professional software developers, generating concise review comments on Java code changes using prompts plus static analysis to extract the enclosing method context.
Static program analysis used alongside the LLM to identify enclosing methods for changed lines and improve contextualization of generated code reviews.

finding.finding_summary: In a 15-day field survey with 9 expert developers, 4/9 reported the tool saved them time and 4/9 rated it effective or highly effective for improving coding efficiency, while 3/9 said it was not very effective. Usage was uneven (2 regular users, 5 occasional, 2 one-time users), and dissatisfaction centered on reviews that merely explained code, were factually incorrect, or focused on irrelevant areas. No standardized productivity effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported time savings, perceived coding efficiency, and frequency of tool use from developer survey

finding.finding_summary: Across a survey of 8 expert developers reviewing 10 LLM-generated code reviews, feedback included positive comments about meaningful suggestions, but also neutral and negative feedback indicating verbosity, incorrect details, irrelevant comments, and missed issues. The study suggests LLM reviews may support code-review reasoning and critical evaluation in some cases, but reliability is inconsistent and no quantitative learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Expert judgments of review relevance, accuracy, usefulness, and qualitative comment categories on generated code reviews

finding.finding_summary: For software engineering task performance, the paper reports preliminary evidence that LLMs could detect injected bugs in 15 snippets (10 short, 5 medium) and generated reviews in roughly 5-6 seconds, but the main formal evaluation relied on expert opinion rather than validated performance outcomes. Pairwise comparisons across 36 evaluations suggested Code LLaMA 13B was preferred more often than other small models, though differences were based on vote counts rather than inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Bug-detection success in adversarial prompt tests, review latency, and pairwise expert preferences between LLM-generated reviews
finding.study_size: 36 pairwise comparisons by 9 experts; 15 adversarial snippets; 5 change IDs for unchanged-line behavior

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can successfully complete Dutch national high school exams in English reading comprehension, and what that implies for educational assessment. The core question is not about improving student literacy learning, but about benchmarking generative AI performance on a high-stakes K-12 reading-comprehension assessment and assessing risks for exam integrity. The author also compares GPT-3.5 with two versions of GPT-4 and explores whether response consistency under repeated sampling can help identify likely errors.

The study used three official 2022 Dutch VWO English national exams, each consisting of reading passages and associated multiple-choice and open-ended comprehension questions. GPT-3.5 was prompted manually through the ChatGPT web interface, sometimes with re-prompting when it failed to provide a valid answer. GPT-4 (March and June 2023 versions) was evaluated through the API using automated prompting with no re-prompting. A bootstrapping/self-consistency analysis was also conducted by submitting items repeatedly with a nonzero temperature setting to test whether inconsistent responses signaled uncertainty or likely error.

The population context is Dutch upper-secondary education: the VWO track is the most academically rigorous high-school program in the Netherlands and prepares students for university study. Although the study compares AI performance with national student score distributions on one exam, no human participants were newly recruited; the primary object of study is the AI system’s performance on authentic K-12 assessment materials. The reading tasks included main-idea identification, inference, and vocabulary-in-context items.

The main conclusion is that GPT-3.5 performed around the level of the average Dutch VWO student, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student on these English reading-comprehension exams. GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without re-prompting, compared with GPT-4 scores of 8.3 and 8.1 for the March and June versions. The findings suggest substantial implications for the security and design of computer-based assessment, while also highlighting possible educational uses of large language models. However, the paper does not study student learning outcomes, classroom use, reading attitudes, vocabulary growth, or broader literacy development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with clear procedures and quantitative results, but it is not a student intervention study and does not estimate causal effects on K-12 learning outcomes. It evaluates AI exam performance rather than comparing student outcomes under different instructional conditions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong immediate task performance by the AI on literacy assessment items, but provides no direct evidence of impact on student literacy learning, reading attitudes, or vocabulary. Educational impact is therefore unclear and indirect, primarily concerning assessment implications rather than demonstrated learner gains.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) as a generative conversational AI on Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exams, including multiple-choice and open-response items, to assess exam-answering performance rather than student learning.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test K-12 students; it evaluated ChatGPT's performance on Dutch VWO English reading-comprehension exams. GPT-3.5 achieved an average grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without re-prompting, compared with the national student mean of 6.99 on Exam 1; GPT-4-0314 and GPT-4-0613 achieved average grades of 8.3 and 8.1 respectively across the three 2022 exams. On Exam 1, student performance was M=35.88/49 points (SD=6.48; n=35,698), while ChatGPT scored 41/49 (GPT-3.5), 46/49 (GPT-4-0314), and 44/49 (GPT-4-0613), indicating strong immediate task performance on reading-comprehension assessment items rather than evidence of literacy learning gains.
finding.measure: Scores/grades on Dutch national high-school English reading-comprehension exams (2022 VWO exams), including total points and converted grades; comparison to published student score distribution for Exam 1.
finding.study_size: n=124 exam questions across 3 exams; human comparison sample for Exam 1 n=35,698 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT's ability to achieve passing-to-high scores on high-stakes reading-comprehension exams raises concerns about the integrity of computer-based or minimally proctored assessments. Quantitatively, GPT-4 scored 8.3 and 8.1 average grades across three exams, outperforming average student performance benchmarks, which the author interprets as evidence that assessment practices may need redesign; however, no institutional intervention was implemented or causally evaluated.
finding.measure: AI performance on high-stakes exams used as evidence for implications for assessment security and policy.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach on learners’ courseware project performances and perceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether integrating ChatGPT into a flipped learning environment can improve learners’ courseware project performance and related perceptions. The author argues that while flipped learning and project-based learning can provide more time for active work, teachers often struggle to give all students immediate, personalised guidance. The study therefore asks whether a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach (ChatGPT-FLGA) can outperform a traditional flipped learning guiding approach (T-FLGA) on project performance, self-efficacy, learning attitudes, motivation, and creative thinking.

The intervention was a ChatGPT-supported flipped learning system built by integrating ChatGPT with Tencent QQ. Students in the experimental condition received flipped classroom instruction plus AI-supported scaffolding through an “AI teacher” that provided instant personalised guidance, continuous conversation, smart reminders about assignments, and participation summaries. Both groups completed flipped learning activities and QQ-based discussions, but only the experimental group had access to ChatGPT-FLGA. Outcome measures included an objective project-performance rubric scored by two instructors and several self-report questionnaires, supplemented by post-study interviews.

Participants were 81 undergraduate students from two intact classes at a public normal university in Mainland China; they were taking a compulsory Modern Educational Technology course and had no prior knowledge of courseware design. One class of 42 students was assigned to the experimental condition and the other class of 39 students to the control condition, with the same teacher teaching both classes. The overall study lasted 8 weeks, including 3 weeks of initial instruction, pretesting in week 4, a 3-week intervention period, and posttesting in week 8.

The study concludes that ChatGPT-FLGA significantly improved project performance and several learner perceptions compared with traditional flipped learning. ANCOVA results showed significant advantages for the experimental group in project performance (F=8.32, partial η²=0.09), self-efficacy (F=4.45, partial η²=0.05), learning attitudes (F=5.10, partial η²=0.06), overall learning motivation (F=5.32, partial η²=0.06), intrinsic motivation (F=7.38, partial η²=0.09), and creative thinking tendency (F=6.85, partial η²=0.08), but not extrinsic motivation. Interview data suggested students valued the immediacy of feedback and personalised support. The author frames the findings as evidence that ChatGPT can serve as an effective scaffold in flipped higher-education project work, though generalisability is limited.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental comparison with a control group, pre/post measurement, and statistical adjustment via ANCOVA, which supports moderate causal inference. However, it is not K-12, uses intact classes at a single university, and lacks random assignment at the individual level and some design details needed for the highest tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports small-to-medium positive effects (partial η² from 0.05 to 0.09) on academic performance, attitudes, motivation, and creative thinking, indicating modest-to-moderate impact. Because the sample is a general higher-education population rather than the priority K-12 literacy population, impact is better classified as green rather than blue.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach in a higher-education multimedia courseware project, where students interacted with an AI teacher via Tencent QQ for instant personalized guidance, conversational scaffolding, reminders, and support during project-based flipped learning.
Traditional flipped learning guiding approach comparator using flipped classroom instruction, video/material access, and Tencent QQ-based discussion without ChatGPT-enabled AI tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experiment with 81 pre-service teachers in China (experimental n=42, control n=39), the ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach produced significantly higher multimedia courseware project performance than the traditional flipped approach after controlling for pretest scores. Posttest adjusted means were 89.93 vs. 87.13, with ANCOVA F=8.32 and partial η²=0.09, indicating a medium effect on vocational/educational technology project performance.
finding.measure: Rubric-scored multimedia courseware project performance across instruction, science, technology, artistry, and operability dimensions

finding.finding_summary: The ChatGPT condition significantly improved multiple learner perception outcomes relative to traditional flipped learning, including self-efficacy, learning attitudes, and overall learning motivation. Self-efficacy showed adjusted means of 34.77 vs. 33.14 (F=4.45, partial η²=0.05), learning attitudes 31.59 vs. 29.91 (F=5.10, partial η²=0.06), and learning motivation 26.01 vs. 25.14 (F=5.32, partial η²=0.06), all favoring the experimental group.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy scale, learning attitudes scale, and learning motivation questionnaire (Likert self-report)
finding.std_deviation: Self-efficacy SDs: 3.73, 4.54; Learning attitudes SDs: 2.76, 4.21; Learning motivation SDs: 2.37, 2.09

finding.finding_summary: Motivation effects were mixed when disaggregated: intrinsic motivation was significantly higher in the ChatGPT group, but extrinsic motivation did not differ significantly from the control group. Intrinsic motivation showed adjusted means of 12.74 vs. 12.12 (F=7.38, partial η²=0.09), whereas extrinsic motivation showed no significant difference (F=1.01, partial η²=0.01).
finding.measure: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation subscales
finding.effect_size: Intrinsic: partial η²=0.09; Extrinsic: partial η²=0.01

finding.finding_summary: Students using the ChatGPT-based flipped learning approach reported significantly higher creative thinking tendency than peers in the traditional flipped condition. Adjusted means were 19.07 for the experimental group and 17.40 for the control group, with ANCOVA F=6.85 and partial η²=0.08, suggesting a medium positive effect on a durable skill related to creativity.
finding.measure: Creative Thinking Tendency Scale (5-item Likert self-report)

paper_profiles.title: A Position Paper: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines the opportunities and risks of using large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT, in education. The authors aim to synthesize the current landscape of possible educational applications of LLMs and to outline major pedagogical, ethical, technical, and policy challenges that must be addressed for responsible adoption. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper discusses how LLMs could support learning, teaching, assessment, content generation, tutoring, accessibility, and professional development.

The paper's approach is conceptual and narrative. It reviews examples from prior literature on LLMs and related conversational AI in education, including uses such as quiz generation, pedagogical agents, code explanation, automated feedback, and assessment support. The authors also propose mitigation strategies for major risks, including bias and fairness, overreliance by learners or teachers, lack of expertise, privacy and security concerns, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work, cost, sustainability, and equitable access.

The paper is not a primary empirical study and does not report a participant sample, intervention duration, or comparative outcomes. Instead, it speaks broadly to educational contexts spanning primary, secondary, higher education, and professional training, considering both student and teacher perspectives. The discussion is framed as guidance for future research and implementation rather than evidence from a controlled or observational evaluation.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial potential to enhance education, but their use must be guided by human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, teacher and learner training, and strong privacy, ethical, and governance frameworks. The authors argue that the risks are manageable if addressed deliberately, and they call for further research on effective integration, user competencies, fairness, and responsible deployment in educational systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and illustrative prior studies; it does not report an original empirical design, sample, comparator, or quantitative outcome analysis. Under the K-12 evidence framework, it therefore lacks the methodological basis required for causal or correlational evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially important educational benefits and risks of LLMs, but provides no direct effect estimates or original impact evidence. Because impact is discussed conceptually rather than demonstrated empirically, the practical impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Position paper discussing prospective uses of large language models such as ChatGPT/GPT-3 in education, including conversational support, content generation, tutoring, question answering, and personalized learning assistance across K-12 and higher education contexts.
Reviews prior examples of NLP/LLM systems for automated or adaptive feedback on student answers, argumentation, and diagnostic justifications.
Discusses LLMs as tools for grammar correction, style suggestions, summaries, translation, vocabulary and language-learning support, especially in reading and writing tasks.

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ over-reliance on incorrect recommendations from ChatGPT. The core problem is that students may uncritically accept large language model outputs even when those outputs are wrong, which could undermine critical thinking and sound judgment. The study focuses on behavioral reliance rather than literacy outcomes, using math-puzzle decisions to test whether students follow correct or incorrect AI advice.

The intervention was a short educational text about ChatGPT covering how it works, its limitations and risks, and tips for wise use; the control group received only a shorter general introduction to ChatGPT. After reading the assigned text, students solved eight Kangaroo math puzzles while viewing screenshots of ChatGPT-4o recommendations, with half of the recommendations intentionally incorrect and half correct. The primary outcomes were over-reliance (accepting incorrect AI advice) and under-reliance (rejecting correct AI advice), along with confidence ratings and decision time.

Participants were 36 Estonian 12th-grade students from 10 high schools, recruited in October 2024 through an online LimeSurvey questionnaire. Students were randomly assigned to intervention (n=19) or control (n=17). The intervention itself lasted about 3.4 minutes on average, and the whole study took about 23.6 minutes. The setting was online rather than classroom-based, and there was no teacher-mediated implementation.

The main conclusion is that the short AI literacy text did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. Students still adopted incorrect suggestions at high rates, and the intervention instead significantly increased under-reliance by making students more likely to ignore correct recommendations. The authors conclude that over-reliance on LLMs is widespread and difficult to counter with a brief literacy intervention alone, and they caution against assuming that simple AI-literacy instruction will be sufficient for safe educational adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled experiment in a K-12 setting with a clear intervention, control group, and reported inferential statistics, which raises it above correlational work. However, the study has substantial concerns including very small sample size (n=36), brief exposure, online task setting, and a narrow outcome context, so it does not meet blue-tier standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The primary intended effect was not achieved: over-reliance was not significantly reduced, and the intervention produced a statistically significant negative effect by increasing under-reliance (d=0.78). Overall impact is therefore best characterized as no impact or harmful impact.

interventions.use_case: High school students used ChatGPT-4o recommendations while solving math puzzles, and the study tested whether a short AI-literacy text could reduce over-reliance on incorrect LLM advice.

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized independent-groups experiment with 12th-grade Estonian students (final n=36; intervention n=19, control n=17), students frequently over-relied on ChatGPT-4o during math puzzle solving: mean over-reliance across all participants was 52.1% (SD=28.90). The AI-literacy intervention slightly lowered over-reliance versus control (48.68 vs. 55.88), but this difference was not statistically significant, Welch's t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25; meanwhile, correct-solution rates across tasks remained modest overall (mean 43.3%).
finding.measure: Rate of over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations during Kangaroo math puzzles; puzzle-level correct solution rates
finding.std_deviation: Overall over-reliance SD=28.90; intervention SD=24.26; control SD=33.69

finding.finding_summary: The short AI-literacy intervention did not improve appropriate critical evaluation of ChatGPT outputs and instead increased under-reliance on correct recommendations. Under-reliance was significantly higher in the intervention group than in control (36.84, SD=24.11 vs. 19.12, SD=20.78), Student's t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78, suggesting the intervention worsened students' calibration in judging when AI advice was trustworthy.
finding.measure: Under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations; behavioral reliance/calibration when evaluating AI advice

finding.finding_summary: Students' self-perceived confidence in their puzzle answers did not differ significantly between groups after the intervention. Confidence was slightly lower in the intervention group (M=3.58, SD=0.46) than in the control group (M=3.67, SD=0.76), but the Mann-Whitney test was non-significant, U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence after each puzzle on a 5-point Likert scale

paper_profiles.title: Complementary Advantages of ChatGPTs and Human Readers in Reasoning: Evidence from English Text Reading Comprehension
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how two generative AI systems, ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4), compare with human readers in reasoning from English text reading comprehension. The core question is not whether AI improves student learning, but whether AI and human readers show different strengths and weaknesses when making inferences from narrative texts. The authors focus on three inference types central to reading comprehension: commonsense inference, emotional inference, and causal inference.

The study uses direct performance comparison rather than an instructional intervention. Chinese senior high school students completed three English reading-based inference tests, and the same tests were repeatedly administered to ChatGPT and ChatGPT Plus to generate comparable numbers of responses. The tests covered local-culture and daily-life commonsense judgments, character emotion inference from short stories, and causal reasoning from a suspense narrative with an omitted ending. The researchers also updated prompts for the chatbots in the causal task to see whether more elaborate instructions improved performance.

Participants were 114 grade-11 students in a mid-level high school in China, approximately age 17, learning English as a second language and preparing for the Gaokao. The context was a school-based offline assessment conducted during flexible class time. Students had studied English for at least six years and had prior instruction in reading comprehension strategies through regular classroom teaching, but there was no experimental teaching treatment, no control group, and no longitudinal follow-up.

The main conclusion is that human readers and generative AI showed complementary strengths. Students outperformed both chatbot versions in local-culture-related commonsense inference and in causal reasoning, especially where logical integration of the whole story was needed. ChatGPT Plus performed best on daily-life commonsense items and generally exceeded students in emotional inference accuracy, while ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) was weakest overall. The authors conclude that AI systems and human readers differ in the kinds of knowledge and reasoning they bring to reading, with GPT-4 showing stronger performance than GPT-3.5 but still notable weaknesses in culturally specific knowledge, false-information detection, and some forms of logical narrative inference.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative quantitative study with a described sample and measures, but it is not a K-12 classroom intervention study, lacks randomization, does not report significance testing/effect sizes, and uses repeated chatbot generations as comparator data rather than a standard human-subject experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows mixed and task-specific comparative performance on literacy-related reasoning, with some advantages for students and some for GPT-4, but no standardized effect sizes or causal evidence of broader literacy learning impact. The practical educational impact is therefore unclear.

interventions.use_case: Direct comparison of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4) against Chinese secondary ESL students on English narrative-text reading inference tasks (commonsense, emotional, and causal comprehension), using prompted chatbot responses rather than classroom instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This was a direct comparative reading-comprehension study, not an intervention trial. Among 114 Chinese senior high school ESL students (with chatbot response sets generated to match valid questionnaire counts: n=87 for commonsense, n=82 for emotional and causal tasks), students outperformed ChatGPT and ChatGPT Plus on local-culture commonsense inference (86.83% vs. 61.98% and 66.58%) and on causal antecedent reasoning, while ChatGPT Plus outperformed students on daily-life commonsense inference (93.33% vs. 67.66%) and slightly on story-ending prediction in one causal task (100% vs. 96.34%). No standardized effect sizes, significance tests, or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on three English reading inference tasks: commonsense inference from narrative/contextual items, emotional inference from short stories, and causal inference from a suspense text
finding.study_size: students n=114; chatbot outputs matched to valid response counts of n=87 (commonsense) and n=82 (emotional/causal)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines reasoning/inference performance as a text-based durable skill embedded in reading. Students showed stronger logical analysis in causal inference and better negative-emotion inference, whereas ChatGPT Plus showed stronger performance in positive-emotion inference and some daily-life/ending-prediction reasoning tasks; the authors characterize this as a complementary human-AI profile rather than a uniform advantage for either side. No inferential statistics or effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Accuracy/frequency of correct responses on commonsense, emotional, and causal reasoning tasks derived from English texts
finding.study_size: students n=114; chatbot outputs n=82 or n=87 depending on task

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students can effectively regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT during science learning tasks. The authors focus on core components of question-asking with generative AI: recognizing effective versus ineffective prompts, evaluating the quality of AI-generated answers, deciding whether to ask follow-up questions, and how these interaction patterns relate to task success. The study is motivated by concern that generative AI may encourage over-reliance, shallow processing, and premature stopping rather than meaningful inquiry and learning.

The study did not test a comparative instructional intervention or control condition. Instead, students completed six science investigation tasks using ChatGPT 3.5 during a one-hour in-school session. Each task included either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, and students judged the prompt, interacted freely with ChatGPT, rated each AI answer, and then wrote a short answer in their own words. The researchers also collected questionnaires on AI attitudes and metacognitive competencies, and they manually coded prompt/answer quality and final task performance. The central analytic approach was correlational, linking students’ interaction behaviors and individual differences to task outcomes.

Participants were 63 French middle-school students aged 14–15 from four public and private schools in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. The context was an in-school science activity conducted during normal class hours with laptops supplied by the research team; task instructions were on paper and AI interaction occurred on a web platform with ChatGPT preloaded. The study therefore concerns adolescent student use of generative AI in a science inquiry context rather than literacy instruction.

The main conclusion is that students showed weak regulation of AI-supported inquiry. On average, they performed near chance in distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts and in discriminating useful from unhelpful AI responses. They rarely asked follow-up questions, often accepted low-quality answers as useful, and achieved only moderate task success despite unrestricted AI access. More positive attitudes toward AI were associated with poorer prompt and answer discrimination, whereas metacognitive regulation and more critical views of AI were linked to better inquiry behavior. The authors argue that AI literacy instruction should emphasize metacognitive regulation and critical evaluation rather than only technical familiarity with AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear methods and quantitative results, but it is a single-group observational/correlational design without a direct intervention-control comparison or random assignment. It provides useful evidence on student interaction quality with ChatGPT, yet causal claims about impact are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports largely negative or null performance patterns: chance-level discrimination of prompt and answer quality, sparse follow-up regulation, and only moderate task success despite AI access. Because there is no direct comparative effect estimate against a non-AI condition and the observed educational impact appears weak/problematic, impact is best classified as red.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as an unrestricted conversational inquiry tool during science investigation tasks, with researchers examining prompt quality discrimination, evaluation of AI responses, follow-up questioning, and resulting conceptual explanations.

finding.finding_summary: In a single-group study of French middle-school students (final N=63), task performance on six science investigation problems remained only moderate despite unrestricted ChatGPT 3.5 access: the average correct solution rate was M=0.51, SD=0.25. Students performed at chance in discriminating efficient from inefficient prompts (d′ mean=0.19, SD=0.8; one-sample t=1.77, p=0.08) and in discriminating high- from low-quality AI answers (d′ mean=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), yet success was higher when students received more expert-rated high-level answers (beta=0.52, p<0.001), better evaluated answer quality (beta=0.10, p<0.001), and asked follow-up questions after low-level answers (beta=0.40, p=0.004) in the best-fitting regression model (F(5,57)=40.29, p<0.0001, adjusted R2=0.81).
finding.measure: Science investigation task success based on binary coding of students' final written explanations for depth, accuracy, and explicit problem addressing; prompt discrimination sensitivity (d′); answer-quality discrimination sensitivity (d′)
finding.effect_size: d′=0.19 for prompt discrimination; d′=0.07 for answer discrimination; regression betas=0.52, 0.10, 0.40; adjusted R2=0.81
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.25 for success rate; SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: Students showed weak metacognitive inquiry regulation while using ChatGPT 3.5: they were unable on average to distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts (d′ mean=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) or useful from low-level AI answers (d′ mean=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Regulatory behavior was sparse, with only 14 of 63 students asking any follow-up questions (22 follow-up questions total across 6 tasks), and even when students identified an answer as unsatisfactory they asked follow-up questions only 31.8% of the time, indicating premature termination of inquiry and poor QA-cycle regulation.
finding.measure: Prompt-quality discrimination d′, AI answer-quality discrimination d′, frequency of follow-up questions, and expert coding of answer level as indicators of metacognitive regulation and inquiry quality
finding.effect_size: d′=0.19; d′=0.07; follow-up rate after unsatisfactory answers=31.8%
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: More positive attitudes toward AI were associated with poorer interaction quality rather than better learning regulation. Path analyses showed prompt-quality sensitivity was negatively predicted by positive AI attitudes (beta=-0.39, p=0.015; bivariate r=-0.49, p<0.001), and answer-evaluation sensitivity was also negatively associated with AI attitudes (beta=-0.30, p=0.018), suggesting overconfidence/trust in GenAI may undermine epistemic vigilance.
finding.measure: Adolescent-adapted GenAI attitudes questionnaire (24 items; attitude/trust/usefulness/fairness/effort dimensions) linked to interaction-quality indicators

paper_profiles.title: Beware of Metacognitive Laziness: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Motivation, Processes, and Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different forms of learning support—especially generative AI in the form of ChatGPT—affect learners’ motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL) processes, and performance. The authors position the study within emerging work on hybrid intelligence and ask whether AI support helps learners in ways comparable to or different from human experts, writing-analytics tools, or no additional support. A central concern is whether generative AI may improve short-term task performance while encouraging over-reliance and reducing deeper metacognitive engagement, which the authors describe as “metacognitive laziness.”

To study this, the researchers conducted a randomized experiment with 117 university students in a lab setting. Participants, all English second-language speakers, completed a two-stage English reading-and-writing task focused on envisioning the future of education using source materials on AI, differentiated teaching, and scaffolding. Students were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: no extra support, ChatGPT 4.0 support, real-time one-to-one human expert support, or checklist-based writing analytics tools. The study collected post-task intrinsic motivation data, detailed trace/process data on SRL behaviors, and performance data including essay score improvement, knowledge gain, and knowledge transfer.

The main findings were that intrinsic motivation did not significantly differ across groups, but SRL processes and performance did. The ChatGPT group showed significantly greater essay score improvement than the no-support, human-expert, and checklist groups. However, the groups did not differ significantly in knowledge gain or knowledge transfer. Process analyses suggested that students using ChatGPT relied more heavily on AI-centered revision loops and engaged relatively less in some metacognitive activities than comparison groups, especially the human-expert condition.

The authors conclude that generative AI can substantially improve immediate task performance, particularly on structured writing tasks, but may not improve deeper learning outcomes such as knowledge gain or transfer. They argue that ChatGPT may encourage dependence on AI and reduced metacognitive engagement, raising concerns for educational use. The paper recommends treating AI as one agent within a broader hybrid-intelligence ecology rather than as a substitute for teachers, and calls for more long-term, multi-task, and cross-context research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized experimental comparison with multiple conditions and quantitative outcomes, which strengthens causal inference. However, it has notable concerns for the requested evidence framework: it is a university lab study rather than K-12, uses a short single-task intervention, and reports limited detail on some outcome metrics and long-term follow-up.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a moderate omnibus effect on immediate essay-score improvement for the ChatGPT condition (eta^2=0.108) but no effect on motivation, knowledge gain, or transfer, making overall impact mixed and largely limited to short-term task performance rather than broader literacy learning.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-4.0 was embedded in a lab writing environment to support university students during revision of an English reading-to-write essay via restricted chat-based advice on task topics, intended to help improve essays without directly generating the full essay.
A checklist-based writing analytics toolkit provided automated feedback on spelling, grammar, academic style, originality, and rhetorical structure during essay revision.
The study evaluated AI-supported English academic writing revision for second-language English learners, including rubric-aligned support for polishing essay quality in an L2 writing task.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized lab experiment with 117 university students, the ChatGPT group showed significantly greater essay score improvement after revision than the no-support, human-expert, and checklist-tool groups. Pairwise mean differences favored ChatGPT versus control (+1.97, p=0.037), human expert (+2.12, p=0.025), and checklist (+2.20, p=0.012), but there were no significant between-group differences in knowledge gain on the AI-in-education test or knowledge transfer on the AI-in-healthcare test.
finding.measure: Essay score improvement after revision; pre/post knowledge test on AI in education; transfer test on AI in healthcare
finding.effect_size: essay improvement omnibus eta^2=0.108; pre-revision eta^2=0.033; knowledge gain eta^2=0.030-0.036; transfer eta^2=0.000
finding.confidence_interval: Pairwise 95% CIs: ChatGPT vs checklist [0.367, 4.033]; vs control [0.083, 3.858]; vs human expert [0.191, 4.049]

finding.finding_summary: Across 114 students with complete IMI data, there were no significant differences among ChatGPT, human-expert, checklist, and control groups on intrinsic motivation after the task. Null results were reported for interest/enjoyment (F=1.087, p=0.358, eta^2=0.029), perceived competence (F=0.453, p=0.716, eta^2=0.012), effort/importance (F=1.152, p=0.332, eta^2=0.030), and pressure/tension (F=0.546, p=0.652, eta^2=0.015).
finding.measure: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales: interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, pressure/tension
finding.std_deviation: Interest/Enjoyment SDs: CN 0.588, AI 0.706, HE 0.831, CL 0.707; Perceived Competence SDs: CN 0.696, AI 0.667, HE 0.715, CL 0.959; Effort/Importance SDs: CN 0.477, AI 0.462, HE 0.681, CL 0.437; Pressure/Tension SDs: CN 0.960, AI 0.695, HE 0.965, CL 0.864

finding.finding_summary: Trace and process-mining analyses indicated that ChatGPT-supported learners relied more heavily on interactions with the AI during revision and showed relatively fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation and orientation than comparison groups, especially relative to the human-expert condition. The authors interpret this pattern as evidence of potential 'metacognitive laziness' or metacognitive offloading: improved short-term essay performance without corresponding gains in knowledge gain or transfer.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning process frequencies and temporal transitions from learning trace data (orientation, planning, monitoring, evaluation, reading, elaboration/organization, agent interaction)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-5 in Secondary Education: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Student Attitudes, AI Anxiety, and Hallucination-Aware Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary students respond to the use of a generative AI chatbot, ChatGPT-5, in a formal school setting, with particular attention to attitudes toward AI, AI-related anxiety, and reactions to hallucinated outputs. The study addresses gaps in K-12 generative AI research by focusing on high school students rather than university learners and by explicitly incorporating tasks that expose students to incorrect AI-generated information. The research questions ask what attitudes students hold toward generative AI, how much anxiety they report, what affordances and constraints they perceive, and how they respond to concerns about accuracy and hallucinations.

The study used a mixed-methods design combining questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. The intervention was integrated into the Greek national curriculum course "Technology" and lasted about eight hours over three days. Students engaged with ChatGPT-5 through seven structured activities: information seeking, CV generation, document summarization, video summarization, image generation, student-generated quizzes, and age-adapted explanations. A central feature of the intervention was deliberate exposure to hallucinations: students were shown pre-identified false outputs, asked the same misleading questions themselves, and then prompted to verify the correct answers. Quantitative data came from the Student Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence scale (SATAI) and selected subscales of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), while qualitative data came from interviews with 36 students.

Participants were 109 sixteen-year-old students in the second year of high school from three Greek high schools in the Attica region, in a rural area of metropolitan Athens. The setting was a formal classroom-based school intervention. Most outcomes were attitudinal and self-reported rather than academic performance measures. Quantitative findings showed moderately positive attitudes toward AI overall, with stronger cognitive and affective attitudes than behavioral intentions. Female students reported significantly more positive cognitive attitudes toward AI than males, while prior ChatGPT users had more positive attitudes across all SATAI dimensions. AI anxiety was moderate overall, with greater concern about job replacement than about learning to use AI.

The paper concludes that students generally saw educational value in generative AI but also recognized important risks related to accuracy, privacy, and overdependence. Qualitative findings identified four affordances—knowledge expansion, immediate feedback, familiar interface, and perceived skill development—and three constraints—uncertainty about accuracy, anxiety related to AI feedback, and privacy concerns. A key contribution is the concept of "epistemic safeguarding," describing how students restricted AI use to topics where they already had enough prior knowledge to verify answers after encountering hallucinations. The author argues that successful K-12 integration of generative AI should emphasize critical AI literacy and hallucination-aware use, not just technical access.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods single-group classroom intervention with validated survey instruments and qualitative interviews, but no control group, randomization, or direct comparative academic outcome design. It provides descriptive and subgroup inferential evidence on attitudes/anxiety, meeting limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear attitudinal differences for some subgroups and meaningful qualitative themes, but impacts are mostly on perceptions rather than direct learning outcomes, and overall educational impact remains unclear. No literacy or broader academic achievement effects were causally established.

interventions.use_case: Secondary students used ChatGPT-5 in a classroom Technology course for multi-purpose conversational tasks including information seeking, CV generation, document/video summarization, quiz generation, age-tailored explanations, and deliberate exposure to hallucinated outputs to build critical AI literacy.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined students’ use of ChatGPT-5 within a secondary 'Technology' course rather than measuring achievement gains with a pre/post academic test. Qualitative data suggested perceived knowledge expansion and clarification of concepts, but no direct comparative academic performance outcome, effect size, or test statistic for course learning was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived learning affordances and knowledge expansion from semi-structured interviews; no standardized academic achievement measure reported

finding.finding_summary: Students reported moderately positive attitudes toward AI alongside moderate anxiety, especially around job replacement. SATAI total attitudes were moderately positive (total M=3.24, SD=0.79, n=109), while AIAS showed modest learning anxiety (M=3.09, SD=1.37) and higher job-replacement anxiety (M=4.07, SD=1.66); prior ChatGPT users had more positive attitudes than non-users (total SATAI: 3.57 vs 3.09, t(68.48)=3.13, p=.003, d=0.63), but attitudes and anxiety were essentially uncorrelated (r=-.05, p=.60).
finding.measure: Student Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence scale (SATAI); Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS); interview reports of perceived affordances/constraints
finding.effect_size: d=0.63 for prior-use vs no-use on total SATAI; gender difference on SATAI total d=-0.38; cognitive subscale gender difference d=-0.91; AIAS-attitude correlation r=-0.05
finding.std_deviation: SATAI total SD=0.79; AIAS learning SD=1.37; AIAS job replacement SD=1.66

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative findings suggest the intervention supported critical evaluation and metacognitive monitoring of AI outputs, especially through what the author terms 'epistemic safeguarding.' In interviews, students reported using prior knowledge to verify chatbot responses and identified skill development themes including computational thinking (n=8), problem-solving (n=6), critical thinking (n=4), and digital literacy (n=2), though no quantitative skill assessment or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on critical thinking, problem-solving, computational thinking, digital literacy, and hallucination-aware verification behavior

paper_profiles.title: DataliVR: Transformation of Data Literacy Education through Virtual Reality with ChatGPT-Powered Enhancements
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an immersive virtual reality application, DataliVR, can improve data literacy learning for university students and whether adding a ChatGPT-powered conversational avatar changes learners’ experiences and outcomes. The core problem addressed is that traditional classroom approaches may not adequately support the multifaceted and applied nature of data literacy, particularly for data collection, cleaning, analysis, and visualization. The authors also note that the educational effects of integrating ChatGPT-based chatbots into VR learning environments remain underexplored.

The intervention was DataliVR, a custom VR learning environment that guides learners through a gamified data-literacy journey using a fruit-classification and machine-learning decision-tree context. The system included scenes for a fruit market introduction, data collection, data cleaning, data analysis, and data visualization. In the treatment condition, learners also had access to a ChatGPT-powered chatbot avatar using GPT-3.5 Turbo with speech-to-text and text-to-speech integration; in the comparison condition, the same VR experience was provided without the chatbot. Participants completed tasks, exercises, and quizzes in VR, and outcomes included user experience, system usability, motion sickness, task completion time, task accuracy, and quiz accuracy.

The study involved 30 university students from diverse academic backgrounds at the Technical University of Munich. Participants had no prior machine-learning knowledge and were randomly assigned to the chatbot or no-chatbot condition. The study took place in a VR lab, with an average intervention duration of about 23.23 minutes in a single session. There is no indication of teacher-mediated use; instead, students worked individually in a controlled lab environment with guided in-VR instructions.

The main conclusions are that DataliVR was generally usable and effective for supporting short-term data-literacy learning, with high user experience and usability ratings and reasonably strong task and quiz performance. The chatbot improved user experience and perceived usability, but unexpectedly did not improve learning performance; participants without the chatbot performed significantly better on task accuracy, while quiz differences were not significant. The authors conclude that ChatGPT-enhanced VR shows promise for improving learning experiences, but its influence on learning outcomes is more complex and requires further investigation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an experimental between-subjects comparison with random assignment, but it is a small-sample university study (n=30) outside K-12 and without reported effect sizes or stronger causal reporting details needed for higher tiers. It provides some quantitative comparative evidence but has notable relevance and credibility limitations for the target framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chatbot intervention improved user experience and usability perceptions, but it did not improve learning efficiency and was associated with significantly worse task performance relative to the no-chatbot condition. Because the AI component showed negative academic impact in the direct comparison, the overall intervention impact is best classified as red.

interventions.use_case: immersive VR gamified simulation for university students to learn data literacy through fruit data collection, cleaning, analysis, and visualization tasks.
ChatGPT-powered embodied conversational avatar integrated into the VR environment to provide on-demand personalized learning assistance during data literacy tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In a between-subjects experiment with 30 university students, DataliVR users showed relatively high overall learning performance in data-literacy task accuracy (M=0.79, SD=0.10) and quiz accuracy (M=0.73, SD=0.11), suggesting the VR simulation supported acquisition of data-literacy skills. However, when comparing chatbot conditions, participants without the ChatGPT chatbot outperformed those with the chatbot on task accuracy (M=0.83, SD=0.07 vs. M=0.75, SD=0.11), t(28)=2.26, p=.032, while quiz accuracy was also higher without the chatbot (M=0.75, SD=0.12 vs. M=0.71, SD=0.11) but not significantly so.
finding.measure: Interactive data-literacy task accuracy and in-VR quiz accuracy on data cleaning, analysis, and visualization-related knowledge
finding.effect_size: t(28)=2.26 for task accuracy comparison; quiz comparison not significant
finding.std_deviation: Task overall SD=0.10; quiz overall SD=0.11; without-chatbot task SD=0.07, with-chatbot task SD=0.11; without-chatbot quiz SD=0.12, with-chatbot quiz SD=0.11

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported high overall user experience in DataliVR (M=5.99, SD=0.58 on a 7-point scale), and the ChatGPT-enhanced version produced significantly better user experience than the no-chatbot version (M=6.24, SD=0.43 vs. M=5.75, SD=0.62), t(28)=-2.3, p=.028. Feedback in the chatbot condition suggested moderate overall positive chatbot experience (M=3.27, SD=0.64/5), with users rating the avatar as authentic (M=4.07, SD=0.83) and interaction as easy (M=3.93, SD=1.07), despite relatively infrequent use.
finding.measure: User Experience Questionnaire scores and chatbot experience ratings reflecting engagement, enjoyment, and perceived learning support
finding.std_deviation: Overall UX SD=0.58; with-chatbot SD=0.43; without-chatbot SD=0.62; chatbot feedback overall SD=0.64

finding.finding_summary: DataliVR task completion time was nearly identical across conditions: 22.56 minutes without the chatbot and 22.49 minutes with the chatbot when chatbot conversation time was excluded, with no significant difference reported. System usability was rated high overall (M=4.05, SD=0.36/5), and higher with the chatbot (M=4.19, SD=0.27 vs. M=3.91, SD=0.38), t(28)=-2.12, p=.044, but participants in the chatbot condition also reported significantly less confidence using the system without technical support on SUS item 4, U=159, p=.004.
finding.measure: Task completion time, System Usability Scale scores, and perceived need for technical support
finding.effect_size: t(28)=-2.12 for usability comparison; U=159 for technical-support item; time difference not significant
finding.std_deviation: Overall SUS SD=0.36; with-chatbot SD=0.27; without-chatbot SD=0.38

paper_profiles.title: LitLinker: Supporting the Ideation of Interdisciplinary Contexts with Large Language Models for Teaching Literature in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge elementary-school literature teachers face when trying to design interdisciplinary teaching contexts that connect literature lessons with other subjects such as science, art, mathematics, and music. The authors argue that although interdisciplinary literature teaching can improve learning and motivation, teachers often lack the time, subject-matter breadth, and support needed to search across disciplines and meaningfully link those materials to reading texts. The paper focuses on this planning and ideation problem rather than on student literacy outcomes.

To address this need, the authors developed LitLinker, a web-based interactive system powered by a large language model (GLM-4). LitLinker recommends interdisciplinary topics connected to selected reading materials, analyzes how literary elements relate to those topics, supports teacher exploration through context and text views, and generates structured lesson plans and suggested classroom activities. The system was developed through an iterative user-centered design process involving Chinese language teachers, with design principles emphasizing step-by-step support, detailed contextual analysis, lesson-plan generation aligned with teaching practice, and grounding in curated databases of contexts and reading materials.

The empirical work took place in China and centered on elementary-school Chinese language/literature instruction. The design process involved 17 Chinese language teachers overall, including 13 teachers in the iterative design and prototype evaluation phases. The main evaluation included two studies: a within-subjects quantitative study with 16 novices of Chinese literature teaching (mainly graduate students and pre-service teachers) comparing LitLinker against a baseline LLM web app, and a qualitative study with elementary Chinese language teachers of varying experience. Participants used the system for lesson-planning and interdisciplinary-context ideation tasks rather than for direct classroom reading instruction.

The paper concludes that LitLinker improved the depth of subject integration in lesson-plan outcomes compared with an LLM chatbot baseline, while also reducing perceived workload and increasing satisfaction and efficiency. Expert interviews further suggested that teachers found the system useful for generating and refining interdisciplinary course ideas. Overall, the paper presents evidence that an LLM-based creativity-support tool can assist teachers in planning interdisciplinary literature instruction, while also noting concerns about the quality and reliability of purely LLM-generated content.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative empirical study with a within-subjects design, but the excerpt provides incomplete quantitative reporting and focuses on teacher users and task performance rather than a stronger causal K-12 learning design. It is stronger than purely qualitative work but falls short of well-reported RCT/QED standards in the provided text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects on teacher ideation quality and workload, but effect sizes and exact statistics are not available in the excerpt, making magnitude unclear. The impact is also on teacher planning rather than direct student literacy outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-powered teacher ideation system (LitLinker) that helps elementary Chinese literature teachers generate and refine interdisciplinary teaching contexts, analyze links between texts and contexts, and draft lesson plans and classroom activities.
General-purpose LLM chatbot/web app using the same underlying model as a baseline comparator for teachers' interdisciplinary lesson-planning and literature-context ideation tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study of novices of Chinese literature teaching (N=16), LitLinker significantly reduced perceived task workload compared with an LLM chatbot baseline during interdisciplinary lesson-planning/ideation tasks. The paper reports lower workload and higher efficiency/satisfaction for LitLinker, but the excerpt does not include exact test statistics, effect sizes, confidence intervals, or subscale means.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX-style workload items; perceived efficiency and satisfaction during interdisciplinary lesson-planning task

finding.finding_summary: LitLinker produced stronger interdisciplinary lesson-plan outcomes than the LLM chatbot baseline in a within-subjects evaluation with N=16. The quantitative results reported in the paper indicate deeper integration of different subjects in the outcome lesson plan, based on expert ratings of content alignment, alignment with educational objectives, and depth of integration, though exact statistics are not provided in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Expert-rated lesson-plan quality for interdisciplinary literature teaching (content alignment, educational objective alignment, depth of integration)

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that LitLinker supported deeper integration across subjects and was perceived as more satisfying for exploratory ideation work, suggesting benefits for teacher creative thinking and interdisciplinary planning processes. However, this is an indirect measure of durable skills related to ideation and planning rather than a direct student skill outcome, and no effect sizes are reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Creativity-support perceptions (e.g., exploration, expressiveness, immersion) and qualitative reports about ideation support
finding.study_size: n=16 quantitative; additional expert interviews n=9 as reported in abstract

paper_profiles.title: Diffusion Models for Generative Artificial Intelligence: An Introduction for Applied Mathematicians
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper provides a mathematically oriented introduction to diffusion models for generative artificial intelligence, aimed at applied mathematicians and statisticians. The authors seek to explain how diffusion models work, especially for image generation, by deriving the core formulas behind the forward noising process and the reverse denoising process. The paper also discusses conceptual links between diffusion models, stochastic processes, and partial differential equations.

The approach is primarily expository and theoretical rather than an educational intervention study. The authors illustrate diffusion models using computational examples based on the MNIST handwritten-digit dataset, showing how images are progressively corrupted with noise and then reconstructed through a learned reverse process. They also present simplified training and sampling algorithms and discuss broader issues such as evaluation, computational cost, privacy, bias, and ethics.

The population is not an empirical study sample; instead, the paper identifies its intended audience as advanced undergraduate students, postgraduate students, and higher education professionals who teach courses in stochastic processes, inference, machine learning, PDEs, or scientific computing. The context is therefore higher education and independent study in mathematics-related disciplines, not K-12 literacy or classroom comparison research.

The main conclusion is that diffusion models can be explained in an accessible but rigorous way to readers with mathematical training, and that understanding their foundations may help researchers and educators engage with rapidly developing generative AI methods. The paper also suggests possible connections between diffusion models and PDE-based formulations, but it does not report learner outcomes, comparative educational effects, or direct evidence about literacy learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methodological introduction to diffusion models in generative AI, not a K-12 empirical education study. It reports no educational intervention, learner sample, comparative design, or quantified literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct evidence of impact on K-12 literacy or related educational outcomes. While potentially relevant as background on generative AI, educational impact is speculative and unmeasured.

paper_profiles.title: Chatting with a Learning Analytics Dashboard: The Role of Generative AI Literacy on Learner Interaction with Conventional and Scaffolding Chatbots
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative-AI-assisted chatbots can help learners better understand complex visualizations in a learning analytics dashboard (LAD), and whether learners’ own generative AI literacy affects how much they benefit. The authors compare two chatbot styles: a conventional reactive chatbot that answers user questions on demand, and a scaffolding proactive chatbot that guides users through the visualizations with structured prompts and feedback. The study also investigates differences in learners’ cognitive interaction patterns with the two chatbot types.

The intervention involved a custom dashboard built from multimodal healthcare simulation data and enhanced with either a conventional or scaffolding GenAI chatbot. Participants first completed a baseline analytical writing task and comprehension questions without chatbot support, then were randomly assigned to one of the two chatbot conditions for a comparable intervention task. Quantitative measures included comprehension improvement from baseline to intervention and a 20-item Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test; qualitative/interaction analysis used epistemic network analysis of learner-chatbot dialogue patterns.

The sample included 81 current or graduated medical or nursing students recruited through Prolific, all with no prior familiarity with the learning context. The visualizations represented teamwork, communication, prioritization, and stress indicators from a nursing simulation. Participants were geographically distributed across multiple world regions, but the study was administered online through Qualtrics and a custom-built website, with the research conducted by Monash University in Australia.

The main findings were that both chatbot types significantly improved comprehension of complex visualizations, with large within-subject effects. Higher GenAI literacy was associated with greater comprehension improvement in both conditions, but the effect was stronger for the conventional chatbot, suggesting that proactive scaffolding may reduce dependence on learners’ prior GenAI literacy. Interaction analyses further showed that higher-literacy learners used more complex and integrative prompting and reflection patterns, while lower-literacy learners relied more on clarification and exploratory exchanges. The authors conclude that GenAI literacy is an important consideration in educational technology design and that scaffolding chatbots may support more equitable access to AI-enhanced learning tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative mixed-method experiment with random assignment to two chatbot conditions and pre/post measurement, providing stronger evidence than correlational work. However, it is not a K-12 study, lacks a no-treatment control, uses a relatively small convenience sample, and focuses on a short-term laboratory-style task in a healthcare higher-education context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Both chatbot conditions showed large short-term gains in comprehension with reported large effect sizes (rank-biserial r=0.87 and r=0.94), indicating substantial immediate impact on the studied task. Impact is limited in external relevance to K-12 literacy, but the measured effects within this context are large.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4o-powered chatbot assistance embedded in a learning analytics dashboard to help learners interpret complex multimodal visualisations; compared conventional reactive chatbot support versus proactive scaffolding chatbot guidance.
Conventional/reactive GenAI chatbot condition that answered learner-initiated questions about dashboard visualisations using retrieval-augmented generation.
Scaffolding/proactive GenAI chatbot condition that guided learners through dashboard visualisations with structured prompts, guiding questions, and feedback.

finding.finding_summary: For comprehension of complex learning analytics visualisations in a healthcare simulation context, the conventional chatbot group improved from a baseline median score of 3.0 (IQR=1.0) to an intervention median of 4.0 (IQR=1.0), with a significant within-subject change (W=71, p<.001) and a large rank-biserial effect size (r=0.87). The study included 41 participants in this condition, and comprehension was measured using six multiple-choice knowledge/comprehension questions tied to the dashboard visualisations.
finding.measure: Comprehension of multimodal learning analytics dashboard visualisations via six multiple-choice evaluation questions

finding.finding_summary: For comprehension of complex learning analytics visualisations in a healthcare simulation context, the scaffolding chatbot group improved from a baseline median score of 3.0 (IQR=2.0) to an intervention median of 5.0 (IQR=1.0), with a significant within-subject change (W=32, p<.001) and a large rank-biserial effect size (r=0.94). The study included 40 participants in this condition, and comprehension was measured using six multiple-choice knowledge/comprehension questions associated with the visualisations.
finding.measure: Comprehension of multimodal learning analytics dashboard visualisations via six multiple-choice evaluation questions

finding.finding_summary: Both chatbot conditions supported learners’ information processing around interpreting visualisations, but higher GenAI literacy was associated with more sophisticated interaction patterns. In the conventional condition, higher literacy predicted greater improvement (OLS beta=0.19, SE=0.07, t=2.84, p=.007; model R²=0.445, n=41), while in the scaffolding condition the literacy effect was smaller but still significant (beta=0.08, SE=0.03, t=2.53, p=.016; model R²=0.502, n=40), suggesting scaffolding reduced dependence on learners’ prior GenAI literacy.
finding.measure: Improvement in dashboard comprehension associated with GenAI literacy; cognitive processing/interaction patterns via OLS regression and epistemic network analysis

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Program Alongside AI: Critical Thinking, AI Ethics, and Gendered Patterns of German Secondary School Students
paper_profiles.venue: 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE-SEET ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how German secondary school students engage with generative AI in programming, focusing on two main questions: how they perceive their own critical thinking in AI-assisted programming and how they understand AI ethics and responsibility. The author positions the study as a response to a gap in prior research, which has focused largely on university students rather than younger learners encountering programming and GenAI at the same time. The paper also investigates whether these perceptions differ by gender.

The study uses a survey-based mixed-methods approach combining Likert-scale items with open-ended questions. Quantitative items were adapted from prior instruments on critical thinking and AI literacy, and qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. Rather than evaluating a learning intervention or comparing treatment conditions, the study documents students’ existing AI-assisted programming practices, including which GenAI tools they use, how often they use them, whether they trust generated code, how they seek help, and how they think about privacy, accountability, and regulation.

Participants were 84 German secondary school students aged 16–19 recruited from two extracurricular software development workshops, one lasting one day and one lasting five days. Students worked collaboratively on small software projects such as Java or Python games and App Inventor apps. All participants reported using GenAI tools for programming, especially ChatGPT, primarily for code generation and debugging. The context was extracurricular rather than regular classroom instruction, and workshop instructors did not provide guidance on AI use so that responses would reflect students’ independent habits.

The main conclusion is that students show an 'AI paradox': they report strong ethical awareness, support for transparency, regulation, testing, and accountability, yet many also report integrating AI-generated code they do not fully understand. Boys were more likely to consult AI before teammates and to use AI more frequently, while girls expressed greater skepticism and stronger emphasis on peer collaboration and accountability. The author argues that programming education should connect ethical awareness to concrete coding practice, for example through code explanation, documentation of AI use, and explicit support for critical AI literacy in culturally responsive software engineering education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-method survey study with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and qualitative thematic analysis, but no experimental or quasi-experimental comparison of learning outcomes.
