finding.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 117 higher-education participants, proactive GenAI agents significantly improved students’ comprehension of visual learning analytics compared with both passive GenAI agents and standalone data-storytelling scaffolds, and these benefits persisted into the post-intervention phase after support was removed. Outcomes were based on corrected scores from six multiple-choice comprehension questions per phase covering knowledge and comprehension of healthcare-simulation visualizations; exact between-group effect sizes and confidence intervals were not reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Corrected comprehension scores on 6 multiple-choice VLA knowledge/comprehension items across pre-, intervention, and post phases

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that proactive GenAI agents improved efficiency in extracting insights from visual learning analytics relative to passive GenAI agents and standalone scaffolding, with efficiency operationalized as success time per correct answer. The paper states proactive agents reduced the time required for insight extraction and that gains persisted post-intervention, but no numeric effect size, standard deviation, or confidence interval is reported in the provided excerpt.
finding.measure: Success time (time spent answering six evaluation questions divided by correct score) for VLA insight extraction

finding.finding_summary: Passive GenAI agents produced comprehension improvements that were comparable to standalone scaffolding during and after the intervention, indicating no clear advantage over the non-AI comparator on the main learning outcome. The study used a randomized design with 117 higher-education participants, but the provided text does not report exact pairwise effect sizes or confidence intervals for the passive-versus-scaffolding comparison.
finding.measure: Corrected comprehension scores on 6 multiple-choice VLA knowledge/comprehension items

finding.finding_summary: Standalone data-storytelling scaffolding yielded improvements comparable to passive GenAI agents but was outperformed by proactive GenAI agents on VLA comprehension and persistence of learning. This comparator condition functions as a non-AI instructional scaffold rather than a generative-AI intervention; exact effect sizes are not reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Corrected comprehension scores on 6 multiple-choice VLA knowledge/comprehension items

paper_profiles.title: Transforming GenAI Policy to Prompting Instruction: An RCT of Scalable Prompting Interventions in a CS1 Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether explicit instruction in pedagogical prompting can help students use generative AI as a learning tool rather than as a shortcut for answers. The study is not about K-12 foundational reading; it is a higher-education computer science study, so it does not provide direct causal evidence for generative AI effects on reading outcomes such as phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or reading comprehension in school classrooms. The authors focus instead on prompting literacy and whether different instructional formats improve students’ ability to ask AI for learning-oriented help.

The intervention was a semester-long randomized trial embedded in a mandatory CS1 lab. Undergraduate students were randomly assigned to one of four conditions that varied in cognitive engagement: a brief text reminder about ethical AI use, scenario-based reading of worked examples, a select-only activity choosing prompt components, or a select-then-write condition where students constructed prompts and received automated feedback from an LLM. The study used pre-test, immediate post-test, delayed post-test, surveys, and qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

Participants were 979 students in an introductory computer science course at a public university in North America; after data cleaning, 431 students with valid data across all phases were analyzed. The setting was a required course lab, and the intervention occurred during an “Ethical Use of AI for Learning Lab,” with delayed assessment on the final exam about six to seven weeks later. The sample was primarily first-year computing students, most intending to major in computer science.

The main findings were that all four conditions significantly improved pedagogical prompting skill immediately and at delayed post-test, with larger gains as conditions became more cognitively engaging; the select-then-write condition produced the strongest gains and retention. However, there were no significant between-group differences on final exam performance, although higher post-test prompting scores predicted better final exam scores after controlling for pre-test performance. Overall, this is adjacent evidence showing that explicit GenAI prompting instruction can causally improve AI-use skills in a university CS context, but it should not be interpreted as evidence about foundational reading or K-12 classroom literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a large initial sample, but it is not K-12, not focused on reading outcomes, and the analytic sample reflects substantial attrition (431 of 979). It provides credible causal evidence for prompting-literacy instruction in higher education CS, but only adjacent—not direct—evidence for the user's target question on K-12 foundational reading.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows moderate-to-large effects on prompting-literacy skills, but no significant causal effect on final academic performance and no evidence on foundational reading or K-12 classroom literacy outcomes. For the target evidence base, impact is therefore unclear and only adjacent.

interventions.use_case: Semester-long randomized prompting-literacy instruction in a university CS1 course teaching students to use generative AI as a tutor rather than a solution provider; highest-engagement condition included iterative prompt writing with GPT-4o-powered validation and feedback.

LLM-powered automated validation and actionable feedback on student-written pedagogical prompts in the select-then-write condition, checking for required prompt components such as guardrails and learner level.
Software-delivered instructional modules with text reminders, scenario-based reading, and component-selection exercises used to teach pedagogical prompting at scale across four randomized conditions.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized trial in an introductory computer science course, all four instructional conditions improved pedagogical prompting skill from pre-test to immediate post-test and delayed post-test. Immediate gains increased from Condition 1 to 4 (0.08, 0.39, 0.45, 0.51), with reported effect sizes ranging from 0.53 to 1.96; delayed gains were 0.06, 0.15, 0.17, and 0.24, respectively, with effect sizes from 0.38 to 1.09. However, there were no significant between-group differences on final exam scores (F(3,427)=1.29, p=.278, eta2=.009), despite modest numerical advantages for Conditions 2-4.
finding.measure: Pedagogical prompting assessments (pre-test, immediate post-test, delayed post-test) and CS1 final exam scores
finding.study_size: n=431 analytic sample from N=979 randomized
finding.effect_size: Immediate gain effect sizes by condition: 0.53, 1.63, 1.96, 1.82; delayed gain effect sizes: 0.38, 0.75, 0.85, 1.09; final exam eta2=0.009
finding.confidence_interval: Final exam condition means reported with 95% CIs: C1 [0.64,0.71], C2 [0.68,0.74], C3 [0.66,0.72], C4 [0.68,0.74]
finding.std_deviation: Immediate gain SDs: 0.15, 0.24, 0.23, 0.28; delayed gain SDs: 0.16, 0.20, 0.20, 0.22

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced strong gains in prompting literacy, a metacognitive/help-seeking skill related to using GenAI for learning rather than answer-seeking. Across the analytic sample (n=431), all conditions significantly improved prompting competencies immediately and at delayed follow-up, with the strongest condition achieving mean immediate gain of 0.51 (SD=0.28) and delayed gain of 0.24 (SD=0.22). Immediate post-test prompting performance also predicted final exam scores after controlling for pre-test score (beta=0.090, t(428)=3.01, p=.003), though this is associational rather than a direct causal academic-transfer estimate.
finding.measure: Prompting competency rubric aligned to five pedagogical prompt components; delayed adoption and self-regulated learning perceptions
finding.study_size: n=431 analytic sample from N=979 randomized
finding.effect_size: Condition-level immediate gain effect sizes 0.53 to 1.96; delayed gain effect sizes 0.38 to 1.09; regression beta=0.090
finding.std_deviation: Immediate gain SDs: 0.15, 0.24, 0.23, 0.28; delayed gain SDs: 0.16, 0.20, 0.20, 0.22

finding.finding_summary: The study showed that even very brief interventions could produce significant prompting-skill gains, suggesting favorable scalability and time efficiency, but higher-gain conditions required substantially more time. Median duration rose from 0.89 minutes in the baseline reminder to 36.92 minutes in the select-then-write condition, roughly tripling at each step, while the highest-gain condition also generated more frustration due partly to system friction in LLM validation.
finding.measure: Time-on-task for intervention completion and self-reported frustration

finding.finding_summary: Condition 4 produced significantly higher frustration than Conditions 1-3 (M=2.07 vs. 1.46-1.58 on a 5-point scale; F(3,427)=7.05, p<.001), although frustration remained below the midpoint. At the same time, students across conditions reported regular subsequent use of pedagogical prompting (M=3.49-3.83, exceeding once per week), and frustration did not predict later usage (beta=-0.010, p=.807).
finding.measure: Post-intervention frustration survey and delayed self-reported prompting usage frequency
finding.study_size: n=431 analytic sample; regression n=418-417 approximately as reported
finding.effect_size: Frustration model F(3,427)=7.05; usage regression beta=-0.010

paper_profiles.title: From Cognitive Relief to Affective Engagement: An Empirical Comparison of AI Chatbots and Instructional Scaffolding in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a custom-configured generative AI chatbot can provide learning support comparable to established instructional scaffolding in secondary physics education, with particular attention to students’ cognitive load and affective experiences during problem solving. The authors position the study against the practical difficulty of implementing resource-intensive tiered supports at scale and ask whether an AI chatbot can offer similar cognitive relief while also improving motivation-related outcomes such as enjoyment, hope, self-efficacy, and situational interest.

The study used a quasi-experimental pre-post field design in regular classrooms with 273 ninth-grade students in Germany. Classes were cluster-randomized at the class level into one of three conditions for solving a buoyancy problem individually: (1) a custom-configured AI chatbot built on OpenAI’s o3-mini model via the Fobizz platform, (2) a digital tiered-support system with sequential hints, or (3) a static textbook-style digital explanation used as the control condition. Students completed validated questionnaire measures before and after the activity; outcomes focused on intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load and affective variables, not reading achievement or other academic performance outcomes.

The main finding was that both interactive support conditions—the AI chatbot and the tiered hint system—significantly reduced intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load relative to the textual support control. The AI chatbot also showed the broadest affective advantages, significantly outperforming the textbook-style support on enjoyment, hope, self-efficacy, and situational interest, while also reducing hopelessness. However, differences between the chatbot and tiered support conditions were not statistically significant. The authors conclude that structured guidance is central for reducing cognitive burden, and that AI chatbots may additionally support positive affect through their interactive and social features.

For the retrieval topic focused on generative AI for foundational reading outcomes in K-12, this paper is only adjacent evidence, not direct evidence. It studies a generative AI chatbot in a school-supported classroom setting and uses a comparative causal design, but the subject area is physics, the population is ninth-grade students, and the outcomes are self-reported cognitive load and affective measures rather than foundational reading outcomes such as phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or reading comprehension.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom field study with class-level random assignment among comparison conditions, but the paper describes the overall design as quasi-experimental, uses post-test ANOVA/MANOVA without full RCT reporting details, and is an arXiv preprint. It offers relatively strong causal evidence for short-term affective and cognitive-load outcomes in school settings, but not the highest-confidence blue-tier evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: For the chatbot relative to static digital text, reported pairwise effects on several measured outcomes were in the medium range, including intrinsic cognitive load up to d=0.72 and affective outcomes around d=0.44. However, these impacts are in secondary-school physics and not foundational reading, so they are adjacent rather than directly responsive to the reading-focused retrieval question.

interventions.use_case: Custom-configured generative AI chatbot (OpenAI o3-mini via Fobizz) used as a task-specific physics tutor for ninth-grade students solving a buoyancy problem, providing conversational guidance, reflective prompts, and feedback to support independent problem solving.
Static digital textbook-style support page used as the non-interactive comparison condition, presenting all information needed to solve the buoyancy task without adaptive guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on physics problem solving around buoyancy, but the reported quantitative results in the provided text focus on perceived cognitive load and affective responses rather than direct achievement or conceptual learning gains. Students used the AI chatbot, tiered hints, or static text while solving the same task (n=273), yet no direct causal estimate for physics achievement, conceptual understanding, or transfer is reported in the provided results section.
finding.measure: physics problem-solving task context; no direct reported achievement outcome in provided text

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental field study with class-level random assignment across 273 ninth-grade students in Germany, the AI chatbot produced significantly better affective outcomes than the static textbook-style support on enjoyment, hope, situational interest, and self-efficacy, and lower hopelessness. Reported pairwise effects for chatbot versus textbook ranged from d=0.44 (situational interest, self-efficacy) to about d=0.37 for hopelessness reduction, with significant post-hoc differences across all affective variables; however, chatbot-versus-tiered-support differences were not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Research-validated self-report questionnaires on enjoyment, hope, hopelessness, situational interest, and self-efficacy
finding.effect_size: d=0.44 (situational interest/self-efficacy vs textbook); d=0.37 (hopelessness vs textbook, approximate from text)
finding.std_deviation: Examples: Enjoyment SD=0.93 (chatbot) vs 0.89 (textbook); Hope SD=0.87 vs 0.84; Self-efficacy SD=0.77 vs 0.81; Hopelessness SD=0.97 vs 0.94

finding.finding_summary: The chatbot was designed to scaffold independent problem solving through reflective questioning and support for conceptual understanding, but the study did not report a direct quantitative outcome on metacognition, critical thinking, or strategy use. Evidence for durable skills is therefore indirect and limited to the intended tutoring design rather than demonstrated causal gains.
finding.measure: No direct durable-skills outcome reported; indirect through tutoring design for reflective problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Classic4Children: Adapting Chinese Literary Classics for Children with Large Language Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making Chinese literary classics more accessible to children. The authors argue that canonical works such as the Four Great Classical Novels are culturally important but often too difficult for children because of classical Chinese, complex plots, and challenging readability. In the context of the user’s research topic, this is not a study of generative AI for foundational reading instruction or reading outcomes in K-12 classrooms; instead, it is an NLP paper on automatic text adaptation and evaluation.

The paper proposes InstructChild, an LLM-based method for child-friendly literary adaptation. The approach fine-tunes Qwen2-7B-Instruct with instructions enriched by character personality information and narrative-structure triplets extracted using GPT-4o. It then adds a custom Chinese readability reward metric (Red-CN), uses direct preference optimization for refinement, and applies a lookahead decoding strategy during inference to improve readability. The authors also construct the Classic4Children dataset, consisting of aligned original and child-adapted fragments from the Four Great Classical Novels, and evaluate system outputs using automatic metrics and human ratings.

No human learner intervention is conducted in schools, classrooms, tutoring settings, or other educational delivery contexts. The “children” in the paper are a target audience for adapted texts, not enrolled participants receiving and being assessed on an instructional treatment. The empirical work is model evaluation on a dataset, plus human judgments of generated text quality by adult volunteers with Chinese educational backgrounds.

The main conclusion is that InstructChild outperforms baseline LLMs and text style transfer methods on their adaptation benchmarks, producing more readable and child-friendly rewritten literary text. However, the paper does not provide direct causal evidence about generative AI improving foundational reading outcomes such as phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension in K-12 students. It is therefore adjacent methodological evidence about text adaptation, not classroom effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an NLP systems paper with benchmark-style evaluation on a curated dataset, not a randomized controlled trial or quasi-experimental study in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings. It provides no direct causal evidence on student foundational reading outcomes and appears to be an arXiv preprint rather than established education-impact evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising task-level improvements in generating child-friendly text, which is adjacent to literacy support, but it does not measure student learning impacts. Any educational impact on K-12 foundational reading is therefore unclear and should not be inferred causally from these results.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based adaptation of Chinese literary classics into child-friendly reading passages, using instruction tuning, readability optimization, and decoding strategies to simplify and rewrite text for children.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that its InstructChild system outperformed baseline LLMs and style-transfer models on automatic and human evaluations for child-friendly literary adaptation. On the Classic4Children test set, InstructChild achieved BLEU-2=13.09, BERTScore F1=70.21, and Red-CN readability=73.12, compared with GPT-4o at BLEU-2=10.42, BERTScore F1=68.04, and Red-CN=68.19; human evaluation on 200 samples also favored InstructChild for character clarity (1.83 vs. 1.52 for GPT-4o) and narrative efficiency (1.78 vs. 0.95 for GPT-4o). However, these are NLP benchmark and human-rating results on rewritten texts, not causal estimates of student reading gains in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Automatic text-generation metrics (BLEU-1/2, BERTScore precision/recall/F1, Red-CN readability) and human ratings of fluency, content preservation, character clarity, and narrative efficiency
finding.study_size: dataset test n=300; human evaluation subset n=200 samples
finding.std_deviation: Reported for human ratings only: GPT-4o Flu 0.25, CP 0.22, CC 0.18, NE 0.12; StoryTrans Flu 0.23, CP 0.21, CC 0.15, NE 0.17; GLM4-9B Flu 0.28, CP 0.16, CC 0.19, NE 0.09; InstructChild Flu 0.19, CP 0.17, CC 0.21, NE 0.14

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the LLM system as a way to automate the otherwise time-consuming and labor-intensive manual adaptation of Chinese literary classics for children. Results show improved automated adaptation quality relative to baselines, suggesting potential productivity gains for content adaptation workflows, but no direct measurement of teacher time, school implementation efficiency, or classroom productivity is provided.
finding.measure: System performance on automated adaptation benchmarks as a proxy for content-production efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Experimental Evidence on Negative Impact of Generative AI on Scientific Learning Outcomes (A Pilot Research)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study investigates whether generative AI helps or harms learning effectiveness when people read academic materials and complete related writing tasks. The paper is motivated by growing interest in using tools such as ChatGPT in education, alongside concern that AI may improve writing productivity while weakening actual comprehension and learning. The study is not about K-12 foundational reading; instead, it examines scientific/academic reading comprehension among highly educated adults.

The intervention compared three experimentally assigned task conditions across three reading-writing cycles: (1) manual summary writing without AI, (2) AI-supported summary writing, and (3) an "Active" AI-assisted reading/chat condition in which participants could use AI to ask questions to support comprehension rather than write a summary. Participants read adapted college/postgraduate-level passages, completed writing tasks under time limits, and then answered five multiple-choice comprehension questions after each passage. Writing quality and time-on-task were also recorded.

The sample consisted of 32 college-educated participants recruited online through Prolific. The paper describes them as college-educated individuals from a range of academic backgrounds; many appear to hold advanced degrees, and the materials were explicitly at college/postgraduate difficulty. The study occurred online over a short period in August 2023, with no classroom or school-supported implementation and no teacher involvement.

The main conclusion is that generative AI use reduced immediate comprehension accuracy relative to manual work in this setting. The author reports average correctness of 66.7% in the manual condition versus 48.4% in the AI-writing condition and 48.9% in the AI-assisted active reading condition, with regression-adjusted declines of 25.1% and 12%, respectively. At the same time, AI improved writing quality and speed. The paper argues that overreliance on generative AI may undermine learning even when it boosts productivity, and that benefits may depend on prior knowledge and language proficiency. For the user's retrieval topic, this is only adjacent evidence: it is not a K-12 study, not about foundational reading outcomes, and not direct causal evidence for classroom reading instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Although the paper uses an experimental design, it is a small pilot preprint with n=32, conducted on college-educated Prolific adults rather than K-12 learners in classrooms or school-supported settings. It is therefore not credible direct evidence for the retrieved K-12 foundational reading question and falls well outside the target population and context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The direct learning outcome most relevant here is negative: AI and AI-assisted conditions reduced reading-comprehension accuracy relative to manual work. Any productivity or writing-quality gains do not offset the negative academic learning result for the target causal-outcome lens.

interventions.use_case: Participants used ChatGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 either to generate summary writing for academic reading passages or to engage in guided chat/active reading to help understand college-level texts before answering comprehension questions.
Generative AI was used as a writing assistant to produce or help produce summaries of assigned readings, with writing quality and completion time compared against manual writing.

finding.finding_summary: In this pilot randomized experimental task study, 32 college-educated participants completed manual, AI-writing, and AI-assisted active reading conditions around college/postgraduate-level reading passages. Relative to manual writing (mean accuracy 66.7%), full AI reliance reduced comprehension-question accuracy to 48.4%, and AI-assisted active reading yielded 48.9%; regression-adjusted estimates reported a 25.1% drop for full AI reliance and a 12% drop for partial AI reliance, both statistically significant. This is direct generative-AI evidence on reading comprehension, but it is not K-12, not foundational reading, and uses adult academic reading materials rather than classroom ELA instruction.
finding.measure: Accuracy on five multiple-choice comprehension questions after each reading/writing cycle
finding.effect_size: 25.1% reduction (AI vs manual, adjusted); 12% reduction (AI-assisted active reading vs manual, adjusted)
finding.std_deviation: Manual SD=0.266287; AI SD=0.287588; Active SD=0.3178209

finding.finding_summary: Generative AI improved task efficiency in the writing component: participants in AI and Active conditions finished earlier on average than those in the manual condition. The paper reports average completion times of 8.7 minutes for AI and 9 minutes for Active, while nearly all manual participants used the full allotted time, indicating faster production with AI support, though no inferential effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Task completion time/productivity during summary-writing or AI-assisted reading tasks

finding.finding_summary: For the writing product itself, AI-generated/assisted summaries were rated higher than manual writing on flow, grammar, and coverage using 1-5 scoring rubrics. The study describes improved writing quality under AI assistance but does not report exact mean differences, standardized effect sizes, or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: Summary-writing quality ratings on comprehensiveness/coverage, grammar, and flow (1-5 scales)

paper_profiles.title: ISSR: Iterative Selection with Self-Review for Vocabulary Test Distractor Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating high-quality distractors for English vocabulary multiple-choice test items. The authors focus on the challenge of using large language models (LLMs) to support teachers in building vocabulary assessments without producing distractors that accidentally create multiple correct answers. The study asks whether LLMs can directly generate distractors effectively and how a system can validate distractors so that only one answer remains correct.

To address this, the paper proposes the ISSR framework (Iterative Selection with Self-Review), which combines a pretrained language model candidate generator, an LLM-based distractor selector, and an LLM-based distractor validator. The framework first generates many candidate distractors, filters them using rules derived from analysis of exam items, then asks an LLM to select plausible distractors and uses a self-review mechanism to remove distractors that could also function as correct answers. The empirical work evaluates distractor-generation quality against teacher-designed distractors from Taiwan’s General Scholastic Ability Test (GSAT) English exam.

The population and context are Taiwanese high school students indirectly represented through archival exam data, along with teachers as the intended end users of the system. The dataset consists of English vocabulary questions from the GSAT, a university entrance exam used with senior high school students in Taiwan. The study is not a classroom intervention and does not test effects on students’ reading or vocabulary learning outcomes; instead, it analyzes item characteristics and benchmarks automated distractor generation methods on exam questions.

The main conclusion is that direct LLM generation of distractors is unstable and weaker than a structured pipeline. ISSR outperforms baseline approaches for generating distractors that better match human-designed exam items, and the self-review mechanism helps filter invalid distractors. However, the paper also notes limitations in computing cost, speed, dependence on the quality of the candidate set, and limited generalizability beyond the GSAT context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a technical preprint evaluating NLP/distractor-generation performance on exam items, not a randomized or strong quasi-experimental study of student learning. It provides no direct causal classroom evidence and no K-12 intervention-outcome design meeting the framework's credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising technical performance for assessment authoring support, but impact on learners or teachers in authentic educational settings is unclear and unmeasured. For the user's target topic, it should be treated as adjacent evidence rather than evidence of reading impact.

interventions.use_case: LLM-supported generation and validation of distractors for English vocabulary multiple-choice test design, aimed at helping teachers construct EFL vocabulary assessments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the ISSR framework outperformed baseline distractor-generation approaches on automatic distractor generation benchmarks for English vocabulary test design, suggesting improved support for teacher item creation. Reported metrics include F1@3=1.55%, F1@10=2.07%, NDCG@3=3.57%, NDCG@10=6.31%, and NDCG@30=9.82% for ISSR versus lower scores for CDGP and direct GPT-based generation/selection; however, no classroom productivity, time-saved, or teacher-use outcomes were directly measured.
finding.measure: Automatic distractor-generation benchmark metrics (F1@k, NDCG@k) for vocabulary test item design
finding.study_size: n=195 exam questions total; 193 test questions in main experiments

finding.finding_summary: Although the system targets English vocabulary assessment design, the paper does not test whether use of ISSR improves student reading, vocabulary, decoding, fluency, or comprehension outcomes. Evidence is limited to item-generation performance on Taiwan university entrance exam vocabulary questions, so there is no direct causal or classroom evidence for foundational reading outcomes in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: No direct student literacy outcome measured; proxied only by exam-item/distractor generation quality
finding.study_size: n=195 exam questions total; no student intervention sample

paper_profiles.title: Investigation of the effectiveness of applying ChatGPT in Dialogic Teaching Using Electroencephalography
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can effectively take on a dialogic teaching role similar to a human instructor in higher education. The core question is whether a large language model can support student learning through back-and-forth instructional dialogue, and how this compares with dialogue led by a human teacher. The study also uses electroencephalography (EEG) to explore differences in students’ cognitive activity while interacting with ChatGPT versus a teacher.

The intervention involved dialogic teaching on a unit about histogram equalization in a digital image processing course. Thirty-four undergraduate science and engineering students who had not previously taken the course were randomly assigned to one of two groups: an experimental group that learned through dialogue with ChatGPT, and a control group that learned through dialogue with a trained graduate student acting as the teacher. Students completed pretesting, then engaged in a short instructional dialogue session lasting about three to ten minutes, followed by a brief break, posttests assessing knowledge retention and transfer, and subjective evaluation forms. EEG data were recorded throughout the dialogue process.

The study was conducted at a large research university in Northwest China with undergraduate students only; it was not a K-12 study and did not address foundational reading outcomes. Thus, for the retrieval topic focused on causal evidence for generative AI and foundational reading in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings, this paper does not provide direct relevant evidence. It is instead adjacent evidence from higher education in an information-related course.

The main findings were that the ChatGPT and human-teacher groups performed similarly on the retention test, but the human-teacher group scored higher on the transfer test, although the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Students also rated the human teacher more favorably for problem solving and preference. EEG results suggested higher theta-band activity, and some higher gamma-band activity, in the ChatGPT group, which the authors interpret as indicating increased cognitive engagement and attention during dialogue. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may help with basic knowledge acquisition but does not fully match human teachers for deeper knowledge application or creativity, and they recommend combining ChatGPT with traditional teaching rather than replacing teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small randomized experiment, which strengthens internal validity, but it is not K-12, not focused on reading or foundational literacy, and reports limited outcome measurement and no effect sizes/confidence intervals. It is therefore only adjacent evidence for the user’s target question rather than strong directly relevant classroom evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic results show no significant advantage for ChatGPT and a negative directional trend on transfer relative to human teaching. For the target evidence question on K-12 foundational reading, this paper provides no direct causal support and only weak adjacent evidence outside mainstream literacy contexts.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a dialogic teaching agent for undergraduate students learning a digital image processing unit on histogram equalization, answering students’ content questions during a short instructional dialogue.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison with 34 undergraduate students (n=17 ChatGPT, n=17 human teacher), ChatGPT-supported dialogic teaching produced retention scores similar to the human-teacher condition but lower transfer performance. Retention posttest means were 32.29 (SD=5.42) for ChatGPT versus 32.53 (SD=4.87) for human teacher, t=0.133, p=0.895; transfer means were 28.59 (SD=8.54) versus 33.06 (SD=7.60), t=1.612, p=0.117, indicating no statistically significant difference but a negative trend for ChatGPT on knowledge application.
finding.measure: Knowledge retention test and knowledge transfer test in undergraduate digital image processing (histogram equalization)
finding.std_deviation: Retention: ChatGPT SD=5.42, Human teacher SD=4.87; Transfer: ChatGPT SD=8.54, Human teacher SD=7.60

finding.finding_summary: Students rated the human-teacher condition more favorably than the ChatGPT condition on perceived problem-solving proficiency and liking for the dialogue. In the preference ratings, 11 of 17 human-teacher students gave the top score of 5 versus 2 of 17 in the ChatGPT group; for problem-solving proficiency, 5 of 17 human-teacher students gave a 5 versus 1 of 17 in the ChatGPT group.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of perceived problem-solving proficiency and liking/enjoyment of the dialogue

finding.finding_summary: The study specifically interprets knowledge transfer as deeper understanding, application, and innovation, and ChatGPT underperformed the human-teacher condition on this dimension. ChatGPT group mean transfer score was 28.59 (SD=8.54) versus 33.06 (SD=7.60) in the human-teacher group, t=1.612, p=0.117; although not statistically significant, the observed pattern suggests weaker support for application/creative transfer.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer test requiring application of learned content to a new problem context

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Education with Generative AI and Digital Twins: VR, RAG, and Zero-Shot Sentiment Analysis for Industry 4.0 Workforce Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training and reskilling the Industry 4.0 workforce using personalized educational technologies. The authors argue that growing technical complexity in advanced manufacturing creates a need for more adaptive training systems, especially for learners from underrepresented or educationally disadvantaged backgrounds. The paper is not about K-12 reading or literacy outcomes, and it does not provide direct causal evidence on generative AI for foundational reading in school settings. Instead, it presents an engineering/workforce development framework for immersive, personalized learning using generative AI, virtual reality, digital twins, retrieval-augmented generation, and zero-shot sentiment analysis.

The main intervention is the gAI-PT4I4 framework, a generative AI-based personalized tutor for Industry 4.0 training. The system combines a Unity-based VR learning interface, low-fidelity digital twins, an interactive AI tutor, GraphRAG for domain-grounded responses, zero-shot LLM-based sentiment analysis of teacher-student dialogue, and a finite automaton that adapts task difficulty based on performance. The paper also introduces a multi-fidelity digital twin education reference model that maps different digital twin capabilities to Bloom's taxonomy and Kirkpatrick evaluation levels. Empirical components include evaluation of sentiment classification on dialogue and Twitter datasets, plus a user experience evaluation of a PPE inspection training module with and without adaptive difficulty.

The population and context are postsecondary and workforce-oriented rather than K-12 classrooms. The framework is described as relevant to undergraduate students, master's and doctoral students, certificate learners, and workforce reskilling contexts. The only direct participant-based intervention result reported is from volunteers using the PPE inspection training in a VR environment; Table IV reports 22 participants without the adaptive mechanism and 6 with the adaptive mechanism, suggesting a small, institution-linked pilot rather than a school-based comparative trial. The paper affiliations indicate a University of Arizona-led project with collaboration from the University of Sonora, but the participant location is not explicitly stated.

The main conclusions are that LLM-based zero-shot sentiment analysis can classify teacher-student interactions with high accuracy on the authors' EduTalk Sentiment Dataset, that GraphRAG may improve domain specificity of LLM tutoring responses, and that an adaptive finite-automaton mechanism in a VR PPE module was associated with improved hit rate and reduced completion time. However, the study does not report a randomized controlled trial or a strong quasi-experimental design, does not involve foundational reading outcomes, and does not establish direct classroom causal evidence for generative AI in K-12 literacy. At best, it provides adjacent pilot evidence in immersive technical training outside mainstream English language arts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not direct K-12 evidence and does not provide a randomized controlled trial or strong quasi-experimental design for generative AI on foundational reading outcomes. It is an ASEE conference/grey-literature style vocational training paper with small volunteer samples, unclear group assignment, and no credible causal classroom reading evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unclear positive results on vocational VR training accuracy and efficiency, not on K-12 foundational reading. Because quantitative impacts are not standardized, causal attribution is weak, and relevance to the target literacy topic is only adjacent, impact should be treated as unclear rather than strong.

interventions.use_case: Generative-AI interactive tutor embedded in a VR Industry 4.0 training environment, using RAG/GraphRAG and conversational guidance to personalize vocational/engineering training tasks in real time.
Virtual-reality digital-twin simulation modules for factory tours, capping-station training, and PPE inspection, with adaptive difficulty controlled by a finite automaton.
Adaptive sequencing of VR exercises based on learner performance thresholds (80% task accuracy) and sentiment-informed personalization of difficulty/content.

finding.finding_summary: In a small volunteer evaluation of the PPE inspection / Industry 4.0 training environment, participants reportedly improved task performance accuracy to above 80% and completed training faster under the adaptive mechanism. Table IV reports Group 2 with adaptive mechanism at mean 83% hits versus 78% without adaptation, and mean completion time 48.94s versus 68.93s; however, this was not a randomized K-12 literacy study, groups were unequal (participants listed as 22 vs 6), and no standardized academic achievement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: VR task performance accuracy (hits percentage) and task completion time in Industry 4.0/PPE training
finding.study_size: participants: 22 without adaptive mechanism; 6 with adaptive mechanism; samples: 82 vs 72
finding.std_deviation: time SD: 34.93s vs 23.89s; hits SD: 17% vs 14%

finding.finding_summary: The adaptive VR training condition was associated with faster completion times, with mean time decreasing from 68.93 seconds without the adaptive mechanism to 48.94 seconds with it. This suggests improved training efficiency in the specific PPE simulation context, but the evidence is based on a small, non-K-12 volunteer sample and lacks causal rigor, confidence intervals, and formal significance testing.
finding.measure: Training task completion time in seconds
finding.study_size: participants: 22 without adaptive mechanism; 6 with adaptive mechanism; samples: 82 vs 72

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims enhanced decision-making capabilities and skill improvement within immersive PPE and Industry 4.0 simulations, with participant performance reportedly improving to over 80% accuracy. However, these outcomes are inferred from simulation-task performance rather than validated durable-skills instruments, and no causal design, effect size, or K-12-relevant measures are provided.
finding.measure: Simulation performance in decision-oriented VR/PPE tasks
finding.study_size: n=22 volunteers mentioned for experimental evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Embrace Opportunities and Face Challenges: Using ChatGPT in Undergraduate Students' Collaborative Interdisciplinary Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using ChatGPT can support collaborative interdisciplinary learning in higher education, specifically among undergraduate students working on digital literacy topics. The authors note that empirical evidence on ChatGPT's educational impact was limited at the time, especially for collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving. Although the retrieval topic concerns causal evidence for foundational reading outcomes in K-12, this study does not address K-12 reading and should be treated only as adjacent evidence on classroom use of generative AI, not evidence for reading instruction outcomes.

The study used a two-week quasi-experimental classroom implementation in which 130 first- and second-year undergraduates in a digital literacy course completed group activities on AI and Blockchain either with or without ChatGPT support. Some groups used standard ChatGPT, while others used a "ChatGPT Persona" mode in which the system was assigned a disciplinary persona to act like an additional teammate. Students worked in face-to-face collaborative groups using Miro in a flipped-classroom format, and the researchers collected weekly self-report surveys on collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving, physical engagement, and cognitive engagement, along with written reflections about ChatGPT use.

Participants were undergraduate students at a single public university in Singapore, drawn from STEM and non-STEM programs. The setting was an in-class university course rather than a K-12 or school-supported literacy setting. Outcomes were not academic achievement or reading measures; instead, they focused on perceived engagement and collaborative problem-solving. Quantitative analyses found significant main effects of topic, but no main effect of ChatGPT condition on the dependent variables. There was a significant interaction between disciplinary background and ChatGPT condition for physical engagement and a marginal interaction for cognitive engagement, with non-STEM students reporting higher engagement in non-ChatGPT conditions.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT should not be applied uniformly; its usefulness depends on task design and learner background. Qualitative reflections showed perceived benefits such as efficiency, brainstorming support, filling knowledge gaps, and human-like responses, alongside concerns about inaccuracy, generic responses, overreliance, and reduced critical thinking. For the purposes of the retrieval question, this paper provides no direct causal evidence on generative AI for foundational reading outcomes in K-12 classrooms; it is adjacent higher-education evidence centered on collaborative learning and self-reported engagement rather than literacy achievement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental study with some comparative structure, but it is outside K-12, not focused on reading, and relies primarily on self-reported engagement/problem-solving rather than direct academic achievement measures. The design lacks the strength and relevance required for strong causal evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Impacts are mixed and unclear: there was no overall ChatGPT main effect on the primary measured outcomes, with only subgroup interactions and qualitative perceptions of benefit and harm. For the user's target domain of K-12 foundational reading, this study provides no direct impact evidence and only adjacent, indirect evidence from higher education collaborative learning.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a conversational peer agent in undergraduate small-group digital literacy activities on AI and blockchain, sometimes in a 'persona' mode to simulate an interdisciplinary teammate contributing ideas during collaborative problem-solving.

finding.finding_summary: In a two-week quasi-experimental study of 130 undergraduates, ChatGPT condition showed no overall main effect on physical or cognitive engagement, but there was a significant interaction with disciplinary background for physical engagement and a marginal interaction for cognitive engagement. Non-STEM students were more physically and cognitively engaged in the non-ChatGPT condition, while STEM students showed no significant engagement difference by condition; topic effects favored the AI module over the blockchain module (physical engagement F(1,202)=15.15, p<.001, η²=.06; cognitive engagement F(1,202)=5.91, p<.05, η²=.02).
finding.measure: Self-report Likert surveys of physical engagement and cognitive engagement completed after class activities
finding.effect_size: η²=.06 for physical engagement topic effect; η²=.02 for cognitive engagement topic effect; interaction η²=.03 for physical engagement and η²=.01 for cognitive engagement
finding.std_deviation: Reported descriptively by subgroup; e.g., AI physical engagement SDs ranged from 0.60 to 0.79 in ChatGPT groups and 0.63 to 0.72 in non-ChatGPT groups

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT did not produce a significant main effect on collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving in this quasi-experiment. Students' collaborative problem-solving ratings were instead significantly higher for the AI topic than for blockchain (F(1,202)=12.40, p<.01), with no significant condition effect and no meaningful interaction attributable to ChatGPT on this outcome.
finding.measure: Three-item self-report collaborative interdisciplinary problem-solving scale adapted from the Team Collaboration Questionnaire
finding.effect_size: Topic effect η²=.05; ChatGPT condition effect not significant
finding.std_deviation: Reported descriptively by subgroup; e.g., collaborative problem-solving SDs ranged from 0.51 to 1.16 across AI subgroups and 0.59 to 0.71 across blockchain subgroups

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative reflections indicated that many students perceived ChatGPT as improving efficiency by quickly generating consolidated information and helping brainstorming, but these benefits were offset by concerns about inaccuracy, generic responses, repetition, and the need for fact-checking and additional probing. Because efficiency was not tested with an objective performance metric and no causal quantitative estimate was reported, the evidence for operational efficiency remains suggestive rather than established.
finding.measure: Post-activity written reflections coded into qualitative themes such as efficiency, idea generation, and need for verification

paper_profiles.title: Stay Hungry, Stay Foolish: On the Extended Reading Articles Generation with LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to reduce the time and effort required to create supplementary educational reading materials and related learning recommendations. The authors investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can automatically generate extended reading articles from TED-Ed lesson transcripts and connect those articles to relevant additional TED-Ed lessons. In the context of the retrieval topic, this paper does not provide direct causal evidence about generative AI improving foundational reading outcomes in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings. It is instead a content-generation and recommendation systems paper focused on educational resource creation.

The proposed approach has three stages. First, an LLM generates an initial extended reading article from a TED-Ed video transcript, adding contextual information such as historical details, terminology, and examples. Second, the system uses a sentence transformer plus an LLM-based ranking process to identify relevant related lessons from a database of 2,930 TED-Ed lessons. Third, the article is rewritten to better integrate the selected recommendations and associated keywords. The evaluation centers on recommendation hit rate, text relevance metrics (BERTScore, BM25, cosine similarity), and LLM-judged coherence, comparing outputs from Llama-3.1-405b and Gemma-2-27b, along with ablation studies.

No human learner sample, grade band, classroom implementation, or reading achievement outcomes are reported. The context is a dataset study using TED-Ed online materials, with students and teachers mentioned only as intended beneficiaries of the generated resources rather than as participants in an intervention study. There is no comparator involving treatment versus control groups, no instructional dosage, and no direct measures of phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, oral reading fluency, vocabulary, or reading comprehension.

The main conclusion is that the proposed pipeline can generate coherent extended reading content and course recommendations that align reasonably well with TED-Ed Dig Deeper materials, with Llama-3.1-405b performing better than Gemma-2-27b on the reported metrics. The paper should be treated as adjacent evidence about AI-assisted educational content generation, not as evidence of effectiveness for foundational reading instruction or student literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systems/content-generation paper with offline benchmark-style evaluation, not a randomized trial or strong quasi-experimental study of student outcomes. It provides no direct causal classroom evidence on generative AI for K-12 foundational reading.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful supplementary reading-material generation and recommendation performance, but impact on learners is unclear because no student outcome effects are estimated. For the user's retrieval goal, evidence is only adjacent and should not be treated as proof of reading gains.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based generation of extended reading articles from TED-Ed video transcripts, combined with semantic-similarity and LLM refinement for recommending related TED-Ed lessons to support supplementary self-study and teacher material design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that its LLM pipeline generated extended reading content and course recommendations with stronger automatic quality metrics for Llama-3.1-405b than Gemma-2-27b, including Hit Rate=0.320, BERTScore=0.642, BM25=2.923, cosine similarity=0.476, and LLM-rated coherence=8.469. These results indicate the system can automate supplementary material production and recommendation with measurable content-quality gains, but there is no direct classroom, teacher-time, or student-learning causal estimate; the evaluation is offline on 2,930 TED-Ed lessons rather than an RCT or quasi-experiment in schools.
finding.measure: Offline automatic evaluation metrics for generated content and recommendations: Hit Rate, BERTScore, BM25, cosine similarity, and LLM-rated coherence

finding.finding_summary: The study concerns generation of extended reading materials, so it is adjacent to literacy, but it does not measure student reading outcomes such as decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension. Reported results are limited to text similarity/relevance/coherence metrics and recommendation hit rate, so there is no direct causal evidence for foundational reading improvement in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings.
finding.measure: Generated-text quality and recommendation accuracy rather than student literacy outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Self-collaboration Code Generation via ChatGPT
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models can improve code generation on complex software tasks by collaborating with themselves through assigned roles, rather than relying on a single model invocation. The authors argue that complex programming problems resemble collaborative human software development, where tasks are divided across analysts, developers, and testers. The study is not about education, reading, K-12 learners, or classroom implementation, so it does not provide direct causal evidence relevant to generative AI for foundational reading outcomes.

The intervention is a self-collaboration framework using ChatGPT and other LLMs in role-based workflows. The framework assigns different agents to act as analyst, coder, and tester, coordinating through structured prompts and a blackboard-style interaction process inspired by software-development methodology. The paper evaluates this framework on multiple code-generation benchmarks including HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, and CoderEval, and also includes qualitative case studies for more complex software tasks such as game and website development.

There are no human learner participants reported. The empirical context is benchmark-based evaluation in software engineering rather than classrooms, schools, or educational programs. The only identifiable institutional context is the authors' affiliation with Peking University in China, but the benchmark tasks themselves do not represent a participant sample in the sense required for educational-intervention evidence extraction.

The main conclusion is that self-collaboration substantially improves code-generation performance over single-agent ChatGPT and several prompting baselines, with reported relative Pass@1 gains of roughly 29.9% to 47.1% depending on the benchmark. The authors conclude that role-playing and structured interaction can elicit stronger performance from LLMs on complex coding tasks. However, because the study uses benchmark experiments plus case studies rather than educational participants or school settings, it should be treated as adjacent technical evidence only, not as evidence for reading instruction or K-12 educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not an education study and provides no K-12 classroom, school-supported, randomized, or quasi-experimental evidence. It is a software engineering benchmark paper on LLM-based code generation, so it does not meet the causal education evidence criteria for the reading-focused retrieval topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact on foundational reading outcomes is studied. Reported gains concern code-generation benchmark performance, which is not relevant evidence for K-12 reading interventions or classroom literacy outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in the Classroom: Boon or Bane for Physics Students’ Academic Performance?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether integrating ChatGPT into instruction affects students’ academic performance in a university physics course. The authors frame the study around a broader debate about whether generative AI tools help or harm learning, and they note the limited empirical evidence available on ChatGPT’s effects in education. For the retrieval topic of generative AI for foundational reading outcomes in K-12, this paper does not provide direct evidence: it is not a reading study, not K-12, and does not assess literacy outcomes such as phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension.

The intervention was the incorporation of ChatGPT 3.5 as a learning aid in a second-semester engineering physics course. A control cohort from Physics 2 2022B received traditional instruction and was prohibited from using ChatGPT, while a later cohort from Physics 2 2023A received similar instruction but was introduced to ChatGPT at the start of the semester, taught how to use it, and strongly encouraged to use it throughout the course for theory questions, problem generation, and clarification. The same instructor taught both cohorts, covering the same topics in the same order and time frame apart from the added time needed to introduce ChatGPT. The study also included a survey of physics students about their perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness.

The population consisted of 76 undergraduate engineering physics students aged 17–20 at Universidad de Ibagué in Colombia, with 40 students in the control cohort and 36 in the ChatGPT cohort. The instructional context was an in-person classroom-based university course using lectures, blackboards, slides, videos, simulation software, labs, assignments, and textbook-based study, with ChatGPT added as a supplemental tool for the experimental cohort. The authors report periodic checks of students’ interactions with ChatGPT to verify use.

The main conclusion is that students in the ChatGPT cohort performed significantly worse than the control cohort on course grades. Mean total course grade was 3.79 in the control group versus 3.35 in the ChatGPT group, with statistically significant differences in two-sample t-tests (p = 0.00518 assuming equal variances; p = 0.00613 with Welch correction). Hake factors were negative across evaluations, which the authors interpret as reduced conceptual learning. Survey responses were more positive than the performance results, with many students reporting that ChatGPT was useful for clarification and understanding, but the authors ultimately argue it should be used cautiously as a supplement rather than a replacement for traditional teaching. As adjacent evidence for the requested topic, this is a quasi-experimental generative AI classroom study, but it is outside mainstream K-12 English language arts and foundational reading, instead focusing on undergraduate physics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not a K-12 reading study and not a randomized trial; it is a two-cohort pre/post-style comparison in higher education with notable selection/history confounds despite same instructor and similar course structure. It provides only limited causal credibility and is adjacent, not direct, evidence for the user's target question on generative AI for foundational reading in K-12.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic outcome shows a statistically significant negative association/intervention effect for the ChatGPT cohort relative to the control cohort, with no reported positive learning gains on the core academic measure. For the target evidence question, this also underscores that direct causal evidence for generative AI improving foundational reading in K-12 is absent here.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 3.5 was introduced as a course learning aid in a second-semester university engineering physics course; students were trained to use it and encouraged throughout the semester to ask content questions, generate theoretical questions/problems, and seek clarifications while studying physics concepts.

finding.finding_summary: In a two-cohort comparison in an engineering Physics II course, students with access to and encouragement to use ChatGPT 3.5 (n=36) had lower final course grades than a prior control cohort taught by the same lecturer without ChatGPT (n=40): mean 3.35 vs 3.79, a difference of 0.44 points. The reported two-sample t-test was statistically significant (equal variances: t=2.881, df=74, p=0.00518; Welch: t=2.835, df=63.67, p=0.00613), and the ChatGPT cohort also had negative Hake factors across three evaluations (-0.31, -0.15, -0.58), indicating worse conceptual performance relative to the control cohort.
finding.measure: Physics course grades across three evaluations, total subject grade, and Hake conceptual gain factor

finding.finding_summary: Student survey results (n=41) suggested generally positive perceptions of ChatGPT's usefulness and motivational value despite the negative grade outcomes. For example, 53.7% reported a positive or very positive effect on motivation/active participation, 68.3% rated response availability/timeliness as good or excellent, and 80.4% said they would recommend ChatGPT as a support tool; however, substantial neutral responses remained on several items.
finding.measure: Student self-report survey on motivation, participation, satisfaction, recommendation, and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Survey evidence on critical thinking and deeper understanding was mixed. While 61.0% of surveyed students felt ChatGPT helped deepen their understanding of physics concepts and 60.9% said it enabled exploration of new perspectives, 9.7% reported that ChatGPT led them to stop thinking and rely on provided answers to some or a large extent, and 26.8% were neutral on that concern.
finding.measure: Student self-report survey on critical thinking, independent thinking, and perceived deepened understanding

paper_profiles.title: Assessing the performance of 8 AI chatbots in bibliographic reference retrieval: Grok and DeepSeek outperform ChatGPT, but none are fully accurate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how accurately eight free-access generative AI chatbots—ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Le Chat, and Perplexity—generate academic bibliographic references. The problem addressed is whether students can rely on general-purpose chatbots to retrieve legitimate, correctly formatted references for university academic work, given widespread concerns about hallucinated citations and inaccuracies in AI outputs.

The authors conducted a comparative evaluation using a standardized prompt asking each chatbot to provide 10 APA-formatted references in each of five university disciplines: cardiology, mechanical engineering, organic chemistry, sociology, and art history. Across the eight chatbots, this produced 400 references total. Each reference was manually checked against Google and Google Scholar for five elements: author, year, title, source, and locating data. The study also analyzed document type, age of references, error counts, citation counts, and overlap across chatbot outputs.

The study context is higher education and is framed around realistic student use of free chatbot versions for coursework or degree projects. No K-12 learners, classroom reading instruction, or school-supported foundational literacy intervention is studied. The population is implicitly university students as intended end users, not intervention participants receiving instruction. The work is therefore adjacent to educational technology use in higher education rather than evidence on learning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that these chatbots are not reliable for unverified bibliographic retrieval. Only 26.5% of generated references were fully correct, 33.8% were partially correct, and 39.8% were wrong or fabricated. Grok and DeepSeek performed best and did not fabricate references in this sample, but neither was fully accurate overall. The paper argues that universities should strengthen AI literacy and information literacy training so students verify AI-generated references rather than trusting them uncritically.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a higher-education preprint, not peer reviewed, and it is not a causal study of student outcomes. Although it has a clear descriptive methodology, it does not meet the K-12 causal evidence standard relevant to classroom effects on reading outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows practically important but non-causal evidence that chatbot use for academic reference retrieval has mixed utility and substantial risk. It does not estimate effects on K-12 learners or foundational reading outcomes, so educational impact is unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Comparative evaluation of eight general-purpose generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude) used by university students to generate academic bibliographic references in APA style across disciplinary domains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates the practical performance of 8 AI chatbots for bibliographic reference retrieval/generation rather than learning outcomes. Across 400 generated references, only 26.5% were fully correct, 33.8% partially correct, and 39.8% wrong or fabricated; Grok (60% fully correct) and DeepSeek (48%) outperformed others, while Copilot fabricated 100% of requested references. This suggests possible productivity benefits for sourcing references, but with severe reliability limitations that undermine dependable academic use.
finding.measure: Accuracy and reliability of generated bibliographic references (fully correct, partially correct, fabricated), mean errors per reference, overlap among chatbot outputs

finding.finding_summary: The study does not directly measure student critical thinking, but its empirical results imply risks for information-evaluation skills because 39.8% of references were wrong or fabricated and many outputs appeared plausible. The authors argue that uncritical reliance on chatbot outputs may impair verification and critical information use, especially among students who do not check sources manually.
finding.measure: Indirect institutional/behavioral implication drawn from hallucination and reference-accuracy analysis; no direct learner assessment

paper_profiles.title: ZPD-SCA: Unveiling the Blind Spots of LLMs in Assessing Students’ Cognitive Abilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can accurately assess the alignment between reading materials and students’ cognitive abilities across school stages, framed through Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development. The authors argue that many educational uses of LLMs implicitly assume that models understand developmental differences in reading comprehension, but that this assumption has rarely been tested—especially for Chinese language education. The study therefore focuses on stage-level classification of Chinese reading texts as appropriate for elementary, middle, or high school students.

The main contribution is the creation of ZPD-SCA, a benchmark dataset for evaluating Chinese reading-comprehension difficulty by school stage. The corpus was built from real-world extracurricular reading materials spanning 12 genres and was annotated by 60 elite “Special Grade” teachers in China, with each book evaluated by at least 20 annotators. The authors then tested 10 LLMs under zero-shot and in-context learning conditions, using accuracy, F1, cross-level migration concentration, and weighted directional bias to assess how well the models matched texts to educational stages. They also explored LoRA fine-tuning on Qwen32B to see whether targeted training improved performance.

The population and context are not classroom learners receiving an instructional intervention; rather, the study concerns Chinese K-12 educational stages represented in benchmark labels and expert teacher judgments. The work is situated in Chinese language education and uses texts intended for elementary, middle, and high school students in China. Teachers serve as expert annotators rather than as implementers of an educational program, and students are not directly observed or tested.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs show limited zero-shot ability to judge reading difficulty in educationally aligned ways, with some models performing near or below random guessing, but they improve substantially when given in-context examples or task-specific fine-tuning. Even the best models retain systematic directional biases and difficulty with deeper dimensions such as thematic depth and logical reasoning. For the retrieval topic, this paper does not provide direct causal evidence about generative AI improving foundational reading outcomes in K-12 classrooms or school-supported settings; instead, it is adjacent benchmark evidence about LLM assessment of reading-material appropriateness in Chinese education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study of a student-facing educational intervention. It is an arXiv benchmark/model-evaluation paper with no classroom causal design and no direct learner outcome estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows technically meaningful but indirect model-performance gains from prompting/fine-tuning, yet provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 student reading outcomes. Educational relevance is adjacent and unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking large language models on classifying Chinese reading texts into elementary, middle, or high school difficulty bands aligned to students' cognitive abilities (ZPD/SCA), rather than delivering instruction to students.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates LLM performance on a Chinese reading-difficulty classification benchmark, not student literacy learning outcomes. Across 10 LLMs, zero-shot accuracy was often poor and in some cases below random-guessing levels (e.g., GLM ACC=0.2659; Qwen-max ACC=0.3061 on the full benchmark), while in-context learning improved performance substantially (e.g., GLM ACC=0.6878; Qwen-max ACC=0.6296; V3 best overall ACC=0.8313, F1=0.8352). These are model-evaluation results on text classification, not causal evidence that generative AI improves K-12 foundational reading in classrooms.
finding.measure: LLM benchmark performance on Chinese reading-stage/difficulty classification: accuracy, F1, CLME, WDBI

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can successfully complete Dutch national high school exams in English reading comprehension, and what that implies for educational assessment. The central question is not a classroom intervention with students, but a benchmark-style evaluation of large language model performance on authentic, high-stakes secondary school literacy assessments. The author also compares GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, investigates the effect of re-prompting, and explores whether repeated stochastic runs can reveal the model’s uncertainty.

The approach involved submitting three 2022 Dutch VWO national English reading comprehension exams to ChatGPT. GPT-3.5 was tested through the web interface with manual item-by-item prompting, and in some cases the researcher re-prompted or clarified questions when the model failed to give a valid answer. GPT-4 was then tested through the API using an automated procedure that fed each reading passage and associated questions together, with no re-prompting and temperature set to 0. The study also included a bootstrapped self-consistency analysis using GPT-4 at temperature 1.0 with 50 repetitions per exam to see whether inconsistent answers corresponded to likely errors.

The context is the Dutch secondary school system, specifically the academically rigorous VWO track for students preparing for university. The exams were official national assessments of English reading comprehension taken by Dutch-speaking high school students. No students interacted with the system as part of the study; instead, the model’s outputs were scored against official answer keys and converted into grades using the formal Dutch grading system. The paper reports one benchmark comparison against the distribution of scores from tens of thousands of students on one exam.

The main conclusion is that GPT-3.5 performed about as well as the average Dutch high school student when re-prompting was allowed, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student and required no re-prompting in the automated API setting. Re-prompting materially affected GPT-3.5 performance, raising its average grade from 6.5 to 7.3, which shows prompt structure and follow-up nudges can alter outcomes. The self-consistency analysis suggested that inconsistent responses were more likely to be wrong, so repeated sampling may help identify uncertain answers, but it did not improve answer accuracy itself. The author argues that these findings raise concerns about assessment security and suggest that LLM capabilities on school literacy tasks are already strong enough to challenge conventional unsupervised digital exams.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmark study with clear methods, but it is not a K-12 intervention study of students and does not estimate causal effects on learner outcomes. It provides descriptive performance evidence about an LLM on literacy assessments, with limited relevance to the requested direct-comparative student literacy evidence base.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial model performance on literacy assessments and plausible institutional implications, but impact on student outcomes is unclear because no students used the tool for learning. Therefore the educational impact for K-12 literacy is uncertain rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: General-purpose ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) was used via web interface and API to answer Dutch national high-school English reading comprehension exam questions, comparing model performance under different prompting and re-prompting conditions.

finding.finding_summary: On Dutch VWO English reading comprehension exams from 2022, ChatGPT GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 with occasional re-prompting, compared with the national student mean grade of 6.99 on one reported exam; without re-prompting GPT-3.5's mean dropped to 6.5. GPT-4 scored 8.3 (March 2023 version) and 8.1 (June 2023 version) without re-prompting, indicating stronger reading-comprehension test performance than average students, but this is a benchmark of model exam answering rather than a student-learning intervention and provides no direct evidence on student literacy gains.
finding.measure: Scores/grades on Dutch national high-school English reading comprehension exams (CITO VWO English 2022) completed by ChatGPT; comparison to published student score distribution for Exam 1
finding.study_size: n=124 exam questions across 3 exams; student comparison for Exam 1 n=35,698

finding.finding_summary: The study concludes that LLM performance at or above average student levels on high-stakes English reading comprehension exams raises concerns for assessment integrity, especially in computer-based or minimally supervised testing. At the same time, the paper argues these results create opportunities for redesigning assessment and educational use of LLMs, but these institutional implications are inferential rather than directly tested outcomes.
finding.measure: Institutional implications inferred from model performance on high-stakes exams; assessment security and policy concerns discussed in relation to exam results

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what its capabilities and limitations mean for learning, teaching, and especially assessment in higher education. The authors frame ChatGPT as a disruptive generative AI tool that has triggered both alarm and enthusiasm, particularly around whether it undermines traditional written assessments. They also situate the discussion within the broader history of educational technology hype and the field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

The paper uses a desktop analysis approach consisting of an extensive literature review and informal experimentation with ChatGPT. The authors review early academic and preprint literature on ChatGPT, GPT-3, and related AI writing tools, and they test ChatGPT with a range of prompts, including conceptual explanations, mathematical explanations, essay writing, and Chinese composition. They also discuss ChatGPT in relation to student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AI applications, comparing it with existing automated writing evaluation and feedback tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune.
