However, the paper also notes that human educators appear to provide higher-quality feedback than generative AI in cited prior work, so efficiency gains may come with instructional trade-offs; no original efficiency data are reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload reduction, immediacy of feedback, administrative assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses institutional implications such as exam redesign, process-based assessment, technological controls, and plagiarism detection challenges in response to generative AI. It presents these as pressing policy issues but does not empirically test institutional outcomes or report implementation effects.
finding.measure: assessment policy, exam security, plagiarism detection, school governance implications

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students actually edit and manipulate AI-generated text while composing expository writing, addressing a gap in the literature on students’ real-time use of generative AI during writing rather than only perceptions or final products. The study asks two questions: what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text, and what broader patterns characterize their AI-assisted drafting and revising processes.

The intervention was a two-hour AI-assisted writing workshop conducted in Hong Kong secondary schools. Students reviewed either process-based or genre-based writing instruction, learned prompt engineering strategies, practiced prompting on the POE app to access chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and then completed at least 30 minutes of an authentic 500-word expository writing task in Google Docs. Students were required to work independently of teacher and peer intervention during the task, and their screens were recorded. The analysis combined quantitative content analysis of 266 edits with qualitative thematic analysis and multiple-case analysis of screen-recorded writing processes.

The population consisted of 29 Hong Kong secondary students aged 12 to 18 from seven schools spanning a range of academic achievement levels; 25 recordings showed AI-generated text edits and were analyzed. This is a K-12 secondary EFL context, not mainstream English language arts. Teachers helped recruit students, chose either genre-based or process-based instructional framing for the workshop, and observed the workshop without intervening, while the first author delivered the instruction.

The study concludes that students’ use of generative AI in writing is more cognitively complex than simple copy-pasting. The authors identified 15 edit types across seven categories, including insertion, deletion, replacement, formatting, and AI-initiated edits from Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs suggestions. Four writing patterns emerged: planning with top-down drafting/revising, top-down without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting/revising, and bottom-up without planning. Most students used planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, suggesting many retained substantial agency in the writing process. The paper does not test effects on writing achievement or compare generative AI against teacher feedback, peer review, or non-generative tools; instead, it offers descriptive evidence about how students interact with AI-generated text during composition.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory mixed-methods study with clear procedures and direct observation data, but it is primarily qualitative/descriptive, lacks a control or comparator group, and does not estimate causal effects on writing outcomes. It therefore fits a yellow tier under the framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides useful evidence that generative AI may support complex writing-process engagement, but impact on literacy achievement is unclear because no standardized, rubric-based, or comparative outcome effects are reported. As a result, practical impact remains suggestive rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used generative AI chatbots via the POE app, along with AI-infused writing environments such as Google Docs and iOS predictive text, to plan, draft, insert, edit, and revise expository compositions during a workshop.

Students prompted conversational generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini through POE) for topic ideas, writing plans, model texts, section drafts, and revision support during machine-in-the-loop writing.

finding.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods exploratory study of 25 analyzable Hong Kong secondary EFL students (from 29 recruited), screen recordings documented 266 AI-related text edits across 15 edit types during expository composition writing. The study found students actively inserted, deleted, and replaced AI-generated text rather than passively copying it, but it did not report externally measured literacy gains, rubric-scored writing improvements, or inferential comparisons of writing quality. Findings therefore show complex writing-process engagement rather than demonstrated achievement gains.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing-process behaviors: frequencies and categories of AI-generated text insertions, deletions, replacements, and editing patterns during expository writing

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative thematic analysis suggested students engaged in cognitively complex planning, drafting, and revising with AI, yielding four writing-process patterns: planning with top-down drafting/revising, top-down without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting/revising, and bottom-up without planning. The dominant pattern was planning with bottom-up drafting/revising (15 students), which the authors interpret as evidence that many students retained agency and strategic control while using generative AI, though no validated metacognition or critical-thinking scale was administered.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of planning behavior, drafting/revising patterns, and observed strategic editing/agency in screen recordings

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing AI Chat Performances on Physics Exams of Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well two large language model chatbots, ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat, can answer high school physics questions from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination. The central question is whether these state-of-the-art LLMs perform at a level comparable to Vietnamese students and whether they can handle questions across increasing levels of difficulty, especially application and high-application physics problems.

The authors evaluated ChatGPT (Feb 13 version) and BingChat (April 15 version) using a subset of the VNHSGE dataset consisting of five illustrative physics exams from 2019 to 2023, totaling 200 multiple-choice questions. The analysis compared model accuracy by question order and difficulty level, reported yearly average performance, and converted scores to compare with Vietnamese student score distributions from national exam data. The study is not an intervention with learners; rather, it is a performance evaluation of AI systems on exam items, with discussion of possible educational uses such as individualized feedback and practice generation.

The context is the Vietnamese high school physics examination system. The questions represent high school physics content in Vietnamese and were drawn from official exam and illustrative materials. The comparison group was not a directly tested human sample within the study but rather national score distributions of Vietnamese students published for the same exam context.

The main conclusion is that both ChatGPT and BingChat underperform relative to Vietnamese students overall and struggle particularly with high-application questions. BingChat was generally more accurate than ChatGPT, while ChatGPT was described as more stable or consistent. The authors conclude that LLMs are not ready to replace human reasoning in physics teaching, though they may still support instruction by offering immediate feedback, individualized help, and practice materials. The paper calls for future work incorporating more domain-specific knowledge and evaluating whether LLM use actually improves student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a direct K-12 intervention study. It contains no student-facing implementation, no experimental or quasi-experimental design, and only descriptive comparisons of model scores to exam and population data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not measure learning gains, writing outcomes, or classroom impacts. Its main empirical result is that the evaluated LLMs underperform students on physics exams, indicating no demonstrated positive educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat on Vietnamese national high school physics multiple-choice exam questions to assess their ability to answer subject-matter questions and approximate student performance; no classroom implementation or tutoring intervention is tested.

finding.finding_summary: Across five illustrative Vietnamese national high school physics exams from 2019-2023 (200 multiple-choice items total), ChatGPT averaged 61% accuracy and BingChat averaged 66% accuracy. Converted average scores were 6.1 for ChatGPT and 6.6 for BingChat, compared with a reported Vietnamese student average of 6.39 and most-attained score of 7.25-7.75 depending on year; the authors conclude both LLMs generally underperformed Vietnamese students and struggled especially on high-application physics questions. No inferential statistical tests, effect sizes, or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Physics exam accuracy on 200 Vietnamese high school graduation examination multiple-choice questions; converted exam scores compared descriptively with national student score distributions
finding.study_size: n=200 items across 5 exam forms; student comparison population in one reported year n=325,525 exam takers

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized grading and feedback for complex, open-ended constructive geometry tasks in online mathematics learning. The authors focus on tasks that require procedural construction, written explanation, and conceptual reasoning, arguing that conventional answer-matching systems are poorly suited to these richer forms of student work. The study asks whether a large language model–supported system can grade student responses in ways aligned with teacher judgment and provide useful formative feedback during multi-attempt problem solving.

The intervention is a hybrid auto-grading and feedback system integrated into Algeomath, a Korean web-based dynamic geometry platform. Rule-based methods were used for closed-ended and constructive-geometry submissions, while GPT-4 with few-shot prompting was used to evaluate open-ended explanations and generate personalized feedback. Feedback was teacher-mediated in design rather than live teacher-delivered: teacher-authored exemplars of anticipated student errors and solution paths were embedded into prompts, and the system adapted feedback based on correctness and attempt number across up to four tries. The feedback became progressively more explicit as attempts were exhausted.

The field study took place in November 2024 with 79 middle-school students across four classes in South Korea working through an 18-question sequence on triangle circumcenters and related geometry concepts. The context was an online platform used in class-based instruction. Quantitative analyses examined agreement between automated grading and teacher judgments, question difficulty and discrimination, cumulative success across repeated attempts, and immediate post-feedback correction rates. The paper also includes qualitative analyses of disagreement cases, feedback quality, and iterative student answer refinement, plus student self-assessment survey data.

The main conclusions are that the system produced strong teacher alignment overall for open-ended grading (overall agreement 0.866; Cohen's kappa 0.737), perfect agreement for rule-based items, and moderate educational value as a formative support. About 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt after feedback, suggesting short-term benefits for revision within tasks. However, longer-term transfer to later tasks was not statistically demonstrated, and feedback quality was uneven, with issues such as terminology imprecision, model-answer leakage, and overly generic or tone-problematic prompts. The authors conclude that LLMs can support scalable, teacher-aligned formative assessment in mathematics, but stronger prompt and feedback design is needed before claiming robust broader learning gains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom field study/pilot with 79 middle-school students and no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison group. It reports descriptive and correlational evidence, agreement analyses, and within-system learning patterns, but causal claims about impact are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: short-term revision success and teacher-aligned grading are positive, yet no standardized effect sizes are reported and longer-term transfer effects were not statistically significant. The evidence supports modest or uncertain impact rather than clear achievement gains.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based auto-grading and adaptive formative feedback for middle-school constructive geometry tasks on the Algeomath online platform, with teacher-authored exemplars and up to four iterative attempts.
GPT-4 prompt-based feedback generation that provides attempt-aware hints, corrective explanations, and final answer explanations during iterative geometry problem solving.
Interactive web-based dynamic geometry environment (Algeomath) used by students to construct, measure, and revise geometric solutions during inquiry-based lessons.

finding.finding_summary: In a field study with 79 South Korean middle-school students, the LLM-enabled grading and feedback system supported frequent short-term corrections in geometry tasks: overall post-feedback correctness conversion was 36.7% (260/708), with cumulative success rising from about 0.60 on first attempt to about 0.80 by the fourth attempt for analyzed questions. However, longer-term transfer to later target questions (Q10, Q11, Q18) was not statistically demonstrated, with all reported comparisons non-significant (all p > 0.05), and some open-ended grading/feedback quality problems remained, especially for terminology-sensitive items such as Q15.
finding.measure: Constructive geometry task correctness by attempt, cumulative learning curves, post-feedback correctness conversion, target-question transfer analyses, teacher-system grading agreement for open-ended explanation items

finding.finding_summary: The automated system showed strong alignment with teacher grading while offering scalable formative assessment for complex geometry responses. Rule-based grading for closed-ended and constructive-geometry tasks reached 100% agreement with teachers, and LLM grading of seven open-ended explanation items achieved overall agreement of 0.866 with Cohen's kappa = 0.737 across 878 responses, indicating substantial consistency with teacher judgment.
finding.measure: Agreement rate and Cohen's kappa between system grading and teacher assessments; qualitative expert ratings of feedback quality

finding.finding_summary: Student self-assessment survey results were favorable, with average ratings reportedly ranging from 4.1 to 4.5 on a 5-point Likert scale across perceived understanding and application items, suggesting generally positive learner perceptions of the activity and system-supported learning experience. The paper also describes encouraging feedback tone as a design feature, but does not provide stronger causal evidence for motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student self-assessment Likert survey and open-ended comments on learning experience

paper_profiles.title: Which Feedback Works for Whom? Differential Effects of LLM-Generated Feedback Elements Across Learner Profiles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how specific design elements of LLM-generated feedback affect student learning and feedback acceptance, and whether those effects differ across learner personality profiles. Rather than comparing AI feedback against teacher feedback or other non-AI supports, the study asks which feedback elements within AI-generated feedback are most useful for helping students revise incorrect answers and which are rated most positively by students. The authors focus on six feedback elements derived from prior work: Baseline, Keywords, Actionability, Novelty, Coverage, and Positivity.

The intervention consisted of GPT-5-generated feedback for multiple-choice high school biology questions. Students answered questions in a web-based system, received immediate feedback tailored to the selected answer option, rated the feedback on six subjective criteria, and, if initially incorrect, revised their answers repeatedly until correct. The feedback was generated in advance and varied by element, such as emphasizing keywords, providing actionable revision guidance, increasing informational coverage, or using positive tone. The study also collected Big Five personality questionnaire data and clustered learners to examine whether feedback preferences varied by personality profile.

Participants were 321 first-year high school students in nine basic biology classes in Japan. The activity was assigned as winter-break homework, so the implementation appears to have been outside regular class time via an online system. The task context was biology problem solving rather than writing, revision of essays, or literacy instruction. Outcomes included two behavioral learning measures related to answer revision and six self-reported feedback evaluation measures including trustworthiness, review guidance, ease of understanding, key-points clarity, expression quality, and new knowledge.

The main conclusions are that Baseline, Coverage, and Keywords were the strongest feedback elements for supporting movement toward correct answers during revision, while Keywords, Baseline, and Actionability tended to receive the highest subjective ratings. Personality-based learner clusters showed different feedback preferences, suggesting potential value in personalizing AI-generated feedback. However, this is not a head-to-head comparator study against teacher feedback, peer review, automated writing evaluation, or other non-generative supports, and it does not address K-12 writing outcomes. Its evidence is therefore more relevant to AI feedback design in science learning than to claims about generative AI as a writing intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a sizable empirical K-12 experiment with direct student outcomes and structured comparisons across feedback conditions, but it is not a head-to-head generative-AI-versus-human comparator study and does not clearly report randomization details, standardized effect sizes, or strong causal controls typical of top-tier RCT evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but uneven benefits for specific feedback designs on immediate answer revision and subjective acceptance, with unclear magnitude because standardized effect estimates are not reported. Effects are short-term, task-specific, and not tied to broader writing or externally measured achievement gains.

interventions.use_case: GPT-5-generated automated feedback on high-school biology multiple-choice responses, varying six feedback design elements (baseline, keywords, actionability, novelty, coverage, positivity) to support answer revision and examine learner perceptions by personality profile.
Use of a modern large language model (GPT-5) to generate personalized-style explanatory feedback for students' incorrect answers in a web-based homework system.

finding.finding_summary: In a learning experiment with 321 first-year Japanese high school students, LLM-generated feedback supported revision on biology multiple-choice items, but effectiveness varied by feedback element. Among students initially incorrect, first revised-attempt accuracy was highest for Baseline (65.66%, n=198), followed by Coverage (53.22%, n=171) and Keywords (52.94%, n=204), while Positivity was lowest (46.63%, n=208); no standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals beyond plotted 95% CIs were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy of first revised attempt after feedback on biology multiple-choice questions; authors also report an 'Effectiveness' metric based on number of attempts to reach the correct answer.
finding.study_size: n=321 overall; per-condition initially incorrect subsamples: Baseline n=198, Keywords n=204, Actionability n=202, Novelty n=213, Coverage n=171, Positivity n=208
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported graphically only; exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Students' subjective evaluations of LLM-generated feedback differed by design element and by personality cluster. Keywords ranked first on 4 of 6 evaluation criteria and Baseline and Actionability were also consistently highly rated, whereas Positivity received relatively low ratings; Kruskal-Wallis tests showed significant cluster differences across all six criteria (p < .05), with Dunn post-hoc tests indicating Cluster 1 differed from other clusters on Trustworthiness, New Knowledge, and Expression Quality (reported p < .01 for Trustworthiness pairwise comparisons).
finding.measure: Three-point student ratings of trustworthiness, review guidance, expression quality, ease of understanding, key-points clarity, and new knowledge; personality-cluster differences in acceptance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined feedback features intended to support revision and metacognitive processing, finding that Actionability was subjectively valued but did not outperform Baseline or Coverage on revision accuracy. Authors interpret effective feedback as that which clearly directs attention to task-relevant information and provides sufficient guidance for revision, but no direct metacognition effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Revision-oriented feedback usefulness, especially 'Review Guideline' ratings and answer-revision performance.

paper_profiles.title: APRES: An Agentic Paper Revision and Evaluation System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models can be used to review and revise scientific papers in a way that improves their clarity, readability, and predicted scholarly impact. The authors argue that human peer review is strained, inconsistent, and difficult to scale, and they investigate whether an LLM-based system can discover useful evaluation criteria and then use those criteria to revise papers without changing their core scientific content.

The intervention is APRES, a two-stage agentic framework. In the first stage, the system searches for a review rubric whose LLM-generated scores best predict future citation counts using negative binomial regression. In the second stage, the discovered rubric is used as an objective function in a closed-loop revision process, where a reviewer agent critiques a paper and a rewriter agent iteratively edits it using diff-based local search/replace changes. The approach is evaluated quantitatively through citation-prediction accuracy and score improvements, and qualitatively through a blinded human preference study comparing original and AI-revised papers.

The population and context are not K-12 learners; instead, the study uses a corpus of 26,707 publicly available machine learning conference papers from ICLR 2024-2025 and NeurIPS 2023-2024, plus human evaluators with PhDs or doctoral-level training in machine learning who judged revised papers. The instructional context is not an educational intervention setting but scientific writing and peer review in research publishing.

The main conclusions are that APRES discovers rubrics more predictive of future citations than human reviewer scores or embedding-based baselines, improving citation prediction MAE by 19.6% over the next best baseline. In paper revision, revised papers were preferred over originals by human expert evaluators in 79% of cases, and the system appeared most effective for improving presentation and clarity rather than fixing fundamental scientific weaknesses. The authors position APRES as a human-augmenting tool for manuscript stress-testing rather than a replacement for expert review.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not a K-12 education study and does not evaluate an educational intervention or learner outcomes. It is a research-paper revision system for scientific manuscripts, presented as an AI systems paper with human preference evaluation outside the K-12 evidence scope.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects on scientific paper revision and reviewer preference, but these impacts are outside the target K-12 educational outcome framework. Therefore its educational impact is unclear/non-transferable for the retrieval question.

paper_profiles.title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students’ motivation relates to their use of generative AI in academic work, focusing specifically on math and writing. The authors argue that students are not a homogeneous group in how they engage with AI tools, and they frame the study through situated expectancy-value theory, emphasizing self-concept and perceived subject value as key motivational dimensions. The main research question is whether students with different motivational profiles show distinct patterns of generative AI use across subject domains.

The study uses a large-scale anonymous online survey administered to public high school students in the state of Chihuahua, Mexico. From 7,739 respondents, the authors retained 6,793 students in the final analytic sample after excluding those who failed attention checks or reported no prior generative AI use. Students reported their motivation in math and writing and their frequency of using generative AI for specific tasks. In writing, these tasks included brainstorming ideas, producing outlines, finding supporting evidence, improving language and grammar, obtaining writing feedback, and adapting text to requirements. The analysis used K-means clustering to identify motivational profiles and then compared AI-use frequencies across those profiles.

The results showed three recurring motivational profiles across both domains: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. In writing, Aspirational students most often used AI for brainstorming and outlining, Confident students most often used AI for language/grammar improvement and writing feedback, and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-related AI use. The authors conclude that generative AI use is patterned by motivation and subject domain, and that educational approaches to AI should be more targeted rather than assuming a one-size-fits-all model.

This is not an intervention or effectiveness study of generative AI for writing achievement, revision quality, or feedback impact. It does not compare generative AI against teacher feedback, peer review, or other writing supports, nor does it measure writing performance outcomes. Instead, it provides descriptive evidence about self-reported student usage patterns in a large K-12 sample, which may inform later design of motivationally sensitive AI-supported learning environments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a large-scale correlational survey with clustering and pairwise comparisons, but no experimental manipulation, comparator intervention, or causal identification strategy. It provides descriptive evidence on student motivation and AI use patterns rather than impact evidence on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study does not estimate effects of generative AI on writing achievement, revision quality, or other educational outcomes, so impact is unclear. Its main contribution is descriptive profiling of usage patterns across motivational groups in a general high-school population.

interventions.use_case: Surveyed Mexican public high school students' self-reported use of generative AI tools for writing tasks such as brainstorming ideas, producing outlines, improving language/grammar, obtaining writing feedback, and adapting writing to requirements, as well as math-related support.

finding.finding_summary: Using survey data from 6,793 Mexican high school students, the study identified three motivational profiles in writing and math (Aspirational, Confident, Disengaged) and found that generative AI use patterns differed by profile rather than reflecting a uniform effect. In writing, Aspirational students most often used AI for brainstorming (M=2.83) and outlines (M=2.72), Confident students most often used it for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67), and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-task AI use; no causal effect sizes for motivation outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-concept and perceived subject value surveys; clustered motivational profiles; self-reported frequency of AI use across writing and math tasks on 1-5 Likert scales

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive differences in how students use generative AI for writing-related activities, not whether AI improves writing achievement. Writing-task use varied by motivational profile: Aspirational students reported more use for brainstorming ideas (M=2.83) and producing outlines (M=2.72), while Confident students reported the highest use for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and seeking writing feedback (M=2.67); no direct writing quality, revision, or literacy gain outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of generative AI use for writing activities including brainstorming, outlining, language/grammar improvement, feedback seeking, and requirement adaptation

finding.finding_summary: The study found distinct math-related AI usage patterns across motivational profiles rather than estimating achievement effects. Aspirational students reported the highest use for step-by-step guides (M=2.81) and interpreting problems (M=2.59), Confident students were less likely than Aspirational students to use AI for formula retrieval (M=2.50 vs. 2.64, p<.001) and step-by-step guides (M=2.60 vs. 2.81, p<.001), and Disengaged students reported the highest direct answer copying (M=2.69), exceeding Aspirational (M=2.53, p<.001) and Confident students (M=2.18, p<.001).
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of generative AI use for math tasks including formula retrieval, direct answer copying, problem interpretation, step-by-step guides, solution verification, and practice problem generation

paper_profiles.title: Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language model (LLM) pedagogical agents can provide adaptive, theory-grounded support in open-ended learning environments without becoming opaque or encouraging student overreliance. The authors argue that many existing LLM tutors use a one-size-fits-all approach, provide insufficiently interpretable reasoning, and may help task performance without supporting durable learning. In response, they introduce the Evidence-Decision-Feedback (EDF) framework, which separates learner-state inference, pedagogical decision-making, and feedback generation into distinct but connected modules.

The framework is instantiated in Copa, a collaborative peer agent embedded in the C2STEM environment for STEM+C problem solving. Copa uses multiple sub-agents to analyze student log data and dialogue, infer learner states and conceptual gaps, select dialogue policies, and generate adaptive feedback. The system was developed through participatory design and prompt refinement, and it was intended to scaffold student inquiry while fading support as students gained mastery.

The empirical evaluation took place in an authentic high school science classroom in Nashville, USA, with 33 sophomore dyads participating in a six-week kinematics curriculum. Students worked on open-ended computational modeling tasks involving 1-D and 2-D motion and interacted with Copa as needed. The study combined system log analyses, conversation analyses, exit surveys, and educator feedback. Quantitative analyses examined whether Copa’s scaffolding changed with student mastery, whether verbalized understanding aligned with mastery, whether students relied less on the agent as mastery increased, and whether the system’s internal evidence-policy-feedback chain was interpretable.

The main conclusions are that Copa’s feedback adapted in theoretically expected ways as mastery rose, students’ verbalized understanding was positively associated with task mastery, requests for support declined as students became more competent, and the system’s intermediate reasoning outputs showed statistically significant grounding, alignment, and faithfulness relative to random baselines. Student perceptions were mixed: they appreciated thought-provoking questions but often wanted more direct answers. The authors conclude that EDF is a viable framework for designing interpretable, pedagogically meaningful LLM agents, while also noting that the evidence is correlational, from a single implementation context, and lacks comparison against alternative systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an authentic classroom empirical study with clear methods and quantitative analyses, but it is a single-group correlational design without randomization or a comparison condition; the authors explicitly note the absence of an RCT and that findings are correlational rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant within-system associations suggesting beneficial adaptive scaffolding and reduced overreliance, but it does not provide causal treatment effects on external learning outcomes or head-to-head comparator evidence. Impact is therefore promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Theory-driven adaptive LLM peer agent (Copa) embedded in a high school STEM simulation environment to provide dialogic scaffolding, probing questions, action suggestions, and feedback during dyadic computational modeling of kinematics.
C2STEM open-ended simulation/modeling environment used as the learning context in which students build 1-D and 2-D kinematics models while interacting with the LLM agent.

finding.finding_summary: In a classroom deployment with n=33 high-school dyads, students' verbalized conceptual understanding was positively associated with task mastery while using Copa. The paper reports a significant Spearman correlation between response success rate after agent probes and mastery deciles (rho=0.40), suggesting that progress in the kinematics modeling tasks aligned with students' ability to explain their reasoning rather than mere task completion; no standardized external science test effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Task mastery in C2STEM kinematics tasks and success rate in verbally explaining code/concepts after agent probes

finding.finding_summary: Students relied less on the LLM agent as mastery increased, which the authors interpret as evidence of growing autonomy/self-regulation rather than overreliance. Across n=33 dyads, requests for support were highest early in learning (about 59% of support while mastery was below 40%) and declined significantly with mastery (Spearman rho=-0.26); student perception ratings were mixed, with appropriate questioning rated moderately positively (mean=3.81/5) but perceived usefulness lower (mean=2.77/5).
finding.measure: Agent support requests across mastery deciles; exit survey perceptions of appropriateness, understanding, and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Copa's scaffolding adapted as students progressed, decreasing probing and increasing implementation/extension-oriented prompts, which the authors frame as support for knowledge construction and collaborative problem solving. In n=33 dyads, PROBE_UNDERSTANDING declined with mastery (rho=-0.34, p=0.034), while SUGGEST_ACTION (rho=0.33, p=0.039) and PUSH_LIMIT (rho=0.42, p=0.007) increased, indicating scaffold fading and deeper challenge as students advanced.
finding.measure: Dialogue policy frequencies across mastery quintiles; correlations between mastery and agent scaffolding moves

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate reading comprehension materials suitable for real educational use, addressing a practical problem identified by middle school English teachers in China: a shortage of diverse, current, personalized reading passages and multiple-choice comprehension questions for students. The authors position the work as an early real-world educational application of large language models, with a focus on evaluating the quality and suitability of generated materials rather than measuring student learning gains.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system that uses manually designed prompts with ChatGPT to generate reading passages and multiple-choice questions for Chinese middle school English learners. The system supports zero-shot and one-shot prompting, with teachers able to specify passage length, genre, topic, and CEFR difficulty level, and to provide a reference passage in the one-shot condition. Generated content is displayed in an editable interface so teachers can revise materials before use, and a toxicity check is applied before materials are made available. The authors compare ChatGPT-generated passages against a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline and against human-written textbook materials using automatic metrics and multiple human evaluation protocols.

The population and context are primarily Chinese middle school English learners and middle school English teachers in Beijing, within an English-as-a-foreign-language setting. However, the formal evaluations also include Chinese college students as evaluators and native English speakers recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing used the system for one week and provided interview feedback. The paper reports use in schools and teacher-facing system evaluation, but it does not present a direct classroom trial measuring K-12 student literacy outcomes.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT, when guided by carefully designed prompts, can generate reading passages that human evaluators often rated as equal or superior to human-written textbook passages on readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. The generated questions were seen as relevant and usable but weaker than human-written questions, especially in the quality and diversity of distractor options. Teachers viewed the system positively as a time-saving, resource-enhancing tool that could provide more diverse and personalized materials, though the authors acknowledge that question generation remains imperfect and that broader deployment and more extensive user feedback are still needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with structured human evaluations and practitioner feedback, but it does not measure direct K-12 student learning outcomes under controlled conditions. Evidence is primarily product evaluation and qualitative/subjective suitability assessment, with notable external-validity and sampling limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect impact: improved perceived quality of reading materials and possible teacher-efficiency benefits, without causal evidence of gains in student literacy outcomes. Because no student achievement effect sizes or post-use learning measures are reported, impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for Chinese middle school EFL teachers/students to generate personalized English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions, with zero-shot and one-shot prompt designs plus editable outputs for teacher revision.
Interface-based delivery system that lets teachers specify topic, genre, length, CEFR level, and question type to produce reading exercises for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT-generated English reading passages were rated as equal to or better than human-written textbook passages for middle school learners in China. In Human Evaluation 1, Chinese student evaluators rated ChatGPT passages higher than human-written passages on overall quality (4.46 vs. 4.18/5) and suitability-related dimensions such as readability, correctness, and coherence; in pairwise comparison, generated passages beat human-written passages 0.87 vs. 0.13 in zero-shot and 0.80 vs. 0.20 in one-shot settings. However, this is evidence about quality/suitability of instructional materials rather than direct student reading-comprehension gains.
finding.measure: Human ratings of generated reading passages and questions: readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality, topic coherence, suitability for middle school EFL reading exercises
finding.study_size: 30 textbook passages + 60 generated passages in Example Set 1; 10 human-written passages + 30 generated passages in Example Set 2; 9 Chinese college student evaluators, 36 native English speakers, and 3 middle school teachers for system feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the system could substantially reduce the time and effort required to create diverse, personalized reading materials and question sets. After one week of use, 3 experienced Beijing middle school teachers described the tool as a 'personalized resource library' that exceeded expectations and could reduce cost and time, though question-option quality still required teacher selection and editing.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usefulness, time/cost reduction, ease of use, and system quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents early practitioner feedback suggesting the system is feasible for school use in Chinese middle school English instruction and has already been used by teachers, but institutional impact is inferred rather than rigorously measured. Evidence comes from limited teacher interviews and claims of real-school use, without adoption metrics, policy change measures, or longer-term implementation data.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of school applicability and potential for broader deployment

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as an automated writing evaluation (AWE) tool: feedback literacy development and AWE tools’ integration framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI and other automated writing evaluation (AWE) tools can support learners’ feedback literacy in writing. The study is motivated by growing interest in ChatGPT for language learning, especially its possible role as a writing assistant and feedback provider, alongside established tools such as Grammarly and Quillbot. The core research question asks to what extent these AWE tools support the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ feedback literacy.

The intervention was the integration of ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot into a writing course. Students were introduced to self-evaluation using these tools, shown how ChatGPT could proofread, provide feedback, and paraphrase, and given a modeled prompt tied to the course writing rubric: “Revise my recount text and show the revision in terms of content, organization, grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics.” Students then used any AWE tool of their choice on draft essays in Google Docs e-portfolios, sometimes combining AI feedback with peer feedback, teacher feedback, Google searches, and word processor spell/grammar checkers. The study also develops an “AWE Tools Integration Framework” based on qualitative analysis of student experiences.

The population was 18 second-semester undergraduate English Education students at a private university in Surabaya, Indonesia, enrolled in a compulsory Recount and Narrative Essays course. The course lasted 16 weeks overall, with the focal data collection concentrated in the first seven meetings and approximately four months of study context described. Data came from semi-structured interviews with 12 volunteers, reflective journals, and student artifacts such as e-portfolios and feedback evidence. The setting was primarily classroom-based instruction with online drafting in Google Docs and LMS submission.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot, used alone or in combination, supported almost all aspects of students’ feedback literacy, but their usefulness varied by student proficiency, motivation, and ability to process automated feedback. ChatGPT was especially valued for generative functions such as paraphrasing, idea development, vocabulary enhancement, and style revision, while Grammarly and Quillbot were preferred for explicit grammar correction. At the same time, students reported limitations including confusion, over-reliance, ethical concerns, and uneven digital literacy. The authors argue that teachers should scaffold students’ use of AWE tools, support critical evaluation of AI output, and consider learner preference, tool features, technical capability, learning affordances, perceived limitations, and personal issues when integrating AI into writing instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative single-case study with clear methods, data sources, and analytic procedures, but it is small, non-K-12, non-experimental, and lacks quantitative outcome estimation. It meets limited credibility criteria and therefore fits yellow rather than green or blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially beneficial but highly mixed and context-dependent impacts, with no causal design or effect sizes and substantial heterogeneity by student proficiency/motivation. Overall impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot were used as automated writing evaluation tools for EFL essay drafting and revision, including grammar checking, paraphrasing, lexical enhancement, proofreading, and feedback on recount/narrative essays.

ChatGPT was specifically used conversationally to review student writing via prompts, generate revisions/feedback across rubric dimensions, paraphrase text, and support students' self-evaluation of essays.
The paper examines AI-enabled automated feedback on student writing, with students using tool-generated comments/corrections during drafting and revision as part of a feedback-literacy intervention.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of 18 Indonesian undergraduate EFL students, ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Quillbot were perceived to support writing revision through grammar correction, paraphrasing, vocabulary enhancement, punctuation, and idea development, but students also reported inaccuracies, over-paraphrasing, text shortening, confusing corrections, and risk of uncritical uptake. Benefits appeared stronger for more proficient and motivated students, while lower-proficiency or less motivated students more often found the tools confusing or unhelpful. No standardized writing effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence from semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, e-portfolio drafts, screenshots of tool use, and feedback artifacts about writing revision and self-evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The primary studied outcome was feedback literacy, with qualitative evidence suggesting the AWE tools supported multiple components such as appreciating feedback, eliciting feedback, and enacting feedback, while 'feedback processing' could be either enhanced or undermined depending on student behavior. Students who iteratively refined prompts, regenerated outputs, compared versions, and cross-checked suggestions showed stronger evaluative judgment and self-regulatory use; others reported overreliance, confusion, or blind acceptance of AI outputs. No quantitative scale scores or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative indicators of feedback literacy from interviews, journals, and writing artifacts, coded against Molloy et al.'s feedback literacy framework

finding.finding_summary: Students reported both positive and negative affective responses to AI-supported writing feedback: some valued the perceived objectivity and helpfulness of AWE tools, while others felt uneasy, considered ChatGPT use 'cheating,' worried about dependency, or found chatbot interaction strange. The paper also notes that Quillbot was perceived by some students as reducing anxiety, but these affective results were not systematically quantified in this study. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported attitudes, emotions, and perceptions in interviews and reflective journals

finding.finding_summary: Participants described AWE tools as making assignment completion and revision easier through rapid grammar checking, proofreading, paraphrasing, and immediate corrective suggestions. The discussion also notes potential workload relief for teachers by shifting surface-level editing to AWE tools, though this was discussed conceptually rather than directly measured. No time-on-task or productivity effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of ease, speed, and convenience of revision; conceptual discussion of teacher workload relief

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the role of ChatGPT in enhancing EFL writing assessments in classroom settings: A preliminary investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can enhance English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) writing assessment in classroom settings, focusing on two core questions: how reliable ChatGPT is when assigning holistic essay scores and how relevant its qualitative feedback is compared with college English teachers. The study is motivated by the need to reduce teacher workload and improve consistency and usefulness in writing assessment, especially given known variability in human scoring and feedback quality.

The intervention was the use of ChatGPT versions 3.5 and 4 as essay raters. Both models were trained briefly on three sample essays aligned to the CET-4 scoring rubric, then used to score and comment on 30 student essays. Four experienced college English teachers from the same university also rated the same essays using the same rubric and provided feedback on language, content, and organization. Quantitative analysis used generalizability theory to compare score reliability across AI and teacher raters, while qualitative analysis examined themes and amount of effective feedback.

Participants were 30 non-English-major undergraduate students and four college English teachers at a university in Beijing, China. Students completed one authentic CET-4 writing task during a normal class session within 30 minutes. The context was higher education EFL writing assessment rather than K-12 literacy instruction, and the AI function studied was assessment support: holistic scoring plus feedback generation, not student-facing tutoring or writing production.

The study concludes that ChatGPT4 showed higher scoring reliability than the human teachers, while ChatGPT3.5 was less reliable than teachers. Both ChatGPT versions provided more numerous and, according to the authors' coding, more relevant feedback than teacher raters across language, content, and organization. The authors argue that ChatGPT4 may be especially promising for supporting or even replacing some aspects of classroom writing assessment, though they also acknowledge important limitations in sample size, single-site design, and generalizability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study with clear methods, but it is not K-12, not experimental on student learning outcomes, and uses a very small single-site sample of 30 university essays. It provides some credible measurement evidence on assessment reliability, yet has limited relevance to the requested direct K-12 literacy implementation map.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially meaningful benefits for writing assessment quality and feedback completeness, especially for ChatGPT4, but no student learning effect sizes were reported and the study is outside K-12. Impact is therefore promising but unclear for the target K-12 literacy population.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 3.5 and 4 used to holistically score university EFL essays and generate qualitative feedback on language, content, and organization in classroom writing assessment.
ChatGPT used as an EFL writing support/assessment tool for English essay evaluation and revision-oriented feedback in a Chinese university context.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 30 university EFL essays, ChatGPT4 showed higher single-rater scoring reliability than teacher raters (G=0.89, Phi=0.88 vs teachers G=0.80, Phi=0.77), while ChatGPT3.5 was lower (G=0.66, Phi=0.65). For qualitative feedback, ChatGPT4 produced more relevant feedback statements than teachers across language (mean=201.25, SD=4.46 vs 54.5, SD=12.56), content (103.5, SD=3.68 vs 20.75, SD=8.72), and organization (106.5, SD=3.98 vs 36.25, SD=12.79), suggesting stronger assessment support for EFL writing than human raters in this setting.
finding.measure: Holistic essay scoring reliability using G- and Phi-coefficients; counts of relevant qualitative feedback statements on language, content, and organization
finding.study_size: n=30 essays; 4 teacher raters; ChatGPT 3.5 and 4 each assessed essays across 4 administrations
finding.std_deviation: Language feedback SDs: ChatGPT3.5=9.25, ChatGPT4=4.46, teachers=12.56; Content SDs: 7.62, 3.68, 8.72; Organization SDs: 9.59, 3.98, 12.79

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could streamline classroom writing assessment by providing automated scoring and extensive feedback, potentially reducing teacher workload, but this was inferred rather than directly tested. No direct time-on-task, cost, or workload measures were reported, so the efficiency benefit remains suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Inferred assessment support/workload reduction from automated scoring and feedback generation; no direct efficiency metric collected

finding.finding_summary: The study presents evidence that ChatGPT4 may support or potentially replace human raters for EFL classroom essay scoring because its reliability coefficients exceeded those of experienced CET-4 teacher raters. However, this institutional implication is based on a small single-site university sample and focused on reliability and feedback relevance rather than implementation at scale.
finding.measure: Comparative reliability of scoring systems and qualitative relevance of feedback, interpreted as implications for assessment practice

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LLaMA, a family of open foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters, with the goal of achieving strong performance at different inference budgets while relying only on publicly available training data. The paper addresses a core question in large language model development: whether smaller, more efficient models trained on large volumes of open data can match or exceed the performance of much larger proprietary systems such as GPT-3, Chinchilla, and PaLM.

The approach is a technical model-development study rather than an education or human-subjects intervention. The authors describe the pretraining data mixture, model architecture, optimization strategy, and efficiency techniques used to train the models on up to 1.4 trillion tokens. They then evaluate LLaMA across a wide set of benchmark tasks, including commonsense reasoning, question answering, reading comprehension, mathematical reasoning, code generation, multitask understanding, and bias/toxicity benchmarks. They also briefly report a small instruction-finetuning experiment showing improved benchmark performance.

No K-12 learners, teachers, or classroom implementations were studied. References to middle school and high school appear only in benchmark descriptions such as RACE and GSM8k, which are evaluation datasets rather than intervention contexts. There is no instructional setting, no teacher-mediated implementation, no dosage or routine-use condition, and no literacy intervention in schools.

The main conclusion is that LLaMA models are highly competitive with leading large language models despite being smaller and trained solely on publicly available data. The authors conclude that open, efficient foundation models can democratize access to LLM research, though they also note continuing concerns about bias, toxicity, and misinformation. For the purposes of K-12 literacy implementation mapping, this paper provides background on the underlying model family but does not report direct educational implementation or moderator evidence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a foundation-model technical paper describing pretraining data, architecture, benchmark performance, and bias/toxicity evaluation. It is not a direct K-12 literacy intervention study and provides no education-context implementation, comparison, or causal evidence relevant to classroom use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong benchmark performance for a general-purpose language model, including reading-comprehension benchmarks, but does not estimate effects on K-12 learners, teachers, or schools. Educational impact is therefore unclear and not directly measured.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of ChatGPT on English Language Learners’ Writing Skills: An Assessment of AI Feedback on Mobile
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT delivered through a mobile application can improve English as a second language learners’ writing more effectively than traditional teacher feedback. The study focuses specifically on grammar-related writing errors and also investigates students’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for English grammar learning. The authors position the work as addressing a gap in direct evidence on AI-generated feedback in school-based ESL writing contexts.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions over an eight-week period. In the experimental group, students wrote a 200-word story based on a picture, typed it into the ChatGPT app, and used a structured prompt asking the system to identify grammatical or structural errors, explain them, and provide examples. Students then reviewed the AI feedback and revised their original handwritten stories. In the control group, students completed the same writing task but received teacher feedback and grammar explanations before revising. Pre- and post-tests used picture-based story-writing tasks, and student attitudes toward ChatGPT were measured with a 12-item Likert-scale questionnaire.

Participants were 132 twelfth-grade ESL students aged 18 to 20 in a senior secondary public school in India. All students were Hindi first-language speakers, had studied English for more than 10 years on average, and were familiar with Android phones and internet use. The same researcher served as instructor for both groups. The study therefore took place in a school-based classroom context, with mobile-supported writing feedback embedded into regular instructional sessions.

The main findings were that the ChatGPT group showed significantly greater reduction in several grammatical error categories than the teacher-feedback control group, including errors involving present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, and possessive forms. Students also reported generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT, including ease of use, clarity of feedback, enjoyment, confidence, and satisfaction. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can serve as an effective supplement to traditional ESL instruction for writing error correction, though they note the short intervention period, lack of long-term evidence, and variability in feedback quality as constraints on interpretation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with pre/post comparison and a control group, which supports a green rating. However, it uses convenience/purposive sampling, lacks random assignment, gives limited reporting on baseline equivalence and implementation fidelity, and relies on automated error scoring plus post-only attitude data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements in writing-error outcomes and positive attitudes, but the practical magnitude is unclear because standardized between-group effect sizes are not reported and outcomes are narrow EFL grammar-error measures during active support. Impact appears promising but insufficiently quantified for a higher tier.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 3.5 mobile app provided automated feedback on senior secondary EFL students’ handwritten picture-based story drafts after students typed them into the app; the system identified grammatical/structural errors, explained them, and supplied example corrections for revision.
ChatGPT was used as a mobile AI writing assistant for English learners to improve grammar and composition accuracy in 200-word story writing through iterative error explanation and revision.
Students interacted with ChatGPT through a prompted conversational interface to obtain individualized grammar explanations and correction guidance during writing practice.
The intervention was delivered through the ChatGPT mobile application on Android phones during repeated one-hour classroom sessions over eight weeks.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental comparison of twelfth-grade ESL students in India (n=132; experimental n=66, control n=66), the ChatGPT mobile feedback group showed significantly fewer writing errors than the teacher-feedback group across targeted grammar categories in picture-based story writing after an eight-week intervention. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant group effect, F(1,65)=13.745, p<.001, and significant pre/post improvement overall, F(1,65)=123.676, p<.001; the paper reports partial eta squared=.860 for the main effect across error categories, but does not provide a direct between-group standardized effect size for the literacy outcome.
finding.measure: Pre/post picture-based 200-word story writing; counts of grammatical errors (present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, possessive, comparative, superlative) analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.860 for main effect of error categories; direct between-group effect size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT as an AI writing/language tool was associated with improved ESL writing accuracy relative to traditional teacher feedback in 132 twelfth-grade students over eight weeks. The gains were concentrated in reduction of grammar errors during supported revision of picture-based narratives, although the paper notes comparative and superlative errors were lower in the control group for some analyses and provides no standardized effect size for overall writing proficiency.
finding.measure: Writing error reduction in picture-based narrative compositions revised after AI feedback

finding.finding_summary: Post-intervention questionnaire data from 132 students indicated generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT for English learning, including motivation, enjoyment, confidence, and satisfaction. For example, 77.27% strongly agreed that interacting with ChatGPT made learning enjoyable, 50.0% strongly agreed and 31.82% agreed they felt motivated to practice grammar regularly, and 68.18% strongly agreed they felt more confident in their English writing; however, these are self-reports without validated scale psychometrics or comparison-group analysis.
finding.measure: 12-item Likert questionnaire on enjoyment, motivation, confidence, satisfaction, usability, and recommendation

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers in U.S. public and charter schools are using ChatGPT and related AI tools to support multilingual learners’ language and literacy learning. The study is motivated by the need to understand whether generative AI can be used in linguistically responsive ways for multilingual learners, especially given concerns about bias, standard-language ideologies, misuse, and limited evidence about classroom implementation. The author frames the analysis through a translanguaging lens and asks how teachers of multilingual learners use ChatGPT in instruction and to what extent those uses align with linguistically responsive pedagogy.

The study draws on a larger professional development initiative, Project ELEECT, focused on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. Data came from classroom observations and post-observation interviews with 42 in-service teachers across pre-K through grade 12 in Washington, DC public and charter schools. Eight observed cases involved instructional use of ChatGPT or related AI tools. Reported uses included teacher-led translation of texts and vocabulary, generation of translated reading-comprehension questions, transcription and translation of students’ oral language, manipulation of text reading levels, creation of exemplar disciplinary writing models, structured prompt frames to guide students’ use of ChatGPT during writing, and a multimodal literacy activity using DALL-E to connect descriptive writing with image generation.

The population and context are primarily multilingual learners in K–12 settings, including English learners, newcomer students, long-term English learners, students in dual-language and Spanish immersion programs, and dually identified multilingual learners receiving ESL/special education support. The uses occurred across elementary, middle, and high school contexts and across subjects such as math, science, ESL, Spanish immersion, social studies, and English language arts. The implementation described is largely teacher-mediated rather than independent student use, with only a few examples of guided student interaction with AI through prompt supports or multimodal experimentation.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT shows promise as a linguistically responsive tool for facilitating communication, differentiating content, and supporting some aspects of translanguaging pedagogy, especially affordances, production, and co-labor. However, reporting is limited and the study does not document effects on student achievement or validated literacy outcomes. The author also highlights notable gaps: little evidence on assessment uses, little reflection on sociopolitical language issues in implementation, limited documentation of students as co-leaders in AI use, and ongoing concerns about translation quality, bias, academic integrity, and the need for explicit instruction and critical AI literacy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study using classroom observations and interviews, with a clear methods section and identifiable sample, but it does not provide causal identification, validated outcome measures, or comparative designs. It meets limited credibility criteria appropriate to descriptive qualitative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but unclear impacts on multilingual learners’ literacy access, communication, and agency, without quantified learning effects or validated post-intervention outcomes. Reported benefits are suggestive and implementation-focused rather than demonstrating measurable impact magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Teachers used ChatGPT and related LLM-enabled language tools to support multilingual learners through translation, transcription/voice-to-text, text simplification or reading-level adjustment, generation of exemplar disciplinary texts, prompt frames for writing support, and image-prompt activities tied to descriptive writing and multimodal literacy.

ChatGPT was also directly engaged by students or teachers as a conversational generative AI for prompt-based writing support, brainstorming, tone checking, and guided interaction around multimodal text/image generation, though not as a full tutoring system.

finding.finding_summary: Across 8 observed AI-use cases within 42 teacher observations, the qualitative findings suggest teachers used ChatGPT to support reading comprehension, writing scaffolds, disciplinary literacy models, and phonological-awareness-oriented text creation for multilingual learners. Evidence is descriptive rather than causal: no standardized literacy outcome data, effect sizes, or pre/post comparisons were reported, and benefits were based on classroom observations and teacher interview accounts rather than validated achievement measures.
finding.measure: Qualitative classroom observations and post-observation teacher interviews about uses for reading comprehension, writing support, disciplinary literacy, and foundational literacy materials
finding.study_size: n=42 teachers observed; 8 AI-use instances identified

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported using ChatGPT to facilitate multilingual communication via translation, transcription, and subtitle generation, with qualitative indications that these uses improved access and participation for multilingual learners. However, no direct assessments of speaking, listening, vocabulary growth, or language proficiency were administered, so the evidence remains practice-based and inferential.
finding.measure: Observed and reported uses of translation, transcription, subtitling, and multilingual prompt support in instruction
finding.study_size: n=42 teachers observed; 8 AI-use instances identified

finding.finding_summary: The study identified teacher-facilitated uses of ChatGPT that appeared to support prompt construction, metalinguistic awareness, multimodal composition, and collaborative discussion, especially in secondary settings. These outcomes were not measured with validated instruments, but the author interprets the observed prompt-framing and image-generation activities as supporting student agency, collaboration, and reflective awareness about language and representation.
finding.measure: Qualitative observation/interview evidence on prompt design, collaborative use, multimodal literacy experimentation, and metalinguistic awareness
finding.study_size: n=42 teachers observed; 8 AI-use instances identified

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described ChatGPT as useful for differentiating content, generating translations, and producing tailored instructional materials, implying potential efficiency gains in preparing multilingual supports. At the same time, at least one teacher reported that adjusting reading levels and obtaining usable outputs required more time and prompt iteration than expected, indicating efficiency benefits were uneven and context-dependent.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports about instructional preparation, differentiation, translation, and prompt-revision workload
finding.study_size: n=42 teachers observed; 8 AI-use instances identified

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers perceive the use of an artificial intelligence-based educational tool designed to support scientific writing in STEM education. The core problem is not whether the AI tool improves student literacy outcomes, but whether teachers see such a tool as useful, appropriate, and feasible for classroom integration. The authors argue that successful adoption of AI in schools depends heavily on teacher attitudes, especially because many teachers have limited firsthand experience with AI-supported instruction.

The intervention studied was an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) built using GPT-2. The system generated text continuations and examples intended to scaffold argumentation and scientific writing through expert modeling, conceptual support, and strategic support. In the study, teachers first received readings and demonstrations about AI in education, then in week 3 they used the AISS themselves to complete an authentic scientific writing task about air quality in the United States. After drafting an essay without support, they used the system to generate follow-up sentences or paragraphs and then reflected on revisions. Data came from log files and short interviews, which were analyzed thematically.

Participants were nine experienced K-12 STEM-related teachers enrolled in a doctoral course at a higher education institution in the southeastern United States. Although they taught across elementary, middle, and high school levels, the actual study participants were educators rather than K-12 students. The activity took place in an online course context at a single institution, and none of the participants had prior experience using AI-based scaffolding in their own classrooms.

The main conclusions were that teachers generally viewed the AI tool positively, especially as a source of immediate, individualized scaffolding and strong models for scientific writing. They believed it could support reasoning, evidence use, and argumentation, and several thought it would be especially useful for middle and high school students. At the same time, teachers raised concerns about transparency, validity, and the potential reduction of the teacher’s role if AI mediates instruction. The paper ultimately presents teacher acceptance and implementation concerns rather than evidence of direct effects on K-12 literacy learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study with a clear methodology, small sample, and systematic thematic analysis, including strong inter-rater reliability. However, it does not test student outcomes experimentally and provides only perception-based evidence, so it fits yellow rather than green or blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but indirect, perception-based benefits with no quantified student outcome effects. Because impact is unclear and based on teacher perceptions rather than demonstrated K-12 learning gains, the appropriate tier is yellow.

interventions.use_case: GPT-2-based scientific writing scaffold that generates continuation text and example paragraphs from a teacher/user prompt to support argumentation, evidence use, and revision in STEM writing tasks.
AI-enhanced scaffolding for essay revision that provides immediate, individualized writing suggestions and expert-model text for reflecting on and revising a science essay.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative study, most of the 9 K-12 STEM teachers reported that the AI-enhanced scaffolding system provided strong expert models for scientific writing, helped with sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, claims-evidence connections, and revision. Findings are based on interview themes and usage logs rather than student achievement data; no effect sizes or validated literacy posttests were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions of scientific writing support; qualitative themes from interviews triangulated with log files and revision reflections

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the AI system as supporting scientific reasoning through argument construction, evidence-based claims, and problem-solving in response to an ill-structured air-quality task. These are perceived affordances rather than demonstrated student learning gains, and no direct student scientific reasoning assessments or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of support for argumentation, reasoning, evidence use, and scientific problem-solving in writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described the tool as promoting higher-order thinking, reflection, self-directed learning, and metacognitive comparison between users' own claims and AI suggestions. Evidence comes from thematic analysis of teacher interviews with high inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha=0.93), but there were no direct student skill measures or causal estimates.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of reasoning, higher-order thinking, reflection, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the system generated writing support quickly (e.g., in under 45 seconds) and could provide immediate individualized assistance, suggesting efficiency benefits. At the same time, they raised concerns that teachers would need time to review AI outputs for accuracy and appropriateness before classroom use, limiting straightforward workload reductions.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of immediacy, individualized support, and review burden

finding.finding_summary: Teachers were generally positive about future school integration of AI-based writing support, but also raised systemic concerns about transparency, validity of AI decisions, and the changing role of teachers in classrooms. The study therefore suggests both implementation promise and governance concerns, without institution-level adoption or outcome metrics.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions about implementation, transparency, validity, and teacher-role change

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
