This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate reading comprehension materials suitable for school use, addressing a practical problem identified by English teachers in Beijing: middle school students often reuse outdated English reading exercises, while producing fresh, personalized, level-appropriate materials is labor-intensive. The study asks whether a ChatGPT-based system can generate reading passages and multiple-choice reading questions of sufficient quality for educational use, and how those outputs compare with human-written textbook materials and a fine-tuned GPT-2 baseline.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system that uses carefully designed prompts with ChatGPT to produce English reading passages and corresponding multiple-choice questions. The system supports zero-shot and one-shot generation, allowing users to specify topic, length, genre, and CEFR difficulty level, and in the one-shot case to provide a reference passage. The generated content is delivered through a graphical interface intended for non-technical users, and teachers can edit outputs before final use. The paper also includes a toxicity check before exercises are shown to teachers or students.

The context is Chinese middle school English education, specifically English as a foreign language reading comprehension for Grades 7-9. The system was built using datasets from Beijing middle schools and was evaluated with multiple groups: Chinese college students with prior experience doing middle school English exercises, native English speakers recruited online, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system for one week and then participated in interviews. Although the target beneficiaries are middle school students, the direct evaluators in the reported study were mostly adult raters and teachers rather than K-12 students in a learning-outcome experiment.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were judged by human evaluators to be high quality and in many cases better than both the GPT-2 baseline and existing human-written textbook passages on dimensions such as readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. Generated questions were rated as relevant but weaker than human-written questions, especially because distractor options were sometimes repetitive or low quality. Teachers reported that the system exceeded expectations and could reduce time and cost while expanding access to personalized materials, but the paper does not test student literacy outcomes, sustained classroom implementation, or effects after support is removed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with clear methods, prompt designs, and human evaluation procedures, but it is not a causal K-12 effectiveness study of student literacy outcomes. Evidence is based mainly on intrinsic quality ratings and small-sample teacher feedback rather than validated pre/post learning measures in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect impact: generated reading materials and some exercises were judged high quality and potentially useful, and teachers reported likely time savings. However, no effect sizes or direct post-intervention K-12 literacy achievement outcomes were reported, so real educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for Chinese middle school English teachers to generate personalized EFL reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions, with editable outputs and teacher review before student use.
Interface-based exercise generation and delivery system that allows users to specify topic, length, genre, difficulty, and question type, then view and edit generated reading materials.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT-generated EFL reading passages were rated higher than human-written textbook passages on several intrinsic quality dimensions by experienced Chinese student evaluators, including overall quality (4.46 vs. 4.18), coherence (4.65 vs. 4.39), and readability (4.61 vs. 4.52). In pairwise comparisons on 10 topic-matched sets, generated passages were preferred over human-written passages in both zero-shot (0.87 vs. 0.13) and one-shot (0.80 vs. 0.20) conditions, and were judged highly topic-coherent (0.97); however, the paper did not measure actual student reading comprehension gains after using the materials.
finding.measure: Human ratings of generated reading passage quality, pairwise preference comparisons, topic coherence, and suitability for middle school EFL reading exercises
finding.study_size: n=9 Chinese college student evaluators for scored passage evaluation; n=36 native English speakers for additional ratings; 30 textbook passages paired with 30 ChatGPT and 30 baseline passages in Example Set 1; 10 topic-matched human passages plus 30 generated passages in Example Set 2

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback suggested the system could substantially reduce the cost and time required to create diverse, personalized reading materials for middle school English classes. After one week of use, 3 experienced teachers described the tool as a valuable personalized resource library and rated it positively overall, though this was based on qualitative feedback rather than quantified workload metrics.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and perceived time/cost savings after using the system

finding.finding_summary: For question generation, ChatGPT-produced multiple-choice items were rated as strongly matching passage content (4.38/5) but below human-written textbook questions on usefulness (3.25 vs. 3.93), suitability (3.48 vs. 3.92), and human-likeness (0.67 vs. 0.27 on appearing machine-generated). Teachers also reported that generated distractors were often weak, repetitive, or too easy, indicating limitations for direct classroom use without teacher curation.
finding.measure: Human ratings of multiple-choice question quality, including passage match, usefulness for training, suitability for middle school EFL learners, and perceived machine-generation
finding.study_size: n=10 exercises with human-written benchmark questions and generated comparison questions; evaluator count not_reported for this section

paper_profiles.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into science lessons: teachers’ experiences and views
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how science teachers experienced and perceived the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) content into regular lower-secondary science instruction. The central problem is how to introduce AI in schools without treating it as a stand-alone subject, especially when most teachers are not formally trained in AI and must integrate it into existing disciplinary curricula. The study asks how teachers perceived the relationship between AI and science, what implementation challenges they encountered, and what improvements they recommended after piloting an AI-integrated science lesson package.

The intervention was a researcher-designed AI-integrated science lesson package aligned with Singapore’s Grade 7 lower secondary science curriculum, specifically the theme of models. The package included pre-lesson video primers on AI and machine learning, review of key science ideas, activities linking science and AI concepts, and a hands-on predictive-modeling task using the Orange software. Students used Mars Rover data to build and test predictive models related to conditions for deploying solar panels on Mars. The approach was explicitly discipline-focused: AI was introduced as a tool for scientific modeling and problem-solving rather than as a separate computing topic.

Participants were three science teachers from three different secondary schools in Singapore and their 37 Grade 7 students. The lessons were implemented after school as a 3-hour session. Data came from teacher reflection sessions, classroom observations, lesson audio/video recordings, field notes, and student worksheets. The study used an instrumental case study approach with qualitative analysis focused on teachers’ views of AI-science connections, implementation barriers, and suggested revisions.

The main conclusions were that teachers saw meaningful overlap between AI and science in model-building, data use, and simplified reasoning, but also viewed the two as playing complementary roles: science provided contextual understanding and judgment about relevant variables, while AI functioned as a tool for generating predictions from large datasets. The biggest implementation challenge was teachers’ lack of confidence in their own AI content mastery, especially regarding machine-learning mechanisms. Teachers also anticipated barriers to broader adoption, including limited teacher buy-in, curriculum adaptation demands, and concerns about targeting the right student audience. They recommended more comprehensive teacher resources and suggested the package may be better suited for after-school enrichment contexts unless stronger supports are provided.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative instrumental case study with classroom observation, teacher reflection, and student worksheet evidence, but no experimental design, no validated outcome measures, and no causal identification strategy. It therefore fits yellow under the framework as a qualitative study with limited credibility for effectiveness claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful but unclear impacts: students may have learned aspects of scientific modeling/AI integration, while implementation feasibility was constrained. Because outcomes are qualitative and effect sizes are absent, overall impact is best classified as unclear rather than clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facilitated AI-integrated Grade 7 science lesson package using pre-lesson videos, Google Quick Draw, and the Orange software to help small groups build a predictive model about Mars solar-panel deployment as part of AI literacy/science integration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative evidence that teachers believed the lesson package helped students connect scientific modeling with AI/ML, especially around using data to build and refine predictive models. Observationally, most students appeared to grasp the broad workflow of model training and testing, and 32 of 37 students reportedly answered a worksheet question correctly about which dataset produced the most accurate prediction; however, no validated pre/post assessment, control group, or effect size was reported, so impact on scientific reasoning remains suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, classroom observations, student worksheets on predictive-model selection and understanding of data/model relationships

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that implementing the AI-integrated lesson package was challenging because of low confidence in their own AI content mastery and difficulty adapting curriculum within regular instruction. They recommended stronger teacher resources and suggested the package may fit better in after-school enrichment contexts, indicating implementation burden and feasibility constraints rather than demonstrated classroom efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Teacher interview/reflection reports on implementation challenges, preparedness, and feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers saw conceptual value in integrating AI into science, but anticipated barriers to broader adoption, including lack of teacher buy-in, curriculum adaptation pressures, and uncertainty about the appropriate student audience. Their recommendation to position the package within enrichment or after-school programs suggests partial institutional fit but limited readiness for routine whole-curriculum uptake.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of curriculum fit, adoption barriers, and recommendations for school implementation

finding.finding_summary: The lesson package was designed around collaborative, inquiry-oriented small-group problem solving, and teacher reflections suggested students engaged in reasoning about relevant versus irrelevant variables, model improvement, and problem solving with data. However, these outcomes were inferred from classroom interaction and worksheet performance rather than measured with validated collaboration, critical thinking, or metacognitive instruments.
finding.measure: Observed collaborative inquiry activity, teacher reflections, worksheet-based reasoning about variables and prediction

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can successfully complete Dutch national high school exams in English reading comprehension, and what that implies for educational assessment. The core question is not whether students learn more with generative AI, but whether large language models can perform at or above the level of secondary students on a high-stakes literacy-related assessment. The author also compares GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 and explores whether repeated querying with stochastic variation can help identify uncertain or potentially incorrect answers.

The study used the three available 2022 Dutch VWO national exams in English reading comprehension, chosen because they postdated ChatGPT’s training cutoff and therefore reduced contamination concerns. GPT-3.5 was first tested through the ChatGPT web interface, with occasional re-prompting when the model failed to provide a valid answer. GPT-4 was then tested through the API in a fully automated workflow without re-prompting. The exams included multiple-choice and open-response items focused on reading comprehension skills such as identifying main ideas, making inferences, and interpreting vocabulary in context. The context is the Netherlands, specifically the academically rigorous VWO high school track.

The main finding is that GPT-3.5 performed roughly at the level of the average Dutch student on these exams, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student. GPT-3.5 obtained a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without it; GPT-4 obtained mean grades of 8.3 and 8.1 for the March and June 2023 versions, respectively. A bootstrapping/self-consistency analysis showed that inconsistent responses were more likely to be wrong, suggesting that output variability can signal uncertainty, though it did not improve final accuracy. The paper concludes that large language models pose clear challenges for the integrity of computer-based literacy assessments and may require educators to rethink assessment design.

The paper does not study a classroom intervention, student learning gains, or durable literacy improvement after AI support. Its conclusions are about AI benchmark performance on high school reading-comprehension exams and the implications for educational assessment. The author also notes an important transferability limit: the exam was English as a foreign language for Dutch-speaking students rather than a native-language English exam, so findings should not be generalized uncritically to other literacy settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with clear methods, but it is not an intervention study on students and has no randomization or causal design for educational outcomes. It offers adjacent K-12 evidence about model capability on literacy assessments rather than direct evidence of student learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial model performance on literacy assessment tasks, but impact on student outcomes is unclear because no students received a generative AI intervention. Thus educational impact is indirect and not quantifiable as a student effect size.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) was used to answer Dutch national high-school English reading comprehension exam items, benchmarking model performance on K-12 literacy assessment tasks rather than delivering instruction to students.

finding.finding_summary: This study does not measure student literacy learning; instead it benchmarks ChatGPT's performance on Dutch high-school English reading comprehension exams. GPT-3.5 achieved a mean grade of 7.3 with re-prompting and 6.5 without re-prompting, compared with the national student mean of 6.99 on one reported exam cohort (Exam 1 student distribution n=35,698; mean points 35.88, SD=6.48), while GPT-4 achieved mean grades of 8.3 (March 2023) and 8.1 (June 2023). Because outcomes are model exam scores rather than student gains, this is only adjacent evidence for literacy intervention effectiveness.
finding.measure: LLM scores on national high-school English reading comprehension exams; number of correct exam items/points converted to Dutch grades
finding.study_size: 3 exams; 124 total exam questions; student comparison for Exam 1 n=35,698
finding.std_deviation: Student Exam 1 points SD=6.48; item-level subgroup SDs reported for some analyses

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that ChatGPT can perform at or above average student level on high-stakes K-12 English reading comprehension assessments, implying meaningful implications for assessment integrity and exam design. GPT-4 scored at approximately the 91st-97th percentiles on Exam 1 relative to Dutch student performance distributions, suggesting potential institutional disruption of unsupervised computer-based assessment, though no direct institutional outcome was experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Comparative exam performance relative to national assessment norms and percentile positioning; implications for assessment integrity
finding.study_size: 3 exams; 124 total exam questions; Exam 1 student comparison n=35,698

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether ChatGPT can be used to generate high-quality, personalized reading comprehension exercises for school use, with a focus on English learning in Chinese middle schools. The authors motivate the work by noting that teachers often reuse outdated reading materials and face substantial effort in adapting texts and writing suitable comprehension questions for students. The study therefore asks whether large language models can produce reading passages and multiple-choice questions that are suitable for authentic educational use.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. Users can specify features such as topic, length, genre, and difficulty level, and the system generates reading passages and associated multiple-choice questions. The authors compare ChatGPT-generated materials against a fine-tuned GPT-2 plus PPLM baseline and against human-written textbook materials. Evaluation includes automatic text metrics, human ratings from Chinese college students and native English speakers, pairwise comparisons with human-written passages, and qualitative interview feedback from experienced middle school teachers who used the system for a week.

The main educational context is middle school English as a foreign language education in China, specifically grades 7-9. The paper also includes undergraduate evaluators (Chinese college students) and adult native English speakers as raters rather than as instructional recipients. Three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing provided direct practitioner feedback on the system after hands-on use. The interface was designed for non-technical teachers and students, and generated text could be further edited by teachers before classroom use.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were rated highly and, in several evaluations, were judged comparable to or better than human-written textbook passages on dimensions such as readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. Generated questions were relevant to passage content but generally weaker than human-written questions, especially because distractor options were often low quality or patterned. Teachers reported that the system could save time and expand access to diverse, personalized materials, but the authors note that question generation still needs improvement and that wider deployment is necessary to assess effectiveness more robustly.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with structured human evaluations and limited practitioner feedback, but it does not test student learning outcomes in K-12 classrooms using a causal design. Evidence is mainly qualitative and rubric/perception-based, with no RCT/QED and no direct literacy gains measured in middle school students.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but unclear impact: perceived gains in passage quality, engagement, and teacher usefulness are positive, yet there is no direct evidence of improved student reading comprehension or durable literacy performance. Question generation quality is weaker than human-written benchmarks, so overall educational impact remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercises for Chinese middle school EFL learners, with editable outputs for teacher use.
A software interface that delivers AI-generated reading passages and comprehension questions for classroom use, functioning as a reading exercise delivery tool rather than an interactive tutor.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated the quality and suitability of LLM-generated reading passages and comprehension questions for Chinese middle school English learners, but did not measure student reading comprehension gains on external assessments. Human raters judged ChatGPT-generated passages higher than human-written textbook passages on several perceived quality dimensions (e.g., among Chinese student evaluators overall quality 4.46 vs. 4.18; readability 4.61 vs. 4.52; coherence 4.65 vs. 4.39), while generated multiple-choice questions were rated below human-written questions for usefulness (3.25 vs. 3.93) and suitability (3.48 vs. 3.92).
finding.measure: Human ratings of passage readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality, suitability, and question usefulness/suitability; no direct student literacy achievement test
finding.study_size: Passages: 30 human-written + 30 ChatGPT + 30 GPT-2 in Example Set 1; 10 benchmark exercises and 20 question sets in Exercise Questions Example Set; evaluators included 9 Chinese college students, 36 native English speakers, and 3 middle school teachers

finding.finding_summary: Engagement was assessed as a perceived property of the generated reading passages rather than as a student motivational outcome. Chinese student evaluators rated ChatGPT-generated passages higher than human-written passages for engagement (4.37 vs. 4.07), and native speakers also rated ChatGPT passages slightly higher (3.93 vs. 3.77), suggesting raters perceived the materials as more engaging, though no direct student motivation or reading-interest measure was collected.
finding.measure: Human ratings of engagement/interestingness of generated reading passages
finding.study_size: 9 Chinese college student evaluators and 36 native English speakers rating passage sets

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback suggested the system could reduce time and cost in preparing diverse, personalized reading materials, but this was based on interviews rather than quantified workload measures. Three experienced middle school teachers who used the system for one week described it as a valuable personalized resource library and indicated that output quality exceeded expectations, especially for passage generation, though question-option quality still required teacher review.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and perceived time/cost reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents early practice-based evidence that the system was used by middle school teachers and was viewed as promising for school implementation, but it does not measure institutional adoption outcomes, policy change, or system-wide effects. Claims of real-world impact are based on limited first-hand feedback and small-scale deployment context rather than formal institutional metrics.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback about school applicability and implementation promise

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second/foreign language writing, particularly for socially vulnerable students with refugee or migrant backgrounds. The research question focuses on the extent to which ChatGPT can contribute to improvements in L2 writing, especially vocabulary and grammar, in a multilingual and multicultural school classroom.

The intervention involved a short classroom-based writing activity integrated into the regular German-as-a-foreign-language syllabus. Students first wrote a personal email in German. The researchers then used ChatGPT to revise the students' drafts for vocabulary and grammar, and students received these improved versions to study and discuss. After that, students wrote a second email on a similar topic, allowing the researchers to compare features of the initial and subsequent texts. The analysis focused on text characteristics such as total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words.

The study took place in a single junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 students aged 15 who had refugee/migrant backgrounds and were learning German at approximately A2 level. The school served a diverse student population, and the participating students were enrolled in the third grade of junior high school. The intervention lasted two weeks within regular classroom instruction.

The authors conclude that the results are promising for using ChatGPT as a language-learning and feedback tool in L2 writing. They report increases in total words, unique words, and average words per sentence in students' later writing samples, which they interpret as evidence of improvement in vocabulary and grammar-related writing performance. At the same time, they stress that this was a pilot study and that broader claims are limited by the very small sample, short intervention period, and need for further research in other contexts and language skills.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot pre/post classroom study with n=8, no control group, no randomization, and mostly descriptive outcome reporting. It is peer-reviewed direct K-12 evidence, but credibility is limited by the very small sample, short duration, and absence of standardized external outcome measures or statistical tests.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially positive but unclear impact: gains were observed on rubric-adjacent/process writing-product metrics in a priority population, but no standardized literacy effects, inferential statistics, or effect sizes were reported. The evidence supports promising but still uncertain impact rather than a clearly established effect.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a foreign-language writing feedback and revision tool to improve junior high school students' German email writing, specifically targeting vocabulary and grammar for refugee/migrant-background learners.

ChatGPT provided AI-generated rewritten versions of students' texts that students reviewed before composing a second, similar email task, functioning as a generative conversational language support tool.

finding.finding_summary: In this 2-week pilot with 8 junior high school students (age 15) learning German as a foreign language, post-support writing samples showed higher word-count and lexical-output metrics after students reviewed ChatGPT-revised versions of their earlier texts. Mean total words increased by 38% (range 2%-62%), unique words increased by an average of 19.1 words per student, and average words per sentence increased by about 42%, though these are descriptive pre/post text metrics rather than externally validated literacy assessments and no inferential statistics or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student writing-product metrics derived from the texts: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words in pre/post German email tasks

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating AI in foreign language education: An investigation into ChatGPT’s effect on foreign language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT affects foreign language learning experiences, focusing on students’ perceptions of its benefits, drawbacks, and possible uses in language education. The study responds to growing interest in generative AI in language learning and seeks to address a gap in understanding how ChatGPT functions in real classroom practice, especially for skills such as writing, grammar, vocabulary, motivation, and engagement.

The intervention was a four-week ChatGPT-integrated English course in which the tool was incorporated into online reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary activities. Students used ChatGPT for tasks such as brainstorming, story generation, social media simulation, vocabulary practice, grammar practice, and receiving feedback on essays. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed thematically in a qualitative case study design.

The participants were 13 preparatory-class students at the School of Foreign Languages of a foundation university in Ankara, Turkey. They were undergraduate students from multiple departments with English proficiency levels ranging from A2 to B2. The course was conducted online because of emergency distance education following a major earthquake in Turkey. One researcher, acting as the language teacher, introduced students to ChatGPT and implemented the activities over the four-week period.

The main conclusions are that students perceived ChatGPT as helpful particularly for writing, grammar, and vocabulary learning, and as supportive of motivation and engagement through quick feedback, accessibility, and versatility. At the same time, participants reported limitations, including minimal benefit for speaking, no benefit for listening, technical problems, possible overreliance, encouragement of shortcuts, and concerns about misuse. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT has promise as a supplementary tool in foreign language learning, but should complement rather than replace teacher guidance and authentic communicative practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed qualitative case study with a clearly described method and thematic analysis, but it is a small non-K-12 sample (n=13 university preparatory students), lacks causal design, and relies on self-reported perceptions rather than direct outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest positive but unclear impact because outcomes are perception-based, effect sizes are not reported, and evidence comes from a small qualitative study in higher-education EFL rather than direct K-12 literacy achievement data.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was integrated into four weeks of foreign-language instruction as a conversational generative AI for reading, writing, grammar, vocabulary, brainstorming, story generation, question answering, and interactive class activities.

Students used ChatGPT specifically as a writing and language support tool for essay brainstorming, drafting assistance, written feedback, grammar practice, vocabulary expansion, and sentence improvement in EFL learning.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study reports student-perceived positive effects of ChatGPT on literacy-related skills, especially writing improvement and vocabulary learning during a four-week EFL course. Evidence comes from interview themes rather than external assessments: participants described better writing, contextual vocabulary learning, and useful writing feedback, but no quantitative literacy gain, effect size, or standardized measure was reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions about writing improvement, vocabulary learning, and reading/writing class experiences

finding.finding_summary: Students reported limited perceived impact on speaking and no impact on listening, despite more positive views for grammar-related language development. Findings are based on thematic analysis of participant interviews after four weeks of use; no direct speaking or listening performance assessment, effect size, or comparative statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions about speaking, listening, and grammar-related language learning

finding.finding_summary: Most participants described enhanced motivation and a more engaging learning experience with ChatGPT, citing instant feedback, accessibility, and interactive activities; however, some students explicitly reported no increase in motivation. These findings are perception-based from interviews with 13 university EFL learners and do not include validated engagement scales or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions about motivation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper contains student-reported indications that ChatGPT supported creativity, idea generation, and more independent prompt-writing over time, but also raised concerns about dependency, shortcut-taking, and possible deterioration of learner autonomy and critical thinking. These are qualitative perceptions rather than demonstrated transfer or post-support-removal outcomes, and no quantitative durable-skill measure was reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions about creativity, independence, dependency, and learner autonomy

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT as time-saving and efficient for research, rapid information access, and quick feedback during language-learning tasks. This reflects perceived productivity benefits from interviews, not observed workflow metrics or experimentally measured time savings.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview perceptions about time-saving, efficiency, and quick feedback

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a very short AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ over-reliance on incorrect recommendations from ChatGPT. The core problem is that students may accept plausible but wrong large language model outputs without sufficient verification, which could undermine critical thinking and decision making. The authors focus specifically on whether a brief educational text about how ChatGPT works, its limitations, and tips for wise use can reduce this tendency.

The study used an experimental design in which 12th-grade Estonian high school students were randomly assigned to either an intervention group or a control group. The intervention group read a short AI literacy text covering ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations and risks, and usage guidance; the control group read only a shorter general introduction to ChatGPT. Students then completed eight math puzzles on an online survey platform while viewing screenshots of ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect. The main outcomes were over-reliance (accepting incorrect AI advice), under-reliance (rejecting correct AI advice), self-reported perceived AI literacy gains, confidence, and decision time.

The participants were 36 final-sample 12th-grade students from 10 Estonian high schools, and the study was conducted online in October 2024. The intervention itself was extremely brief, averaging about 3.4 minutes of reading time beyond the control text. The educational context is secondary education rather than higher education, which the authors position as important because many prior over-reliance studies have used university students.

The main conclusion is that the short AI literacy intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. Students still adopted incorrect suggestions at high rates overall, with mean over-reliance of 52.1%. The intervention did, however, significantly increase under-reliance, meaning students became more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations. Students in the intervention group reported greater perceived knowledge about how ChatGPT works and how to use it, but not significantly greater knowledge about its limitations. The authors conclude that over-reliance on ChatGPT is widespread among secondary students and is not easily reduced by a brief informational intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled K-12 experiment, which strengthens causal inference, but it has substantial concerns including a very small final sample (n=36), likely limited power, and use of researcher-created task measures in a narrow context. These issues keep it below blue tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention did not improve the main targeted behavior and produced a statistically significant negative effect on under-reliance toward correct ChatGPT recommendations (d=0.78 in the undesirable direction). Overall impact is therefore best classified as no impact or negative impact.

interventions.use_case: High school students solved math puzzles while receiving ChatGPT recommendations, with the study testing whether a short AI-literacy text changes students’ reliance on correct versus incorrect LLM advice.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized high-school experiment, students used ChatGPT recommendations while solving eight math puzzles (final n=36; intervention n=19, control n=17). Over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT advice was high overall (52.1%, SD=28.90) and was not significantly reduced by the AI-literacy intervention, t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25; however, the intervention significantly increased under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations (36.84% vs. 19.12%), t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78, suggesting worse uptake of correct support.
finding.measure: Rates of over-reliance and under-reliance while solving Kangaroo math puzzles with correct/incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
finding.effect_size: d=-0.25 for over-reliance; d=0.78 for under-reliance
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported in figure only; exact values not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Over-reliance SD=28.90 overall; intervention SD=24.26, control SD=33.69. Under-reliance SD=24.00 overall; intervention SD=24.11, control SD=20.78

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies critical evaluation of AI outputs and over-reliance as a durable-skill issue. Students adopted at least one incorrect ChatGPT recommendation in 94.4% of cases, and longer decision time was associated with less over-reliance (rs=-0.41, p=.013), while the intervention itself did not improve deliberation and appears insufficient to reduce uncritical acceptance of AI output.
finding.measure: Over-reliance on incorrect AI recommendations, initial decision time, and critical evaluation of AI outputs
finding.effect_size: rs=-0.41 for over-reliance with incorrect-item decision time; rs=0.35 for under-reliance with correct-item decision time

finding.finding_summary: Students in the intervention group reported higher perceived knowledge about ChatGPT usage and working mechanism, but not limitations, after reading the educational text. Specifically, self-reported knowledge increased for usage, t(34)=2.26, p=.030, d=0.76, and working mechanism, t(34)=2.09, p=.044, d=0.70, while confidence in puzzle answers did not differ significantly between groups (U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17).
finding.measure: Self-reported AI-literacy perceptions and self-perceived confidence in answers
finding.effect_size: d=0.76 (usage), d=0.70 (working mechanism), d=0.19 (limitations, non-significant), rrb=0.17 (confidence, non-significant)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported in figures only; exact values not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Usage SD=0.77 vs 0.97; working mechanism SD=0.76 vs 0.90; limitations SD=0.91 vs 1.03; confidence SD=0.46 vs 0.76

paper_profiles.title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students’ motivational profiles relate to their use of generative AI in academic work, specifically in math and writing. The authors frame the problem around the rapid adoption of generative AI in education and the lack of understanding of how different kinds of students actually use these tools in everyday learning. Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory, the study examines whether students’ self-concept and perceived subject value are associated with different patterns of AI use.

The study did not test an intervention or measure learning gains from AI. Instead, it used an anonymous online survey to capture students’ reported motivation and AI use. Students rated their self-concept and perceived value in math and writing, with and without generative AI availability, and reported how often they used AI for specific tasks. In writing, these tasks included brainstorming ideas, producing outlines, finding supporting evidence, improving language/grammar, obtaining writing feedback, and adapting writing to requirements. The authors then applied K-means clustering to identify motivational profiles and compared AI usage patterns across groups.

The population consisted of 6,793 public high school students in the final two years of high school in Chihuahua, Mexico, after excluding respondents who failed attention checks or had no prior generative AI experience. The context was a large-scale survey administered online in collaboration with the state Ministry of Education and public high schools. The study therefore reflects student self-reports about existing AI use rather than observed classroom implementation.

The main conclusion is that students with different motivational profiles use generative AI in distinct, domain-specific ways. Across both math and writing, three profiles emerged: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. In writing, Aspirational students most often used AI for brainstorming and outlining, while Confident students most often used AI for language/grammar improvement and writing feedback. Disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-related AI use. The authors argue that these findings challenge one-size-fits-all approaches to AI integration and support more motivationally informed educational interventions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a large-scale K-12 correlational survey with clear methods and a substantial sample, but it does not identify causal effects of generative AI on student outcomes. It provides one credibility criterion through transparent methodology and direct K-12 relevance, but lacks experimental or quasi-experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows meaningful variation in self-reported AI use across motivational profiles, but it does not estimate effects on literacy or other student outcomes. As a result, impact is unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Survey of Mexican high school students' self-reported use of generative AI tools in writing and math, including brainstorming, outline generation, language/grammar improvement, writing feedback, and step-by-step guidance.
Writing-focused generative AI use for brainstorming ideas, producing outlines, improving language and grammar, adapting writing to requirements, and obtaining writing feedback.

finding.finding_summary: In a survey of 6,793 Mexican high school students, distinct motivational profiles (Aspirational, Confident, Disengaged) were associated with different self-reported generative AI use patterns in writing and math. In writing, Aspirational students reported more brainstorming (M=2.83) and outline production (M=2.72), Confident students reported the highest use for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67), and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-task AI use; no causal effect sizes were reported because this was a cross-sectional clustering study.
finding.measure: Self-reported motivation profiles (self-concept and perceived subject value) and frequency of AI use across writing and math tasks on 1-5 Likert scales

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined how students reported using generative AI for writing-related tasks, but it did not measure literacy performance outcomes such as reading comprehension, vocabulary, writing quality, revision quality, or error reduction. Therefore, no direct evidence of academic literacy gains or losses can be inferred from this study.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use for writing tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, language/grammar improvement, feedback seeking, and requirement adaptation

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to teach K-12 students, specifically secondary students, to use generative AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning. The authors focus on "prompting literacy"—students’ ability to understand when AI can support learning, how to form effective prompts, and how to interact with AI in ways that support rather than replace learning. The study also examines whether an AI-based auto-grader can reliably assess student-written prompts and whether the accompanying assessments are suitable for measuring prompting literacy.

The intervention was a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based practice in which students wrote prompts for hypothetical learning situations in biology, geography, and math. Students interacted with an AI chatbot, then received AI-generated rubric-based feedback on their prompts. The module emphasized learning-by-doing and immediate elaborated feedback. Across two classroom deployment iterations, the authors evaluated the quality of the AI auto-grader, student performance on prompt-writing dimensions, confidence in using AI for learning, student perceptions of the experience, and the quality of assessment items. Study 1 used pre/post surveys, multiple-choice assessments, human-graded prompt artifacts, and thematic analysis of open-ended reflections; Study 2 revised the assessment to include true/false and open-ended items and analyzed item quality.

The population consisted of students in 11 authentic secondary education classrooms, with Study 1 explicitly reporting 111 valid student participants in six secondary classrooms in East Asia. Teachers were present to facilitate implementation in class. The setting was a classroom-based deployment of a web platform, with no control group. The paper does not report a multi-week duration; the intervention appears to have been delivered as an in-class practice activity with immediate post-activity measures.

The main conclusions are that the AI auto-grader achieved generally strong agreement with human grading, with average accuracy around 0.92, though some rubric dimensions were weaker than others. Students improved in including background/context in prompts and reported higher confidence in using AI for learning after the activity, while conceptual test scores showed no significant gain due to ceiling effects in the original assessment. Qualitative responses suggested students perceived the module as useful and engaging, especially the interactive AI practice and feedback. The second study showed that revised true/false and open-ended assessment items had better difficulty and discrimination characteristics than the original multiple-choice items. Overall, the paper presents promising early evidence for a scalable prompting-literacy module, while emphasizing the need for broader studies, stronger assessment design, and further refinement of the auto-grader and instructional materials.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom deployment study in authentic secondary settings with pre/post measures, human-validation of AI grading, and qualitative analysis, but it lacks a control group or random assignment and is primarily exploratory/design-based. The evidence is therefore direct K-12 but methodologically limited relative to causal standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings show positive but modest and uneven effects: confidence improved and one prompting dimension improved, while broader test gains were not significant and no literacy achievement outcomes were measured. Impact is therefore promising but unclear for general educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Web-based prompting literacy module in which secondary students interact with an LLM chatbot across biology, geography, and math learning scenarios to practice responsible AI use for learning.

AI auto-grader evaluates student-written prompts against a rubric and provides immediate elaborated feedback on dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, background/context, elaboration, and avoiding direct-answer seeking.
Scenario-based instructional platform delivering practice items, feedback, and assessments to teach prompting literacy in classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 111 secondary students in Study 1, students improved on one targeted prompting component—embedding background/context in prompts—over repeated practice, with McNemar test showing higher success on Q3 than Q1 (p=.039). However, there were no significant gains on relevance (p>.90), conciseness (p=.286), or purpose (p=.617), and no pre/post gain on the 6-item conceptual test among the 98 students completing both assessments (p=.377), indicating selective rather than broad prompting-literacy improvement.
finding.measure: Human-scored prompt quality by rubric dimensions across practice tasks; 6-item pre/post prompting-literacy assessment
finding.study_size: n=111 for classroom deployment; n=98 for matched pre/post test

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after the module, with self-reported confidence rising by 10.4% on average and a statistically significant Wilcoxon test (p<.001). Qualitative responses also indicated high interest in interacting with AI and favorable perceptions of the learning design, though some students reported challenges related to typing, login issues, and scenario relevance.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-reported confidence item and open-ended perception survey responses
finding.study_size: n=111 for confidence analysis; n=131 open-ended responses reported

finding.finding_summary: The AI auto-grader showed satisfactory agreement with human grading, achieving average pass/fail accuracy of 0.92 across rubric dimensions and overall explanation accuracy of 0.95. Accuracy was strongest for relevance (0.98), background (0.96), and elaboration (0.90), but weaker for purpose (0.85) and no-direct-answer judgments (0.88), suggesting the system can support scalable feedback with some reliability limitations.
finding.measure: Accuracy of AI auto-grading versus human rubric scoring; explanation accuracy

finding.finding_summary: Assessment revision in Study 2 improved item quality relative to the original multiple-choice version: 60% of open-ended items and 30% of true/false items fell into desired difficulty/discrimination ranges, whereas none of the original MCQs did. However, internal reliability remained only moderate and slightly lower for the iterated version (Cronbach's alpha 0.58 vs 0.68), so efficiency for robust measurement remains promising but not yet established.
finding.measure: Assessment item difficulty, discrimination, and Cronbach's alpha reliability

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students can productively regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT for learning. The core problem is not literacy instruction but students’ ability to initiate, evaluate, and regulate question-asking cycles with generative AI during school tasks. The authors investigate whether students can distinguish effective from ineffective prompts, judge the usefulness of AI responses, ask follow-up questions when needed, and ultimately reach accurate conceptual understanding. They also test how these behaviors relate to metacognition, prior knowledge, and attitudes toward AI.

The study used six science investigation tasks in which students interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 during a one-hour school session. For each task, students saw either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, judged that prompt’s quality, optionally used it or wrote their own, evaluated every AI response they received, and then wrote a short answer in their own words. Researchers analyzed prompt discrimination, answer-evaluation sensitivity, follow-up behavior, and final task success, while also collecting questionnaire data on AI attitudes and metacognitive competencies.

Participants were 63 French students aged 14–15 from four middle-school institutions in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. The study took place during normal school hours with laptops provided by the research team, while task materials were given on paper. This was an observational study rather than a controlled intervention trial: although prompt suggestions were randomized at the task level, the paper primarily analyzes students’ naturally occurring behaviors, individual differences, and associations with performance rather than treatment effects between groups.

The main conclusion is that students showed substantial over-reliance on ChatGPT and weak metacognitive regulation. On average, they were near chance in distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts and informative from uninformative AI answers, seldom asked follow-up questions, and achieved only moderate task success despite unrestricted AI access. More positive attitudes toward AI were associated with poorer judgment of prompt and answer quality, whereas metacognitive regulation was associated with better prompt discrimination. The authors argue that AI literacy instruction should move beyond technical familiarity toward explicit training in metacognitive regulation, epistemic vigilance, and strategically effortful use of generative AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear methods and quantitative analyses, but it is a small single-group observational/correlational design without a control group or random assignment to intervention versus non-intervention conditions. As a preprint, it also has some peer-review uncertainty and does not meet stronger causal credibility standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Observed outcomes are predominantly negative: students showed chance-level discrimination of prompt and answer quality, very limited follow-up regulation, and only moderate science-task success despite AI access. The paper does not report positive literacy or academic effect sizes, and the main implication is risk of over-reliance rather than demonstrated benefit.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as an unrestricted conversational inquiry partner during science investigation tasks, with researchers analyzing prompt quality judgments, evaluation of AI responses, follow-up questioning, and resulting science explanations.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 63 French middle-school students (ages 14–15), task performance with unrestricted ChatGPT access remained only moderate despite all tasks being solvable with effective prompting. Mean success rate across six science problems was M=0.51 (SD=0.25), and students performed at chance in discriminating efficient from inefficient prompts (t=1.77, p=0.08) and useful from uninformative AI answers (Md′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), indicating weak support for conceptual understanding via spontaneous LLM use.
finding.measure: Binary-coded quality of students' final science explanations across six investigation tasks; prompt discrimination sensitivity (d'); AI answer evaluation sensitivity (d')
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.25 for success rate; SDd′=0.8 for prompt sensitivity; SDd′=1.2 for answer-evaluation sensitivity

finding.finding_summary: Students showed limited persistence/regulation in AI-mediated inquiry: only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions, totaling 22 follow-up questions across all six tasks. Even when students recognized an answer as unsatisfactory, they initiated follow-up questions only 31.8% of the time, suggesting premature termination of inquiry and low sustained engagement in repairing understanding.
finding.measure: Behavioral regulation during inquiry, including frequency of follow-up questions after AI responses and premature termination of QA cycles

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial weaknesses in metacognitively regulated use of ChatGPT: students could not reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) or informative from low-level AI answers (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Positive AI attitudes predicted worse prompt-quality sensitivity (β=-.39, p=.015) and worse answer-evaluation sensitivity (β=-.30, p=.018), while higher metacognitive regulation correlated with better prompt discrimination (r=.30, p=.022).
finding.measure: Prompt-quality discrimination, AI-answer evaluation sensitivity, follow-up regulation behavior, metacognitive and AI-attitude correlates

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy intervention can improve how middle-school students regulate their use of large language models during school-like problem solving. The authors focus on a key concern in K–12 generative AI use: students may over-trust fluent but incorrect AI outputs, fail to question weak prompts or answers, and delegate too much reasoning to the system. The study asks whether explicit instruction about how LLMs work, how they fail, and how to interact with them critically can improve both students’ interaction strategies and their task performance.

The intervention was a two-hour workshop delivered two days before the test session. It combined a conceptual component about LLM mechanisms and limitations (such as hallucinations, bias, and sycophancy) with a procedural component teaching transferable heuristics for prompting, evaluating answers, asking follow-up questions, and checking plausibility. Afterward, students completed six science investigation tasks with access to a generative AI chatbot. The study compared an intervention group with a control group that completed the same science task session without prior workshop training. Outcomes included final answer quality, prompt acceptance or rejection, follow-up questioning, and correctness judgments about AI responses, along with self-report questionnaires on GenAI attitudes and metacognition.

Participants were 116 students from grades 8–9 in one French middle school, tested during regular class hours. The final sample included 76 students in the intervention group and 40 in the control group. The context was LLM-supported science inquiry rather than literacy instruction; students used chatbots to help solve science exercises and then wrote final answers in their own words. The study therefore provides direct K–12 evidence about AI literacy training and GenAI-supported academic work, but it is adjacent rather than direct evidence for literacy outcomes.

The main conclusion is that a short, classroom-feasible AI literacy workshop modestly but significantly improved students’ final task performance and several behavioral indicators of better regulation. Trained students were less likely to accept underspecified prompts, more likely to ask follow-up questions when needed, and more accurate in judging response correctness. Self-reported GenAI knowledge, attitudes, and metacognitive scores did not predict performance. The authors argue that effective educational use of generative AI depends less on students’ self-perceived competence and more on explicit training in how to regulate interactions with the system.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is direct K-12 controlled classroom evidence with a comparison group and behavioral/performance outcomes, which is stronger than correlational work. However, it is a single-school preprint with non-randomized group assignment, attrition/exclusions, and some measurement concerns, so it falls short of blue-tier causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic effect is statistically significant but modest (r=0.19) in a general middle-school population, with clearer gains on process/regulation measures than on large performance outcomes. This supports a modest positive impact rather than a medium/large one.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used a generative AI chatbot during six science inquiry/problem-solving tasks, and the study tested whether a brief AI literacy workshop improved how students regulate prompting, evaluate chatbot responses, ask follow-up questions, and produce final answers.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with grades 8–9 students (N=116), the intervention group that received a 2-hour AI literacy workshop scored higher on final science-task answers than controls when both used an LLM during six inquiry tasks. Mean performance was 11.38/20 (SD=3.87, n=76) versus 10.29/20 (SD=3.04, n=40), with Mann–Whitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19, indicating a modest positive effect on LLM-supported science problem solving.
finding.measure: Final written-answer validity/performance on six science inquiry tasks, scored on a 0–20 scale from a 0–2 rubric per item

finding.finding_summary: The AI literacy workshop improved behavioral regulation of LLM use: trained students accepted fewer suggested prompts overall, were less likely than controls to accept underspecified prompts (51.5% vs 66.7%, p=.044), made more accurate correctness judgments, and were more likely to ask follow-up questions after accepted underspecified prompts (59.2% vs 27.9%, p<.001). Across participants, prompt discrimination sensitivity and conservative response bias predicted better performance (sensitivity β=1.76, 95% CI [1.06, 2.46], p<.001; bias β=1.65, 95% CI [0.25, 3.05], p=.021), suggesting the workshop strengthened regulation/monitoring-to-control processes in LLM-supported inquiry.
finding.measure: Behavioral indicators of interaction regulation during LLM-supported tasks: prompt acceptance/rejection, follow-up questioning, correctness judgments, signal-detection indices (d′, β)
finding.effect_size: β=1.76 for sensitivity; β=1.65 for response bias
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [1.06, 2.46] for sensitivity; 95% CI [0.25, 3.05] for response bias

finding.finding_summary: The workshop did not produce significant pre–post changes in GenAI self-report dimensions within the intervention group, and baseline self-report dimensions did not differ significantly between intervention and control groups after correction. Repeated-measures MANOVA found no overall intervention effect on GenAI self-reports (Pillai's trace=.116, F(6,62)=1.36, p=.247), with only small non-robust trends for Attitude and Fairness & ethics.
finding.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaire dimensions including attitude, trust, social influence, fairness/ethics, usefulness, and effort/ease of use
finding.study_size: n=112 for questionnaire analyses; n=72 intervention students for pre-post comparison

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that “AI literacy” has become a prominent but inconsistently defined concept, especially after the rise of generative AI. The authors ask how researchers conceptualize and approach AI literacy in K-12 and higher education, and what trends have emerged since generative AI became publicly available. Rather than evaluating one intervention, the paper synthesizes a broad and heterogeneous body of literature to clarify the field’s changing definitions, goals, and pedagogical approaches.

The study uses an integrative review methodology to analyze 124 empirical and theoretical studies published between 2020 and July 2024. The authors searched ERIC and Scopus, supplemented this with purposive citation tracing, and included peer-reviewed English-language studies in K-12 or undergraduate settings that focused on teaching or promoting AI-related skills or awareness. From these studies, they derived a conceptual framework with three ways of understanding AI—technical details, tools, and sociocultural impact—and three ways of understanding literacy—functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial. They then organized the reviewed literature according to these combinations and compared pre-generative-AI and post-generative-AI trends.

The review covers studies conducted across K-12 and undergraduate education globally. In K-12, the literature prominently includes machine learning curricula, AI ethics instruction, and comprehensive curricula combining technical and sociocultural content. In higher education, pre-generative-AI work was relatively sparse, but post-2023 studies increasingly focused on teaching effective use of generative AI tools, especially prompt engineering and critical use of ChatGPT-like systems. The paper also notes age-related access restrictions for some generative AI tools that may constrain direct K-12 use.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy is best understood as an umbrella term spanning substantially different objectives and approaches, and that more precise terminology is needed. The authors find strong growth in studies treating AI as a tool, especially in postsecondary contexts after generative AI’s emergence, while K-12 work remains more centered on technical and sociocultural instruction. They conclude that the field now includes multiple distinct strands—such as machine learning education, AI ethics, and generative AI tool use—and that the proposed framework can help researchers and practitioners communicate more clearly about which form of AI literacy they are targeting and where important research gaps remain.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed integrative review that synthesizes 124 AI literacy studies, but it is not a meta-analysis of a specific intervention and does not provide causal estimates for K-12 generative AI literacy outcomes. For the requested K-12 generative-AI-and-literacy question, it offers only indirect, narrative evidence rather than direct outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate a specific intervention effect on student literacy outcomes, so impact on K-12 literacy is unclear. Its contribution is conceptual and descriptive rather than demonstrating measurable academic impact.

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students engineer prompts when using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a writing task. The central problem is that effective use of generative AI for writing support depends on prompt engineering skill, yet non-technical students often have to learn this through trial and error. The study asks what types of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge in their prompt-engineering pathways while completing the same classroom writing task.

The researchers conducted a qualitative multiple-case study focused on students’ turn-by-turn interactions with chatbots. Four students completed a timed blog-writing task using iPads, Google Docs, and the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. Screen recordings were transcribed and coded for prompt types, such as auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, search-engine-like queries, greetings, and combinations of these forms. The analysis emphasized the sequence, quantity, and content of prompts rather than measuring literacy gains.

The population was four high-achieving form one students in a Hong Kong secondary school English class, using state-of-the-art chatbots for the first time in this context, although they had prior experience with other generative AI tools. The task took place during a single after-school classroom lesson of up to 45 minutes, taught by the first author. The study context is therefore a highly specific EFL secondary-school setting with novice chatbot users.

The main conclusion is that students followed distinct prompt-engineering pathways, showing different levels of sophistication and substantial trial-and-error behavior. Some students relied on simpler prompt forms, while others began combining prompt elements such as exemplars, instructions, and questions. The authors argue that EFL students would benefit from explicit prompt-engineering education so they can use chatbots more strategically to support writing, rather than relying on unsystematic experimentation. The paper does not provide direct evidence of literacy improvement; its contribution is descriptive evidence about how students interact with generative AI during a writing task.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative multiple-case study with clear methods, direct K-12 relevance, and systematic coding of screen recordings, but it lacks a comparison group, causal design, and standardized outcome measures. Under the framework, that fits yellow-tier evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report effect sizes or direct measured learning gains; impacts are descriptive and unclear rather than demonstrated. That supports a yellow impact tier for uncertain practical effect.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to help complete a blog-writing task, with the study focusing on how students engineered prompts during human-AI collaborative writing.
Students interacted conversationally with ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly to generate ideas and text continuations while composing an English writing assignment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides descriptive evidence that four Hong Kong secondary EFL students used chatbots to help complete a writing task and produced final blog entries, but it does not evaluate writing improvement with pre/post tests, rubric-based gains, or comparative performance against a control condition. Findings are limited to qualitative descriptions of prompt types, prompt sequences, and completed texts, so literacy impact on writing quality remains suggestive rather than causally established.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of prompt content/pathways and collection of completed blog-writing products

finding.finding_summary: Across 36 coded turns from 4 secondary EFL students, the authors identified multiple prompt-engineering pathways and interpret some pathways as becoming more sophisticated through trial-and-error, including use of auto-complete, natural-language instructions, and combined prompt forms. The study argues that students were learning prompt-engineering strategies and AI literacy practices, but these conclusions are based on qualitative case interpretation with no standardized durable-skills assessment or transfer test.
finding.measure: Screen-recording-based content analysis of prompt engineering behaviors, prompt types, sequencing, and cross-case pathway patterns

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses that chatbots may provide a supportive, non-judgmental environment for EFL writers and notes students' exploratory trial-and-error engagement with the tools, but it does not directly measure motivation, confidence, or affective outcomes. Any social-emotional implications are therefore inferred rather than empirically tested in this sample of 4 students.
finding.measure: Indirect qualitative observations and discussion; no direct validated engagement or motivation instrument

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether current large language models can perform fine-grained error analysis for K-12 English writing and provide pedagogically useful feedback. The authors argue that prior work in automated essay scoring and grammatical error correction focuses either on overall scores or surface-level corrections, leaving underexplored the more educationally relevant task of identifying specific error types, rating their severity, and explaining them in ways that support learning. To study this, they introduce FEANEL, a benchmark for fine-grained error analysis for English learners.

The approach is the construction and evaluation of a benchmark dataset rather than an instructional intervention with students. FEANEL contains 1,000 student essays annotated by English education experts. The benchmark includes 500 essays from elementary students and 500 from secondary students, with each error labeled for type, severity, and explanatory feedback using a 29-category taxonomy co-developed with educators. The authors then evaluate a range of state-of-the-art LLMs under different prompting conditions, including zero-shot and one-shot detailed prompts, using metrics for classification accuracy, severity rating error, and explanation quality.

The population consists of K-12 learners writing in English, primarily non-native speakers. Elementary essays came from students aged 9-11 on a global online education platform, and secondary essays were drawn from the TECCL corpus of Chinese EFL learners, focusing on students aged 12-18. Annotation was carried out by experienced English teachers, and additional teachers not involved in dataset creation were used for human benchmarking. The context is English writing by school-age learners, especially in EFL settings, not mainstream English-medium literacy instruction.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs show some foundational capacity for fine-grained writing error analysis but remain clearly below human performance on this nuanced educational task. Models struggled with complex and compound errors, long-tail error categories, and producing explanations with strong pedagogical nuance and consistent formatting. Performance improved when prompts included detailed definitions and examples, and some larger or reasoning-oriented models performed better on classification, but no model matched human teachers overall. The authors position FEANEL as a benchmark to expose these limitations and guide future development of LLM-based feedback tools for K-12 English writing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/evaluation study with clear methods and K-12 data, but it is not an intervention study measuring student outcomes, nor an RCT or quasi-experiment. It provides direct evidence about tool performance, not causal evidence about educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear educational impact because it does not measure student literacy gains, motivation, or transfer after use. Findings mainly document technical limitations and some workflow promise, so practical impact on K-12 learners remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking LLMs for fine-grained English writing error analysis on K-12 student essays, including error classification, severity rating, and explanatory feedback generation.
Evaluating large language models as English writing support tools for K-12 learners, especially for grammar, lexical, and pedagogical feedback in EFL writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on a benchmark of 8,676 annotated writing errors from 1,000 K-12 essays rather than student learning gains. Results show substantial limitations in literacy-relevant automated feedback quality: in the zero-shot setting, average error-classification accuracy was 63.13% and macro-F1 was 50.16, rising to 66.85% accuracy and 54.22 macro-F1 with one-shot detailed prompting; explanation metrics remained low, and human teachers outperformed most models on a 1,000-error subset. These findings indicate current LLM feedback systems are not yet at human-level for fine-grained K-12 writing support.
finding.measure: Error-classification accuracy and macro-F1, severity MAE, BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE for generated explanations on K-12 English writing errors
finding.study_size: n=1,000 essays; 8,676 annotated errors; human comparison on 1,000 sampled errors

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark suggests LLMs have some potential to automate parts of writing feedback, but current performance is inconsistent and prompt-sensitive. Performance improved when detailed prompts and examples were supplied, implying possible efficiency gains under structured use, yet the persistent gap from human teachers and low explanation scores indicate these systems are not ready for dependable autonomous deployment in K-12 feedback workflows.
finding.measure: Model benchmarking under zero-shot versus one-shot prompting; comparative performance versus human teachers

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing to Improve Health Literacy and Communication in Pediatric Populations and Beyond
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether publicly available large language models (LLMs)—ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing—can generate explanations of pediatric medical conditions at reading levels appropriate for children and lay audiences. The motivating problem is health literacy: the authors argue that children, adolescents, parents, and other non-expert users may benefit from clearer explanations of medical information, but there is limited evidence on effective interventions and increasing public reliance on online information sources.

The study evaluates LLM outputs rather than testing a classroom or clinical intervention with human participants.
