paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study does not estimate causal effects on learning and reports no effect sizes, so educational impact is unclear. Its strongest contribution is documenting widespread adoption and mixed perceptions rather than demonstrating measurable gains.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of U.S. secondary students' real-world use of general-purpose LLMs such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, and Bing Copilot for schoolwork help across subjects including language arts, history, math, and foreign languages.

finding.finding_summary: The survey of 306 U.S. students in grades 6-12 found very high uptake of LLMs (71% had used them at least once; 9% daily), but students expressed mixed views about usefulness and trustworthiness. Open-ended responses suggested perceived help with simplifying complex topics alongside concerns about overreliance and inaccuracy; 20% wanted better emotional understanding/conversation while 51% wanted more coherent and accurate responses.
finding.measure: Self-reported usage frequency, perceived usefulness/satisfaction, open-ended perceptions of impact, ethical concern ratings

finding.finding_summary: Students reported widespread LLM use despite generally restrictive school policies, with average perceived policy strictness of 3.48/5 and average ethical concern of 2.83/5. The paper also identified access gaps by region, school type, and paid-model access: 80.2% usage in top technology-index states versus 64.3% elsewhere, and 76.7% in private schools versus 71.3% in public schools.
finding.measure: Self-reported school policy strictness, ethical concern ratings, demographic/access subgroup differences in LLM use

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students use LLMs for language-arts-related tasks and that 57% of LLM users found them useful for writing text, but it does not directly measure reading or writing achievement. Evidence is limited to student self-report on perceived usefulness rather than externally assessed literacy outcomes, rubric-scored writing products, revision quality, or error reduction.
finding.measure: Self-reported subject use and perceived usefulness for writing text

paper_profiles.title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers actually revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before it is sent to students. Rather than evaluating AI feedback in isolation, the study asks three questions: what textual features are associated with teacher revisions, whether revision decisions can be predicted from the AI-generated text alone, and how revisions change the pedagogical type of feedback. The core problem is that teachers act as gatekeepers in AI-supported feedback systems, so the educational impact of generative AI depends not just on model output quality but on how educators accept, edit, or reshape that output.

The authors analyze log data from Tutoria, an AI-supported feedback platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom. In the platform, an LLM generates draft feedback for short open-ended student responses, and teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite it before delivery. The dataset contains 1,349 AI-generated feedback instances and corresponding final teacher-delivered messages from 117 teachers. Quantitatively, the study uses descriptive statistics, semantic similarity measures, and predictive modeling to analyze revision behavior. Qualitatively, it applies theory-informed coding to classify feedback as corrective, high-information, reinforcement/punishment, or other, enabling analysis of how teachers reshape the pedagogical character of the feedback.

The population and context span multiple Brazilian educational settings, including high school chemistry classes and undergraduate computer science contexts, along with additional extracurricular computing-related settings. Teachers were the main focal users, though students were the recipients of the feedback. Across all instances, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in about 78% of cases, and roughly half of teachers never edited any AI-generated feedback. When edits did occur, they usually shortened the feedback while preserving most semantic content. Teacher editing behavior varied substantially across individuals.

The main conclusion is that teacher mediation of AI feedback is selective rather than constant. Default AI behavior matters because most feedback is passed on unchanged. When teachers do intervene, they often simplify verbose, high-information explanations into more concise corrective forms, suggesting that AI-generated feedback may frequently overscaffold or misalign with teacher priorities. Predictive models using only feedback text achieved modest above-chance performance in identifying which messages would be revised, indicating that revision depends partly on the text itself but also on contextual and teacher-specific factors not captured in the models. Overall, the paper argues that AI feedback should be evaluated as a co-created artifact shaped through teacher-AI interaction, not just as raw model output.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational/log-analysis study with quantitative and qualitative coding, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experiment and does not estimate causal effects on student learning. It provides direct classroom-process evidence on teacher mediation of LLM feedback, with clear methods but limited causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially useful operational benefits and significant shifts in feedback form, but impacts on student outcomes are unclear and no direct literacy effect sizes are reported. Thus the practical impact is modest or uncertain rather than clearly positive on learner achievement.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback drafts for short open-ended student responses in a classroom platform, with teachers accepting, editing, or rewriting feedback before delivery.
Generative-AI-supported educational writing feedback, including teacher mediation of feedback language, explanatory density, and corrective wording for student-written responses.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers accepted AI-generated feedback without modification in 77.8% of 1,349 cases, suggesting the system often reduced editing effort. However, editing behavior was heterogeneous across 117 teachers: about 51.3% edited at least once, roughly half edited fewer than 6% of messages, and the top decile revised about two-thirds; text-only prediction of revisions achieved modest performance (AUC up to 0.75), indicating some ability to anticipate where human effort will be needed.
finding.measure: Teacher acceptance/edit rates, feedback length differences, cosine similarity between AI and final feedback, and prediction metrics for revision decisions (AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen's kappa)
finding.effect_size: AUC=0.75; Cohen's kappa up to 0.387; within-teacher Wilcoxon W=460.5, p=.024 for length difference
finding.std_deviation: AI feedback length SD=19.60; final feedback length SD=19.81; similarity SD=0.09

finding.finding_summary: This paper examines literacy-related feedback processes around student written short responses, but it does not measure student literacy learning gains directly. Qualitative coding of 834 deduplicated messages showed that unrevised feedback was more often corrective (58.1%) than high-information (41.9%), while revised cases started more often as high-information (59.9%) and shifted after teacher editing toward more concise corrective or other forms; the pre/post shift was statistically significant but small (chi-square=4.55, p=.033, Cramer's V=0.12).
finding.measure: Pedagogical feedback-type coding of AI-generated versus teacher-revised written feedback messages
finding.study_size: n=834 deduplicated feedback messages coded; full log n=1349 instances
finding.effect_size: Cramer's V=0.12; Cohen's w=0.16 to 0.20 for distributional differences

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language students use and edit AI-generated text while composing expository writing. The central research questions are what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text and what broader patterns characterize their writing processes when working with generative AI. The study is motivated by concern that students may simply paste AI output with little cognitive effort, and by the lack of fine-grained evidence about what students actually do during AI-assisted writing.

The intervention was an AI-assisted writing workshop in which students received instruction on either process-based or genre-based writing, along with prompt engineering for generative AI tools. Students then used the POE app to access chatbots and wrote a 500-word expository article in Google Docs, highlighting AI-generated text and recording their screens. The researchers analyzed 25 usable screen recordings from 29 recruited students using a mixed-methods design combining content analysis, descriptive statistics, thematic analysis, and multiple case studies.

Participants were secondary students in Hong Kong from seven schools, spanning a range of academic achievement levels and grade levels one through five, with ages 12 to 18. The context was a two-hour workshop conducted at schools, with teachers helping recruit students, arrange venues and hardware, and choose an instructional orientation, while the first author delivered the workshop. The study focused on the writing process itself rather than externally measured literacy outcomes.

The authors identified 15 types of AI-generated text edits across seven categories, including insertions, deletions, replacements, formatting actions, and unanticipated AI-initiated edits from Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs suggestions. They also identified four writing patterns: planning with top-down drafting and revising, top-down drafting and revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, and bottom-up drafting and revising without planning. The paper concludes that students' AI-assisted writing behavior is more active and cognitively complex than simple copy-pasting, but that the Hong Kong EFL context, small sample, and brief single-instance recordings limit generalization.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory mixed-methods study with clear methods and direct K-12 relevance, but it is primarily qualitative/descriptive, lacks a control group, and does not estimate causal effects on literacy outcomes. It therefore fits yellow-tier evidence under the framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides useful but indirect evidence of process-level engagement with generative AI in secondary EFL writing, not quantified impact on learning outcomes. Because outcome effects are unclear and no effect sizes are reported, the impact tier is best classified as yellow.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-assisted EFL secondary composition writing, focused on how students insert, edit, replace, and delete AI-generated text while drafting and revising expository essays using chatbots and embedded writing suggestions.
Students used POE-accessed chatbots such as ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini to generate ideas, plans, model text, sections, and revisions during machine-in-the-loop writing.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory mixed-methods study of 25 analyzable Hong Kong secondary EFL screen recordings (from 29 recruited students) found extensive AI-supported writing-process activity, identifying 266 edits across 15 edit types and 7 categories. However, it did not directly measure externally assessed literacy gains, rubric-scored final writing quality, revision quality, or error reduction; the empirical contribution is therefore mainly descriptive process evidence showing students actively modified AI output rather than passively inserting it. No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing-process behaviors; frequencies and categories of AI-generated text insertions, deletions, replacements, and editing patterns during expository composition

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret the observed editing behaviors as evidence of complex cognitive engagement, planning, and agency management in machine-in-the-loop writing. Four writing-process patterns were identified—planning with top-down drafting/revising (n=1), top-down without planning (n=6), planning with bottom-up drafting/revising (n=15 as reported in text/table, though one subsection says n=13), and bottom-up without planning (n=3)—but these are descriptive patterns rather than validated gains in transferable metacognition or independent performance. No standardized durable-skills outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative/thematic coding of planning, drafting, revising, and editing-pattern behaviors from screen recordings

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Persian: A Preliminary Study Focusing on ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how well large language models perform on a broad set of Persian-language NLP tasks, motivated by the concern that models such as ChatGPT have been studied much more extensively in English than in lower-resource languages like Persian. The authors ask how GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and OpenChat-3.5 perform on Persian tasks under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, how prompt language affects results, and how these models compare with task-specific fine-tuned state-of-the-art systems.

The study benchmarks the models across classic NLP tasks, reasoning tasks, and knowledge tasks. Tasks include sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, named entity recognition, machine translation, reading comprehension, textual entailment, multiple-choice math and logic QA, elementary school math questions, mathematical problems from Iranian entrance exams for 7th and 10th grades, and knowledge-based multiple-choice questions. The intervention is not an educational implementation with learners in classrooms; rather, it is an evaluation of LLM performance on Persian benchmarks using different prompt languages (Persian vs. English) and prompting setups (zero-, one-, and three-shot). The authors also test whether translating Persian samples into English improves performance.

The context is primarily Persian-language benchmarking, with some educationally themed datasets drawn from Iranian elementary school math exams and entrance exams for middle- and high-school levels. The paper does not study human participants directly; instead, student-related populations appear only indirectly through exam-question datasets. Geographic context is tied to Iran and Persian-language use, with authors based in Iran and Canada and some datasets sourced from Iranian exams.

The main conclusions are that GPT-4 is generally the strongest of the evaluated LLMs on Persian tasks, followed by GPT-3.5 and then OpenChat-3.5. However, task-specific fine-tuned models still outperform LLMs on many classic tasks such as named entity recognition, emotion recognition, reading comprehension, and textual entailment. The authors also find that English prompts often outperform Persian prompts, and translating Persian inputs into English can improve GPT-3.5 performance. Overall, the paper argues that Persian LLM performance is promising but uneven, with strong results in some reasoning and knowledge tasks and weaker performance on several task-specific language understanding benchmarks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a model benchmarking paper, not a K-12 intervention study. It does not evaluate effects on students, classrooms, or literacy outcomes, and therefore does not meet the direct-education evidence criteria for stronger empirical tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mixed benchmark performance on literacy-related tasks and stronger benchmark performance on math reasoning, but it provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learners. Any educational impact is therefore unclear and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking general-purpose large language models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, OpenChat-3.5) on Persian NLP tasks, including reading comprehension and school-level question answering, as an evaluation study rather than an educational intervention delivered to K-12 learners.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports benchmark performance on Persian reading comprehension rather than student learning outcomes. On a 200-sample subset of the ParsiNLU reading-comprehension test, GPT-4 reached F1=0.687 with English prompts and 3-shot prompting, slightly below the task-specific SOTA model at F1=0.691; GPT-3.5 peaked at F1=0.644 and OpenChat-3.5 at F1=0.613. The authors note zero-shot models often produced overly long answers, and one-/three-shot prompting improved extractive answer matching.
finding.measure: Model performance on benchmark reading comprehension task (F1 score on answer-span matching)

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong LLM performance on Persian math and logic benchmarks, though these are model benchmark results rather than student outcomes. GPT-4 achieved accuracy=0.725 on ParsiNLU math-and-logic multiple-choice QA (outperforming the SOTA model at 0.395), accuracy=0.740 on a 50-item elementary-school math set, and Math metric=0.564 on a 179-item mathematical-problems set; GPT-3.5 and OpenChat-3.5 performed lower.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy / Math metric on math-and-logic QA, elementary school math questions, and mathematical problem solving
finding.study_size: n=200 benchmark items for math & logic subset; n=50 elementary school questions; n=179 mathematical problems

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI can be integrated into secondary classroom instruction through a classroom co-design pilot with teachers. The paper asks how teachers design and implement AI-assisted tools in typical instruction, how teacher judgment and AI competency shape student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes, and what supports are needed for effective K-12 AI integration. The focus is not on a controlled test of achievement effects, but on early implementation lessons, teacher experiences, and patterns of classroom use.

The intervention studied was the Colleague AI Classroom platform, which included four generative AI features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment with AI Feedback for rubric generation and automated formative feedback, AI Tutor for on-demand student support, and Student Growth Insights for summarizing patterns in student interactions. Teachers used these tools as part of regular instruction, with AI positioned as a support for inquiry, feedback, revision, and instructional adjustment rather than as a replacement for teacher judgment. Data came from surveys, planning and reflection forms, weekly meetings, interviews, and platform usage logs.

The study took place over seven weeks in spring 2025 with 21 in-service teachers across four public school districts and one independent school in Washington State, involving more than 600 students in grades 6-12. Contexts included ELA, social studies, math, science, Spanish, and other secondary subjects. Teachers varied in prior AI experience, and the study emphasized teacher co-design, with participants choosing how and when to integrate the platform into live classroom instruction.

The main conclusions are that generative AI showed early promise when tightly scaffolded by teachers and aligned to instructional goals. Teachers reported that AI was most useful as a formative feedback and revision support, especially through narrative comments and rubric-guided feedback, while automated scoring was less trusted. Student engagement and perceived learning depended heavily on teacher framing, subject area, grade band, and interface design. The authors conclude that AI can act as a productive 'third agent' in classrooms, but only when teacher oversight remains central; they also stress that findings are exploratory and limited by regional sampling, self-report, platform specificity, and lack of direct learning outcome measures tied to student artifacts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory classroom co-design pilot with mixed qualitative data, surveys, interviews, teacher reflections, and platform logs, but no randomized or quasi-experimental design and no direct validated literacy outcome testing. It provides direct K-12 implementation evidence, yet most findings are teacher-reported and descriptive.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear student impact, with stronger evidence for workflow efficiency than for literacy attainment. Because no effect sizes or externally measured literacy gains are reported, overall impact on K-12 literacy outcomes remains modest/uncertain rather than established.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-guided generative AI classroom partner used in grades 6-12 for structured student-AI conversations via Teaching Aide and open-ended AI Tutor support across subjects, including some ELA/social studies uses such as prewriting, brainstorming, seminar preparation, and multilingual participation support.

AI-assisted assessment and grading system that generates/edit rubrics, scores student submissions, and provides narrative formative feedback to support revision and teacher feedback workflows across grades 8-12, including ELA and Spanish writing-related tasks.
Student Growth Insights aggregates patterns from student-AI interactions to surface misconceptions, questions, and progress summaries for teachers to guide reteaching and instructional adjustment.

Generative AI used in language-related contexts such as high school English prewriting/brainstorming, Spanish writing support, and proficiency-aligned feedback for multilingual/language-learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Direct literacy evidence is limited and exploratory. In ELA/social studies/language-related implementations, teachers reported that high school English teachers used AI for prewriting and brainstorming that improved essay quality, Spanish teachers used AI for ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback, and one example tied Teaching Aide to a Spanish writing assignment; however, the report provides no standardized reading/writing outcome measures, no rubric score distributions, and no effect sizes. Assessment logs covered 936 submissions across 33 classrooms and 58 assessments, but literacy-specific gains were not disaggregated and findings rely largely on teacher report.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported improvements in essay quality, writing support, and language-task usefulness; platform submission/resubmission logs rather than direct external literacy tests
finding.study_size: More than 600 students overall in grades 6-12; literacy-specific sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The report includes limited but favorable direct K-12 language-related evidence, especially in Spanish and multilingual participation contexts. Teachers reported that multilingual learners who practiced with AI conversations gained confidence and then contributed more to whole-class discussion, and Spanish teachers used AI for real-time ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback; however, these are descriptive teacher observations without validated fluency assessments or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of multilingual learner participation and AI-supported language/proficiency feedback in Spanish
finding.study_size: not_reported for language subgroup; overall pilot involved 21 teachers and more than 600 students

finding.finding_summary: Student engagement and confidence outcomes were generally positive but variable and heavily teacher-mediated. For Teaching Aide, 28% of implementations were rated as showing thoughtful engagement, 66% mixed engagement, and 6% limited engagement; 35% of teachers said the tool helped most students learn, 62% said some students learned, and repeated implementation was associated with higher engagement. In assessment contexts, some students valued low-pressure immediate feedback, but others were overwhelmed by long comments or interface friction.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of engagement, perceived learning benefit, student confidence/comfort, and descriptive reports of student reactions to AI feedback
finding.study_size: Teaching Aide feedback from 18 teachers; assessment feedback survey from 13 teachers; platform use included over 600 students

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described AI as supporting inquiry, revision, self-advocacy, and critical thinking when prompts were structured and tied to visible end products, suggesting possible benefits for durable skills. However, the same report warns about overreliance, younger students' need for scaffolds, and lack of direct measurement; no independent post-support removal performance or transfer outcomes were tested.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported inquiry quality, revision behavior, self-advocacy, and critical-thinking related classroom behaviors
finding.study_size: More than 600 students overall; durable-skills-specific sample not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Operational benefits are among the strongest findings in the report. AI grading coverage was high (median 92.2% of submitted work AI-graded), teachers reported faster turnaround for personalized feedback, and Student Growth Insights/conversation summaries reduced oversight burden and helped target reteaching; assessment logs covered 58 assessments, 936 submissions, and 33 classrooms with mean submission rate 54.8% (SD=27.9%) and average resubmission rate 8.7%.
finding.measure: Platform logs on grading coverage, submission/resubmission rates, and teacher reports of time savings, oversight reduction, and feedback workflow efficiency
finding.study_size: 19 teachers used assessment features; 58 assessments; 936 submissions across 33 classrooms

paper_profiles.title: Unlocking Scientific Concepts: How Effective Are LLM-Generated Analogies for Student Understanding and Classroom Practice?
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language model (LLM)-generated analogies can effectively support students’ understanding of scientific concepts and assist teachers in classroom practice. The authors focus on two educational scenarios: students using LLM-generated analogies without teacher intervention, and teachers integrating LLM-generated analogies into classroom teaching. The central questions are whether such analogies improve student understanding, what kinds of analogies teachers actually need, and how useful these analogies are when teachers can adapt them.

The intervention centers on GPT-4o-generated analogies for high school biology and physics concepts. In Study I, the authors ran a controlled in-class test in which one group of students used textbook explanations only, while another used textbook explanations plus LLM-generated analogies; outcomes included multiple-choice accuracy and self-confidence ratings, followed by student interviews. In Study II, the authors first interviewed teachers and senior students to identify requirements for classroom-useful analogies, then conducted a one-week classroom field study in which teachers used and modified generated analogies in one class while teaching another class as usual. Based on these findings, the authors also developed and evaluated a practical system to help teachers generate and refine analogies.

The study was conducted in a Chinese high school with first-year high school students, two teachers, and additional senior students consulted during interviews. Across the studies, the context was in-person school instruction in biology and physics classes. The classroom field study covered 12 lessons over one week, and the authors observed how teachers selected, refined, and used analogies, along with student feedback and homework-related performance impressions.

The main conclusions are that LLM-generated analogies can sometimes improve student understanding, particularly for biology concepts, but are unreliable for unsupervised student use because errors, omissions, and student over-reliance can undermine learning while increasing confidence. In classroom settings, teachers were able to refine and selectively use generated analogies in ways they found useful, reporting positive classroom feedback and perceived homework performance gains. Overall, the paper argues that LLM-generated analogies are more promising as teacher-facing supports for lesson preparation and guided classroom use than as standalone student self-learning tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study with a controlled in-class comparison and classroom field study in K-12, but it is not a literacy study, uses small samples from one Chinese high school, and reports limited causal design detail and no standardized effect sizes. Evidence is therefore stronger than opinion but below well-designed RCT/QED standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially beneficial but uneven effects: significant gains for some biology concept understanding and positive teacher-reported classroom use, alongside no clear physics benefit and risks of overconfidence or misunderstanding. Because impacts are mixed, domain-specific, and mostly lack effect sizes, overall impact is best classified as unclear/modest rather than clearly positive.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated analogy generation and teacher-facing refinement support for explaining high school biology and physics concepts in classroom instruction and student concept learning.

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies high-school students’ understanding of unfamiliar biology and physics concepts using LLM-generated analogies versus textbook explanation alone in a Chinese high school. In the controlled in-class test, biology accuracy showed a significant advantage for the analogy group (p=0.042), whereas no clear advantage appeared for physics; the authors also report mixed item-level patterns, including some lower performance when analogies omitted essential information or were incorrect. In the classroom field study, teachers reported positive classroom feedback and homework performance boosts when they refined and selectively used generated analogies, but these results were qualitative and no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice concept question accuracy; item-level accuracy differences; teacher-reported classroom feedback and homework performance in biology/physics concept learning
finding.study_size: n=49 enrolled, 44 valid test papers in Study I; 50 students across 2 classes in Study II field study

finding.finding_summary: Students using LLM-generated analogies reported significantly higher confidence overall and by subject, including physics and biology, despite weak alignment between confidence and actual correctness. The paper reports negligible correlations between accuracy and confidence (absolute Kendall's tau <= 0.2), and interviews suggested over-reliance and overconfidence, especially when analogies were vivid but incomplete or erroneous.
finding.measure: 5-point self-confidence ratings; interview-reported perceptions of helpfulness, over-reliance, and classroom feedback
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers; 8 post-test student interviews; 2 teacher interviews plus classroom observations in field study

finding.finding_summary: Teachers in the field study and system evaluation found that LLM-generated analogies could be refined to teacher satisfaction and used to inspire additional analogies and teaching approaches during lesson preparation. The paper's evidence here is qualitative: teachers selected, modified, and reused generated analogies, and the authors subsequently built a practical system to support analogy generation and refinement, but no time-saved metric or workload reduction effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness for lesson preparation, analogy refinement, and ideation during classroom planning
finding.study_size: 2 teachers in pre-class interview and field study; 6 teachers in system evaluation

paper_profiles.title: PARTNERING WITH AI: A PEDAGOGICAL FEEDBACK SYSTEM FOR LLM INTEGRATION INTO PROGRAMMING EDUCATION
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be used to provide pedagogically sound feedback in programming education, rather than simply generating generic automated hints. The authors argue that prior LLM feedback systems in programming often overlook established pedagogical principles such as adapting feedback to student mastery, task progress, and the nature of students’ help requests. Their research questions focus on how to design an LLM-based feedback system aligned with pedagogical theory and how such feedback compares with human teacher feedback.

To study this, the authors first conducted a preliminary interview with one secondary-school computer science teacher to identify useful adaptation criteria for feedback. They then developed a pedagogical framework that conditions LLM feedback on task description, student mastery, student attempt, and optional student text input. The framework was implemented in a web-based Python programming application using GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, with multiple specialized agents for error analysis, teacher-style feedback generation, and pedagogical validation. The system was evaluated using a mixed-methods design with semi-structured interviews and rating tasks.

The population consisted of eight secondary-school computer science teachers in Germany who had experience teaching Python across grades spanning roughly middle and high school. Teachers interacted with the system and evaluated pre-generated LLM feedback responses to synthetic student programming requests based on recursion tasks. The evaluation included both qualitative interview data and quantitative ratings of correctness, pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, effectiveness, comparison to teachers’ own feedback, and need for edits.

The main conclusions are that teachers generally viewed the LLM-generated feedback as pedagogically sound, understandable, and effective when it was structured according to the proposed framework. Teachers especially valued the speed and precision of LLMs for error detection and their potential to support both high- and low-performing students. At the same time, the study found important limitations: LLMs could not adapt well to dynamic classroom context, lacked interactive real-time awareness of student thinking, and could not use the visual and situational teaching strategies that human teachers employ. The authors conclude that LLMs are best understood as complements to, rather than replacements for, teachers in programming feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method qualitative study with small-sample teacher evaluations (n=8) using synthetic student scenarios rather than direct student outcome data. It provides useful practitioner evidence but lacks causal student-learning estimates and has limited external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impact, based mainly on teacher perceptions of pedagogical quality and efficiency rather than measured student effects. Positive signals exist, but no direct effect size on learner outcomes is reported.

interventions.use_case: LLM-driven pedagogical feedback generation for secondary-school Python programming tasks, using adaptive prompts and multi-agent validation to provide mastery- and progress-sensitive code feedback.
Conversational help interface embedded in a web-based programming practice tool where students request support and receive LLM-generated responses tailored to coding attempts and questions.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure student learning gains directly; instead, eight German secondary computer science teachers evaluated pre-generated LLM feedback on recursion tasks. Teachers rated responses as generally pedagogically sound (Mean=3.84, SD=1.10), comprehensive (Mean=4.04, SD=1.01), and effective for supporting learning (Mean=3.89, SD=1.14), but qualitative data emphasized important limits in contextual adaptation and classroom responsiveness.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, effectiveness, and qualitative interview judgments about support for programming learning
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers; 60 sampled requests/responses discussed from a mock dataset of 329
finding.std_deviation: Pedagogical soundness SD=1.10; comprehensiveness SD=1.01; effectiveness SD=1.14

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the LLM feedback system as more efficient than human teachers for routine error detection and timely support, especially for identifying small code errors quickly and providing parallel assistance in larger classes. Accuracy judgments were high, with 91.7% of evaluated responses rated correct and 8.3% partially correct, though these are perception-based rather than direct workflow productivity measurements.
finding.measure: Teacher judgments of correctness and qualitative perceptions of speed, precision, and ability to reduce teacher workload through instant feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM feedback systems can complement teachers and may help address class-size and support-all-students challenges, but teachers also stressed that these systems cannot replace human expertise because they lack situational awareness and alignment with classroom context. Findings therefore support augmentation rather than substitution at the classroom-system level.
finding.measure: Teacher interview perceptions about fit with classroom practice, scalability, and role of AI versus teachers

paper_profiles.title: Exposía: Academic Writing Assessment of Exposés and Peer Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Exposía, a public higher-education dataset designed to support research on academic writing assessment, peer feedback, and revision. The authors aim to address the lack of integrated resources that connect student drafts, peer and instructor feedback, revisions, and fine-grained human assessment scores. Rather than testing a literacy intervention, the paper focuses on documenting a dataset and benchmarking large language models for automated scoring of student writing and student reviews.

The approach centers on data collection from a real university course, "Introduction to Scientific Work," in which students wrote research project proposal drafts, received peer and instructor feedback, revised their work, and submitted final versions. The dataset includes draft and final exposés, inline comments, free-text reviews, and instructor-assigned rubric scores for both writing and feedback quality. The authors also evaluate several open-source LLMs on two tasks: criterion-based scoring of exposés and criterion-based scoring of student reviews.

The population consisted of undergraduate computer science students in a bachelor-level course, along with instructional staff who produced and scored feedback. The study took place in a single university setting in Germany, within topics related to computer science and AI. Of 193 enrolled students, 159 completed course requirements, and the released dataset includes materials from those who consented to public sharing, resulting in 55 exposés, 306 reviews, and 2,253 inline comments.

The main conclusions are that Exposía captures a novel draft-feedback-revision workflow useful for educational NLP research, that student exposés improved from draft to final version especially on content-related rubrics, and that LLMs can achieve relatively high agreement with human raters on scoring dimensions that require less domain expertise. However, the authors emphasize that performance degrades on more content-expert criteria and explicitly caution against using LLMs for fully automated grading, recommending human-in-the-loop decision support instead.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmarking and dataset paper in higher education, not a K-12 intervention study. It provides descriptive and comparative evidence with transparent methods and sample sizes, but no causal design, no K-12 population, and no externally validated learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful but unclear impact: writing products improved after feedback and LLM scoring may support efficiency, but no standardized achievement effects are reported and effects are limited to rubric-based higher-education outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automated scoring of undergraduate academic writing proposals and peer feedback reviews using fine-grained rubric criteria, intended as decision-support for assessment rather than tutoring.
Open-source LLMs are evaluated as writing-assessment tools for scoring proposal quality and review quality, especially on language/form versus content dimensions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that draft exposés improved from draft to final after receiving peer/instructor feedback, with the largest mean rubric gains in Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology. However, these are rubric-scored university academic-writing products rather than externally measured literacy gains, and no standardized reading or writing achievement outcomes are reported. For automated scoring, the strongest LLMs reached human-LLM agreement around QWA=0.75-0.76 on exposé scoring across 31 criteria, with weaker performance on content-heavy expert criteria.
finding.measure: Instructor rubric scores on draft and final academic writing proposals; human-LLM quadratic weighted agreement for criterion-based exposé scoring
finding.confidence_interval: Bootstrap 95% CIs shown for draft-final rubric score changes in Figure 3, numeric values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that feedback and revision support development of peer review and academic writing skills, and reports that final exposés improved particularly on conceptual/argumentative rubrics after feedback. Student reviews were also graded on 24 criteria tied to pedagogically grounded feedback quality dimensions, but outcomes are rubric-based and situated in higher education rather than direct K-12 durable-skill measures.
finding.measure: Instructor rubric scores for peer feedback quality and revised writing quality across criteria such as Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward, content quality, and errors

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions LLM-based scoring as a way to reduce assessment workload and shows that combined prompting is both more effective and more computationally efficient than scoring one criterion at a time. Stronger LLMs achieved human-LLM agreement near human-human agreement on less expertise-dependent criteria, supporting use as human-in-the-loop decision support, though the authors explicitly caution against fully automated grading.
finding.measure: Human-LLM agreement (QWA) for scoring accuracy and comparative computational efficiency of prompting strategies
finding.study_size: n=55 exposés; n=110 student reviews; 4 open-weight LLMs evaluated

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines how different configurations of generative AI assistance affect students’ writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing. Rather than asking whether AI helps in general, the paper focuses on where in the writing process AI intervenes—idea generation, sentence construction, both, or neither—and whether those different forms of support shape confidence, agency, and perceived writing ability differently.

The intervention used ChatGPT in a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design crossing AI support for idea generation and AI support for text construction. This created four conditions: No AI, Sentence AI, Ideation AI, and Full AI. Participants completed two 30-minute argumentative essay tasks in Korean during a 100-minute online session, with post-task self-efficacy surveys after each task. The study also reviewed participant reflections and ChatGPT interaction logs descriptively to contextualize the quantitative patterns.

The population consisted of 13 Korean undergraduate students, recruited voluntarily, after 8 of 21 initial recruits were excluded for non-attendance or procedural noncompliance. The study was conducted online via Google Meet in South Korea, using the free web version of ChatGPT. The primary measured outcome was writing self-efficacy, assessed on a 0–100 self-report scale covering writing ability, process management, and writing experience.

The main conclusion is that generative AI did not have uniform effects: outcomes depended strongly on the configuration of support. Full AI support produced the highest but largely stable self-efficacy, yet participants also reported diminished ownership and authenticity. Ideation-level AI showed the most promising pattern, combining high self-efficacy with positive change over time and preserved learner agency. Sentence-level AI showed a concerning pattern of universal self-efficacy decline across participants, suggesting that revision-focused support may undermine confidence when it functions as a comparative standard. The authors frame the study as preliminary and argue that future larger-scale, longitudinal research is needed to test whether these configuration-specific effects persist.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot experimental study with n=13 undergraduate participants, exploratory analyses, wide uncertainty, and no direct K-12 sample. It has clearer methodology than opinion pieces but does not meet strong causal evidence standards for the target K-12 question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on self-efficacy are suggestive and sometimes large in magnitude, but estimates are unstable, confidence intervals include zero, and literacy performance impacts are not directly measured. Overall impact is therefore unclear rather than clearly positive or null.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT configured as a writing assistant for undergraduate argumentative writing, with condition-specific support for ideation only, sentence-level drafting/revision, or full-process writing assistance.
Conversational use of ChatGPT through prompt-constrained dialogue to support brainstorming and/or text revision during essay writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This pilot experiment examined writing self-efficacy across four ChatGPT assistance configurations in 13 Korean undergraduates. Full AI support showed higher average self-efficacy than no AI (M=82.2 vs. 61.8; g=1.23, 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]) and higher than sentence-level AI (g=0.73), but confidence intervals spanned zero and authors emphasize the study was underpowered. Over time, ideation-only AI showed the largest within-person gain (ΔM=+11.1, SD=16.2), full AI was stable (ΔM=+0.5, SD=6.7), no AI changed little (ΔM=+1.3, SD=2.4), and sentence-level AI declined for all five participants (ΔM=-5.7, SD=5.6).
finding.measure: Post-task writing self-efficacy ratings on a 0-100 scale across writing ability, process management, and writing experience subdomains
finding.effect_size: g=1.23 (Full AI vs No AI); g=0.73 (Full AI vs Sentence AI); g=0.99 (Sentence AI vs No AI); g=0.31 (Ideation AI vs Sentence AI)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07] for Full AI vs No AI; other CIs not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Full AI SD=6.4; Ideation AI SD=16.1; Sentence AI SD=7.2; No AI SD=24.0; change-score SDs: 16.2, 6.7, 5.6, 2.4

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about AI-assisted argumentative writing, but it does not directly measure writing quality, revision quality, reading, vocabulary, or error reduction as literacy outcomes. Literacy-relevant evidence is indirect through self-efficacy items about grammar correction, vocabulary choice, coherence, evidence use, and writing to task; qualitative observations suggest ideation support preserved personal voice while full AI reduced ownership, but no rubric-scored product outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-perceived writing ability and qualitative reflections, not externally assessed literacy performance

finding.finding_summary: The study reports exploratory evidence relevant to learner agency and independent problem-solving rather than direct performance transfer. Participants in the ideation AI condition reported writing in their own language and showed positive self-efficacy trajectories, whereas full AI users reported reduced ownership and one no-AI participant who habitually used AI struggled to write independently when support was removed; however, no formal transfer task or post-removal performance measure was administered.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy items on independent resolution of writing difficulties and qualitative observations about ownership/agency

paper_profiles.title: Predicting the Quality of Revisions in Argumentative Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically predicting whether a student’s argumentative revision is successful or unsuccessful. The authors argue that revision quality depends on argumentative context: the same added sentence may improve one essay but weaken another depending on surrounding claims, evidence, and reasoning. Their research questions ask whether argumentative contexts help revision-quality prediction, which type of context is most useful, and whether ChatGPT prompts can generate these contexts effectively.

The approach combines annotated student revision data with large language model prompting. The authors define three kinds of argumentative context—claim, reasoning, and evidence—and use ChatGPT, including zero-shot Chain-of-Thought prompts, to extract or summarize those contexts from essays. These generated contexts are then paired with student revisions and fed into a DistilRoBERTa-based classifier to predict whether revisions are successful or unsuccessful. The study compares these context-based methods against prior location-based baselines that use nearby sentences around a revision.

The empirical data come from two corpora: 596 essays from grade 5–6 students responding to automated formative feedback in an Automated Writing Evaluation system, and an existing benchmark of 60 college students’ argumentative essays. The elementary students revised essays written for Response to Text Assessment prompts about the Millennium Villages Project or Space Exploration; the college corpus involved essays about technology proliferation revised after feedback. The paper reports 10-fold cross-validation results on annotated sentence-level revisions of evidence and reasoning.

The main conclusion is that argumentative contexts generated with ChatGPT improve prediction of revision quality over location-based baselines in both elementary and college corpora. In the elementary corpus, reasoning-context prompts were especially helpful, and Chain-of-Thought prompting generally outperformed single-pass prompting by small margins. The study does not evaluate student literacy gains from using generative AI directly; instead, it shows that generative AI can support automated assessment of revision quality within writing-feedback systems. The authors conclude that argumentative context is a promising direction for improving automated writing evaluation and feedback on student revisions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical modeling study on K-12 student writing data, but it does not test effects of the AI system on student literacy outcomes through an RCT or quasi-experiment. The evidence is primarily benchmark/classification performance on annotated essays, so it fits correlational/developmental evidence rather than causal impact evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports positive improvements in automated prediction accuracy for revision quality, but no direct effect sizes or demonstrated student outcome gains after using the system. Impact on learners is therefore promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted prediction of the quality of students’ argumentative writing revisions, intended to support automated writing evaluation and formative feedback on evidence and reasoning revisions in grade 5-6 essays.

Use of ChatGPT with single and chain-of-thought prompts to generate argumentative context summaries (claims, reasoning, evidence) that improve automated assessment of revision quality in student essays.

finding.finding_summary: On an elementary corpus of 596 students’ grade 5-6 argumentative essays, LLM-generated argumentative contexts improved prediction of successful vs. unsuccessful writing revisions over location-based baselines. For all reasoning and evidence revisions, the best model (AC-Reasoning with CoT prompts) reached macro F1=70.81 versus 68.06 for the strong baseline; for reasoning revisions F1=72.63 versus 69.71; for evidence revisions F1=67.16 versus 64.71. These are improvements in automated classification of revision quality rather than direct gains in students’ writing performance.
finding.measure: Macro precision, recall, and F1 for classifying revision quality in argumentative writing revisions
finding.study_size: n=596 elementary students; 3267 annotated elementary revisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that using ChatGPT-generated argumentative contexts can improve automated detection of revision quality compared with standard short- and long-context baselines, potentially making automated writing evaluation more informative for formative feedback workflows. However, no direct measures of teacher time savings, grading speed, or workflow efficiency were reported; the evidence is based on model-performance gains only.
finding.measure: Model performance improvement for automated revision-quality prediction as a proxy for improved feedback-system capability
finding.study_size: n=596 elementary students; 60 college students benchmarked secondarily

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines the opportunities, risks, and implementation challenges of large language models such as GPT-3 and ChatGPT in education. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, it synthesizes emerging examples from the literature and argues for a cautious but constructive approach to using generative AI in teaching and learning. The paper is concerned with how these systems may affect educational content creation, student support, assessment, feedback, and broader educational technology ecosystems.

The authors discuss potential educational uses of large language models for learners and teachers, including generating quizzes and reading-comprehension materials, supporting writing and language learning, providing explanations and adaptive feedback, assisting lesson planning, and helping with assessment. They also review selected prior studies and examples from the literature involving quiz generation, pedagogical agents, peer assessment, language learning chatbots, and automated feedback, but they do not present original intervention data of their own.

The paper addresses education broadly, mentioning primary, secondary, university, and professional-training contexts, but it does not study a defined participant sample or a specific implementation setting. Its perspective is conceptual and policy-oriented, emphasizing that successful adoption of large language models in education depends on human oversight, critical thinking, teacher and learner AI literacy, privacy and fairness protections, and careful pedagogical integration.

The main conclusion is that large language models have meaningful potential to enhance both learning and teaching, but that their use must be governed responsibly. The authors highlight risks including bias, overreliance, privacy concerns, plagiarism, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work, unequal access, and sustainability costs. They recommend ongoing human monitoring, educator training, critical evaluation of model outputs, and stronger governance frameworks before large-scale educational integration.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and examples of large language models in education rather than reporting an original K-12 empirical study with a clear sample, intervention implementation, comparator, or outcome evaluation. It therefore does not meet criteria for direct empirical evidence and is best classified as non-empirical/opinion-oriented background literature.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses potentially important educational impacts of LLMs but does not provide direct causal effect estimates or original outcome data. Its practical influence may be conceptual or agenda-setting, but empirical impact is unclear from this source alone.

paper_profiles.title: Ethical use of ChatGPT in education—Best practices to combat AI-induced plagiarism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT create new risks for academic integrity, especially plagiarism, while also offering possible educational benefits. The central question is how educators and institutions can respond to AI-enabled misconduct without losing the instructional opportunities of these tools. The article is framed as an opinion or position piece rather than an empirical study.

The paper proposes a set of institutional, pedagogical, technological, and assessment-design strategies to reduce AI-induced plagiarism. These include clearer AI-use policies, plagiarism and AI-detection tools, adaptive testing, reflective writing, peer review, oral examinations, multimodal assessments, portfolio work, personalized assignments, and breaking large tasks into staged submissions. The author also emphasizes awareness campaigns and explicit instruction in ethical AI use.

The discussion is situated broadly in education, but the article does not report a specific participant sample, site, intervention implementation, or grade-bounded study context. It refers generally to students, educators, and institutions, with many examples oriented toward universities and academic settings rather than a direct K-12 literacy intervention. No direct experimental or observational data are presented.

The paper concludes that effective responses to AI misuse require a multi-faceted approach combining technology-based detection, curriculum and assessment redesign, and education for ethical AI use. It argues that institutions should continually adapt policies and teaching practices as generative AI evolves, and that human oversight remains essential. Because the article is a non-empirical opinion piece, it does not provide direct evidence on learning outcomes or intervention effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is explicitly labeled an opinion article and does not present original empirical methods, sample, comparator, or analyzed outcome data. Although peer-reviewed, it does not meet the framework's standards for empirical causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article suggests potentially important institutional implications, but impact is unclear because no direct effect estimates or original outcome evidence are reported. It should not be treated as direct evidence of effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: Opinion paper discussing ethical use of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools in education, focused on plagiarism prevention, assessment redesign, AI-detection tools, and institutional policy rather than evaluation of a learning intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This is a non-empirical opinion article arguing that generative AI creates institutional risks around plagiarism, policy, privacy, and assessment integrity, while also offering potential benefits for engagement and personalized learning. The paper cites prior literature and proposes strategies such as AI-use policies, oral exams, adaptive testing, and AI-detection tools, but reports no original sample, no direct outcome data, and no effect sizes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI tools may improve efficiency through personalized feedback, adaptive testing, and streamlined assessment processes, but also notes implementation burdens such as cost, false positives, privacy compliance, and increased teacher workload for monitoring and oral assessment. These claims are conceptual only and are not supported by original empirical measurements in this article.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a technical report on GPT-4, a large multimodal generative AI model developed by OpenAI. The report focuses on describing the model’s capabilities, predictable scaling behavior, benchmark performance, and safety properties. It is not an education study and does not investigate a K-12 literacy intervention, classroom implementation, or learner outcomes in schools. Instead, it documents model development and evaluation across professional exams, NLP benchmarks, multilingual tasks, and safety testing.

The approach studied is the creation and evaluation of GPT-4 as a Transformer-based model trained with large-scale pretraining and post-training alignment using reinforcement learning from human feedback. The report summarizes benchmark results on exams such as the bar exam, LSAT, SAT, GRE, AP exams, coding tasks, and standard NLP datasets, alongside discussion of multilingual performance and visual input capabilities. It also describes safety mitigations including expert red teaming, refusal tuning, and rule-based reward models.

No human participant sample is reported in the sense required for an educational intervention study. Although human labelers, domain experts, and benchmark test populations are referenced, the paper does not present a direct empirical study of students, teachers, or schools using GPT-4 for literacy instruction. There is therefore no K-12 population, implementation setting, dosage, comparator classroom condition, or instructional protocol that can be extracted as direct evidence for school-based literacy outcomes.

The main conclusions are that GPT-4 demonstrates strong performance on a wide range of benchmarks, shows predictable scaling from smaller models, improves over prior OpenAI models on many tasks, and has safety improvements alongside ongoing limitations such as hallucinations, calibration problems after post-training, and persistent misuse risks. For the user’s review purpose, this paper is not strong enough to include as direct evidence on K-12 literacy effects of generative AI, because it is a general model technical report rather than a direct education efficacy study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical report on GPT-4 model development, benchmarking, and safety rather than an education study. It does not report a K-12 literacy intervention, learner sample, classroom implementation, or causal/observational study design relevant to educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report shows strong general language-model capability on benchmarks, but it provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 literacy learners or classrooms. As such, educational impact is unclear and should not be treated as direct evidence for the review thesis.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid emergence of generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT. The author argues that effective educational integration of AI depends on three core capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than testing a specific K-12 literacy intervention, the paper is a conceptual discussion focused on the challenges and opportunities of AI adoption in education, especially around academic writing, classroom use, and institutional policy.

The paper uses a two-part approach: an institution-based case study at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, combined with a narrative literature review. The case study draws on the author's teaching experience, participation in the university's AI taskforce, and informal, unstructured discussions with students and staff. A central institutional intervention described is the development of internal AI guidelines that permit but regulate student use of generative AI in written work, requiring transparency about which tools were used, why they were used, how outputs were critically evaluated, and where AI contributed to the manuscript. The paper also discusses possible classroom uses of AI, including experiments with chatbots, AI-supported case study generation, curriculum support tools, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The population and context are primarily higher education, not K-12. Participants are not formally sampled or quantified, but the text refers to students, lecturers, supervisors, and university leadership at a single Swiss university of applied sciences. The setting is mainly classroom and institutional practice in a higher-education environment, with the author explicitly noting that the discussion is focused on higher education, even if some ideas may also be relevant to children.

The main conclusion is that simply allowing or banning AI is insufficient. Institutions should cultivate an 'AI culture' through explicit guidance, workshops, AI literacy instruction, and deliberate teaching of prompt engineering and critical evaluation. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires not just access to tools but also educator support, institutional resources, and sustained attention to ethical and pedagogical issues. It does not provide direct experimental evidence on student literacy outcomes and is not a direct K-12 generative AI literacy effectiveness study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review focused on higher education, not an empirical K-12 evaluation. It does not report a defined K-12 sample, intervention implementation study, comparator, validated outcome measurement, or causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article makes broad claims about potential relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking, but provides no direct empirical effect estimates. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive the use of generative AI for creative mathematical writing in real classroom settings. The central problem is that creative mathematical writing may help students express mathematical ideas imaginatively, but many elementary learners struggle to generate stories, connect them to mathematical concepts, and sustain engagement. The authors argue that generative AI may provide useful scaffolding, but its classroom value depends on how students and teachers actually experience it in practice.

The intervention was a GenAI-powered learning technology developed by the research team, using GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to support a three-step instructional process: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed a math story, then visually represented mathematical ideas, and finally used GenAI to help draft and revise their own culturally relevant math stories tied to equations or mathematical goals. The system generated story drafts and images based on structured student prompts, and students evaluated the generated stories using a checklist.

The study took place in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools and involved 79 students and six teachers. Data collection was qualitative: semi-structured focus group interviews with 10 students, individual interviews with all six teachers, open-ended student surveys, and classroom observations. The analysis used thematic analysis with triangulation across these sources. The setting was classroom-based mathematics instruction, with sessions ranging from four class periods in one school to eight sessions in another.

The main conclusions are that students and teachers perceived several benefits of GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing, including support for creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, they identified important challenges: students sometimes lacked skill in critically evaluating AI output, the AI could feel "too perfect," the system did not provide sufficient pedagogical feedback, and it limited autonomy, peer interaction, and accessibility features such as speech-to-text. Overall, the paper offers design implications for classroom GenAI tools but does not provide causal evidence of literacy or academic effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom implementation study with clear methods, multiple data sources, and triangulation, but no control group, randomization, or quantitative outcome testing. It meets limited credibility criteria and is best classified as yellow-tier evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but perception-based benefits with no effect sizes or objective pre/post achievement estimates. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrably positive at a quantified level.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4- and DALL·E-3-powered classroom tool supporting 5th-grade students in creative mathematical story writing by generating draft math stories and images from student prompts, then allowing students to review and revise them.
Generative text support for drafting and refining student-authored math stories, including prompt-based story generation and revision support within a writing task.

finding.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews, surveys, and observations from 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, participants reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing improved problem understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and helped uncover misconceptions. Findings are perception-based rather than causal estimates; no standardized math achievement gains, inferential tests, or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions from semi-structured interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations about mathematical understanding during fraction story-writing activities
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers; interview subset of 10 students

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported activity increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning during elementary math instruction. Evidence comes from qualitative thematic analysis across 79 students and 6 teachers, but no validated motivation scales or statistical estimates were provided.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers; interview subset of 10 students

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the tool supported creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses, suggesting gains in AI literacy and critical/creative thinking. At the same time, students and teachers also identified barriers including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent prompts, and reduced autonomy/social interaction, indicating mixed durable-skill implications.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of creativity, flexible thinking, AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation skills
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers; interview subset of 10 students

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of fine-grained error analysis for K-12 English writing and asks how well large language models can identify, classify, rate the severity of, and explain specific writing errors made by school-age learners. The authors argue that existing work in automated essay scoring and grammatical error correction does not provide sufficiently interpretable, pedagogically useful feedback at the level of individual learner errors. To support more rigorous evaluation, they introduce FEANEL, a benchmark focused on fine-grained error analysis for English learners.

The core contribution is a benchmark dataset and evaluation framework rather than a classroom intervention. FEANEL contains 1,000 student essays annotated by English education experts, including corrected versions, extracted edits, error types, severity ratings, and explanatory feedback. The authors also develop a 29-category error taxonomy and test a range of state-of-the-art large language models under zero-shot and one-shot prompting conditions to assess performance on three subtasks: error classification, severity rating, and explanation generation.

The population consists of K-12 learners writing English essays. The benchmark includes 500 essays from elementary students aged 9-11 collected through a global online education platform with primarily non-native speakers from around the world, and 500 essays representing secondary-level Chinese EFL learners aged roughly 12-18 drawn from the TECCL corpus. Annotation was performed by experienced English education experts, and additional English teachers not involved in dataset construction were used for a human comparison subset.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs show some promise but still fall well short of human teachers on this fine-grained educational feedback task. Model performance improves when prompts include richer instructions and examples, and some reasoning-oriented models perform better on classification, but all systems struggle with complex, compound errors and with generating pedagogically nuanced explanations. Overall, the paper concludes that fine-grained educational feedback remains a challenging area for LLMs and that FEANEL provides a useful benchmark for future research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/model-evaluation paper, not a direct K-12 intervention study measuring learner outcomes against a comparator. It is useful technical evidence about AI feedback quality, but it does not provide causal educational evidence for student impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear practical impact for K-12 learners: models exhibit some capability and improve with prompting, but overall results reveal substantial gaps from human performance and no direct student outcome effects are estimated.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking large language models for fine-grained analysis of K-12 English writing errors, including error classification, severity rating, and explanatory feedback on student essays.
LLMs are used as language-analysis tools to detect and explain grammatical and lexical errors in English learner writing rather than as interactive tutors.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on a benchmark of 8,676 annotated writing errors from 1,000 K-12 English essays rather than student learning gains. Results show substantial performance gaps versus human teachers in fine-grained writing-error analysis: average zero-shot classification accuracy across models was 63.13% and average one-shot accuracy was 66.85%, while human performance on a subset reached 79.90%; explanation quality metrics were also well below human levels. These findings indicate current LLM-based feedback tools are not yet reliably accurate enough for high-stakes K-12 writing support without further improvement.
finding.measure: LLM benchmark performance on K-12 writing error analysis: classification accuracy, macro-F1, mean absolute error for severity, BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE for explanations
finding.study_size: 1,000 essays; 8,676 annotated errors; human comparison on 500 elementary + 500 secondary errors

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark suggests LLMs have emerging utility for automating aspects of writing feedback, but current performance remains inconsistent and prompt-sensitive. More detailed prompting improved average classification accuracy from 63.13% to 66.85% and explanation metrics also increased, yet the models still lagged human teachers and struggled with rare and compound errors, limiting dependable efficiency gains in classroom deployment.
finding.measure: Automated feedback performance under different prompting conditions as a proxy for feasibility/efficiency of AI-assisted error analysis

paper_profiles.title: SingaKids: A Multilingual Multimodal Dialogic Tutor for Language Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design a child-friendly generative-AI tutoring system for early language learning that works robustly across multiple languages and cultural contexts. The authors argue that although large language models and multimodal systems offer strong potential for personalized language support, they often perform unevenly across languages, are not optimized for children’s speech and interaction patterns, and require age-appropriate scaffolding to support motivation and learning.

The intervention is SingaKids, a multilingual multimodal dialogic tutor for picture-description-based language learning. The system combines dense image captioning, multilingual LLM-based dialogue, automatic speech recognition, and text-to-speech generation in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil. It was optimized through multilingual pretraining, instruction tuning, scaffolding-guided augmentation, and improvements to speech components for lower-resource languages and children’s voices. The tutor is designed to provide guided questioning, hints, explanations, feedback, and social-emotional support while children describe images orally.
