The empirical study involved 35 first- and second-grade elementary students in Singapore with varying language proficiency levels. Students used the system with parental consent and guidance. The paper reports an utterance-level analysis of scaffold types delivered to higher- and lower-performing learners and describes observational findings from real-world use, including challenges with noisy environments, speech recognition errors, learner frustration, and attention management when images were visually complex.

The main conclusion is that SingaKids shows promise as an effective multilingual dialogic tutor for elementary language acquisition, particularly by adapting scaffolding to learner performance and supporting descriptive language, vocabulary, and conversational fluency. However, the evidence remains preliminary: the study appears to be a small-sample deployment without a control group, with limited reporting on duration, implementation fidelity, and long-term learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preliminary arXiv study with a small user study (n=35) and no clear experimental comparator, randomization, or fully reported causal outcome analyses. It provides some direct K-12 empirical evidence but only limited credibility criteria are met.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially beneficial effects on young learners' oral language practice and support for lower-performing students, but impact magnitude is unclear because no standardized outcome estimates or effect sizes are reported.

interventions.use_case: Multilingual multimodal dialogic tutor for grade 1-2 students practicing oral picture description, using an LLM to provide scaffolded questions, hints, explanations, feedback, and social-emotional support in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

AI-supported language-learning tool integrating child speech recognition, speech generation, and language evaluation to support oral vocabulary, sentence production, and conversational practice during picture-description tasks.

finding.finding_summary: A preliminary user study with 35 grade 1-2 students reported that learners improved in descriptive language skills, vocabulary usage, and conversational fluency after interacting with SingaKids during picture-description tasks. However, the paper does not report pre/post test statistics, exact effect sizes, standard deviations, or confidence intervals, so the magnitude of improvement cannot be quantified from the available text.
finding.measure: Descriptive language skills, vocabulary usage, conversational fluency during picture-description interactions

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the system provided dynamic scaffolding and social-emotional support, with lower-performing students receiving more social-emotional support than higher-performing students (31% vs. 17% of scaffolding moves) and more hints (12% vs. 5%). The paper suggests these supports helped maintain confidence and engagement, but it does not include validated motivation or engagement scale results or inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Utterance-level distribution of scaffolding types, especially social-emotional support and hints, across student performance groups

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI can be integrated into secondary school instruction when teachers act as co-design partners rather than passive adopters. The core questions are how teachers design and implement AI-assisted tools in regular classrooms, how teacher judgment and AI competency shape student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes, and what support conditions enable effective classroom use. The study is framed as an early-stage classroom pilot of AI as a "third agent" that can support inquiry, formative feedback, and instructional decision-making while teachers retain authority.

The intervention was the Colleague AI Classroom platform, which included four features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment with AI Feedback/Grading, AI Tutor for student help-seeking, and Student Growth Insights for summarizing student interaction patterns. Over a seven-week professional learning and implementation arc, teachers attended weekly meetings, planned AI-integrated lessons, implemented activities in live classes, and provided reflections through surveys, forms, interviews, meetings, and platform logs. The design combined qualitative feedback with quantitative descriptive usage and survey data.

Participants were 21 in-service teachers and more than 600 students in grades 6-12 across four Washington State public school districts and one independent school. The contexts were regular synchronous classrooms spanning math, science, ELA, social studies, and other subjects. Teachers designed the activities and students used the platform during class, with participation voluntary and non-AI parallel versions available. The study therefore reflects teacher-mediated classroom integration rather than student-directed independent use.

The main conclusions are that generative AI showed promise when tightly scaffolded by teachers, aligned to instructional goals, and used primarily for formative purposes. Teachers reported that AI could support student inquiry, personalized feedback, revision, and instructional adjustments, but effectiveness depended heavily on teacher framing, prior AI experience, interface usability, and subject/grade-level fit. The report emphasizes that AI worked best as a teaching partner rather than a replacement, with teachers retaining evaluative authority and mediating trust, interpretation, and personalization. The findings are explicitly exploratory and limited by geography, self-report, lack of direct observation, and use of a single platform.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory co-design pilot using teacher surveys, reflections, interviews, and platform logs, with no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison and no direct validated student outcome analysis. It provides useful implementation evidence but only limited causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: teacher-reported benefits for engagement, inquiry, and efficiency are positive, but effects are descriptive, mixed across contexts, and not supported by causal effect sizes or standardized achievement outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-mediated classroom use of a generative AI platform ('Teaching Aide' and 'AI Tutor') to support student inquiry, discussion, brainstorming, and guided academic help in grades 6-12 across subjects.
AI-assisted rubric generation, automated grading, and narrative formative feedback on student work, with teachers reviewing and retaining final grading authority.
Student Growth Insights aggregates patterns from student-AI interactions to surface misconceptions, common questions, and progress indicators for teachers' instructional adjustments.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot reported strong descriptive evidence that the platform reduced teacher workload in feedback and monitoring workflows. Across 58 assessments in 33 classrooms, median AI grading coverage was 92.2%, suggesting high automation of first-pass scoring/feedback, and teachers reported faster turnaround for personalized feedback and lower oversight burden via conversation summaries and Student Growth Insights. No causal estimate or standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Platform usage logs (AI grading coverage, submission/resubmission rates), teacher survey/reflection reports on feedback turnaround and monitoring burden
finding.study_size: 21 teachers; >600 students overall; 58 assessments across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions
finding.std_deviation: Submission rate SD=27.9%; other SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported improved student engagement with AI-supported classroom conversations when activities were well scaffolded: 28% of implementations were rated as showing thoughtful engagement, 66% mixed engagement, and 6% limited engagement. Teachers also described increased confidence and lower-pressure participation for some students, especially multilingual learners, but these findings are perception-based and varied substantially by subject, grade band, and implementation quality.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported engagement ratings and qualitative reflections on confidence/participation
finding.study_size: 18 teachers reporting on Teaching Aide implementations; up to 600 students in 21 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests AI-supported conversations and feedback may promote inquiry, revision, self-improvement behavior, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers provide strong framing, but outcomes were inconsistent across contexts. For Teaching Aide, 35% of teacher-reported sessions said the tool helped most students learn, 62% said some students learned, and 3% said none benefited; however, these are descriptive teacher judgments rather than direct performance measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported learning benefit, observations of revision behavior, inquiry depth, and reasoning during AI-supported tasks
finding.study_size: 18 teachers for Teaching Aide learning reports; >600 students overall

finding.finding_summary: ELA-related results were described as promising but uneven. High school English teachers reportedly used AI for prewriting and brainstorming that improved essay quality, and some students used AI feedback to revise writing, but the report provides no direct literacy test scores, writing rubric gains, or effect sizes, and notes weaker ELA engagement patterns than in some other subjects.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on writing quality, brainstorming/prewriting support, and AI-assisted revision
finding.study_size: ELA teachers/classes included within 21 teachers and >600 students overall; exact ELA n not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Truly Perform Multimodal In-Context Learning?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) truly perform multimodal in-context learning, or whether their apparent few-shot adaptation is driven mainly by text rather than by both text and images. The authors study two core questions: how demonstration content in different modalities affects in-context learning performance, and how demonstrations should be selected to improve performance on multimodal tasks.

To address these questions, the paper evaluates several existing MLLMs, including OpenFlamingo and IDEFICS, on visual question answering, visual reasoning, and image captioning benchmarks. The authors manipulate the content of in-context demonstrations by removing or corrupting images and text, and compare different demonstration-selection strategies. Based on these analyses, they propose a new retrieval strategy called Mixed Modality In-Context Example Selection (MMICES), which first filters candidate demonstrations using visual similarity and then reranks them using textual similarity.

The study is not an education study and does not involve human learners, teachers, or K-12 settings. Instead, the population consists of AI models evaluated on benchmark datasets such as VQAv2, OK-VQA, GQA, and MSCOCO. The work is conducted as a machine learning benchmarking and method-analysis paper rather than an intervention study with participants.

The main conclusion is that current MLLMs' in-context learning performance is driven predominantly by textual information in demonstrations, while visual content in the demonstrations contributes little directly to task performance. However, visual information remains useful for selecting better demonstrations. The proposed MMICES method improves performance over random selection and image-only retrieval across multiple models and tasks, suggesting that mixed-modality example selection is more effective than relying on a single modality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a computer vision / multimodal in-context learning methods paper, not a K-12 education intervention study. It reports benchmark results on vision-language datasets rather than learner outcomes, and provides no educational sample, classroom implementation, or causal evidence relevant to the requested K-12 literacy review.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows technical performance improvements for multimodal example selection in AI benchmarks, but there is no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learners, teachers, or literacy outcomes. Educational impact is therefore unclear and not usable as direct evidence for the review.

paper_profiles.title: Prompting in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Prompt Evolution in Software Repositories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how developers manage and evolve prompts embedded in real-world large-language-model-integrated software systems. The core research problem is that prompts have become a new kind of software artifact, but little is known about how they change over time, how those changes relate to code maintenance, how well they are documented, and whether prompt edits actually produce intended changes in model behavior.

The authors conduct an empirical observational study of prompt evolution in open-source software repositories. Starting from the PromptSet dataset, they clean and filter prompts, then analyze 1,262 unique prompt changes across 243 GitHub repositories. Their approach combines qualitative coding of prompt change types and components with quantitative analysis of commit histories, documentation practices, and limited manual evaluation of prompt impact on LLM responses. They classify prompt changes such as additions, modifications, removals, rephrasing, formatting, and restructuring, and examine how these changes align with software maintenance activities like feature development, bug fixing, and refactoring.

The population and context are not educational participants but open-source software repositories and software developers working on LLM-integrated applications, primarily in Python projects hosted on GitHub. There is no K-12, literacy, classroom, or student-focused intervention in this paper. Instead, the context is software engineering practice in public repositories, with analysis centered on developer-written prompts and commit histories.

The main conclusions are that prompt evolution is common and is driven mostly by additions and modifications, especially during feature development. Documentation of prompt changes is poor, with only 21.9% of prompt-changing commits explicitly mentioning prompt changes. Prompt modifications can introduce logical inconsistencies, and intended prompt changes do not always lead to expected LLM response changes. The authors argue that LLM-integrated software development needs better documentation practices, validation tools, and testing frameworks for prompts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is an empirical software engineering study of prompt evolution in GitHub repositories, not a K-12 education intervention study. It provides no direct learner-level educational evaluation, no school-based sample, and no literacy outcome design relevant to the requested review question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports descriptive findings about developer prompt-maintenance practices and LLM-integrated software reliability, but it does not estimate educational effects on students, teachers, or literacy outcomes. Any relevance to education is indirect and insufficient for impact claims in the K-12 evidence framework.

paper_profiles.title: SYSMOBENCH: Evaluating AI on Formally Modeling Complex Real-World Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces SYSMOBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating whether generative AI systems, especially large language models and agents, can produce formal models of complex real-world software systems. The core problem the authors address is that formal system models are valuable for verification and testing but are expensive and difficult for humans to create, and it remains unclear whether modern AI can generate such models for realistic concurrent and distributed systems rather than only small code snippets or function-level specifications.

The approach is the creation of a benchmark centered on TLA+ system modeling tasks derived from real-world artifacts such as Etcd Raft, Redis Raft, ZooKeeper leader election, and synchronization/data-structure components from the Asterinas operating system. SYSMOBENCH evaluates AI-generated models using automated metrics for syntax correctness, runtime correctness, conformance to system implementations via trace validation, and invariant correctness through model checking. The paper also reports baseline evaluations using several agents and LLMs, including Claude-Sonnet-4, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1.

The paper is not an education study and does not involve K-12 or other learner populations. Its empirical context is software engineering and formal methods research, with benchmark tasks based on open-source system artifacts rather than human participants in instructional settings. The only human-related context described concerns benchmark developers adding tasks and inspecting some LLM-assisted mappings, not study participants.

The main conclusions are that current generative AI systems can sometimes generate high-quality formal models for relatively small and simple systems, such as a spinlock, but perform poorly on larger and more complex systems such as Etcd Raft. The authors conclude that contemporary LLMs remain limited in comprehending, abstracting, and specifying large complex systems, though benchmarks like SYSMOBENCH can help drive future progress in AI-assisted formal modeling.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a computer systems/AI benchmark paper about generating formal models of distributed and concurrent software systems, not an education study. It contains no K-12 learners, no literacy intervention, and no education-relevant empirical design for the target review question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct evidence on K-12 literacy, language, motivation, or classroom outcomes. Any reported results concern benchmark performance of AI systems on formal specification tasks, so the paper cannot materially inform the educational review thesis.

paper_profiles.title: AAAR-1.0: Assessing AI’s Potential to Assist Research
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AAAR-1.0, a benchmark for evaluating how well large language models can assist researchers with high-expertise research tasks. The motivating question is not about K-12 learning or literacy outcomes, but about whether AI systems can support researchers in tasks such as inferring equation correctness, designing experiments, identifying paper weaknesses, and critiquing peer reviews. The authors argue that existing evaluations of LLMs in research assistance are either too subjective or focus on broader autonomous workflows rather than well-specified research subskills.

The approach is the construction and evaluation of a benchmark dataset spanning four tasks: EQUATIONINFERENCE, EXPERIMENTDESIGN, PAPERWEAKNESS, and REVIEWCRITIQUE. The dataset is built using accepted AI papers from sources such as ACL Anthology, arXiv, and OpenReview, with substantial expert involvement in annotation and review. The study then evaluates a range of open-source and closed-source LLMs using task-specific metrics, including F1 for classification tasks and custom semantic or entailment-based measures for generative tasks.

The empirical human population involved in the paper is senior AI researchers or advanced PhD students who served as annotators and reviewers for benchmark construction and validation. The paper does not study K-12 students, teachers, classrooms, or literacy instruction. Instead, its context is AI research workflows and scientific-document evaluation. The setting is effectively online or computational, using paper repositories and model evaluation pipelines.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs show some promise for assisting researchers but remain limited on expertise-intensive tasks. Performance is often only modestly above simple baselines, and generated outputs can be vague, insufficiently specific, or poorly aligned with expert reasoning. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful as support tools for researchers, especially junior researchers, but are not yet reliable substitutes for expert scientific judgment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is an AI benchmark/methods paper about LLM assistance for research tasks, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It does not evaluate learning outcomes for students, and thus does not provide direct education evidence under the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student, teacher, or school intervention impact is estimated. Reported results concern benchmark performance of LLMs on research-assistance tasks, so there is no direct educational impact to map.

paper_profiles.title: THINKING LIKE AN EXPERT: MULTIMODAL HYPERGRAPH-OF-THOUGHT (HOT) REASONING TO BOOST FOUNDATION MODALS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to improve the reasoning ability of foundation models beyond standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. The authors argue that CoT is limited because it is linear and better suited to ordinary step-by-step reasoning, whereas expert reasoning often involves higher-order multi-hop inference and multimodal comparative judgment. The paper therefore asks whether a new reasoning paradigm, Hypergraph-of-Thought (HoT), can better model expert-like reasoning for complex multimodal tasks.

The proposed approach constructs both a textual and a visual hypergraph-of-thought. In the textual component, triplets are treated as basic thoughts and linked through multi-hop random walks to form hyperedges that capture higher-order relations. In the visual component, image patches are clustered into hyperedges. These textual and visual hypergraphs are encoded with an AllSet Transformer, and then connected through a cross-modal co-attention graph to support multimodal interaction. The full system is implemented in a two-stage reasoning framework for rationale generation and answer generation, evaluated on the ScienceQA benchmark.

The study is not an education intervention with human learners or teachers; instead, it is a machine learning benchmark study using the ScienceQA dataset, which contains science questions spanning grade bands including grades 1-6 and 7-12. No human participant sample, school implementation, or classroom deployment is reported. The context is model development and offline evaluation on an existing dataset rather than instruction in a real educational setting.

The main conclusion is that the HoT-enhanced T5 models outperform several baseline VQA and CoT-based models, including CoT-based GPT-3.5 and ChatGPT, and approach GPT-4-level performance on ScienceQA with a smaller model. The authors conclude that multimodal hypergraph reasoning can strengthen high-order multi-hop reasoning and multimodal comparative judgment, though they also note that the current method still has room for improvement and should be seen as opening a new paradigm for future multimodal foundation models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv preprint on multimodal reasoning for foundation models evaluated on the ScienceQA benchmark, not a direct K-12 educational intervention study. It does not study learners, classrooms, literacy instruction, or educational implementation, so it does not meet the evidence criteria for inclusion as direct K-12 evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports benchmark performance gains on science question answering, but these are model-level results rather than measured student impacts. Any educational relevance is indirect and unclear, so impact on K-12 learning outcomes cannot be established.

paper_profiles.title: Revisiting Entropy in Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates entropy collapse during reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large language models. The authors study how model entropy changes during training, how those changes relate to response diversity, calibration, and benchmark performance, and what factors contribute to entropy collapse. The work is motivated by the concern that RLVR can push models toward premature convergence and reduced exploration, potentially limiting reasoning performance.

The paper studies RLVR training of large reasoning models, primarily Qwen2.5-Math-7B trained with GRPO on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset, and evaluates variants such as adaptive entropy regularization, clipping modifications, and a proposed method called Positive-Advantage Reweighting. The authors combine theoretical analysis with extensive computational experiments to argue that tokens with positive advantages are the main drivers of entropy collapse. Based on this, they introduce Positive-Advantage Reweighting, which dynamically adjusts loss weights for positive-advantage tokens to regulate entropy while maintaining competitive performance.

There is no K-12, literacy, classroom, teacher, or student population in this study. The context is machine learning experimentation on benchmark datasets in mathematical reasoning, coding, and instruction following, rather than an educational intervention. Experiments are conducted in an AI training/evaluation setting using benchmark tasks such as AIME, MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and IF-Eval.

The main conclusions are that entropy is strongly associated with response diversity and model calibration, but is not a consistent proxy for task performance across benchmarks. The authors identify clipping thresholds, off-policy updates, and training data diversity as key factors shaping entropy dynamics. They conclude that Positive-Advantage Reweighting can mitigate entropy collapse and preserve strong benchmark performance, though evidence is limited to mathematical-domain RLVR experiments rather than broader application domains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a machine learning methods paper on reinforcement learning for large language models, not a K-12 education intervention study. It contains no student sample, no educational implementation, no direct literacy instruction context, and no credible causal or observational design relevant to schooling outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports benchmark performance changes for math/coding/instruction-following LLMs, not learner outcomes in K-12 literacy. Therefore it provides no direct evidence of educational impact for the review thesis.

paper_profiles.title: Rethinking Easy-to-Hard: Limits of Curriculum Learning in Post-Training for Deductive Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether curriculum learning—especially easy-to-hard ordering of training examples—improves large language model post-training for deductive reasoning. The authors note that curriculum learning is widely used and intuitively appealing for compositional reasoning tasks, where harder problems are built from simpler inference steps, but that its actual value in LLM post-training has not been systematically established.

To study this question, the paper compares several curriculum schedules against standard random sampling during post-training. The experiments use synthetic arithmetic and logical reasoning datasets with explicitly defined structural difficulty, allowing the authors to test whether ordering examples by difficulty affects out-of-distribution generalization to harder problems. They evaluate both supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards across multiple medium-sized open-weight language models.

The study does not involve human learners, teachers, or K-12 educational settings. Instead, the "population" is a set of language models trained and evaluated on synthetic benchmarks including MathGAP arithmetic tasks and knights-and-knaves logic problems. The work is conducted in a computational/online experimental setting rather than a classroom or school context.

The main conclusion is that curriculum learning provides no robust or consistent advantage over standard random sampling for deductive reasoning post-training under a fixed training budget. Across datasets, model families, and training methods, the ordering of examples had little effect on accuracy or response length. The authors further report that reinforcement learning generally improved out-of-distribution performance more reliably than supervised fine-tuning, while supervised fine-tuning could sometimes underperform even zero-shot baselines. Overall, the paper argues that example sequencing is less important than feedback mechanisms and training data structure for compositional reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is an AI/ML methods study on curriculum learning for post-training large language models on synthetic deductive reasoning benchmarks, not a K-12 education intervention study. It provides no school-based sample, no learner population, and no direct educational evaluation relevant to K-12 literacy evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports no direct K-12 educational outcomes and therefore cannot contribute evidence on literacy or related student impacts. Its main empirical conclusion is also null within its own technical context: curriculum-based sequencing showed no robust advantage over standard sampling.

paper_profiles.title: LLM-REVal: Can We Trust LLM Reviewers Yet?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be trusted as reviewers in academic peer review, especially when LLMs are also increasingly used to help generate or polish research papers. The core question is whether deep integration of LLMs into both research production and manuscript evaluation creates systematic fairness risks. Rather than studying education or K-12 literacy, the paper focuses on scholarly publishing and simulated conference peer review.

The authors build a multi-round simulation called LLM-REVal consisting of a research agent and a review agent. The research agent generates LLM-authored papers from topic keywords and revises rejected papers based on review feedback; the review agent simulates reviewer assessment, rebuttal, reassessment, meta-review, and final decisions. Human-authored ICLR papers and LLM-authored papers are compared, and rejected papers are iteratively revised and resubmitted. The study also includes human annotation to compare LLM review judgments with human judgments and analyzes possible sources of bias such as linguistic style preferences and aversion to critical framing.

The context is academic machine learning research, using public ICLR submissions and simulated reviewing with models such as DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, Qwen3, and Gemini-2.5. There are no K-12 learners, teachers, classroom interventions, or literacy instruction participants in the study. The unit of analysis is papers and reviews rather than students or schools.

The main conclusions are that LLM reviewers systematically favor LLM-authored writing styles, inflate scores for LLM-generated papers, and tend to undervalue human-authored papers containing critical statements about risks or fairness. At the same time, revision guided by LLM review can improve manuscripts. Overall, the paper argues that LLM reviewers may be useful as assistive tools for early-stage feedback, but they are not yet trustworthy as impartial evaluators in high-stakes peer review due to fairness and bias concerns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not a K-12 education intervention study. It is an arXiv simulation paper about LLMs as academic peer reviewers, with no learner-facing educational sample, no school implementation, and no direct literacy instruction evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct K-12 literacy or student outcome impacts, so it cannot contribute evidence on the review thesis about generative AI in K-12 literacy instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive the benefits and challenges of using generative AI to support creative mathematical writing. The core problem addressed is that creative mathematical writing may help students express mathematical ideas imaginatively, but many elementary learners struggle to generate and develop such stories without support. The study asks what educational opportunities and barriers students and teachers perceive when generative AI is introduced into this process.

The intervention was a researcher-developed GenAI-powered learning technology that supported a three-step instructional process: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed a math story, then represented their thinking visually, and finally used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to help draft and revise their own culturally relevant math stories. The system generated story drafts from student-provided prompts including mathematical goals, characters, settings, and events, and students then evaluated the generated stories using a checklist.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. elementary schools with 79 students and six teachers. Data were collected through student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended student surveys, and classroom observation notes. The analysis used thematic analysis and focused on perceived experiences rather than measuring achievement effects.

The main conclusions were that students and teachers perceived several benefits: greater creativity in math, improved mathematical understanding, increased AI literacy, and stronger interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning. They also identified notable challenges, including weak student critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating effective prompts and coherent stories, lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, limited peer interaction, and accessibility constraints such as lack of speech-to-text. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI has promise for elementary math-related writing tasks, but effective educational use depends on careful instructional and system design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative classroom study with clear methods, authentic K-12 implementation, and multiple data sources, but it lacks a control/comparator, quantitative outcome measures, and causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impact based on self-reported perceptions rather than measured achievement or validated psychosocial outcomes; effect magnitude is not estimable.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4- and DALL·E-3-powered co-creative math story generation platform for 5th graders, where students prompt the system to draft and revise culturally relevant mathematical stories and images during fraction learning.
Generative writing support embedded in a math learning activity, helping elementary students turn prompt inputs into narrative math stories and revise wording, detail, and structure.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative classroom implementation with 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, students and teachers reported that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity improved problem understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and the surfacing of misconceptions. Evidence came from thematic analysis of student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations; no quantitative achievement gains or standardized math effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, visual knowledge representation, and identification of misconceptions from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI-supported mathematical story writing increased interest, enjoyment, curiosity, and ownership of learning. These findings are based on qualitative thematic evidence from 79 elementary students and 6 teachers after classroom use across multiple sessions, but no validated motivation scale scores or effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, enjoyment, curiosity, and ownership from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: The study found qualitative evidence that the intervention supported creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses, suggesting gains in AI literacy and higher-order thinking. However, participants also reported weaknesses in students’ critical evaluation of AI-generated content and difficulties formulating coherent prompts and stories, making the overall durable-skills pattern mixed.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, AI literacy, and critical evaluation skills from interviews, surveys, and observations

paper_profiles.title: THE IMPACT OF AI AND PEER FEEDBACK ON RESEARCH WRITING SKILLS: A STUDY USING THE CGSCHOLAR PLATFORM AMONG KAZAKHSTANI SCHOLARS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how familiarity with AI tools and peer feedback relates to openness to revising academic writing among Kazakhstani scholars. The central question is whether AI-assisted feedback and peer review, delivered through the CGScholar platform, can support development of research writing skills and how participants perceive these feedback mechanisms.

The study focuses on CGScholar, a platform that integrates AI-generated feedback, peer feedback, and structured rubrics for academic writing. Participants completed a 15-question bilingual survey with multiple-choice, Likert-scale, and open-ended items, and the course structure included repeated project updates, AI feedback on drafts, peer review, and final revision. The authors describe the work as design-based research, but the empirical data reported are survey-based descriptive statistics, correlations, and thematic interpretation.

The population consisted of 36 Kazakhstani scholars in a pedagogy cohort completing a scientific internship at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. They were enrolled in a course on transformations in higher education and engaged with both in-person and online sessions over one academic semester. All participants were female, citizens of Kazakhstan, and reported Kazakh as their first language. The context is higher education / scholar professional development rather than K-12.

The paper concludes that participants had low familiarity with AI tools but moderate familiarity with peer feedback and were generally open to feedback overall. Reported findings include a moderate positive correlation between familiarity with AI tools and openness to making changes based on feedback, and a stronger positive correlation between research writing experience and expectations for peer feedback, especially on research methodology. The authors argue that AI feedback may be useful for surface-level aspects of writing, while peer feedback remains especially valued for higher-order methodological guidance. They recommend broader and longitudinal future research to assess longer-term writing improvement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample correlational survey study with descriptive and thematic analysis, no control group, no randomization, and no direct pre/post performance outcome for writing skill. It provides only limited causal evidence and is not a direct K-12 study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially positive but unclear impact, based mainly on attitudes and correlations rather than demonstrated learning gains. Reported associations are promising but insufficient to establish meaningful educational impact.

interventions.use_case: CGScholar platform providing AI-generated feedback on scholars’ research writing drafts using a rubric covering experience, empirical evidence, conceptualization, analysis, application, and presentation.

finding.finding_summary: The study concerns research writing and feedback processes, but it does not report pre/post writing performance gains, rubric score improvements, or experimental comparisons in writing quality. Instead, it reports correlational survey results among 36 Kazakhstani scholars, including a moderate positive correlation between AI familiarity and openness to revising based on feedback (r=0.35), which is only indirect evidence for writing improvement.
finding.measure: Self-reported familiarity with AI tools, openness to feedback, expectations for peer feedback, and experience in research writing; no direct post-intervention writing achievement measure reported
finding.effect_size: r=0.35 (AI familiarity with openness to making changes based on feedback)

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported generally positive openness to feedback, with an average openness score of 3.83, and the study found a moderate positive correlation between familiarity with AI tools and openness to making changes based on feedback (r=0.35). Although no causal design was used, the results suggest more AI-familiar participants were more receptive to revision-oriented feedback.
finding.measure: Openness to feedback via survey/Likert-style items

finding.finding_summary: The study found a strong positive correlation between research writing experience and expectations for peer feedback, especially on research methodology (r=0.68), and a very strong correlation between AI familiarity and expectations for peer feedback on research methodology (r=0.82). These findings suggest perceived support for feedback-related revision and methodological thinking, but they do not demonstrate measured gains in critical thinking or collaboration skills.
finding.measure: Survey-based expectations for peer feedback on research methodology and self-reported research writing experience/AI familiarity

paper_profiles.title: LLMs as Writing Assistants: Exploring Perspectives on Sense of Ownership and Reasoning
paper_profiles.venue: The Third Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how people perceive ownership and authorship when using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT for writing. The core questions are whether sense of ownership varies by content type—especially creative versus non-creative writing—and how LLM use affects the relationship between feeling like an owner of text and being willing to claim authorship. The study is framed as an exploration of human-centered cognitive and psychological dilemmas in AI-assisted writing rather than an evaluation of learning outcomes.

The authors conducted a short survey of 35 participants. Survey items asked whether participants believed they contributed to ChatGPT-assisted non-creative writing (e.g., assignments) and creative writing (e.g., stories or poems), whether they would submit LLM-generated content under their own name, whether they felt they owned LLM-generated content, and whether prompting or editing the output changed that ownership perception. The intervention is therefore not an instructional program but a survey-based elicitation of attitudes toward LLM-assisted writing under different scenarios.

Participants were predominantly university students aged 18-24, mostly from science backgrounds, and described as technologically aware. The paper text identifies the lead author's institution in Bangladesh, but it does not explicitly state that all participants were located there; thus the study context is higher education students, likely in a university-affiliated context, but not a K-12 literacy setting. No direct educational implementation details such as classroom instruction, teacher involvement, or fidelity procedures are reported.

The main findings are that participants reported greater perceived contribution and ownership in non-creative writing than in creative writing, where they tended to credit the LLM more. The study also found a mismatch between authorship and ownership: many participants were willing to submit AI-generated text under their own name while not fully claiming ownership of it. Reminding participants about their role in prompting increased perceived ownership, and reminding them about editing increased ownership further. The authors conclude that active human involvement shapes ownership perceptions and that future writing-support systems should better account for transparency, collaboration, and attribution.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small descriptive survey study with a clear empirical component, but it is not K-12, has no experimental or quasi-experimental design, and reports no validated causal estimates. It meets limited credibility criteria and is better classified as exploratory human-subjects research.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests unclear, self-reported shifts in perceived ownership/authorship rather than demonstrated educational learning effects, and no effect sizes are reported. Impact is therefore uncertain and not directly tied to K-12 academic outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of ChatGPT/LLM use as a writing assistant for generating and editing non-creative assignments and creative writing, examining users' perceived ownership and authorship rather than learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: In a short survey of 35 participants, respondents reported lower perceived contribution/ownership for creative writing tasks (e.g., stories, poems, birthday wishes) and higher perceived contribution for non-creative writing (e.g., STEM assignments, formal letters). Ownership judgments also shifted after prompts reminding participants of their role: reported ownership increased from 17.1% to 28.6% after a prompting reminder, and to 62.9% after being reminded about editing the LLM output; no inferential statistics or standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported survey responses on sense of ownership, self-declared authorship, and perceived contribution in LLM-assisted writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential risks that extensive LLM use may reduce autonomy, critical reasoning, and promote thought outsourcing, but these constructs were not directly measured in the survey. Because these claims are interpretive discussion points rather than tested outcomes, the evidence for durable-skills effects is weak and non-causal.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; speculative discussion of autonomy and critical reasoning risks

paper_profiles.title: Writing With Machines and Peers: Designing for Critical Engagement with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students engage with generative AI and peer feedback during academic writing, and how they develop reflective relationships with both human and AI reviewers. The central problem is that although generative AI is increasingly used in education, there is limited classroom-based evidence showing how students actually use AI feedback across iterative writing processes, especially alongside peer review.

The study investigates an 8-week pedagogical design in which students in a graduate-level educational technologies course developed literature review or landscape review papers through multiple drafts. Students first received feedback from a custom AI reviewer, CyberScholar, which used rubric-aligned generative AI feedback and follow-up chat. They then revised and received structured peer feedback using the same rubric, followed by additional revision and reflection. Data included AI log files, draft versions, peer reviews, and written reflections, and the authors combined descriptive quantitative analyses with qualitative thematic analysis.

Participants were 10 consenting students from a single graduate course at a large research university in the United States, most of them doctoral students in social-science-related fields. The context was a classroom course hosted in a learning management system, with synchronous discussions, AI-supported review, peer review, and reflective writing. The study focused on authentic academic writing tasks rather than experimental comparison of outcomes across groups.

The main conclusion is that students used AI and peer feedback in complementary ways. AI was primarily valued for rapid, rubric-aligned, surface-level, and organizational feedback, while peer feedback was more useful for conceptual development, disciplinary relevance, and dialogic clarification. Students varied substantially in depth of AI engagement: some used the system transactionally as a scoring/checklist tool, whereas others engaged critically and strategically. The authors argue that hybrid human-AI feedback designs can support writing development, AI literacy, and critical engagement, but that meaningful outcomes depend on pedagogical scaffolding and students’ ability to evaluate and selectively use AI feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-methods qualitative/case study in higher education with descriptive revision metrics and no control group, randomization, or causal identification. It provides useful implementation evidence but meets only limited credibility criteria for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear positive impact on writing development and critical AI engagement, without reported effect sizes or rigorous comparison. Impact is therefore best characterized as positive but uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Custom GPT-4o-based rubric-aligned writing feedback system (CyberScholar/CyberReview) used to review graduate students’ literature-review drafts, score rubric dimensions, provide actionable revision suggestions, and support follow-up dialogue about revisions.
Conversational follow-up chat with the GenAI reviewer to clarify feedback, request examples, negotiate revision decisions, and ask questions about academic writing moves during iterative drafting.
Generative AI used for surface-level writing support such as grammar correction, wording improvement, coherence, and rubric-aligned academic writing refinement.

finding.finding_summary: In this 8-week mixed-methods case study with 10 graduate students, the hybrid AI-plus-peer feedback design was reported to support writing development across iterative drafts, with students using AI mainly for rubric alignment and surface-level edits and peers for conceptual development and disciplinary relevance. Revision analyses showed substantial text changes for several students across draft stages, but no standardized writing gain, inferential statistical test, or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student writing artifacts across three draft versions, revision trajectory metrics (Jaccard similarity; added/deleted n-grams), peer feedback, reflections, and AI chat logs

finding.finding_summary: The study found evidence of improved critical engagement with AI, reflective decision-making, and strategic use of different feedback sources among 10 graduate students. Qualitative cases showed that some students evaluated AI suggestions, negotiated whether to adopt them, and used peers for epistemic validation, indicating growth in metacognition and critical AI literacy, though effects were descriptive rather than statistically estimated.
finding.measure: Reflection notes, AI chat histories coded for depth of engagement, thematic analysis of revision decisions and feedback uptake

finding.finding_summary: Student reflections suggested increasing confidence and comfort in using AI over time, alongside appreciation for the encouragement and affective support provided by peers. The evidence indicates positive shifts in students’ perceived confidence and relational stance toward AI, but these findings were qualitative and no validated socio-emotional scale or effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Student written reflections about confidence, encouragement, and evolving relationships with AI and peers

paper_profiles.title: Search for a massless particle beyond the Standard Model in the Ξ0 → Λ + invisible decay
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a particle-physics search for a beyond-Standard-Model massless invisible particle in the flavor-changing neutral current decay Ξ0 → Λ + invisible. The scientific question is whether this rare hyperon decay occurs at an observable rate that would indicate new physics contributions, such as from a QCD axion or a massless dark photon. The study is not about education, literacy, K-12 learners, or generative AI use in classrooms.

The approach is an experimental analysis of high-energy collision data collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider. Using (1.0087 ± 0.0044) × 10^10 J/ψ events, the collaboration reconstructs tagged anti-Ξ0 decays and searches on the recoiling side for Ξ0 → Λ + invisible, where the invisible final-state particle leaves no detector signal. The analysis uses single-tag and double-tag event selection, Monte Carlo simulation, control-sample corrections, and a likelihood-based extraction of signal yield.

No human participant population is studied; the relevant context is a collider-detector experiment in China. After event selection and background modeling, no significant signal is observed. The fitted yield is consistent with background, and the collaboration sets an upper limit on the branching fraction B(Ξ0 → Λ + invisible) < 2.3 × 10^-4 at 90% confidence level.

The main conclusion is that this is the first search for this decay mode and it places a new experimental constraint on massless beyond-Standard-Model particles contributing to Ξ0 decays. The result remains consistent with existing dark-photon expectations and improves constraints relevant to some axion-coupling scenarios. However, it provides no direct evidence relevant to K-12 literacy, educational interventions, or generative AI in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a particle physics search study and does not concern any K-12 educational technology or AI intervention. It therefore provides no relevant educational study design, learner sample, or education outcome evidence for the requested review.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or learner outcome is evaluated, so the paper has no measurable impact for the K-12 literacy/GenAI review question.

paper_profiles.title: Reviewriter: AI-Generated Instructions For Peer Review Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how generative AI can support students during peer review writing, particularly to help with writer’s block and idea generation. The authors argue that while large language models have strong potential for educational writing support, there is limited evidence on how such systems should be designed for authentic learning settings and how students perceive them in practice.

To address this, the authors develop Reviewriter, a web-based tool that provides AI-generated inline writing instructions for peer review tasks in German. The system was designed using a student-centered process that combined a literature review with semi-structured interviews of 12 graduate students to derive user requirements and seven design principles. On the technical side, the authors fine-tuned three language models on a corpus of 11,925 German student-written peer reviews and selected German GPT-2 based on training loss, inference time, and human judgments of fluency and correctness. The tool offers multiple suggestions, keyboard-based acceptance/rejection, inline display of generated text, and word-count support.

The empirical evaluation involved 14 students from a public university in Europe, including 3 undergraduates and 11 graduate students, all native German speakers. Participants completed a 30-minute peer review writing task on a business model after a short introduction, then completed questionnaires and open-ended interviews. The setting appears to be a controlled evaluation session conducted either face-to-face or remotely, rather than a K-12 classroom implementation.

The study concludes that students generally perceived Reviewriter positively, especially in ease of use, ease of interaction, enjoyment, and excitement, with usefulness rated moderately positively. Qualitative feedback suggested that the system sometimes helped students overcome writer’s block, generate new ideas, and speed up writing, but also revealed concerns about hallucinated, irrelevant, or ungrammatical suggestions and waiting time for generation. Overall, the paper presents a promising higher-education prototype and design study, but it does not provide direct evidence of learning gains or effectiveness in K-12 literacy contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-method pilot in higher education with n=14, no control/comparator group, no randomization, and mostly self-reported acceptance/usability outcomes rather than validated learning gains. It has a clear methodology but only limited causal credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports favorable user perceptions and some qualitative signs of benefit, but no direct learning effect sizes or rigorous achievement impacts are provided. Impact on substantive educational outcomes is therefore unclear rather than established.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted peer review writing tool ('Reviewriter') that generates inline German text suggestions/instructions to help higher-education students continue writing peer reviews and overcome writer's block.
Adaptive suggestion system embedded in a peer-review writing interface, providing next-sentence recommendations based on the student's ongoing text rather than scoring or full tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The mixed-method pilot with 14 higher-education students examined AI-supported peer-review writing, a literacy-related writing outcome, but did not report direct pre/post writing-quality gains, standardized writing scores, or inferential statistics. Qualitative feedback suggested some students used suggestions to generate ideas and structure reviews, while others found outputs irrelevant or unusable; thus evidence on actual writing improvement is suggestive but inconclusive.
finding.measure: Peer-review writing process perceptions and self-reported usefulness for writing reviews; qualitative comments on idea generation and review composition

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive affective responses to Reviewriter in a pilot evaluation (n=14). Mean ratings on 1-7 scales were above neutral for perceived excitement (M=5.64, SD=1.15) and enjoyment (M=5.43, SD=1.16), and qualitative comments indicated the tool reduced feelings of being 'alone' while writing and helped with writer's block.
finding.measure: Post-use Likert scales for excitement and enjoyment; qualitative interview feedback on motivation/engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames peer review writing as related to critical thinking and review structuring, and some participants reported that Reviewriter helped generate new ideas and support structured reviewing. However, no validated direct assessment of critical thinking, metacognition, or peer-feedback skill improvement was reported, so evidence for durable skill gains remains indirect and mixed.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of improved reviewing/writing structure and qualitative comments about idea generation

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative findings suggested the tool sometimes improved writing efficiency by helping students continue when stuck, with some reporting faster review writing and support overcoming writer's block. At the same time, several participants complained that the 8-second delay for suggestions slowed the process, indicating mixed effects on productivity.
finding.measure: Qualitative feedback on speed, efficiency, and workflow during peer-review writing

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper documents early uses of generative AI in research and education within data-driven materials science. The authors ask how generative AI can support software learning, tutorial generation, and interface development for scientific tools. Rather than evaluating a formal educational intervention with controlled outcomes, the paper presents descriptive examples from a July 2024 hackathon (AIMHack2024) focused on integrating generative AI into materials science workflows.

The intervention consisted of three demonstration activities using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and MyGPT: (1) AI-assisted trial use of ImageJ for image-based particle counting, including overlapping-object detection; (2) creation of an AI tutor for the Bayesian optimization package PHYSBO using MyGPT with official documentation and papers as source material; and (3) development of a Windows GUI executable for PHYSBO with AI assistance, including automated manual creation. The paper emphasizes that AI outputs required human verification and iterative refinement, especially when initial responses were inaccurate.

The context was a hackathon with approximately 30 participants from diverse backgrounds including students and industry researchers in materials science, information science, bioinformatics, and condensed matter physics. The educational setting was not K-12; participants ranged from students to adult researchers, and the activity appears to have been conducted in a workshop/hackathon format at institutions in Japan. The paper does not report a formal sampling frame, participant breakdown, or standardized learning assessments.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can substantially reduce the effort required to learn unfamiliar software, generate usable tutorials, and create simple GUI applications and manuals in scientific domains. However, the authors also conclude that AI responses are not consistently reliable and must be checked against documentation, literature, and actual software behavior. Overall, the paper is best understood as an illustrative descriptive report of exploratory practice rather than rigorous evidence of educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive hackathon/report paper in higher education/research training rather than a K-12 empirical impact study. It lacks a clear causal design, validated outcome measures, statistical analysis, and direct literacy-relevant methodology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful but unquantified positive effects on efficiency and learning support, with no reported effect sizes or rigorous evidence of impact. Impacts are promising but unclear and not directly tied to K-12 learner outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT/MyGPT as a conversational assistant to help learners and researchers learn unfamiliar materials-science software, generate tutorials for the PHYSBO Bayesian optimization package, and guide software operation through step-by-step instructions.
Software-based instructional use of ImageJ and PHYSBO/GUI demonstrations as learning tools during a materials-science hackathon, with AI supporting access to tutorials and usage guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI reduced the effort and time required to learn unfamiliar software and generate user-facing materials such as tutorials, manuals, and GUI wrappers. Evidence is descriptive rather than experimental: approximately 30 hackathon participants observed or used AI-assisted workflows, and the authors state that several participants successfully used previously unfamiliar software, but no controlled comparison, effect size, or formal productivity metric is reported.
finding.measure: Descriptive reports of reduced workload, faster software onboarding, successful software use, and successful creation of tutorials/GUI/manuals

finding.finding_summary: A central stated goal of the hackathon was to strengthen participants' ability to critically evaluate AI-generated content by checking outputs against literature, domain knowledge, and software execution. The authors describe this as fostering critical thinking and verification practices, but provide no direct pre/post assessment, quantified learning gain, or validated measure.
finding.measure: Qualitative emphasis on critical evaluation, verification, and technical problem-solving practices

finding.finding_summary: Within the domain of materials-science education, the paper presents examples where AI-supported tutorials enabled users to perform image analysis tasks and understand PHYSBO acquisition functions and hyperparameter optimization workflows. However, the evidence is based on demonstrations and successful execution examples rather than formal assessment of scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Task completion in scientific software use; correct explanation of Bayesian optimization functions; executable tutorial performance
finding.study_size: approximately n=30 participants in hackathon; some demonstrations are single-case examples

paper_profiles.title: Business (mis)Use Cases of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines potential harmful business misuse cases of generative AI rather than educational applications or learning outcomes. The authors ask how generative AI might be misused at scale in business contexts, and they use participatory design fictions to explore how AI experts judge the plausibility, seriousness, and preventability of such futures.

The study used three fictional scenarios focused on generative text, audio, and video misuse: automated derivative novel writing, fake video evidence affecting insurance claims, and fabricated audio evidence in criminal cases. These scenarios were discussed in co-creation interview sessions with six AI software engineers, who first imagined their own future misuse scenarios and then reacted to the researchers’ 2030 scenarios. The data consisted of interview discussions that were thematically reviewed by two members of the research team.

Participants were adult AI professionals from a single research organization (IBM Research), not students, teachers, or school stakeholders. The context was a research interview setting rather than a classroom or educational implementation. No literacy intervention, K-12 population, or generative AI instructional use was studied.

The main conclusions are that experts saw generative AI misuse futures as partly plausible but contested in seriousness, with recurring themes around ubiquity of fakes, quality degradation, ownership questions, new market structures, and an arms race between generation and detection. Participants suggested that technological safeguards, provenance tools, regulation, legislation, and public education might mitigate harms. The paper is best understood as a qualitative HCI and ethics exploration of future risks, not as direct evidence about K-12 literacy uses of generative AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a workshop position/qualitative design-fiction study about business misuse cases of generative AI, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It includes only six AI engineer participants, no student sample, no instructional implementation, and no educational outcome measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learners, literacy, or classroom outcomes. Any educational implications are speculative rather than empirically estimated.

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) adequately addresses emerging market-power risks in generative AI. The authors argue that the DMA, which was designed to regulate dominant digital “gatekeepers” such as major platform providers, does not explicitly cover generative AI services even though these services may increasingly function as gateways for business users and end users. The paper focuses on policy and regulatory analysis rather than educational or learning outcomes.

The core approach is a legal and conceptual argument that certain generative AI services should be added to the DMA’s list of “core platform services,” and that some AI developers should be treated as gatekeepers under the regulation. The authors discuss mechanisms by which gatekeeping may arise in generative AI, including concentration of computing power, early-mover advantages, and control over data resources and integrated systems. They also review how existing DMA obligations might apply to standalone generative AI platforms if the regulation were amended.

There is no empirical study population, intervention trial, or educational implementation context in this paper. Instead, the context is the broader European digital policy environment, especially interactions among the DMA, the Digital Services Act, and the proposed AI Act. The paper uses examples from industry developments involving firms such as OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, and Meta to motivate concerns about competition, fairness, and contestability.

The main conclusion is that the DMA should be updated to explicitly encompass generative AI services before market dominance becomes entrenched. The authors contend that this would help preserve openness, diversity, innovation, and fair competition in the generative AI ecosystem. This paper is not a direct K-12 literacy study and does not provide evidence relevant to educational effects of generative AI interventions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a non-education policy commentary/legal analysis rather than an empirical K-12 study. It provides no direct intervention evaluation, no learner sample, and no causal or correlational outcome methodology relevant to the review.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses potentially important institutional implications for regulation of generative AI, but it contains no measured educational impact estimates. Its practical impact on K-12 literacy conclusions is therefore unclear and indirect.

finding.finding_summary: This is a policy/legal analysis arguing that generative AI services may become gatekeepers under the EU Digital Markets Act and that the DMA should be amended to classify certain generative AI services as core platform services. The paper cites illustrative market developments and alleged anti-competitive behavior but reports no original empirical education data, no K-12 participants, and no effect sizes or statistical tests.
finding.measure: legal/policy analysis of market structure, contestability, fairness, and regulatory fit under the EU Digital Markets Act

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how well current vision-language models (VLMs) can answer visually grounded, subject-specific questions based on real German middle-school knowledge. The authors argue that widely used multimodal benchmarks are often English-dominant, overly benchmark-optimized, and insufficiently representative of realistic school-level visual reasoning tasks. They therefore introduce a new German-language benchmark intended to test whether state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs can combine image understanding with background knowledge across authentic school subjects.

The study’s main approach is the creation and evaluation of a benchmark dataset built from German educational materials. The dataset contains 2,038 open-ended questions linked to 486 images across nine domains: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. The benchmark includes both standard questions and adversarial questions that intentionally ask about information not actually shown in the image. Thirteen open-weight VLMs were evaluated, and answers were scored using an automated LLM-as-a-judge approach with multiple judge models.

The context is German schooling, specifically grades 8 to 10 and school types including Gymnasium and Realschule. Although no human participants were recruited as study subjects, the benchmark content is explicitly drawn from middle-school curricula and educational resources intended for students in that range. The paper is therefore about AI system performance on tasks representing middle-school learners’ curricular knowledge rather than an intervention delivered to students or teachers.

The main conclusion is that current open-weight VLMs perform poorly on this benchmark, with the best model scoring below 45% overall accuracy and much lower performance in domains such as music and mathematics. Models performed especially badly on adversarial questions, indicating persistent difficulty recognizing when an image does not support an answer. The authors conclude that middle-school-level multimodal tasks in German are a meaningful and underused stress test for VLMs, and that performance on established public benchmarks does not reliably predict real-world multimodal reasoning performance in non-English educational contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/model-evaluation paper, not a K-12 intervention study with learners. It provides no student sample, no educational treatment, and no causal or correlational design about learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct impact on K-12 learners, teachers, or institutions from an educational intervention. Findings are about AI model performance limitations, so it does not provide evidence of positive educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates 13 open-weight vision-language models on a German middle-school benchmark and finds weak performance on mathematics items that require combining image understanding with background knowledge. Best math accuracy is only 34.09% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with many models far lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B = 9.09%, InternVL3 8B = 19.32%), indicating poor multimodal mathematical reasoning rather than educational gains for learners. No human student sample, effect size, or intervention comparison is reported.
finding.measure: Model accuracy on middle-school mathematics benchmark questions derived from German curricular materials
finding.study_size: 486 images; 2,038 questions overall; math domain includes 112 images and 308 questions

finding.finding_summary: Across science-related domains such as biology and physics, the benchmark shows that current VLMs perform far below mastery on German middle-school multimodal tasks. Best reported scores are 48.53% in biology and 47.65% in physics, with models often failing diagram interpretation, causal explanation, and domain-specific identification, especially on adversarial questions. The study reports no student learning outcomes, only model-performance limitations.
finding.measure: Model accuracy on biology and physics benchmark questions, including adversarial items
finding.study_size: 486 images; 2,038 questions overall; biology includes 33 images/169 questions and physics includes 52 images/234 questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central finding is that state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs perform poorly on authentic German middle-school knowledge tasks spanning history, geography, arts, music, religion, and sports. Overall accuracy ranges from 23.53% to 43.26%, and even the best model remains below 45% overall; adversarial-question performance is worse, often near or below 30%, suggesting substantial limits in real-world multimodal school knowledge understanding. These are benchmark results on AI systems, not educational impacts on K-12 students.
finding.measure: Overall and domain-specific model accuracy on a German multimodal middle-school benchmark, including adversarial-question accuracy
finding.study_size: 13 models evaluated on 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across 9 domains

paper_profiles.title: Most Language Models can be Poets too: An AI Writing Assistant and Constrained Text Generation Studio
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on When Creative AI Meets Conversational AI (CAI2), COLING 2022
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of constrained natural language generation: how to make language models produce text that obeys hard lexical, semantic, or phonetic constraints, such as banning a letter, matching a syllable count, or satisfying rhyme-related properties. The authors argue that while large language models are strong generators, prior work has paid limited attention to simple, plug-and-play ways of enforcing these kinds of token-level constraints during decoding. They position the work mainly as a creative writing and research tool rather than as an educational intervention study.

The core approach is to filter a language model’s vocabulary before each token is generated, compositionally applying user-specified constraints without retraining or modifying the underlying model. To demonstrate this, the paper introduces Constrained Text Generation Studio (CTGS), a graphical AI writing assistant, and a Hugging Face web app called Gadsby. The system supports a wide range of lexical, semantic, and phonetic filters, including banning specific letters, forcing letter inclusion, semantic similarity thresholds, syllable count, meter, rhyme, and phonetic matching. The paper also introduces a new constrained-writing dataset, Lipogram-e, composed of book-length English texts omitting the letter “e.”

No K-12, higher education, or other human participant population is empirically studied. The paper discusses possible users such as poets, creative writers, recreational linguists, and researchers, but does not report a formal user study, educational deployment, or participant sample. Its empirical component is instead a technical evaluation using GPT-2-medium on the Lipogram-e dataset, comparing base, fine-tuned, and over-fine-tuned models with and without the vocabulary constraint filter.

The main conclusion is that vocabulary filtering can effectively enforce hard constraints while preserving usable text generation, and on the Lipogram-e benchmark it yields strictly better performance than fine-tuning alone: lower perplexity and zero ignored-constraint errors across tested conditions.
