The authors also note important caveats, including degenerate generation behavior under heavy filtering and limitations caused by subword tokenization. Overall, the paper is best understood as a technical systems and methods contribution, not a direct education study and not direct evidence for K-12 literacy impacts of generative AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a workshop technical paper evaluating model behavior, not a K-12 education study. It provides no learner sample, no educational study design, and no causal evidence about student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows technical performance improvements for constrained text generation, but educational impact is unclear because no K-12 learners, teachers, or direct learning outcomes were studied.

interventions.use_case: Constrained text generation writing assistant (CTGS/Gadsby) that helps users generate or manually select creative writing continuations under lexical, semantic, and phonetic constraints such as banning letters, enforcing syllable counts, rhyme, or meter.

finding.finding_summary: In a technical evaluation on the Lipogram-e dataset, applying vocabulary-level constraint filters to GPT-2 variants reduced perplexity relative to the same models without filters and eliminated ignored-constraint errors. Reported results were GPT-2 perplexity 237.37 vs 211.53 with filter, GPT-2 fine-tuned 5 epochs 78.24 vs 77.99 with filter, and GPT-2 fine-tuned 20 epochs 75.58 vs 75.10 with filter; ignored constraint error rates fell from 28.2%, 0.5%, and 0.3% respectively to 0%.
finding.measure: Language-model perplexity on test split; ignored constraint error percentage on Lipogram-e dataset

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Summarization: Designing AI Support for Real-World Expository Writing Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the underexplored problem of how to design AI support for expository writing tasks that involve both reading source materials and generating new knowledge from them. The authors argue that most prior AI-assisted writing work has focused on tasks such as creative writing, editing, and summarization, while real-world expository writing—such as literature reviews or clinical documentation—poses distinct challenges because it requires evidence-based synthesis rather than simple text generation.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the paper is a position piece that proposes a conceptual framework for AI support in expository writing. The authors describe expository writing as both evidence-driven and knowledge-generating, and they outline three major design components for AI support: augmenting reading and evidence collection, supporting information synthesis, and facilitating text composition. They emphasize that AI should assist users in ways that preserve human control, reduce cognitive load, and allow verification of extracted evidence and generated content.

The paper does not report an empirical study with participants, so no learner population, educational sample, or implementation setting is described. Instead, it discusses potential applications in expert real-world domains such as scholarly writing and medical writing. The context is therefore conceptual and design-oriented rather than classroom-based or intervention-based.

The main conclusion is that expository writing presents a valuable and distinct design space for AI-assisted writing research. The authors conclude that effective systems should not simply generate full texts, but should instead provide modular support across stages of reading, synthesis, and drafting, while minimizing hallucination, bias, and overreliance on AI outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position/theoretical paper, not an empirical K-12 study. It presents design arguments and examples but no evaluative study design, sample, comparator, or measured learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially high real-world value of LLM-supported expository writing, but provides no direct causal evidence of impact. Impact is therefore speculative and unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual design of large-language-model support for expository writing tasks, including evidence collection, synthesis, and text composition for real-world document-based writing.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of using large language models (LLMs), including GPT-style systems and ChatGPT, in education. The central question is not the effectiveness of a specific classroom intervention, but how LLMs might be used productively and responsibly across learning and teaching, and what pedagogical, ethical, and institutional challenges must be addressed for their integration into education.

The paper discusses a wide range of possible educational uses for LLMs, including generating educational content, quizzes, feedback, summaries, explanations, tutoring support, lesson-planning materials, and adaptive assistance for both students and teachers. It also provides a narrative overview of prior research on LLMs and related NLP applications in education, spanning examples such as quiz generation, pedagogical agents, code explanation, automated assessment, and feedback systems. However, the paper does not report a new empirical intervention, experimental comparison, or implementation study.

The discussion spans multiple educational levels, explicitly mentioning elementary, middle and high school, university, professional training, and teacher use cases. In the K-12 context, the paper highlights possible applications to reading, writing, language learning, critical thinking, collaborative writing, and support for learners with disabilities, but these are presented as opportunities rather than tested implementations. The teacher perspective is also central, especially around personalization, lesson planning, assessment, and professional development.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have substantial promise for transforming education, but only if used with strong human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking practices, teacher and student AI literacy, and attention to privacy, bias, fairness, access, and sustainability. The authors argue against uncritical adoption and recommend that educational systems develop clear pedagogical strategies, governance structures, and training supports before integrating LLMs widely.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper synthesizing opportunities, risks, and examples from prior literature rather than reporting an original empirical study with a defined sample, design, or causal identification strategy. It therefore does not meet empirical evidence criteria in the K-12 evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper makes claims about potential benefits and risks of LLMs in education, but it does not estimate intervention effects or report outcome data. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Position paper discussing potential educational uses of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-3 for conversational support, tutoring, question answering, personalized guidance, and dialogue-based learning across school and higher-education settings.
Discusses LLM/NLP systems for automated or adaptive feedback on student writing, answers, peer assessment, and diagnostic responses, including semi-automated grading and revision support.
Describes LLMs as writing and language supports for grammar correction, style suggestions, summaries, translations, vocabulary support, and writing assistance for school-age learners.
Covers AI-generated instructional materials such as quizzes, flashcards, practice problems, summaries, and reading-comprehension questions for software-supported learning activities.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-assisted language learning using ChatGPT can improve academic writing skills and writing motivation for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The study is motivated by common challenges in writing instruction, including limited time for individualized feedback, difficulties improving organization and grammar, and low learner motivation. The authors aim to determine both the measurable effects of AI-supported instruction and students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in writing development.

The intervention involved a 12-week AI-assisted writing program in which the experimental group used ChatGPT twice per week for approximately 60 minutes per session. Students interacted with ChatGPT through a web-based platform that provided real-time feedback on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, coherence, and organization, and allowed students to ask questions and request examples or clarification. The control group received traditional writing instruction from an experienced teacher using the same instructional materials and similar writing tasks, with feedback delivered by the teacher rather than the AI system. The study combined quantitative pre-test/post-test comparisons with qualitative semi-structured interviews.

Participants were 50 Chinese undergraduate EFL students enrolled at a national university in China, with intermediate to upper-intermediate English proficiency. They were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. The study took place during the regular academic year using university language laboratories and computer facilities, while the experimental group also had flexibility to use ChatGPT at home. Outcomes included IELTS-based writing assessments rated by two independent raters, a writing motivation scale, and interview data from a subset of students in the AI condition.

The study reports that students in the ChatGPT condition outperformed the control group on overall writing, writing content, organization, language use, and writing motivation. Interview findings suggest that students perceived ChatGPT as innovative, accessible, and helpful for immediate personalized feedback, and many reported increased motivation and engagement. At the same time, the paper notes concerns about contextual accuracy, possible over-reliance on AI, and the need for ethical guidance to avoid plagiarism. Overall, the authors conclude that ChatGPT can be an effective support for EFL academic writing instruction, though careful implementation and continued development of AI tools are necessary.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods experimental comparison with random assignment to experimental and control groups, pre/post measurement, and statistical controls via ANCOVA. However, it is a small single-site study in higher education rather than K-12, and reporting leaves some credibility concerns (e.g., limited implementation detail and no confidence intervals).
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on writing outcomes and motivation are moderate to large, with Cohen’s d ranging from 0.52 to 0.88 and partial eta squared values indicating substantial group differences. The magnitude of impact is clearly above the 0.20 threshold, although the population is not K-12.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based AI-assisted EFL academic writing support providing real-time feedback and suggestions on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, coherence, and organization during writing and revision.
Conversational interaction with ChatGPT as an on-demand virtual writing tutor that answers questions, gives explanations, and offers examples during writing practice.

finding.finding_summary: In a mixed-method pretest-posttest comparison with 50 Chinese EFL university students, the ChatGPT group outperformed the traditional instruction group on post-test writing outcomes after a 12-week intervention. Reported post-test differences favored ChatGPT for overall writing (59.12 vs 45.18; t(48)=3.79, p<0.001, d=0.76), content (15.96 vs 13.71; t(48)=3.01, p=0.003, d=0.65), organization (16.56 vs 13.63; t(48)=4.12, p<0.001, d=0.84), and language use (19.89 vs 15.89; t(48)=4.34, p<0.001, d=0.88). ANCOVA controlling for pretest also showed a significant group effect for global writing, F(1,47)=19.01, partial eta squared=0.27.
finding.measure: IELTS Academic Writing Tasks 1 and 2 scored with IELTS band descriptors for overall writing, content, organization, and language use
finding.effect_size: d=0.76 overall; d=0.65 content; d=0.84 organization; d=0.88 language use; partial eta squared=0.27 overall
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=14.23 overall, 3.71 content, 3.54 organization, 4.82 language use; Control post-test SD=15.62 overall, 3.12 content, 3.63 organization, 4.12 language use

finding.finding_summary: The ChatGPT group showed higher writing motivation than the traditional instruction group after the 12-week intervention. Post-test motivation means were 20.06 (SD=3.33) for the experimental group and 18.21 (SD=3.58) for controls, with t(48)=3.34, p=0.001, d=0.52; ANCOVA controlling pretest found F(1,47)=29.62, p=0.00, partial eta squared=0.38. Qualitative interviews also indicated greater enjoyment, confidence, and engagement during writing with AI support.
finding.measure: Writing Motivation Scale questionnaire (7-item adapted WMS) and semi-structured interviews
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=3.33; Control post-test SD=3.58

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines concerns about using ChatGPT in education, treating ChatGPT as an instrumental case of advanced AI chatbots among early adopters. The central research question is: what are the concerns of using chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, in education? Rather than testing a literacy intervention or measuring learning gains, the study focuses on perceptions, risks, and practical issues surrounding adoption, such as cheating, response quality, ethics, fairness, privacy, and implications for teaching practice.

The study uses a three-stage approach: (1) social network analysis and sentiment/content analysis of 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT in education, collected over roughly two weeks; (2) content analysis of interviews with 19 early adopters from varied roles including educators, students, developers, and AI freelancers; and (3) a one-week hands-on user experience investigation in which three experienced educators tested ChatGPT across ten educational scenarios. These scenarios explored issues such as essay cheating, inaccurate or inconsistent content generation, uneven response quality across users, poor assessment design, dependence on prompting quality, lack of emotional/reflection capacity, misleading privacy claims, and possible manipulation beyond the user’s request.

The population and context are broad and cross-contextual rather than tied to a single formal school implementation. Participants included students and educators, with interviewees drawn from multiple countries including the USA, China, and the UK, and tweets drawn from public discourse in English on Twitter. The paper discusses educational settings generally, including schools and universities, but does not report a specific classroom-based implementation, grade-banded sample, or direct instructional trial.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT has strong transformative potential in education, but its use should be approached cautiously and governed by clearer policies and pedagogical redesign. The authors argue that educational systems should not simply ban the technology; instead, they should develop new teaching philosophies, strengthen users’ prompting and critical-thinking competencies, and prioritize responsible, human-centered chatbot design. The paper highlights the need for future research on safe adoption, human-machine collaboration, fairness, privacy, and the competencies required for effective educational use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative instrumental case study using triangulated methods (tweet analysis, interviews, and user-experience scenarios), but it does not provide causal identification, controlled comparison, or validated quantitative outcome estimates. It meets limited credibility criteria appropriate to qualitative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper documents potentially meaningful but mixed and largely perception-based implications for educational practice and policy, without quantified learning impacts or effect sizes. Overall impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Qualitative case study of ChatGPT as an educational chatbot/conversational AI, examining perceived uses such as answering student questions, generating instructional materials and quizzes, providing learning assistance, and raising concerns about cheating, accuracy, ethics, and policy.

finding.finding_summary: Participants and user-experience scenarios suggested ChatGPT could reduce teacher workload by quickly generating outlines, quizzes, and other instructional materials, often within minutes. However, the paper also documents substantial limitations in output quality, inconsistency, and formatting that could increase checking and revision demands. No effect sizes or controlled comparisons were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview perceptions and hands-on scenario-based observations of usefulness for material generation and workload reduction
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in 1-week user-experience exercise; 2330 tweets for public discourse context

finding.finding_summary: Across interviews and discussion, the authors report recurring concerns that student reliance on ChatGPT may reduce critical thinking, innovation, and independent problem solving. Evidence is based on stakeholder perceptions and illustrative scenarios rather than direct pre/post assessment of durable skills, so the direction reflects reported concern rather than causal estimation. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions about critical thinking, innovation, and independent reasoning
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in 1-week user-experience exercise

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds generally positive but fragmented public discourse around ChatGPT in education, with tweet sentiment showing more positive than negative sentiment (5% vs 2.5%), while 92.5% were uncategorized/undecided. The authors also identify institutional concerns including cheating, privacy, fairness, and the emergence of bans and policy responses, concluding that adoption requires governance and guidance rather than simple prohibition. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Social network analysis and sentiment analysis of tweets; qualitative synthesis of policy and governance concerns

finding.finding_summary: Interviewees described ChatGPT interactions as exciting, fun, and in some cases emotionally engaging, with one participant likening it to a personal tutor. At the same time, participants reported disappointment, frustration, and lack of emotional trust when outputs were inaccurate or when the system failed to provide genuine empathy. Findings are qualitative only, with no validated social-emotional scale or effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of emotions, engagement, attachment, trust, and perceived human-likeness

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots—especially ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and considers their implications for higher education. The authors aim to situate these tools historically and commercially, review early English- and Chinese-language academic literature, and compare leading chatbots on capabilities relevant to higher education assessment, teaching, and learning. A central concern is how these systems may disrupt traditional academic practices, especially writing-based assessment and academic integrity.

The paper does not report a participant-based intervention study. Instead, it combines historical overview, literature review, and comparative analysis of chatbot systems. The authors describe the development of chatbots from ELIZA to current large language model systems, discuss the role of major US and Chinese technology firms, and review early scholarly discussions on chatbot use in higher education. They also outline a comparative testing approach to assess chatbot performance on tasks relevant to academic assignments and examinations.

The context is higher education rather than K-12 schooling. The discussion concerns students, faculty, and institutions broadly, with examples drawn from university assessment, learning support, and disciplinary applications such as medicine, law, IT security, and language learning. The article also references institutional and policy responses, including bans, revised assessments, and concerns about plagiarism detection.

The paper concludes that, despite substantial hype, current chatbots are far from consistently reliable or truly intelligent. GPT-4 and earlier ChatGPT models performed best among the systems discussed, while Bing Chat and Bard were characterized as less dependable in the authors’ comparison. The authors argue that higher education should neither ignore nor simply ban these tools; instead, institutions, faculty, and students should respond critically and adapt assessment and teaching practices to the new generative AI landscape.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Although published in a peer-reviewed journal, this paper is primarily a narrative review and comparative commentary focused on higher education, without a clear K-12 empirical design, student sample, or causal methodology aligned to the requested evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important but unclear institutional and productivity implications of chatbot adoption; however, it does not report direct learner impact estimates or effect sizes, so impact remains speculative and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Comparative review and benchmark-style evaluation of general-purpose generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bing Chat, Bard, Ernie) for higher-education-relevant tasks such as answering questions, generating text, providing explanations, and supporting academic work.

finding.finding_summary: This article argues that rapidly developing chatbot systems are likely to substantially affect higher education assessment, teaching, learning, and institutional policy, but it does not present original causal evidence from learners or schools. Its own comparative bot test concluded that no chatbot in the sampled cohort achieved top-tier performance, with GPT-4 performing best and Bing Chat/Bard performing poorly on the authors' higher-education-relevant benchmark; however, no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or student outcome statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Comparative author-designed chatbot performance test and narrative review of implications for higher education policy, assessment, and teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential productivity gains from generative AI for drafting, editing, summarising, and producing materials, while simultaneously emphasizing unreliability, hallucinations, and accuracy problems that limit safe educational use. These claims are based on literature review and illustrative examples rather than an empirical study of teacher or student efficiency outcomes, and no quantitative workload or time-savings estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of productivity/workload affordances and risks of chatbot use in academic tasks

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging question of what benefits and challenges ChatGPT may present for higher education, framed through constructivist learning theory. The authors explicitly pose two research questions: identifying the key benefits of ChatGPT for the future of higher education and identifying the key challenges. Rather than reporting results from an empirical intervention, the paper offers a perspective-based analysis and develops propositions for future research and practice.

The approach studied is conceptual rather than experimental. The paper discusses potential applications of ChatGPT in higher education, including adaptive learning, individualised feedback, research and writing support, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment design. It also examines risks such as academic integrity violations, ethical and equity concerns, bias and falsified information, limitations in evaluating graduate skills, and difficulties in assessing student learning outcomes. Across these areas, the authors argue that ChatGPT can align with constructivist principles when used to scaffold learning, provide feedback, and support active knowledge construction, but may undermine those same principles when used as a shortcut or substitute for authentic learning.

The population and context are higher education broadly, including tertiary students, academics/educators, administrative staff, and institutions. The paper does not report a specific participant sample, site, intervention duration, or country of study because it is not an empirical study. Its discussion is situated in university and tertiary education contexts rather than K-12 settings.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT has substantial promise to enhance higher education through personalised learning, feedback, writing support, and administrative efficiency, but its use must be carefully governed. The authors recommend responsible-use education, new assessment strategies that cannot be easily replicated by AI, attention to equity and bias, and inclusion of AI literacy in graduate capabilities. Overall, the paper argues for a balanced approach that leverages ChatGPT’s benefits while mitigating ethical, pedagogical, and assessment-related risks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical discussion paper, not an empirical study. It presents propositions and literature-informed claims but no original sample, intervention implementation, comparison group, or outcome measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially important benefits and risks, but provides no direct causal evidence or measured effects. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Perspective paper on using ChatGPT in higher education as a conversational AI for adaptive learning, personalised feedback, research/writing support, administrative assistance, and assessment design; it does not report an implemented intervention trial.
Discusses ChatGPT as a tool for automating or augmenting formative feedback and grading support for student work.
Discusses ChatGPT as a writing and language support tool for drafting, summarising, translating, and assisting academic writing, especially for non-native English users.

paper_profiles.title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a viable source of feedback for complex writing tasks, specifically argumentative essay writing, and how the quality of AI-generated feedback compares with peer-generated feedback. The authors frame the study around a practical educational problem: teachers often struggle to provide timely, high-quality feedback on essays, especially in large classes, and peer feedback can also be inconsistent because students may lack sufficient expertise or feedback skills. The study asks two main questions: whether ChatGPT-generated and peer-generated feedback differ in quality, and whether essay quality is related to the quality of feedback produced by either source.

The intervention involved an online argumentative essay writing module delivered through the Brightspace platform. In week one, students individually wrote essays on course-related controversial topics. In week two, students provided asynchronous written peer feedback on two peers’ essays using a structured prompt through the FeedbackFruits tool, while the researchers also submitted the same essays to ChatGPT using a closely matched prompt to generate AI feedback. The researchers then analyzed both the essays and the feedback using established coding schemes that assessed essay quality and feedback features such as affective, cognitive, and constructive elements.

The study took place at a Dutch university specializing in life sciences and involved 74 graduate students in food sciences. The context was fully online and focused on higher education rather than K-12. Quantitative analyses included MANCOVA to compare peer and ChatGPT feedback quality and Spearman correlations to examine relationships between essay quality and feedback quality.

The main conclusion is that peer feedback was overall higher quality than ChatGPT feedback, largely because peers were better at identifying problems in essays, whereas ChatGPT was stronger at descriptive feedback such as summarizing essay content. The authors argue that ChatGPT may still be useful as a complementary feedback source rather than a replacement for peer or teacher feedback. They also found no overall significant relationship between essay quality and the quality of feedback generated by peers or ChatGPT. The paper emphasizes the promise of AI-supported feedback while noting important limitations regarding sample scope, short duration, and lack of evidence on how students used the feedback for revision.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study with structured coding and statistical analysis, but it is exploratory, non-K-12, from a single graduate course, and not a randomized impact evaluation of student outcomes. It provides some methodological rigor but does not meet stronger causal evidence standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study finds small differences in feedback characteristics between ChatGPT and peer feedback, but it does not measure downstream learning gains, revision quality, or independent writing outcomes. As a result, educational impact is unclear rather than clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-generated written feedback on graduate students’ argumentative essays, using a fixed prompt to provide 250–350 word feedback about argument elements, problems, and improvement suggestions.

finding.finding_summary: In a comparison of ChatGPT-generated versus peer-generated feedback on argumentative essays, ChatGPT produced significantly more descriptive feedback, while peers were significantly better at identifying problems in essays. Reported effects were small: description F(1,146)=3.25, p<0.05, η²=0.03; identification F(1,146)=4.38, p<0.01, η²=0.02; no significant differences were found for affective, justification, or constructive feedback dimensions. The study did not test revision gains or independent post-writing performance, so literacy improvement from AI feedback was not established.
finding.measure: Coded quality of essay feedback on argumentative writing (affective, cognitive: description/identification/justification, and constructive components) using rubric-based ratings
finding.effect_size: η²=0.03 for description; η²=0.02 for identification
finding.std_deviation: Peer description SD=0.29; ChatGPT description SD=0.00; Peer identification SD=0.49; ChatGPT identification SD=0.70

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could potentially complement peer feedback and help reduce teacher feedback workload in large-enrolment writing contexts, but this was not directly tested empirically. No time, cost, productivity, or workload outcome measures were collected, so any operational benefit remains inferential rather than demonstrated.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; discussion-based implication about scalability and teacher workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used to generate high-quality, personalized English reading comprehension materials for school use, addressing a practical problem identified by middle school English teachers in China: students often reuse outdated reading passages and teachers face high workload when adapting texts and writing questions. The study asks whether a ChatGPT-based system can generate suitable reading passages and multiple-choice questions for middle school English learners, and whether such a system could be useful in real educational settings.

The authors build a reading exercise generation system with a graphical user interface that allows users to specify passage length, genre, difficulty level, and topic. ChatGPT is used in zero-shot and one-shot prompting modes to generate reading passages and comprehension questions, with an added toxicity check before materials are made available. The study also includes a GPT-2 + PPLM baseline for passage generation comparison. Evaluation combines automatic text metrics, structured human ratings of generated passages and questions, pairwise comparisons against human-written textbook materials, and qualitative feedback interviews from teachers who used the system.

The educational context is Chinese middle school English learning, especially Grades 7 to 9, with source materials and evaluation framed around reading comprehension exercises used in Beijing schools. Participants in the evaluations included Chinese college students with prior experience doing such exercises, native English speakers recruited online, and three experienced middle school teachers in Beijing who used the system for one week. The system is intended for teachers and students, but the direct first-hand implementation feedback comes primarily from teachers.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were rated as high quality and, in several human evaluations, even outperformed human-written textbook passages on dimensions such as readability, coherence, engagement, and overall quality. Generated questions were judged relevant to passages but weaker than human-written questions, especially because distractor options were often repetitive or low quality. Teachers reported that the system was useful, easy to use, and promising for providing diverse and personalized reading materials, though the authors note that broader deployment and more extensive user feedback are still needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation study with structured human assessment and limited teacher field feedback, but it does not measure K-12 student learning outcomes directly and lacks a causal design such as an RCT or strong quasi-experiment. Evidence is mainly based on content-quality ratings and qualitative implementation feedback.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear educational impact: materials were judged high quality and teachers perceived workload benefits, yet no direct independent literacy gains or quantified effect sizes on student outcomes were reported.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-based system for generating personalized English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercise questions for Chinese middle school learners, with editable outputs for teacher use and adaptation in school contexts.
Graphical reading-exercise generation system that delivers AI-generated reading practice materials through a teacher-facing interface for classroom or school-based English practice.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were rated as higher quality than both a fine-tuned GPT-2 baseline and, in several human evaluations, higher than human-written textbook passages for middle school English reading practice. In Human Evaluation 1, Chinese student raters scored ChatGPT passages higher than human-written passages on overall quality (4.46 vs. 4.18), readability (4.61 vs. 4.52), correctness (4.60 vs. 4.32), coherence (4.65 vs. 4.39), and engagement (4.37 vs. 4.07); however, no direct student learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Human ratings of reading-passage quality, suitability, topic coherence, and comparison with textbook passages for English reading comprehension materials
finding.study_size: 30 human-written passages + 30 ChatGPT passages + 30 GPT-2 passages in Example Set 1; 10 human-written passages + 30 generated passages in Example Set 2; 9 Chinese college student evaluators and 36 native English speakers for passage evaluation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the system could substantially reduce the time and cost of creating diverse, personalized reading comprehension materials, and that output quality exceeded expectations despite weaknesses in distractor-option generation. This finding is based on one-week first-hand use and interview feedback from three experienced Beijing middle school teachers, without quantified time-savings or workload effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and perceived reduction in workload/cost

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the system was utilized by middle school English teachers and was perceived as promising for school implementation, with teachers describing it as a personalized resource library that could support broader provision of diverse reading materials. However, this was based on limited pilot use and perception data rather than measured school-wide adoption or institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of school applicability and implementation promise

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating AI in foreign language education: An investigation into ChatGPT’s effect on foreign language learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how ChatGPT affects foreign language learning experiences and how students perceive its strengths, challenges, and possible uses in language education. The authors position the study as addressing a gap in understanding the practical classroom use of generative AI, especially ChatGPT, in foreign language instruction. The research questions focus on how ChatGPT shapes learners’ experiences, motivation, engagement, and skill development, and what students see as the tool’s benefits, drawbacks, and recommendations for improvement.

The intervention was a four-week ChatGPT-integrated English course conducted online. ChatGPT was embedded into reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary lessons, each 45 minutes long, using tailored lesson plans based on coursebook units. Students used the tool for activities such as warm-ups, pre-reading exploration, vocabulary practice, creative writing, grammar practice, brainstorming, story generation, social media simulation, and receiving writing feedback. The teacher initially provided prompts, then encouraged students to generate their own prompts in later weeks to support greater independence and creativity.

The study involved 13 preparatory-class university students at a School of Foreign Languages at a foundation university in Ankara, Turkey. Participants were 18–20 years old, came from multiple academic departments, and had English proficiency levels ranging from A2 to B2. Because of a post-earthquake shift to emergency distance education, both the instructional activities and the semi-structured interviews were conducted online. Data were collected through interviews and analyzed thematically within a qualitative case study framework.

The main conclusions are that students generally perceived ChatGPT as beneficial for writing, grammar, and vocabulary learning, and as increasing motivation and engagement through immediate feedback, accessibility, and versatility. Students also reported value for creativity and cultural exploration. At the same time, they noted limited usefulness for speaking and no impact on listening, plus concerns about overreliance, technical issues, misuse, and weak responsiveness to emotional or highly personal communication. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a useful supplementary tool in foreign language education but should complement rather than replace teacher guidance and authentic communicative practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study with a clear methodology, intervention description, and thematic analysis, but it lacks a control group, causal identification, and objective outcome measures. It meets limited credibility criteria and is therefore best classified as yellow.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts are generally positive but based on small-sample self-reports without effect sizes or independent assessments, making magnitude unclear. In addition, the study is outside K-12 and thus offers only limited evidence for the school-age literacy review context.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was integrated into online foreign-language instruction over four weeks for reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary activities, including brainstorming, question answering, story generation, role-play creation, research proposal ideation, and teacher-provided or student-generated prompting.

ChatGPT was used specifically as a language-learning and writing support tool to help students draft essays, brainstorm ideas, practice grammar, expand vocabulary, and receive written feedback on essays in EFL instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study, students reported that ChatGPT positively supported writing improvement, vocabulary learning, and some reading/writing classroom tasks during a four-week intervention. Evidence comes from interview themes rather than standardized literacy assessments; no effect sizes or comparative statistics were reported, and the study involved 13 university EFL preparatory students rather than K-12 learners.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on writing improvement, vocabulary learning, reading/writing activity experiences

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived benefits for grammar-related language development, but speaking improvement was reported as limited and listening improvement as absent. These findings are based on participant perceptions from interviews after four weeks of ChatGPT-assisted online EFL activities, with no direct fluency test scores or effect sizes reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on grammar, speaking, and listening impacts

finding.finding_summary: Most participants described increased motivation and engagement from ChatGPT's interactive, accessible, and versatile use in online classes, though a few reported no increase in motivation. Findings are qualitative and perception-based, derived from interviews with 13 learners after a four-week implementation; no validated motivation scale or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on motivation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT supported creativity, brainstorming, and interactive learning activities, but also raised concerns about overreliance, shortcut-taking, and possible weakening of autonomy or critical thinking. These conclusions are based on thematic analysis of interview data rather than direct performance measures.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on creativity, interactivity, dependency, and shortcut-taking

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT saved time and made information access and research tasks more efficient during language-learning activities. However, these efficiency findings were self-reported qualitatively and were not quantified with task-time or productivity metrics.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview reports on time-saving and efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Metacognitive Awareness and EFL Learners' Perceptions and Experiences in Utilising ChatGPT for Writing Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how EFL learners perceive and experience using ChatGPT for writing feedback, with particular attention to the role of metacognitive awareness. The study asks three main questions: how ChatGPT influences students’ writing experiences and metacognitive awareness, how levels of metacognitive awareness relate to perceptions and practices of ChatGPT use, and what factors shape effective use of ChatGPT for writing feedback.

The intervention took place in a semester-long practical writing course in which one class used AI tools including Poe as an access point to ChatGPT during writing tasks, while another class followed a teacher-led, peer-collaboration approach without AI. The study used a mixed-methods design combining questionnaires, pre/post comparisons, regression analyses, and semi-structured interviews. Outcomes focused on self-reported writing motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, collaborative writing tendency, and metacognitive awareness dimensions such as declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge, planning, monitoring, and evaluation.

Participants were 40 EFL undergraduates in two English Practical Writing classes at the same institution in Macau, SAR, China. Students were described as mainly from Macau, with Cantonese as a first language for most and some Mandarin speakers from mainland China, and their English proficiency was low to intermediate. Ten students from the AI group also participated in interviews, split between higher and lower metacognitive awareness.

The main findings were that the AI-using group showed significantly higher post-test scores on most self-reported writing and metacognitive outcomes than the non-AI group. Regression and interview findings suggested that metacognitive awareness was strongly associated with more productive use of ChatGPT. Students with higher metacognitive awareness described using ChatGPT more critically and strategically, whereas lower-awareness students were more likely to copy output or struggle to obtain useful feedback. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support EFL writing development, but its effective use depends heavily on learners’ metacognitive awareness, critical thinking, and cognitive effort.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method comparative study with a small sample (n=40) in higher education, using two intact classes and quantitative plus interview data. It is not a K-12 study, not a randomized controlled trial at the student level, and reports no standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals, so it fits correlational/quasi-experimental evidence with notable limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported post-test and gain-score differences are consistently positive across motivation, engagement, collaboration, and metacognitive outcomes, with several statistically significant group differences suggesting modest practical impact. However, effect sizes are not reported and the sample is small and non-K-12, so impact is better characterized as modest rather than clearly medium/large.

interventions.use_case: EFL university writing course using Poe/ChatGPT as a writing feedback and revision aid for students to seek comments on their writing, compare suggestions, and support editing/revision during class.
Generative AI used specifically as machine-generated feedback on student writing, contrasted with a non-AI teacher-led and peer-collaboration writing approach.

finding.finding_summary: Across a 15-week writing course, the AI group (n=20) showed significantly higher post-test writing-related outcomes than the non-AI group (n=20), including self-efficacy for writing and other writing experience indicators. Post-test self-efficacy for writing was 3.96 (SD=0.52) in the AI group versus 3.66 (SD=0.34) in the non-AI group (p=0.037), although gain-score differences for self-efficacy were only marginal in the Mann-Whitney test (p=0.064), suggesting literacy-related benefits but with some inconsistency across writing submeasures.
finding.measure: Writing-related questionnaire outcomes in an EFL writing course, especially self-efficacy for writing as part of writing experiences/perceptions
finding.std_deviation: AI post SEW SD=0.52; non-AI post SEW SD=0.34

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported writing group (n=20) reported significantly stronger motivation, engagement, and collaborative writing tendency than the comparison group (n=20) after the semester-long course. Post-test means favored AI for motivation for writing (4.34 vs 3.59, p<0.001), collaborative writing tendency (4.14 vs 3.58, p<0.001), and writing engagement (4.26 vs 3.48, p<0.001); gain-score tests also favored AI for motivation, collaboration, and engagement (all p<=0.0024, except self-efficacy marginal at p=0.064).
finding.measure: Questionnaire scales for motivation for writing, writing engagement, collaborative writing tendency, and self-efficacy for writing
finding.std_deviation: Motivation post SDs: 0.38 vs 0.35; collaboration post SDs: 0.45 vs 0.37; engagement post SDs: 0.54 vs 0.39

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial positive effects of AI-supported writing on metacognitive awareness dimensions. Relative to the non-AI group (n=20), the AI group (n=20) scored higher at post-test on declarative knowledge (4.40 vs 3.46), procedural knowledge (4.09 vs 3.54), conditional knowledge (4.26 vs 3.44), planning (4.14 vs 3.64), monitoring (3.97 vs 3.40), and evaluating (4.22 vs 3.50), all p<0.001; regression further showed metacognitive awareness strongly predicted perceptions/experiences of ChatGPT use (b=1.2398, p<0.001, model R²=0.8631).
finding.measure: Metacognitive Writing Strategies Questionnaire dimensions: declarative, procedural, conditional knowledge; planning, monitoring, evaluating; plus regression of metacognitive awareness on ChatGPT-related perceptions/practices
finding.std_deviation: Representative post SDs—DK: 0.27 vs 0.32; PK: 0.47 vs 0.38; CK: 0.36 vs 0.36; Planning: 0.31 vs 0.27; Monitoring: 0.28 vs 0.19; Evaluating: 0.22 vs 0.18

paper_profiles.title: TEACHERS’ AND STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS TOWARDS THE USE OF CHATGPT TO IMPROVE WRITING IN THE MALAYSIAN SECONDARY SCHOOL CONTEXT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Malaysian secondary school students and English teachers perceive the use of ChatGPT for improving students’ English writing. The study is motivated by growing interest in generative AI in education and the relative lack of evidence focused on secondary school settings, especially compared with the larger literature in higher education. The authors specifically investigate perceived effectiveness, how ChatGPT is used for writing-related purposes, and what factors shape adoption.

The approach studied is the use of ChatGPT as a writing support tool rather than a formally implemented experimental intervention. Participants described using ChatGPT for drafting essays, revising text, grammar checking, vocabulary development, proofreading, idea generation, and obtaining feedback. Teachers also reported using ChatGPT to create more personalized lesson materials and, in at least one example, assigning homework in which students used ChatGPT to write an essay and then discussed feedback and revisions in class.

The study used a qualitative design with open-ended online questionnaires. The sample included 20 respondents from six public secondary schools in Sabah, Malaysia: 12 students and 8 English teachers. Students were described as having varied English proficiency levels and differing prior exposure to ChatGPT. Data were thematically analyzed to identify common perceptions, reported uses, and adoption factors.

The main conclusion is that both students and teachers generally viewed ChatGPT positively as a helpful aid for English writing, especially because it can provide fast, personalized feedback and support tasks such as proofreading and idea generation. At the same time, participants identified important challenges, including limited access to devices or internet, uneven digital literacy, and concerns about overreliance on AI that could undermine independent writing development. The authors conclude that AI integration in writing instruction has promise, but should be balanced with conventional teaching and supported by attention to infrastructure and teacher support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study with a clear methodology, sample, and thematic analysis, but it does not use experimental or quasi-experimental designs and provides only self-reported perceptions rather than direct outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially beneficial but unclear impact on secondary students’ writing and teacher efficiency because findings are based on perceptions only, with no causal design, standardized outcome data, or effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by Malaysian secondary school students and English teachers to support English writing through drafting, revising, proofreading, grammar correction, vocabulary expansion, idea generation, and creating sample texts or lesson materials.

ChatGPT used conversationally to provide personalized feedback and suggestions on students’ writing, including asking how to improve original work and discussing AI-generated feedback in subsequent class sessions.

finding.finding_summary: Across 20 participants (12 students, 8 teachers) from six Malaysian secondary schools, respondents generally perceived ChatGPT as effective for improving English writing, especially grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, drafting, revision, and overall writing quality. Evidence is based on qualitative self-reports rather than direct pre/post writing assessments, and no effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended questionnaire responses about perceived improvement in English writing proficiency and writing-related uses of ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT saved time in writing and teaching-related tasks by offering rapid feedback, grammar checking, and quick generation of example texts or personalized lesson materials. These efficiency benefits were described qualitatively by students and teachers, with no quantified time-saved metric reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of time savings, convenience, and usefulness for teaching/material preparation

finding.finding_summary: Some teachers perceived ChatGPT as encouraging critical thinking because students must formulate questions or prompts to obtain useful answers, but participants also expressed concern that overreliance could undermine students’ ability to write independently. These findings are perception-based and not supported by direct performance measures of critical thinking or independent writing transfer.
finding.measure: Open-ended questionnaire responses on critical thinking, independence, and overreliance concerns

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as an AI L2 Teaching Support: A Case Study of an EFL Teacher
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT can support second-language teaching, focusing on one English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teacher’s use of the tool over a seven-month period. The study asks how the teacher integrated ChatGPT into teaching, how effective it was for her instructional goals, how she learned to craft prompts, and how she checked the reliability of the AI’s outputs. The broader problem addressed is whether generative AI can function as practical teaching support in real language-learning contexts while avoiding inaccuracies and bias.

The intervention studied was the teacher’s ongoing use of the free version of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) to assist with lesson planning, in-class implementation, and assessment. Data came from the teacher’s ChatGPT history, lesson plans that incorporated ChatGPT, and a semi-structured interview. The analysis used thematic analysis to categorize uses of the tool, including curriculum suggestions, activity generation, vocabulary support, real-time classroom Q&A, interactive language practice, text editing, automated grading, and self-assessment materials. A major emphasis of the paper is the teacher’s development of more effective prompt-crafting strategies over time, culminating in a five-step prompt framework.

The study took place in a private language school in Spain serving Spanish learners preparing for Cambridge English exams. The focal participant was one experienced EFL teacher, while her students were described as subsidiary participants spanning children ages 4–12, teenagers ages 12–18, and adults. The context was face-to-face language teaching in small groups across proficiency levels from A1 to C1. The paper reports that ChatGPT was especially useful for producing lower-complexity materials, expanding resources for younger learners, and supporting classroom engagement and feedback processes, though outputs for advanced learners were sometimes too superficial or off-target.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT can be a valuable support tool for EFL teaching when used critically and skillfully, especially for lesson planning, classroom material generation, and some assessment functions. The authors stress that prompt crafting and critical evaluation of outputs are essential competencies for teachers. They also conclude that teachers must verify AI-generated content for reliability, bias, and pedagogical fit. Because the study is a single qualitative case, the authors present the findings as exploratory and useful for informing future larger-scale studies rather than as broadly generalizable evidence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative single instrumental case study with clear methods and rich implementation detail, but it includes only one teacher, lacks experimental or quasi-experimental design, and reports no standardized outcome estimates. It meets limited credibility criteria appropriate to qualitative evidence but cannot support strong causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests useful and potentially meaningful benefits for teacher workload, classroom engagement, and literacy/language support, but impacts are mostly perception-based and unquantified, with at least one concrete limitation in writing-score accuracy. Overall impact is promising but unclear in magnitude and generalizability.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) used by an EFL teacher over seven months to support lesson planning, generate classroom materials, enable in-class question answering and interactive language practice, and assist with assessment and feedback in a private language school serving children, teenagers, and adults.
ChatGPT used to assess learner writing, generate rubrics, provide automated grading/feedback, and compare AI scoring of Cambridge-style B2 writing against official handbook-based scoring criteria.

ChatGPT used as a language-support tool for grammar, vocabulary, reading, writing, and sentence/text editing tasks, including generating exercises, model texts, vocabulary tables, and revision support for EFL learners.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative single-case study, the teacher reported that ChatGPT provided significant support for lesson planning, material generation, and some assessment tasks, reducing workload and saving time while broadening the range of resources she could prepare for different proficiency levels. Evidence comes from analysis of 68 ChatGPT-supported productions collected over seven months plus a post-interview; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness/productivity in lesson planning, material development, classroom implementation, and assessment support; qualitative thematic analysis of chat history, lesson plans, and interview

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT helped generate writing tasks, reading-comprehension activities, vocabulary materials, and writing feedback, and the teacher perceived these supports as helpful for student comprehension, vocabulary retention, and writing-related instruction. However, when ChatGPT scored a Cambridge FCE B2 essay, its ratings diverged from the official benchmark by 3 total points, indicating limitations in assessment accuracy despite utility for drafting and feedback support.
finding.measure: Teacher-observed literacy support in writing/reading activities; AI scoring accuracy against Cambridge FCE writing scale benchmark
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; student counts not reported

finding.finding_summary: The teacher used ChatGPT for interactive language practice, simulated conversations, role-play, vocabulary development, and real-time Q&A, and reported increased participation and enthusiasm as well as better tailoring of materials for different EFL levels. These findings are based on teacher perceptions and implementation records rather than independent pre/post fluency measures, so impact on speaking proficiency remains suggestive rather than causally established.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness of ChatGPT for speaking/writing practice, role-play, vocabulary support, and classroom participation
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; small groups averaging about 8 students, total not reported

finding.finding_summary: The teacher reported increased student participation, enthusiasm, and engagement when incorporating ChatGPT-supported activities, especially among adolescent learners who showed high willingness to use AI in class. These engagement findings are qualitative and observational, with no standardized engagement survey or effect size reported.
finding.measure: Observed participation, enthusiasm, and willingness to use AI in class

finding.finding_summary: A central qualitative finding is that effective use of ChatGPT required and appeared to foster prompt crafting, critical evaluation of outputs, cross-checking with sources, and collaborative review by students, the teacher, and colleagues. The paper frames these as important AI-related competencies and describes their development over the seven-month period, but does not quantify gains with validated instruments.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence of prompt-crafting skill, critical thinking, source verification, and collaborative review practices

Adjacent and postsecondary studies are likely contaminating retrieval; the thread requires direct K-12 evidence with adjacent evidence explicitly flagged, not blended in.

Direct K-12 evidence is currently too thin on reading outcomes: the sweep includes AI doing exam/comprehension tasks and LLM-generated reading exercises, but not enough studies where K-12 students used generative AI and then had measured reading comprehension, reading motivation, or vocabulary outcomes.

Outcome-family coverage is incomplete. Writing/revision is represented, but vocabulary, reading motivation, and durable independent performance after support removal are not yet covered with direct K-12 studies.

The stronger-claim test ('better supported as a feedback/revision aid than as a reading intervention') cannot be defended confidently from the current set because the reading-intervention side is undersearched in the sweep, not because contrary evidence has been ruled out.

Transferability limits cannot yet be well characterized because the current direct K-12 items appear skewed toward secondary and likely EFL/foreign-language contexts; mainstream English-medium K-12 contexts and elementary grades are undercovered.

Several retained items are adjacent rather than direct K-12 literacy evidence (e.g., studies of ChatGPT taking exams, generating exercises, science/SRL contexts). More targeted retrieval is needed for student-outcome studies in literacy classrooms.

Key evidentiary tiers are missing or underrepresented: externally measured literacy gains versus rubric-scored products versus process/error/attitude measures are not yet populated across all required outcome families.

None of the four priority direct K-12 literacy studies appear to have been actually located or extracted; the current finding is an unrelated discourse-analysis paper that only cites broad ChatGPT-in-education literature.

No direct article page, abstract, conference record, accepted manuscript, repository copy, or indexing record has been surfaced for Balantekin on ChatGPT-4-generated texts for reading comprehension and motivation.
No direct record has been surfaced for Fauzi on elementary fiction-writing prompt engineering, including whether it is truly K-12, literacy-focused, and intervention-based.
No direct record has been surfaced for Huang on middle-school generative AI integration with teacher feedback and peer feedback.
No direct record has been surfaced for Liu et al. on elementary LLM-supported CALLA writing instruction.

Because the target studies were not found, required extraction fields remain missing: sample size, grade band, subgroup, EFL vs mainstream ELA, design, comparator, duration, dosage, mediation, tasks, outcomes, effect direction, and limitations.
No determination can yet be made about whether any priority study is strong enough to include as direct evidence in the final thesis.
None of the four priority direct K-12 literacy studies appears to have been located as a direct article, abstract, conference record, repository copy, or indexing record.
Current evidence shown is off-target secondary/background literature rather than direct K-12 intervention/evaluation studies of generative AI for literacy outcomes.

Required extraction fields remain largely unfilled for the priority studies: sample size, grade band, context (EFL vs mainstream ELA), design, comparator, duration, dosage, outcomes, effect direction, and limitations.
Coverage is especially weak for elementary and middle-school studies and for conference/accepted-manuscript/repository versions that may be the only discoverable records.
No clear determination can yet be made about whether any of the named studies are strong enough for inclusion as direct evidence in the final thesis.

Only two surfaced items are visible here, and one (CyberScholar) appears likely descriptive/initiative-level rather than a direct literacy outcome study; this is not enough to build the requested implementation/moderator map.

Core named studies requested by the thread are still missing or unverified: Kaplan, Balantekin, Liu CALLA-LLM, Huang, Fauzi, Meyer et al. on secondary text revision, Woo prompt-engineering study, and comparator studies with teacher or peer feedback.

The sweep has not yet established which studies are truly K-12 or clearly school-age; several AI writing papers in this area are university/EFL higher-ed, so age/school-level filtering remains unresolved.

Implementation variables are largely unanswered: duration, number of sessions, minutes per session, classroom vs homework, teacher-led/guided/independent use, individual vs group format, and prompting structure are not extractable from the current evidence base shown.
Tool-function coding is incomplete: whether each intervention generated text, generated feedback, generated materials, or provided tutoring has not been systematically mapped.
Outcome-context coding is missing: whether outcomes were measured during supported use versus independently after support is not yet covered.
Moderator angles requested by the thread are not yet addressed: grade band differences, EFL vs mainstream English-medium settings, and teacher-mediated vs student-directed use.
Primary/secondary comparator studies involving teacher feedback or peer feedback have not been surfaced, limiting the requested comparative interpretation.

Most surfaced items are descriptive or conceptual snippets; the sweep does not yet recover enough direct K-12/school-age literacy intervention studies with implementation details (duration, session count, minutes, setting, mediation, grouping, prompting structure).

Named target studies are not adequately pinned down or extracted: Kaplan, Balantekin, Liu CALLA-LLM, Huang, Fauzi, Meyer et al. on secondary text revision, and Woo prompt-engineering/editing studies remain partially identified or not verified as K-12 literacy studies.
Comparator studies involving teacher feedback or peer feedback are missing or underdeveloped, which is central to the moderator map and to judging teacher-mediated versus student-directed effects.

The current evidence does not clearly separate EFL/ESL school settings from mainstream English-medium K-12 settings, so the requested moderator comparison by language-learning context is not yet answerable.
Outcomes measured during supported use versus independent post-use are not systematically extracted; this is one of the key requested implementation dimensions.
CyberScholar appears surfaced, but it is unclear whether it is a direct literacy study with school-age outcome data rather than a broader initiative description.
Grade-band coverage is incomplete: no clear implementation map yet spanning elementary, lower secondary, and upper secondary literacy uses of generative AI.
The sweep does not yet establish whether tools generated text, feedback, materials, or tutoring support on a study-by-study basis for the named studies.
The sweep has not yet established the core tier-one definitional boundary: an explicit inclusion/exclusion rule distinguishing generative AI from adjacent AI categories in K-12 literacy research.

The requested use-case taxonomy is incomplete: studies/systems for draft-feedback generation, text simplification/material generation, automated writing evaluation/grammar correction, non-generative ITS, speech recognition, plagiarism detection, automated scoring, and AI-literacy-only interventions have not been systematically identified and separated.

The named anchor studies are not all confirmed or surfaced. At minimum, Balantekin is not verified here; Kaplan, Liu CALLA-LLM, Huang, Fauzi, Meyer et al., Steiss, Wan and Chen, Fokides and Peristeraki, AWE systems such as EssayCritic/Criterion, and Xiao et al. reading-material generation are not all clearly retrieved and classified.
Direct-study classification is missing. The review needs a table assigning each surfaced study to a use-case category and to one of: direct evidence, adjacent comparator evidence, or out of scope.

Comparator technologies central to the boundary question are undercovered, especially automated writing evaluation, grammar correction, automated scoring, plagiarism detection, speech recognition, and classic intelligent tutoring systems without open-ended text generation.

The current evidence appears skewed toward broad discussion pieces or initiative descriptions (e.g., CyberScholar) rather than K-12 literacy outcome studies that can test the proposed inclusion framework.

K-12 literacy-specific outcome coverage remains uncertain across reading versus writing domains; reading-material generation/text simplification studies and writing-feedback studies need targeted retrieval to support the framework's application.
The sweep has not yet produced the requested tier-one definitional boundary: a concrete inclusion/exclusion framework separating generative AI from adjacent AI categories in K-12 literacy research.

The named studies have not been systematically verified and classified. At minimum, Kaplan, Balantekin, Liu (CALLA-LLM), Huang, Fauzi, CyberScholar, Meyer et al., Steiss, Wan and Chen, Fokides and Peristeraki, AWE systems such as EssayCritic/Criterion, and reading-material generation studies such as Xiao et al. still need direct retrieval and coding.

There is no study-level mapping of surfaced evidence into the required use-case categories: student-facing text generation, formative draft feedback, text simplification/material generation, automated writing evaluation/grammar correction, non-generative ITS, speech recognition, plagiarism detection, automated scoring, and AI-literacy-only interventions.
The sweep has not yet determined for each main study whether it is direct evidence for K-12 literacy outcomes, adjacent comparator evidence, or out of scope.

Coverage appears thin on classic pre-LLM literacy technologies that the review explicitly needs to distinguish from generative AI (AWE, automated scoring, grammar correction, speech recognition, plagiarism detection, ITS without open-ended generation).

Coverage also appears thin on K-12 reading-material generation/text simplification studies and on AI-literacy interventions with no literacy outcome, both of which are necessary to set the boundary correctly.

The current findings snippet shows at least one likely adjacent/non-literacy paper (genetics classroom creative writing), suggesting retrieval noise and insufficient precision for the actual review boundary.
